He set his own foot beside one of them. It did not fit. He went through the mourners: the Widow's small boot, the clerk's town shoes, the tinners in their hobnails. It was none of theirs.

passages.heading: Boots, blacked.
passages.text:
The size matched no one in the house.

They went up the stair.

passages.heading: Stair. Study door, locked.
passages.text:
He followed them up, lamp in one hand and ring in the other. He had stopped asking whose they were. He had run out of people.

The prints climbed the stair steadily and without hurry, the way a man walks up his own stairs. On the landing they turned left and stopped at the study.

He had locked the study door himself, at three o'clock before the reading, and tried it twice. It was locked now. He put his hand on the knob and it did not give.

Black crepe hung on the door.

He knew that crepe. It had hung on the front door for three nights, and he had taken it down at noon because the Widow said a will is business, and business does not come in through crepe. He had folded it and laid it in the linen press. Now it was tied across the study door in his own knot: a reef with the tail tucked under, the knot his mother taught him.

passages.heading: Stair. Study door, locked.
passages.text:
Crepe goes on the front door of a house with a death in it, where the street can see it.

This door was inside.

The house was mourning someone behind the study door. Not Vane.

passages.heading: Study.
passages.text:
He did not knock.

Opening doors was what he was for. He knew every door in Hollowmere: which ones stuck in wet weather, which ones a woman could lean against in the dark and weep, and which ones he must never open without being asked.

The ring was in his hand. He counted for the study key by its teeth, as he had counted all his life.

Study.

Study.

Study.

There were three. One was his. The second had barn straw caught in its bow and a pale twist of goat hair. The third was so cold it ached, and when he raised it to the lamp it smelled of the Undercroft's gas.

He had never hung either of them. He had never cut a copy of a key in his life.

The ring was no longer his count.

He stopped counting.

He fitted a key without choosing which one, and it turned.

The study was as it had always been. The desk. The master's chair, with its back to the window. The curtains drawn, as he had drawn them.

He put his hand on the chair. It was warm.

The day-book lay open on the desk.

He had left it downstairs, on the hall table, to dry. He knew that as surely as he knew the teeth of the keys. Now it lay open on the desk with tonight's page written all the way down. The ink was still wet, and every word was in his hand.

*Front door, barred. Hall, dark. Clock, as ever.*
*Clock. Cold in the brass.*
*Safe, locked.*
*Boots, blacked.*
*Stair. Study door, locked.*
*Study.*

Then the lines he had not walked yet.

*Crepe, front door.*
*Key, Hale Barn.*
*Key, Undercroft.*
*Clock, wound.*
*Hall. One clock, standing.*
*11:47.*

He read it twice. It was a good round. He would have written it the same way himself. He had.

The night was already written, and it ended at 11:47.

So he walked it.

He untied the crepe from the study door and carried it down, and he tied it across the front door in a reef with the tail tucked under.

He drew back the bar and went out across the wet ground to Hale Barn, where the wolf pelt hung on the door. The goat watched him, as goats watch everyone, and he hung the key with the straw in its bow where it would be found.

He crossed the square. Every window was dark. He went down the Well Ladder rung by rung, into the cold and the smell of gas, and laid the third key in the Undercroft where it would be found.

He came back in by the front door. He had barred it. He did not wonder about that.

His boots were not dry any more.

In the hall he opened the case and took the chain in his wet hands and drew the weight all the way to the top.

The hands did not move.

He did not put out the lamp. He did not ask himself why.

In the hall of Vane Manor it was eleven forty-seven, and it always had been.

works.title: What the Well Remembers
works.blurb: a girl who counts things hides on the Well Ladder at curfew, is driven down by a stranger washing at the well-head, and crosses the Undercroft into St Brannock's, where a sleeper's pallet, a post-dated Gazette and a red-darned glove in the bell rope take Father Bray's train east away from her.

passages.heading: What the Well Remembers
passages.text:
Father Bray went back east on the train.

My mother said it at supper, the week he went, the way you say the pump is frozen. She said it to the bread. Nobody at the table asked her anything else.

I remember him in three things.

He set the hymn numbers on the board every Sunday, and while he set them he made me read them back to him, and that is how I learned numbers. After Mass he read the Gazette on the chapel step and let me sound out the big letters at the top. That is how I learned letters.

He let me stand inside his arms when he rang the Company bell. The rope went up past my face and came down past it again, and the floor hummed.

His gloves were worn through at the palm from that rope. He darned them himself in red wool, badly. The darn sat right in front of my eyes when I stood inside his arms. I used to count the stitches. Nine on the left hand. I never saw the right one close enough.

passages.heading: What the Well Remembers
passages.text:
I count things. Planks on the platform: forty-two. Lanterns on the square: four. Plates on Crumb's wake table: ten, every time, whether there are ten mourners or two. Counting is how I keep things. If you have counted it, it happened.

So I believed it. Trains go east. Priests go with them.

Saloon was over. The Curfew bell rang. The wolves came down to the fence the way they do, and the Watchman walked the lanes knocking on shutters and sending children in.

I did not go in.

There is a ladder in the well on the square. Iron rungs, set into the shaft wall, going down to the shortcut under the town. Grown men use it sometimes in the day, sideways, cursing, because the rungs sit too close to the stone for a man's shoulders. They don't fit me badly at all. I have hidden on it on curfew nights since I was seven. You go down three rungs, where the light from the square still reaches, and you sit with your knees against the wall, and when the Station Rush starts you climb out and walk home like you've been to the pump.

Three rungs down. Knees on the stone. Four lanterns on the square. I counted them lit, one, two, three, and I was still waiting on the fourth when I stopped watching for it.
Up was always the way home. Up was the only way home I knew.

Boots on the well-head.

Not the Watchman's. The Watchman drags his left heel. These didn't drag.

The bucket came down past my face on its chain and went into the water below me and came up again full, close enough that it brushed my hair. Then washing. Hands, by the sound. Rubbing. Rinsing. Rubbing. A long time. Longer than flour takes. Longer than mud.

Water spilled over the lip and came down the shaft onto me. It was colder than well water. In the little light it was darker than well water, too. I did not look at my sleeve after. I am telling you that so you know I didn't.

Then the washing stopped, and he did not leave.

He stood at the top of the well with his hands held out, maybe, waiting for something to dry. I could not see a face. I could only see that something was standing between me and the lantern, because the light on the rungs above me had gone.

You cannot climb past someone at the top of the only ladder. You can't even breathe loudly. The ladder up was held by whoever had washed there, and I was small, and quiet, and I stayed still the way you stay still.

He did not go.

So I went down.

Below the rungs I knew there were more rungs, and below those there was a passage, low and wet, and at the end of the passage there was the Undercroft.

I had never gone that far. I knew where it came out, the way you know what is behind a door you've been told not to open. The Undercroft lies under St Brannock's. There is a stair from the Undercroft up into the chapel. The chapel door is never barred, because Father Bray said God's house has no bar, and nobody since has thought to fit one.

That was my plan. Down. Across. Up the stair. Out the chapel door. Home by the back lanes before anyone at the well thought to look down it.

And nobody would be in the Undercroft. I was sure of that. Nobody comes down there at night. It is a cellar. Cellars are for the dead and the potatoes.
Dark. Cold. A smell of gas.

The Undercroft has two alcoves for the gas, one north and one south. The north one was dark.

The south one was lit.

The lamp was turned down to a bead, a blue drop on the end of the pipe, but it was burning. Under it was a pallet made of sacking, pressed flat in the shape of a body that had lain there more than once. A tin cup. A candle stub, burned to a puddle. On the shelf over the pallet, a key with a brass tag. I could read the tag. STUDY, and under it, smaller, VANE.

Someone sleeps here.

I knew it the way you know a bed has been slept in. You don't need to touch it.

So I made it into something. A stowaway off the train. The Gazette says they come in the freight crates, under the flour, and they have to sleep somewhere when they get out. Somewhere dry. Somewhere nobody comes down to at night. A stowaway had found the Undercroft before I did, and that was all.

I took the key. I don't know why. Children keep things. It went into my pocket and it stayed there.

A stowaway. That was all.

There was chalk on the wall by the pallet. Low down, where a man lying on his side would write if he had a piece of chalk and nothing to do with the night.

Four numbers.

23. 140. 8. 271.

I knew them. I knew them the way you know your own name said in another room. They were the hymn numbers from Father Bray's last Sunday. I read them back to him that morning while he slid the cards into the board, and he said *good*, and he said *again*, and I said them again. They are still on the board upstairs. Nobody has changed them since he went. Nobody has set any numbers at all.

A stowaway off the train would not know those numbers. Nobody off the train would.

So that wasn't it.

So it was him. It was Father Bray who slept here, and it was before his train. A night, maybe two, before he went east. He came down under his own chapel to say goodbye to it from underneath, and he wrote his last hymns on the wall so he'd have them. That is a thing a priest might do. It is.
Before his train. Before.

If Father Bray slept here before his train, then something of his might still be here. I wanted something of his. I had kept his hymn numbers in my head all that time and nobody had told me I could keep anything else.

I lifted the head of the pallet to look underneath it.

A Gazette, folded flat. Folded the way he folded it on the chapel step, in half and in half again, so it would fit in a coat.

Mine now, I thought. His or not.

I unfolded it to see what he had been reading.

You read the date first. He taught me that. *Before you believe a paper, find out what day it thinks it is.*

I read it the way he taught me. Letter by letter, under the blue bead of the lamp. The day. The month. The number.

The number was after his last Sunday. Not much after. Enough.

The Gazette comes in on the Daily Train. That is the only way it comes. So this one came in on a train after the train that took him east.

Someone else brought it down, then. That's what I said. Anyone could have. Anyone could fold a paper in half and in half again. I said it in my head twice, the way he made me say the hymns twice, and the second time it was thinner than the first, and I did not believe it either time.

And the lamp.

The lamp in the south alcove was turned low. Not out. Turned down to a bead, the way you leave a lamp you are coming back to. You turn a lamp out when you go away. You turn it down when you are going up to do something and you will want it again before morning.

Whoever slept here was out, and the alcove's sleeper was coming back tonight.

The lamp was turned down, not out.

Up the well was the washer. Down here was a bed someone was coming back to. The chapel was the only other way out I knew.

I took the stair.

St Brannock's at night. Plank walls. Pews. The smell of cold wax. The hymn board, white cards in black slots, *23 140 8 271*, still. The windows grey. The door at the far end. And between me and the door, the place under the bell, where the rope comes down.

The chapel was empty. I told myself that. It was empty, and the door was ten steps away, and the way to it ran under the bell and past the rope, the way it always had.

Ten steps. I counted them.

The Company bell hangs over that spot with the Company's mark stamped on its shoulder. I have looked up at it every Sunday of my life.

The rope was moving.

Only a little. A slow sway, side to side, getting smaller. The way a rope does after. After someone has let go of it. After something has come off it. So the chapel was not empty. Or it had not been, a moment before I came up the stair.

There was something caught in the rope. Twisted into the lay of it, about where a grown man's hands would be if he reached up to ring.

A glove.

Not a whole one. The cuff, and half the palm, the rest torn away. The palm worn through from rope. Darned over the worn place in red wool. Badly.

I knew it.

I have stood inside those arms with that darn in front of my eyes. I have counted those stitches.

I started to tell myself something. Other men darn their gloves. Other men ring bells. Red wool is cheap. Everybody has red wool. I got that far. I could not get any further. I could not get to the end of it, and I have never got to the end of it since.

I did not count the stitches. I did not want to know if there were nine.

What the glove did not tell me: whether he rang that bell until the rope tore his hand out of it. Whether he climbed. Whether the rope was for something else. Whether someone took it off him. Whether he pulled his hand out himself and left the glove behind and walked down to the platform and got on the train like they said.

The bell did not ring. Nothing rang.

I did not take the glove. I had the key.

I knew whose it was.
I could not unknow it. I have tried. It does not go back.

I went out by the chapel door, which has no bar, and home by the back lanes, and I was in my bed with my wet sleeve under the blanket before the Station Rush.

The whistle out of the pines. The platform lantern going pale. The well-head stones, when I went out for water, dark and wet, and nobody standing at them.

The train had brought a Vicar. He came up the square in a coat too good for the mud, with his bag in one hand, looking at everything the way you look at a house you have been told is yours. He stopped at the pump, where I was. He bent down, because grown men do that to children, and smiled, and asked me.

Where did Father Bray go?

The key was in my pocket. My mother was at our door. Mrs Grieves was sweeping the tavern step, and she had stopped sweeping.

"Father Bray went back east on the train," I said.

The Vicar nodded. My mother nodded. Mrs Grieves nodded, and went back to her sweeping.

Three.

I counted them.

works.title: The People against ______
works.blurb: the transcript of the Tribunal at the Bell, Tuesday 28 November 1893, kept by a clerk lent for the day: a boot-mender hanged on an unsigned ledger slip after his alibi witness, Gert, is entered Indebted at the Midday Shift and struck, the gallows pine charged to her household, and a new slip on the board naming the widow who vouched.

passages.heading: The People against
passages.text:
IN THE TRIBUNAL AT THE BELL
HOLLOWMERE, COLDWATER TERRITORY

passages.heading: THE PEOPLE against ______.
passages.text:
Tuesday, 28 November 1893. Sat from the Station Rush.
Before: the Judge, by the Daily Train.
Recorder: second hand, Clerk's Office, lent for the day.

passages.heading: FIRST SITTING. The Station Rush.
passages.text:
The Judge stepped off the train at 7.10 with his own bag and nobody to carry it. The tarpaulin was taken off the bench. It had rained on it in the night, and the water ran off the far end onto the board where the three verdicts are painted for those who cannot read. Acquittal. A Heavy Fine. Death.

The gallows stood behind the bench. Trap bolted. Rope not yet out. Crows along the beam.

THE JUDGE: The train goes at Dusk. So do I. Read it.

**EXHIBIT 1.** A Dirty Deed Ledger Slip, Company form, taken down from the notice board by the Police Officer at 7.15. Pencil, a hand nobody owns to. Unsigned. Lodged with the Clerk on Monday at the Station Rush, within the hour Mabel was found, so it has lain one day. Under Article IX §2 it is a Tribunal Indictment without further act, and it may not be withdrawn, the Company having already read it.

passages.heading: FIRST SITTING. The Station Rush.
passages.text:
The slip reads in full:

> the boot-mender at the pump. Mabel. Sunday night or Monday. ask him.

RULING: Admitted.

*[I entered it word for word, the full stop after "Mabel" included. I keep the rolls. The form is the fairness: a slip, a day, an indictment, a bench, a judge. I only write it down.*

*It names a trade and not a man. But there is only one boot-mender. — R.]*

---

The defendant was brought from the Constable's in iron cuffs and set on the stool before the bench. He is middling tall and grey at the temples. His hands are cracked at the knuckle and black in the lines, the way a cobbler's hands go. He sat with them in his lap and looked at the crows.

THE JUDGE: Your name.

THE DEFENDANT: ______.

*[He said it. I took it down. Then I went through the rolls for it, Mill Row, Pump Row, the railyard bunks, Schedule A, all of it, because the Judge asked me to. It is not there. He never signed with the Company. He mends boots on a box by the pump for whoever brings them, and he is paid in scrip or in bread.*

passages.heading: FIRST SITTING. The Station Rush.
passages.text:
*The Postmaster wired it to Thorne Junction at 7.30 to be verified.*

*The Judge ruled that the record follows the Gazette's rule, since the record goes east on the train to be printed. No name that has not been verified. Where a name is not verified, a blank is left.*

*So I struck what I had and set the line. A blank until the wire answers. A blank accuses no one. — R.]*

THE DEFENDANT: ______.

---

The square had come up to the fence line while we were at the rolls. Station Rush crowd, flour on some of them, and the platform crew still in their gloves. They stood the way people stand at a well when somebody has dropped something down it.

A VOICE: The whistler.

A VOICE (the same?): Him.

A VOICE: The one by the pump.

RECORDER: I ask the bench whether noise from the square is to be entered.

passages.heading: FIRST SITTING. The Station Rush.
passages.text:
THE JUDGE: The case is the People against. The People are a party. Enter them.

*[Entered because ordered. Voices are not evidence. I wrote it in the margin small enough that nobody east would need to read it.*

*Three lines, three words for one man. None of them is his name. — R.]*

---

passages.heading: SECOND SITTING. The Law.
passages.text:
**EXHIBIT 2.** The Detective's case file, Company paper, one folio. Three traits, each Verified, each stamped.

- *Height.* A bootprint in the lane behind the Drowned Lantern, where Mabel was found at the Station Rush on Monday. Company boot, middling.
- *Scarf.* A thread of brown wool, caught on the lane fence at shoulder height.
- *Hat.* Felt nap, brown, on the same fence, higher.

THE JUDGE: How many men in HollowMere answer all three?

THE DETECTIVE: Nineteen. That I have counted.

THE JUDGE: Did you send it up?

THE DETECTIVE: No, sir. Verified clues narrow the board. They don't name.

THE JUDGE: Then who sent it up?

THE POLICE OFFICER: The Indictment, sir. It lay a day.

THE DETECTIVE: Article IX. No rung shall be skipped —

THE JUDGE: — except by the Company. Then the Company has not skipped it. Go on.

*[I wrote "nineteen" out in letters. A figure can be made into another figure with one stroke, and I would rather nobody east had the chance.*

passages.heading: SECOND SITTING. The Law.
passages.text:
*So the arrest stands on the slip alone. The square isn't evidence and the Detective will not make it evidence. Then whatever is still to come will have to carry it. — R.]*

---

Because nothing but the slip was under the arrest, the Police Officer had gone to the box by the pump at first light and brought back what was on it. He laid it on the bench one thing at a time.

**EXHIBIT 3.** An awl, bone-handled. A boot-knife, short, the edge worn hollow from stropping. Both from the box.

**EXHIBIT 4.** A rag, cotton, folded in four. Stained red in two places. From the box, under the last.

**EXHIBIT 5.** A woman's left boot, size four. Resoled, with a new heel. The welt is stitched in a double row, waxed thread, the knots on the inside. The defendant owned to the stitch without being asked.

Inside the boot, as an insole, a hymn sheet folded twice. Copied out in pencil in a round hand: the words of a hymn, numbered 212, with the alto line marked under each word in small strokes.

passages.heading: SECOND SITTING. The Law.
passages.text:
Mabel took in mending on Mill Row. She charged by the button, not the hour, and kept the buttons she was paid in, and the buttons she found, in a cocoa tin by the door, sorted by colour. She lined her boots with hymns because paper was cheaper than felt and she could read them at the bench while she waited. She sang alto at St Brannock's. She came in a half-beat behind the rest, every verse, as if checking that the others meant it.

A VOICE: There.

*[I have stood behind her in the chapel. That half-beat. I thought she was slow. I think now she was listening.*

*Every cobbler owns a knife. Every cobbler has a rag. Every boot on Mill Row has his stitch in it, because he is the only one. Mine too. I owe him for the heel on my right boot. Eleven cents scrip. I was going to pay him Saturday. — R.]*

passages.heading: SECOND SITTING. The Law.
passages.text:
The tools prove nothing about a cobbler but his trade. So the court turned, as the town always turns, from the knife to the hour.

DOC MALLORY, sworn. Opened the dead at the Morgue on Monday.

[Summarised: The cause was a cold edge, once. The witness gives no further particular and the bench asks for none. The hour, by the cooling and the stiffening, between eleven on Sunday night and one on Monday morning. Not before eleven. Not after one.]

THE JUDGE: The rag. Exhibit 4. Is it hers?

DOC MALLORY: It is red.

THE JUDGE: Is it blood?

DOC MALLORY: It is red, sir. I would not swear it is anyone's.

RULING: The Doctor declines.

*[Then it hangs on the hour between eleven and one. Not on the knife, not on the voices. The hour. — R.]*

---

THE WITNESS, sworn. Gert, of Pump Row, a widow, laundress. One boy, eight.

passages.heading: SECOND SITTING. The Law.
passages.text:
She stood before the bench with her hands under her shawl. She did not look at the defendant. She looked at me, because I was writing.

[Summarised in her words, which I have kept: The defendant sleeps in her lean-to against the wash-house wall since August, for a bed and his supper, and pays when he has it. On Sunday night her boy's boot had come away at the toe. The defendant brought his last in from the lean-to and sat at her table and resoled it by her candle. He was at the table before the chapel bell rang eleven. She heard eleven. She heard twelve. She heard one. She had the one candle and she sat up because of it. When he had done he held the boot up to the light, turned it over, and whistled two notes, up and down, the way you'd call a dog you were fond of. Then he went out to the lean-to. She heard the latch. Her boy wore the boot to the Station Rush on Monday.]

passages.heading: SECOND SITTING. The Law.
passages.text:
THE JUDGE: You heard one.

THE WITNESS: I heard it. I was waiting for the candle to go.

*[I took her down in full. Every word. My best hand, the one I keep for the Company's letters east. If the hour is what hangs men here, the hour is covered now. It is covered by a witness, and I have written it fair.*

passages.heading: The alibi will hold. — R.]
passages.text:
THE JUDGE: The witness will stay by the bench in case she is recalled. It is noon. No sentence falls during the Shift. We rise.

---

passages.heading: THE SHIFT. Not in the record.
passages.text:
*[Entered later as Exhibit 6, by order. A leaf of the rent roll, Pump Row, in my hand. — R.]*

The Clerk collects at Midday in person, at the Rows. I carry the roll. I have carried it every day for two years.

We went down Mill Row and up Pump Row. Doors opened. Scrip. My pen. Doors opened. Scrip. My pen. The Clerk does not speak at the doors. He holds out his hand.

Gert's door, fourth from the pump. He knocked once. No answer.

She was not at it. She was under the bell, by the bench, where the Judge had told her to stand. I could see the bench from her step. I could see her shawl.

"Enter her," the Clerk said. "Every bed slept in."

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| GERT | Pump Row, 4th door | **Indebted.** |

The ink was the same ink. The hand was mine.

passages.heading: THE SHIFT. Not in the record.
passages.text:
I did not say where she was. He knew where she was. Everyone on the Row knew where she was.

*[Her door. Her name. My hand. Gert is entered Indebted, and the ink was dry before we reached the pump. — R.]*

---

passages.heading: THIRD SITTING. After the Shift.
passages.text:
The Clerk handed the roll up to the bench himself. The Judge read it where I had left it open.

THE JUDGE: Article V §3. The Indebted may not bear witness before the Tribunal. The witness Gert is entered Indebted as of Midday. Her testimony is struck.

passages.heading: RECORDER: Sir, she was —
passages.text:
THE JUDGE: Strike it.

I drew the line.

> ~~The defendant sleeps in her lean-to against the wash-house wall since August, for a bed and his supper, and pays when he has it. On Sunday night her boy's boot had come away at the toe. The defendant brought his last in from the lean-to and sat at her table and resoled it by her candle. He was at the table before the chapel bell rang eleven. She heard eleven. She heard twelve. She heard one. She had the one candle and she sat up because of it. When he had done he held the boot up to the light, turned it over, and whistled two notes, up and down, the way you'd call a dog you were fond of. Then he went out to the lean-to. She heard the latch. Her boy wore the boot to the Station Rush on Monday.~~
>
> ~~THE JUDGE: You heard one.~~
>
> ~~THE WITNESS: I heard it. I was waiting for the candle to go.~~

passages.heading: RECORDER: Sir, she was —
passages.text:
A WOMAN (Indebted; not a witness): I was here. You told me to stand here. I was *here.*

*[Struck. Legible. You can read every word of it through the line. That is how the Company likes a strike made, so that the east can see what was taken out.*

*The alibi is struck. The hour lies open again, from eleven to one, with nobody in it. — R.]*

---

Because the hour lay open, the Judge put it to the only one left who could fill it.

THE JUDGE: Where were you between eleven and one?

THE DEFENDANT: Let it stand.

THE JUDGE: Let what stand?

THE DEFENDANT: What she said. Or what you've got. Let it stand.

The square pressed on the fence. A VOICE, then many. The Police Officer blew the riot whistle, one long blast, and the square went back a step.

passages.heading: THE DEFENDANT: [whistles]
passages.text:
*[Two notes. Up, then down. I have no sign for a whistle in my shorthand and there is none in the Company's. I wrote what I could.*

*He said nothing more. The Judge asked him twice more and he looked at the crows. His silence is entered as his answer. I do not know what it answered. — R.]*

---

The Judge looked at his watch, and then up the Line, and then at the square.

THE JUDGE: The People are a party. The People will say.

VOICES.

I could not take them down singly. I took them down as they came and in the order I heard them, and the first that was a word and not a noise was *Death*, said loud, from somewhere at the fence between the pump and the well. Then the rest said it too.

THE JUDGE: Death. By the trapdoor at the Bell. At four o'clock, which is after the Shift and before the train. *The Town has spoken.*

passages.heading: THE DEFENDANT: [whistles]
passages.text:
*[Four words. The Article allows no others. I wrote them in the form and blotted them.*

*The sentence is Death, and the record is closed, and God help me I was glad of it. A closed record is one I don't have to keep. — R.]*

---

**EXHIBIT 7.** An invoice of the Waterwheel Lumber Mill, sent up at 2.40 under Article IX §4. Scaffold, trap and rope, at the Schedule rate. Pine. Charged to the account of the condemned. The charge survives the condemned.

The record was closed. The invoice came anyway.

The Clerk looked at the account line.

THE CLERK: There is no account. There is no name.

THE JUDGE: Then whose house?

THE CLERK: He slept at the widow's. Every bed slept in.

The Judge did not rule. The Clerk did, and the Judge let him.

RULING: The charge for the pine to stand against the household of Gert, Pump Row, 4th door, already Indebted.

passages.heading: RETURN.
passages.text:
**EXHIBIT 8.** Return of Execution, Company form, the blanks filled in by the Recorder.

> Sentence carried out at **4.00** in the afternoon upon **______**, at the Bell, HollowMere. Witnessed by the Judge, the Police Officer, and the Town. Body to Car 3 for the up-train. Rope taken in at dusk.

He went up the steps without being helped. He looked once along the square at the lanterns, which were not lit yet. That is all I will enter. The form does not ask for more.

At Dusk the Judge got onto the train with his bag. It did not wait. It never has. One coffin went out in Car 3. Name not entered.

The square did not go home. It stood in the cold where the crows had been.

And when the train was gone, a voice from the square, from the fence, between the pump and the well:

passages.heading: RETURN.
passages.text:
A VOICE: Who did it?

Nobody answered. Then again, nearer, or the same voice nearer:

A VOICE: Who *did* it?

*[I was ordered to enter them all. There is no line in the record for a question with no witness, so I made one, and I left it open at the end because nobody closed it. The man is in Car 3 and the square is still asking. — R.]*

---

passages.heading: AFTER.
passages.text:
At 6.20, after the train had gone, the Postmaster sent a boy up with the wire from Thorne Junction. It had been answered at 5.55.

> REPEAT NAME STOP

I turned back to the first page to repeat it. The first page says:

THE DEFENDANT: ______.

I wrote that.

I sat on the bench under the bell with the wire on my knee and tried to hear him say it, the way he said it at seven in the morning, looking at the crows. I can hear his voice. I can hear the two notes. When I reach for the name, what comes up is *the boot-mender*. What comes up is *the whistler*. What comes up is *him.*

I did not wire anything back. Across the square the Lamplighter was out on her round, ladder on her shoulder. Nobody whistled at it.

*[I had it. Until the wire answered, it was a blank. Now the wire has answered, and it is still a blank. I wrote the blank instead of the name. — R.]*

passages.heading: AFTER.
passages.text:
Station Rush, Wednesday. The notice board.

A new slip, Company form, pencil, the same kind of hand nobody owns to. Unsigned.

> the widow on Pump Row who vouched for him.

It has to lie a day.

I have the rolls to carry at Midday. I have a heel I owe eleven cents for, and no one to pay.

I took a fresh sheet, and I wrote the heading in my best hand.

works.title: The Loudest Voice
works.blurb: one night and morning in the second person, under the Killer card's clauses as headings: the stone names Hattie the washerwoman, the other one's false cry draws the Watchman off her door, a child's chalk tally is wiped and a thread left, and at the Bell the loudest voice asking who did it turns the square onto the Watchman's dragged heel.

passages.heading: The Loudest Voice
passages.text: Somebody has to ask first.

passages.heading: Walk in a borrowed character.
passages.text:
The stone is up before the train.

It stands at the edge of the square where the lanes give out. Grey. About the height of a child. Tomorrow's date cut in it, the way it always is, and under the date a name. Nobody has ever seen a name being cut. There is a new one every morning anyway.

Agnes reads it to the Row at dawn, because half the Row can't, and you hear her from the pump. One word. Then the Row goes quiet, the way a kitchen does when a cup breaks.

HATTIE.

You chose her last night. You lay on your back in the dark and went through the town door by door, and you stopped at hers, and you slept. Then the stone. You have never settled which of you goes first, you or the stone, which of you is following the other. You don't try to settle it this morning either. You get up.

passages.heading: Walk in a borrowed character.
passages.text:
Coat. Hat. Scarf.

They go on the way weather does. It is not your coat. It has never been your coat. The square says good morning to it every day of the week, and that is the whole trick: nobody looks twice at a thing they already say good morning to.

Hattie is at the pump with her two buckets. Her hands are red to the wrist from the copper, the way a washerwoman's are once the cold sets in. She has heard the stone. Everyone has. She fills the first bucket, looks up at the borrowed face, and nods.

passages.heading: Morning.
passages.text:
"Stone's got me today," she says. "Wash still wants doing." She works the handle. "I've asked the Watchman. He'll stand at my door tonight. Paid him in sheets. First bed he's had with no holes in it."

She says it the way you'd mention a debt you've settled. Then she lifts both buckets and goes down the Rise to the wash-house with the water slopping. She doesn't look back at the stone. You understand that she has decided not to.

So the whole town knows the Watchman will stand at her door tonight.

So do you.

passages.heading: Curfew.
passages.text:
The Lamplighter comes round at dusk. Platform first, then the square, and the fourth lantern, the one over the chalk and the well, last of all. She always leaves that one till last. The Saloon empties. The Curfew bell rings. The wolves come down to the fence and walk the length of it.

By then the Watchman is at the wash-house door: lantern on the step, collar up. When he settles his weight his left heel drags on the stone, one short scrape, and stops.

You are across the lane at the foot of the Rise, in the borrowed coat, doing nothing a neighbour wouldn't do at curfew. Walking home slowly. Looking at nothing.

Then a voice from the pines side.

passages.heading: Wolves! Wolves in the square!
passages.text:
High. Pitched to carry. Pitched, exactly, to carry to the bottom of the Rise and no further.

You know that voice. You do not turn your head toward it. That is the one rule between you and the other one, older than any other: you never look at the other one where anyone can see. *You never hold the knife, only the alibi.* That is their card, not yours, and they keep it better than you keep yours.

The Watchman looks at Hattie's door. He looks at the dark toward the fence. He looks at the door again.

He goes, lantern swinging, heel scraping, scrape and scrape up the lane, out of hearing.

Her door is unwatched. You didn't even have to ask.

## Strike after dark when the room is empty.

The room is empty. The card promised it would be, and the card is right.

Sheets, rows of them, pegged on lines across the room so that the room is all corridors. The copper, banked low. The mangle. Lye. A jar on the sill.

passages.heading: Wolves! Wolves in the square!
passages.text:
Some things go into you whether you want them or not.

Over the copper, chalked big in careful capitals: HATTIE. It is the one word she can write, and she has written it where she'll see it every morning. On the shelf there is a letter half done in somebody else's hand. *Dear son, the work is steady and the* — and nothing after. The Postmaster writes it for her at a scrip a week, a line at a time, and this week's scrip hasn't been paid.

The jar is buttons. You tip it to the window and they slide: horn, bone, brass, one shell. One from every dead man's shirt she washed for the box. Somebody ought to keep something. You don't know that she ever said that. You think she must have.

You put the jar back where the ring in the dust says it goes.

On the nail by the door hangs her own shawl, washed thinner than anything she takes in. Everyone's washing comes before hers. Under the copper there's a pair of boots, the soles stuffed with Gazette against the wet, set side by side, toes to the wall, the way you'd set them if somebody had once told you to and you'd never stopped.

passages.heading: Wolves! Wolves in the square!
passages.text:
Then you stand between two sheets and wait.

She comes in with the last basket on her hip, humming. It isn't a hymn, just a tune with no words left in it. An hour ago she heard the Watchman settle at her door, and she believes he is still there. You can see her believe it: her shoulders down, the latch left up behind her.

"Night, then," she says, over her shoulder, to the empty step.

She sets the basket down. She stands a moment with her hands in the small of her back, looking at her rows, counting them the way she must count them every night. She has had all day to run, and she spent it on the town's sheets. There is a second where you think she knows. Then she reaches up to unpeg the nearest sheet, and the nearest sheet is the one you are behind.

passages.heading: Wolves! Wolves in the square!
passages.text:
A cold edge, and the lantern goes out.

Her hand comes up. It finds the end of the borrowed scarf and closes on it, and it does not open again.

You work at her fingers. A thread comes away into them. One thread, the weave of every scarf on the square. You could get it out. You stop, because the card says one clue, and you haven't seen what else there is yet.

Nobody saw. You believe that all the way to the door.

passages.heading: Clean one clue.
passages.text:
The doorframe. At the height of a child's shoulder.

Four strokes and a bar across them, in white chalk, the dust still loose on the wood. It was not there when you went in. You came in by this door. You would know.

Children chalk every door in this town. There is hopscotch under the fourth lantern every morning, and nobody ever seen drawing it. There are marks on the shutters. Townsfolk carry chalk and mark what they see; it's written on their cards. So it's a wash tally. Five sheets owed. A game.

Nothing.

That is three explanations, each one shorter than the last. You stand in the doorway with the shelf half built and you decide: children's chalk. That is what it is.

But the card says one.

A thread is a weave, and half the square wears it. A tally is somebody who stood here and counted.

passages.heading: Clean one clue.
passages.text:
You take the rag from your pocket and wipe the frame until the wood there is darker than the wood around it. You leave the thread where it is, in her fist.

The chalk is gone. Your hands are wet to the wrist.

passages.heading: Wash at the well.
passages.text:
The square is empty, and the fourth lantern burns over the chalk and the well.

The bucket goes down on its chain, past the rungs in the shaft, into the water, and comes up full.

Hands first. Rub. Rinse. Rub. Longer than flour takes, longer than mud. What you tip back over the lip looks darker than well water in that light. You don't look at it twice.

Then, below you, a breath.

Three rungs down. Maybe four. One breath, held too long and let go. Then nothing. Nothing at all, which is worse than the breath.

You stand at the lip with your hands out as if you are waiting for them to dry. You are between the lantern and the shaft, so whatever is down there has no light now except what gets past you. You don't call down. You don't leave. You stand, and the wet goes cold on your hands, and you listen.

passages.heading: Wash at the well.
passages.text:
Then iron. A small sound on the rungs, going down. Slow. Careful. Away.

Mere-rot. The fen puts feet where there aren't any, and everyone in HollowMere knows it. The Lamplighter has heard steps on these rungs and not gone to look. That's all it is.

"Mere-rot," you say out loud, to nobody. You dry your hands on the borrowed coat and walk home across the square in boots that don't drag.

## Then be the loudest voice asking who did it.

She is found at first light by somebody coming for their sheets. The Bell goes. The square fills the way it always does: coats over nightshirts, the platform crew straight off the Rush, Mrs Grieves on the tavern step holding a broom she hasn't put down.

passages.heading: Who did it?
passages.text:
You say it first, and loudest, before the Bell has finished. It is the borrowed character's voice, the part of the borrowed character that has always fitted best.

The Detective has a table set up at the Bell: magnifier, notebook, the case file. And on a square of clean paper, the thread, out of her hand.

The Detective holds it up to the light. The square looks at it. Then the square looks at scarves.

It isn't slow. It runs along the crowd like wind along wheat. Eyes drop to the throat of the man alongside, the woman alongside, their own. Half the square wears that weave, and yours is in that half. One pair of eyes rests on your scarf and stays there for the length of a breath. Then another pair.

You don't touch it. You don't look at anybody else's either. You say it again, louder: who did it? You say her name with it this time. You say what she was. A good woman, you say. Did the town's wash. The crowd murmurs yes, and the yes comes back to you warm, and you hold on to it.

passages.heading: Who did it?
passages.text:
There's a girl in the crowd by the pump, about nine. The one who counts things. Everyone knows she counts things. She isn't looking at faces. She is looking at feet, the whole front row of them, and her lips are moving.

The Detective says, "Anyone with something to say, step up."

You step up. You have something to say.

Her eyes come with your boots. One. Two. Three.

You stop.

You stand still the way you stood still at the well. She goes on watching your boots, lips going, then moves to the next pair and the next. It's nothing. She counts everything. She counts the planks on the platform. But now you can hear your own steps, every one of them. You couldn't cross the square without hearing each one land, and you know you'll still be hearing them tomorrow.

The Detective has a second find, and it isn't on the paper. It's in the mud: a trail from the fence line down the lane to the wash-house door. Boot prints, and behind each one a long gouge where a heel was dragged.

passages.heading: Who did it?
passages.text:
The square turns its head. Nobody has to tell it whose heel drags.

The Watchman tells them the truth. He stood at her door. There was a cry at the fence, wolves in the square, and he went, because that is what the lantern is for.

"There were no wolves in the square last night," you say.

You heard the cry. You were at the foot of the Rise when it came. You say it louder than he told the truth, and your voice goes over the heads of the crowd and comes down on him.

Somebody near the table turns to you. Where were you, then, at curfew?

Before you can open your mouth, a voice at the back says, "At the pump. With me."

You don't turn round. You never turn round.

The square's eyes come off your scarf. They drop, all together, to the Watchman's heel.

passages.heading: The town has spoken.
passages.text:
The Tribunal sits at the Bell. It doesn't take long; it never does. It can say three things: Acquittal, a Heavy Fine, or Death.

"Rope," you say.

Just the one word, loud. It leaves you and goes into the crowd, and the crowd takes it up, mouth to mouth, *rope, rope*, until it isn't your word any more. It belongs to the square, and nobody remembers who said it first.

The Tribunal gives a Heavy Fine: three months' scrip. Then it takes his lantern off him, there on the table beside the thread, and stands him down.

Nobody will stand at a door tonight. No one stands at any door in HollowMere now.

The girl is there for the vote. She watches the Watchman's heel all the way off the square, and if she knows anything about heels, she doesn't say it. She counts the hands that went up for the rope. You watch her count them. You know you are one of the hands.

passages.heading: The basin.
passages.text:
Home. The door barred. Basin, jug, water.

Hat. Scarf. Coat.

You look for your face.

Not in a glass. You don't need a glass. You look from the inside, the way you know your own hand in the dark. You go looking for the face under the borrowed one, the one that was there before the coat, and there is nothing where it ought to be. Not a blank. Not a dark. Just the coat on the chair, and the voice in your throat still asking who did it. It is the coat's voice, and it is the only one you have.

The square says good morning to the coat. Hattie said good morning to the coat. The coat is the one with the voice.

You put it back on. It goes on easier than it ever has. You know it will not come off again.

The girl counted your steps. One day she will say a number out loud to somebody who writes things down. So you take out the knife and lay it on the sill, under the sacking, in the place the other one knows to look if you don't come home. If they come for you, the other one finishes it. It is the one thing you have done all day that was not for the square, and even that is for whoever comes after you.

passages.heading: The basin.
passages.text:
Dawn. The stone. A new name. You read it, and you already know the door.

The square is filling. The Bell hasn't finished.

Somebody has to ask first.

works.title: The Dead Man's Lamp
works.blurb: Arvo Lahti, Workings No. 6, is sent below the winze boards on Tuesday 28 October 1952 with one carbide charge to bring up a VANE TIN CO crate; inside are stopwatches and a Form 9-D with his number, and when his light dies he sits in the refuge lamp's light among the Crawlers, fills it from the can he carried, and goes into the water.

passages.text:
There's a lamp burning down there nobody fills.

The Collier said it on Tuesday, the twenty-eighth of October, with his back to the clamp and his arms black to the elbow. He said it the way a man tells you it will rain.

Six was carrying stone. The Workings crew had been lent to the kilns for the week, and the stone was for the clamp, and the Collier did not look up when the detail officer came down the skid road with a clipboard under his arm.

"Six," the officer said.

Six put the stone down.

The officer read from the top half of a form. *Form 9-D. Detail: Recovery, Deep Level. Item: one crate, stencilled VANE TIN CO. Light issue: one charge. Return: by whistle.* He held the clipboard so the bottom half folded under his thumb.

"Yes," Six said.

In Grounds 99 you said yes or you said nothing, and nothing was written down as no.

They gave him a rope and a camp lamp, a carbide cap lamp gone green at the seams. He shook it by his ear. The charge was light. Half, maybe. He thought: they ration everything. He thought: it's a crate, not a shift.

The Collier spoke as he passed, still not looking up.

passages.heading: Down the winze.
passages.text: "Lamp's still burning down there, then. Nobody fills it."

passages.heading: Whose lamp?
passages.text:
"Him off the board. The German, or the Swede." The Collier spat into the ash. "Depends who tells it."

His name was Arvo Lahti. He had been twenty-six years underground in Butte before the leaflet, and the leaflet was a single sheet about the strike in 1948 that he had not written and had handed out at a mine gate, to men he knew, in the rain. His classification said *enemy of the state*. He had always thought the state would be bigger than that.

He knew lamps. That was the use of him.

The tram rails took him up through the adit into the ore chamber, past the last shift's tally board. Names went on that board in chalk when men went down and came off when they came up. One at the bottom had been rubbed so many times it had gone to ghosts, a smear the shape of a name the way a cloud is the shape of a horse. He did not try to read it. Nobody on the crew tried.

passages.heading: Whose lamp?
passages.text:
At the winze gallery the water stood black round the ladder shaft. Two guards in gas masks pried the boards up with a bar and stacked them against the wall.

Six took off his helmet to settle the liner. Inside it, in pencil, was *Aili*. He wrote it there every morning because pencil fades by night, and because the camp used numbers, and he would not let a number be the only thing written on him. He put the helmet back on.

He went over the edge and counted the rungs the way his father had, in Finnish, under his breath. *Yksi. Kaksi. Kolme.*

Above him the boards stayed on the stack, against the wall. Not on the hole. He noticed that, and was glad of it.

He was below the boards with one charge.

The winze landing was a shelf of rock over water. The flooded stope opened beyond it, wide and black, crossed by two plank walkways on trestles. His lamp reached a few yards and gave up.

Across the water, low in the southwest corner, a light was burning.

Yellow. Small. Steady.

Six stood with his hand on the ladder and knew who it was.

No. 3 had slept in the bunk above his. Nineteen, classed *other*, a boy who wore a red bootlace round his wrist, double-knotted, cut from his sister's skates. On his first night he had told Six about the skates: a pond at home, his sister faster than him every winter and never letting him forget it. He went on this same detail on Saturday. On Sunday his billet came off the crew's rack, and the roll said *not recovered* against his slot.

Six had thought then: *recovered* means a body. *Not recovered* means they did not look.

And here was a light. The boy had got down, found the refuge, found oil, and lived on something, and the camp had written him off because writing was cheaper than coming down.

It went through Six like heat off a stove. He had not been glad of anything since intake.

A ledge ran round the west wall to the refuge, clear of the water. He took it fast, one hand on the rock, expecting a living man.

"Three!" he called.

He had never asked the boy his name.

The refuge was a room cut square into the rock: timber frame, plank door hanging open, a table, a bunk, a hook on the wall with nothing on it.

Nobody.

Dust lay on the table and the bunk thick and unbroken, like felt. Rat tracks stitched across it. No boots. No boy. No mark where a boy had sat.

The lamp stood in the middle of the table.

It was not a camp lamp. It was brass, a flame safety lamp with a glass and a gauze chimney, the kind men carried before carbide, the kind his father had carried. Older than the camp. Older than the program, whatever the program was. Its flame burned small and yellow and did not move.

So it was not the boy. The boy was gone. Six took that and set it down where he would not have to look at it.

The lamp, then. Under the old tin there was coal; every man on the crew knew that. Coal meant gas. A seep through a crack in the floor, gas creeping into the gauze, and a flame could feed on it for a long time if the gas kept coming. He had heard coal men in the bunkhouse tell it. It happened.

He shelved the lamp as a gas seep, the way a miner shelves anything he has a word for.

"It happens," he said, to nobody.

Then he heard what he had just said, and he went cold.

Gas. He had walked into a gas room with an open carbide flame on his head.

He backed out, set the cap lamp on the ledge outside, and came in again by the light of the brass lamp alone, slowly. If it was gas, there was a test, and the old men had taught it to him before he could shave: turn the flame down to a bead and look for the cap. Gas sits on a low flame like a blue hood. The more gas, the taller the hood.

He found the pricker on its wire and worked the wick down.

A bead of clean yellow. No hood. No blue. Nothing.

No gas.

He picked the lamp up. It was heavy, and the weight moved in it. Oil. He tilted it and heard it slosh in the pot, a third full, maybe. The wick was trimmed square. The glass had been wiped.

A lamp like this burned a shift on a full pot, two if you were mean with the wick. Whoever had filled it had filled it since Sunday. Since yesterday, maybe.

He set it down exactly where it had been, on the square of clean wood where the dust had never settled.

Somebody filled the lamp. He decided not to think about who.

He turned his back on it.

The job was the only thing down here with a shape, so he did the job.

The crate was in the old workings, east, across the stope. He took his cap lamp off the ledge and went out on the nearer walkway. The planks were dry and gritty with old dust, and his boots left prints in it. The water below lay flat and black. Off to the west the drowned adit opened in the rock, a dark mouth with nothing in it.

He did not look at the water. He counted the planks instead. *Neljä. Viisi. Kuusi.*

On the far side he stopped and turned, the way you check the road home, with the walkway behind him.

The planks were wet.

Not splashed. Wet on top, in marks. Two and two, all the way back, the shape of hands and the shape of knees, as if something had come up out of the stope behind him and crawled along the boards in his own tracks. The hands were wrong. Too long in the finger. Too narrow in the palm. A man's hand, drawn out.

The water lay flat.

Then, somewhere out on it, a breath let go. A long one, the sound a man makes coming up after too long under.

No current. No wind. No drip, now that he listened.

Nothing.

Drip, he told himself. Rats. Rats swim; a wet rat leaves a mark, and water spreads a mark long. Big rats. He did not believe in rats that big, but he believed in them as hard as he could.

He stopped looking behind him.

The crate stood among the ore pillars, where the order said it would be. VANE TIN CO, in black stencil, the letters worn.

The wood under the letters was new.

Pale. Sawn this year. Raw at the corners. The lid was not even nailed.

He lifted it.

Three stopwatches, in felt.

A clipboard. On it, a column of numbers, and against each number a time. Some were crossed through. Against *3*: *4 min 10 s.* Under that, a ruled line.

A carbon of Form 9-D, the same form the officer had read to him at the kilns. The top half said what the officer had said. The letterhead above it was blacked out with a solid bar, and under the bar, in type: ANOMALY UNKNOWN. The number in the box was *6*, typed. He had never seen the bottom half. He saw it now.

passages.heading: Observer: ________.
passages.text:
And in the corner of the crate, a square can of lamp oil, stencilled REFUGE LAMP — MAINTAIN.

He stood with the lid in one hand.

Nobody sent a man down a boarded winze for a crate they could have winched. Nobody put new wood under an old name for nothing. The crate was never the cargo. The detail is the test, he thought. The cargo was the man who came to fetch it.

He put the lid down. He picked up the can. He did not know why. His hands wanted something to hold.

Neither box on the form was ticked yet.

He ran.

Back over the walkway, on the wet marks, not looking down. Along the ledge. Up the ladder, counting, losing the count, starting again. *Yksi, kaksi, kolme, neljä.* The can banged against the rungs.

His helmet hit wood.

The boards were back over the winze.

He pushed. They did not give. He found the ends of nails with his fingers where they had come through from above. He had not heard the hammer. He had been counting.

passages.heading: Six!" he shouted. "Six, on detail!
passages.text:
His number. Not his name.

Nothing came back. The order said *by whistle*. It did not say before it. The winze was shut above him until the whistle, and the whistle was hours off, and whatever the form meant by *duration*, it was not going to be decided up there.

On his head, the carbide flame shrank to a blue tongue. Half a charge. He had known on the skid road. It sputtered once and went out.

Black.

No light. No sound above. No sound below, except the water.

Then, far down and across the stope, small and yellow and steady, the refuge lamp.

The only light on the Deep Level.

He climbed down to it. He went along the ledge with his hand on the rock and his eyes on the bead of yellow, the can held against his chest, and he went into the refuge and sat on the bunk, in the dust, with the can between his boots.

passages.heading: Six!" he shouted. "Six, on detail!
passages.text: He sat in the dead man's light because it was the only light there was.

He did not know how long. The flame did not tell time, and he had no other clock.

The sound of the water changed. It rose and fell in the sump, slow, like breathing. Long in. A long hold. Out.

It came up the stope and lay along the refuge sill, black and level, and stayed there.

The cold came with it. Not mine cold. A cold that got into the teeth.

Then they came.

They came up out of the water at the sill, one, then another, then more, and sat at the edge of the light the way men crouch round the bunkhouse stove before the morning whistle. Close enough for the warmth. No closer.

Men. They had been men.

Long. That was the first thing. Too long in the arm and the shin, as if the cold had stretched them and they had set that way. Pale as tallow. The skin drawn so tight over them that he could count them by their bones: ribs standing out like the slats of a bunk under wet sheeting, hip bones like handles, the cords of the neck. Lips gone thin and back from the teeth. Ears and fingertips black with frost. Nails gone. On one, in the crook of the arm, a stub of rubber tube still taped to the skin, the tape gone grey.

They did not breathe. He watched the nearest one's chest for a long time, and it did not move. Then it heaved, once, all the air going out of it at once, and was still again.

They did not cross into the light.

He had thought, if he had thought anything, that the lamp kept them off.

It did not keep them off. They had come straight to it, and they sat at its edge, and they watched it. Not him. The lamp.

They kept things. That was the worst of it. One rubbed a thumb along two long fingers, over and over, rolling a cigarette that was not there. One tapped the plank of the sill, a count, stopping and starting again the way a man loses count on a ladder. One sat with his head bowed and his long hands folded, the way a man sits in chapel when he has stopped believing and still goes.

One of them had a red bootlace round its wrist, double-knotted.

The wrist was not right any more. Thin as a broom handle, the bone white through the skin, bent back further than a wrist goes and resting that way, as if it did not hurt now. The lace had sunk into it. With his other hand he turned it, slowly, round and round, the way the boy used to turn it in the bunk above Six when he could not sleep.

Six thought about a pond, somewhere, and a girl faster than her brother every winter, and whether anyone had told her what he was now.

The flame was lower. He leaned over and looked into the pot. Nearly dry.

They were waiting the way he had waited at the top of the ladder, for something above them to open. Every number before him had come down with a carbide lamp and a can from the crate, and ended here, on this bunk, in this light, and filled the lamp last thing. The dead man's first. Then Three's. Then theirs. Nobody filled it, the camp said. Everybody filled it. The lamp was theirs to keep lit. It was the only light any of them had.

He could let it go out.

Then there would be nothing down here for Eight but the dark and the water breathing, and these men sitting in it.

He unscrewed the pot and filled it from the can, slowly, not spilling, the way his father had taught him. He trimmed the wick square. The flame stood up. Along the sill, something in them eased. He saw it go through them like heat.

He took off his helmet and turned it over and read the liner once. *Aili.* The pencil was faint. It was evening, somewhere.

He set the helmet on the table beside the lamp, name-side up, for whoever reads names.

At the sill the one with the bootlace moved over to make room.

The water was colder than anything he had touched. Shins. Knees. His belt. It took his breath before he could give it, and he stood with his chest locked and his hands open, and then he made himself breathe once more, deep, because the form had a box for it and somebody up there was holding a watch.

He went under.

Black. Cold in the eyes. Cold in the ears.

He counted. *Yksi. Kaksi. Kolme.* His chest went tight, then tighter, then it was all he was. Hands came round his arms in the dark, long and thin and not unkind, the way men hold a man in a cold river so he does not go alone. *Kymmenen.* He lost the count. He started again. He thought of Aili's handwriting, which was better than his. His chest pulled at him to open.

He held.

He held.

He let go.

The lamp burned, full, for the next number.

passages.heading: Form 9-D
passages.text:
> **[████████████████████████]**  
> **ANOMALY UNKNOWN — GROUNDS 99**  
>
> **Detail:** Recovery, Deep Level  
> **Item:** one crate, stencilled VANE TIN CO  
> ~~Subject~~ / **Worker:** 6 (Workings)  
> **Light issue:** one charge  
> **Return:** by whistle  
> **Midnight Roll, Tue 28 Oct:** excused (detail)  
> **Duration (held):** 4 min 31 s  
> **Outcome:** ~~Recovered~~ / Not recovered ✓  
> **Observer:** ████████  
> **Remarks:** Boards lifted at whistle. Refuge lamp observed burning. Item not returned. Rack slot 6 cleared, Wed 29 Oct 1952. Next detail: 8.

Whether those hands felt like God's eternal presence, or sleeping with the devil, we'll never hear it from those drowned lips.

That afternoon, at the kilns, somebody told Eight.

There's a lamp burning down there nobody fills.

works.title: Fifteen Seconds
works.pov: first-person (Bunkhouse No. 4, a radio man from Dayton)
works.blurb: when his bunkmate Five is entered as transferred at the Midnight Roll of 13 November 1952, Bunkhouse No. 4 finds a ciphered enlistment slip with his own number on it in Five's lunchbox, hears the Sleepless knock fifteen under the floor, has his report drowned by the Choir, hides the slip in Three's lunchbox, and is posted to the kilns past the whistle.

passages.text:
The whistle at the Foundry did not begin. It was simply there, all at once, the way the cold is there when the blanket goes.

Fifteen seconds.

I was on my feet by two. Boots by four. By six I had the button in my cheek, the brown one off my good coat, the coat they took at the gate. You hold a button in your cheek and your teeth can't chatter. A man whose teeth chatter is a man who is saying something.

Slot four. My slot. A number painted on the post at the foot of my bunk, and the same number burned into a pine billet on our crew's rack by the door. Every crew keeps its own rack of ten. The bunkhouse crew's hangs where we can see it while we eat.

Nine. Ten.

Three was on my left, breathing through his nose. On my right, slot five.

Slot five was empty.

Twelve. Thirteen.

I didn't look. You don't look. I counted his blanket instead, folded the way he folded it, corners in. His hymn card on the shelf. His boots not under the bunk.

Fifteen.

The whistle stopped and the arc-lights came up through the one window. White. Flat. No shadow anywhere in the room except under us. Then the door. Then the masks.

Two of them. Rubber faces, glass eyes, the canister snouts. They walk the row with a clipboard and a lamp. They don't say your number. They look at it.

At five, one of them stopped.

"Five," the mask said. It came out wet and far off, a man talking from the bottom of a well.

Nobody answered. That is the answer.

Outside, the alert. The big light on the Foundry roof swung once across the yard and once across the pines. The dogs went out. You can hear dogs go out: the chains first, then nothing, then a long way off.

Slot five was called missing on the roll, and the pencil wrote it down.

I lay back down with my boots on and told myself the plain thing. Five was late at the kilns. They'd had him on clamp work all week. An old man, a slow path, a bad knee. The dogs would find him on the skid road and walk him back, and tomorrow he'd lose his sugar for it and hum about it, flat, all day.

Fifteen seconds is long enough to see who isn't there.

The dogs came back at two.

I know because I was counting. Not sleeping. Counting the slats over my face, eleven, and the nails in the slats, thirty-four.

Chains. Boots. The handler said something to the mask on the porch, and the mask said nothing back. No argument. No second team. No lamps going out again along the woods trail.

No scent. Fine. The rain, the kiln smoke. Dogs lose things.

Then the mask came in alone, sat at the end of the mess table with the roll sheet and the lamp turned low, and wrote.

I can read upside down. Eleven years at a repair bench in Dayton, reading the dial plates of radios across a counter. I read it from my bunk through the gap in the half wall.

TRANSFERRED.

One word. Block capitals. Beside five.

Nobody had looked for him. The dogs had gone out and come back, and in between nobody had looked anywhere, and the word was already in the pencil. Waiting. As if it had been written in the morning and only needed the night to catch up to it.

Five was entered as transferred.

All right, I thought. All right. Transferred means a train. The payroll train comes Fridays, and tomorrow was Friday. Men go out on it sometimes, men with papers, men somebody higher up has made a decision about. He was in the Office with a blanket and a cup of something. He was going somewhere else.

The sugar twist was still under his pillow. I could see the newspaper edge of it.

Eight weeks of sugar, for a grandson in Scranton he'd never met.

You do not leave the sugar.

At morning tally a mask laid a form on my blanket and a pencil on the form.

FEDERAL ███████ OF ██████████████ — GROUNDS 99
PRODUCTION IS OBLIGATION.
EFFECTS OF TRANSFERRED PERSONNEL
(NEIGHBOUR TO SIGN)

Five was entered as transferred, and the form for transferred men wants the man in the next slot. So I was the one who emptied his bunk.

Two shirts, grey. One hymn card, soft as cloth from his thumb. One comb, three teeth gone. One twist of sugar, newspaper.

Boots: none. I wrote *none*.

One lunchbox, tin, dented on the lid where somebody's heel had been.

I knew that box. He kept his bread in it and his tonic ticket and nothing else, and it was too heavy for that. I tipped it. The bottom moved an eighth of an inch. Someone had set a second floor into it and pressed it down tight.

Under it, one slip of paper.

Not camp paper. Camp paper is grey and furry and drinks pencil like a blotter. This was thin and white and crackled, and someone had covered it in typed letters in groups of five, five, five, none of them words.

passages.heading: I wrote: *One lunchbox, tin.
passages.text:
I didn't write the slip.

I put it in my boot, under my heel, and signed. The mask took the form without looking at it, and the bunk was just a bunk again, a board and a ticking, waiting for a number.

Escape money, I told myself, walking out to the yard. That's what it was. A price. Some arrangement with somebody for a key, or a gap in the wire, and the arrangement came due and he went. Good for him. Good for Five.

I had signed for a man. That's what the line said. Neighbour to sign.

Friday night the arc-light came through the cracks between the boards in stripes. Under the blanket I laid the slip on my knee in one of them.

Groups of five. I tried them every way a radio man knows: backward, every second letter, a shift of three, a shift of four. Nothing. It wasn't written for me to read.

Except for three things.

At the top, typed and then struck through: DEPT. and a black bar where the department should be. Somebody had sat down with a ribbon and inked out whose paper this was.

Bottom corner, in pencil, not typed: a canteen. A child's drawing of one, a circle with a neck and a strap.

And beside it, a number.

4.

Not a group, not part of the cipher. A four on its own, the way they paint it on the post at the foot of my bunk.

So it wasn't escape money. Nobody buys his way out with a department and a picture of my canteen.

I sat with the stripe of light across my knee and my number in it, and I did what I do. I counted what I knew.

One. Somebody with a typewriter and a department had put this in an old man's lunchbox. Nobody in this bunkhouse owns paper that white.

Two. It was about slot four. About the water in slot four's canteen. That was how I read it. That is how anyone would read it.

Three. Five had held it. One night, two, a week. I didn't know.

Four. He hadn't done it. I was alive. I'd drunk from that canteen every day.

Five. He was gone.

So he'd said no. That was the shelf I put it on, and it was a narrow one. He had said no, in whatever way you say no to a slip of paper, and been taken for it, and the word was in the pencil before the dogs got back.

I folded the slip into my boot again.

Five had been keeping me alive. With a lunchbox.

Because the slip named slot four, I stopped drinking from the canteen.

On Saturday I drank at the pump from my hands, when the line was long and nobody watched hands. Sunday the same. It tastes of the pipe. Everything here tastes of something else.

I stopped sleeping, too. Not on purpose. I lay down and my eyes stayed open, and after a while I sat up with my back to the half wall, where I could see the door, the window and the hatch.

Old men talk in the dark. Eight said there was a lamp down in the Deep Level, in the refuge, a miner's lamp from before the camp, still burning, and nobody fills it. Two said that was a story for new men. Eight said go down and look, then. Nobody said anything after that.

Sunday's roll came and went. I stood. I was counted. I sat back against the wall.

Somewhere after one, under the floor, something knocked.

The root-cellar hatch is between the end bunks, a square of planks with an iron ring. Turnips once. Nothing now, the cook says.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

I counted. Of course I counted.

Fifteen. Then quiet, about as long as two breaths. Then fifteen.

Fifteen is the whistle. Fifteen is the one number every man in this room has in his bones.

Five, I thought. Five in the cellar. Not on a train, not in the woods, nowhere the dogs go. Under the boards, alive, hiding from whatever he'd said no to, and knocking the only count we all share, so that whoever heard would know it was one of us.

I got down on the floor by the ring and put my knuckle to the plank.

I knocked back. Fifteen.

It knocked fifteen again.

The bunk room was asleep the way men sleep here, shallow and all at once. Three was turned to the wall. The window was white.

I put two fingers through the ring and lifted.

Cold came up. Earth. Roots. Something sour under it, a sickroom smell.

The arc-light fell in behind me, one square of it down the ladder and across the floor.

At the edge of the square, against the joist, someone was sitting up.

Not lying. Sitting straight, the way you sit when you've been told to. Hands in the lap. One knuckle lifted an inch from the wood.

Eyes open.

Not open the way mine were, sore and red after two nights. Open past that. The lids gone thin as cigarette paper, raw at the rims, and they did not close. Not once while I looked. I don't think they knew how any more.

The rest came at me in pieces, the way a thing comes when you can't take it whole.

Skin gone tight over the skull, a drumhead over a frame. Temples sunk in. Lips drawn back off the teeth, split, dried black in the splits.

No shirt. Ribs standing out through the skin, every one. I counted them. God help me, I counted them.

A tube taped into the crook of one arm, the tape gone brown. It ran down into nothing, its end knotted off.

Fingertips black at the ends, the cellar cold had them. The knocking knuckle was worn through to something white.

A jaw that never stopped moving. Under its breath, all the time, it was counting.

And the boots. Laced and double-knotted, the ends tucked down the sides because he couldn't stand them flapping. I knew those boots. I had looked at them every night for four months, under the bunk on my right.

The knuckle came down on the joist once and stopped, because of the light.

It flinched from the square like a dog flinches from a raised hand. A sound came out of it, high in the nose. Not a word. Then the face came up into the light anyway. Thin. Not Five's. Nobody's I knew. Somebody's, once. Somebody who had been made to stay awake past where a body stops. And then past that. And then past that.

passages.heading: It said, "Four.
passages.text:
Not loud. The way the mask says it at roll. Exactly that way, with the same weight on it. Someone had taught it how a number is said.

I dropped the hatch and sat on it.

Below me, after a while, very gently: one. Two. Three.

Five wasn't under the boards. His boots were, and whatever was in them had my number.

It wasn't signalling. It was practising.

There was a tribunal in the yard at dawn on Monday. Scrip Forfeiture, nobody from our crew. I stood at the back and learned how it goes. They read. They weigh. They decide. A man who goes to them first is a witness. A man they come for is a case.

I had no shelves left. The thing under the floor had my number, the slip in my boot had my number, and the only door in Grounds 99 that opens from the inside is the one you report through.

So I chose.

After roll the mess hall stays lit. One mask keeps the night desk by the iron range, and a man who has something to say goes then, counted and accounted for, with the whole room watching him walk.

A dozen men were at the long table. Not our crew; men from all over, men I'd seen at the pump and never heard speak. They sat with their hands flat on the boards. When the last echo of the whistle died in the rafters, they turned their heads together, the twelve of them, as smooth as a door on a hinge.

Then they hummed.

One note. Low, and all of it at once, the way the whistle is all at once.

I walked to the desk with the slip in my hand.

passages.heading: There's a contract—
passages.text:
The note rose. Not louder, fuller. It filled the hall to the rafters, and my words went into it the way a stone goes into the Blackwater. I could feel my mouth working. I could not hear it. I said *lunchbox*. I said *Five*. I said *canteen*. Nothing came out of the hum.

The mask didn't hear any of it. The mask looked at the paper.

White paper. Typed groups. A black bar where a department should be. A pencilled canteen, a pencilled four, in the hand of the man standing in front of it.

The glass eyes stayed on it a long time. Then the mask wrote something down on the night sheet, waved me off with the pencil, and didn't take the slip. It didn't need to.

The humming stopped when I sat down. Not before.

Nobody heard me. Everybody saw it.

On Tuesday the seam in the Workings burned. A dust fire, the men said, and nobody said who. Smoke lay over the yard all morning, and the Workings crew came up coughing black and were sent to the tonic line.

At noon the work sheet went up on the board.

*4 — KILNS — LATE DETAIL — RELIEVE 23:50.*

The kilns are out on the woods trail, past the skid road. On a clear path, running, a man is ten minutes from the bunkhouse door. Fifteen seconds is fifteen seconds.

I read it twice, and then I understood about Five.

He hadn't been late at the kilns. They had put him at the kilns. The mask had seen the slip in my hand and written it down, and now the sheet put me where the whistle would end with me outside. A man missing at roll is a man the dogs are for. Nobody has to decide anything. The count decides.

A man searched with that slip in his boot was finished. So I did the one thing left to me.

Three was on his bunk mending a sock, badly, the needle going in and out of the same hole. When he went to the pump I opened his lunchbox. I pressed the slip flat under his bread, under the tonic ticket, and closed the lid soft so the tin wouldn't speak.

I am not going to say why. I know why. Fifteen seconds is not enough time to be a better man.

He came back and picked up the sock again.

Three's sock had a hole in the heel. I didn't tell him.
The Collier gave me the torch at the clamp and looked at the sheet in my hand and didn't say anything about it.

passages.heading: Keep that torch up.
passages.text:
I kept it up. The kilns ticked. The morning's smoke still hung in the pines. 23:50 came on the Collier's watch and nobody came to relieve me. I hadn't thought anybody would.

Then the whistle.

It didn't begin. It was there.

I ran. Torch in one hand, the button in my cheek, counting. Five. Six. My wife's kitchen clock ran four minutes fast so we would never be late, and I thought of it, four minutes, I'd have taken four minutes. Nine. The skid road under my boots. Ten. Eleven. The lantern posts in the yard, very small, very far.

Fifteen.

The whistle stopped, and I was a long way from anywhere.

And in the quiet where it had been, far off, past the kilns, past the ridge, somewhere I have never been, something sounded. Low. Long. Like breath drawn across the mouth of a bottle. Almost a flute.

Once.

passages.heading: Keep that torch up.
passages.text:
I stood in the road and for one breath I was not afraid. I don't know why. I will not know why.

Then the arc-light swung off the Foundry roof and out across the yard. It went over the woods trail, over the pines, over me, and kept going.

Carried thin across the yard, a mask's voice through the bunkhouse window.

passages.heading: Four.
passages.text:
Nobody answered. That is the answer.

I know where Three was standing. Slot three, boots on, his breath through his nose, beside a board and a ticking and a blanket folded corners-in. Not looking. Counting it instead.

The chains went first. Then nothing.

And under the bunkhouse floor, I know, something in an old man's boots had lifted one knuckle an inch from the wood.

Three's lunchbox. Tomorrow.

Fifteen seconds is long enough to see who isn't there.

works.title: The Burlap Cowl
works.blurb: spring 1790: the Leaven-Rot kills the Abbot, Dom Ambroise, and his burlap cowl comes down the dish-pit stair to bless the Commons; a Plongeur girl, named aloud for the first time by the cowl and registered after the first blessed burning, finds the Abbot's body under kelp and does not report it, because the blessed bread is the only bread, and ends as the Cellar-Ghoul, keeping him.

passages.heading: 1. Salt
passages.text:
Once a year the Abbot came down the dish-pit stair and said our names.
