Nobody else came down. Not the Aboyeur, not the Council's clerks, not the Commons' committee, who had held the Square since the ferry brought the news and who said, now, that all of us were citizens. Citizens of the pit. We scrubbed their plates the same as we had scrubbed the Gallery's.

I was born down there. My mother was sent to the pit for a crumb, in a year before I can remember, and a child born in the pit is a Plongeur by birth. I have no platter in the Hall. A soul without a platter has no name in law. I had a name anyway. The Abbot kept it for me.

The eve of the Blessing of the Flour. Upstairs the Aboyeur carried the dusk loaf down the Hall and set it on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal. We heard his feet through the ceiling. The night began.

passages.heading: 1. Salt
passages.text:
We knelt. That is the custom: on the eve you kneel where you work. I knelt where I always knelt, on the old seal of Le Champignon that was ground into the floor before anyone's grandmother. The office of the first heresy. My knees know it better than my hands know my face.

First bell. Nothing.

Second bell. The burlap came down the stair.

It was the cowl. The patch at the knee, the rope belt, the wooden thumb-bowl. It went along the row. It did not stop at the old man beside me and say his name. It did not stop at me. It put its thumb to each brow the way the Abbot did, quick, like a seal on wax, and moved on.

His thumb smelled of hearth-ash. Always. Twenty blessings in my life and every one smelled of the Hearth.

This one smelled of salt.

When it lifted, my brow was cold where it had been. I put my fingers up. They came away green.

passages.heading: 1. Salt
passages.text:
I bowed into it anyway. I had waited a year.

I did not wipe it off.

passages.heading: 2. Damp
passages.text:
I lay on my pallet and explained it to myself.

The Starter had turned. That was all. The Abbot carried the Apostolic Starter in that little bowl from the Abbey to the pit, and the pit is wet, and the stair is wetter, and anything alive goes strange in the wet. Green is a colour bread goes. Everyone in a kitchen knows it.

The Abbot was old. Old men forget names. He had said ours for forty years; one year he could be tired.

And the salt. The Commons had their watch on the Square every night now, red crust on their sleeves, lanterns at every lane. An old man in burlap who would not bless their fire would not walk past them for pleasure. He would have come the long way. By the Salt-Flats. Salt on the hem, salt on the hands.

There. Three things, three reasons.

I did not wash my face. The old man beside me did not wash his.

passages.heading: 2. Damp
passages.text: The damp, I decided. Damp gets into everything down here.

passages.heading: 3. The bowl
passages.text:
At dawn the flour carts stood at the foot of the Windmill Cliffs, the way they stand every year on the Blessing, the sacks open at the neck. The Abbot blesses the flour of the first grinding, and the island eats clean for a year. That is what the Abbey is for.

A Plongeur does not leave the pit at the Blessing. A Plongeur does not leave the pit. I left it.

I came up the back stair with a tub of plates as my reason and put the tub down at the head of the lane.

The cowl walked past the carts. It did not look at them. It did not lift a hand. The carters stood with their caps off, and it went by them like a man passing a stall he does not owe.

It went to Gallows Square.

The Hall's great south doors stood open onto the Square, as they had since the autumn, so the Commons could see the Hearth from the stage and the Hearth could see them. The committee sat at the long table where the Gallery used to take its supper. Red crust. Ink. A seal on a ribbon.

passages.heading: 3. The bowl
passages.text:
The cowl climbed the stage. It blessed the committee one by one, thumb to brow. Then it turned to the open doors and lifted both hands to the Hearth itself.

The Square made a sound I had never heard it make. It was not a cheer. It was what a dog does when it is fed after a long time.

Then the cowl dipped its thumb in the wooden bowl for the next brow, and held the bowl high, and I was close enough to see inside.

Grey-gold. The Apostolic Starter, the colour it always was. Dry at the rim. Clean.

The green was not in the bowl. It was on the thumb. It had always been on the thumb.

Not the damp, then. Not the Starter. Not the stair.

For a whole year the Abbot had stood in that Square and refused. The Gallery asked him to bless their Trial by Fire, and he would not. The Commons asked him to bless theirs, and he would not. He blessed bread and he blessed us. That was all he would bless.

passages.heading: 3. The bowl
passages.text: He never blessed a fire. Not theirs, and not the Gallery's.

passages.heading: 4. The platter
passages.text:
With the Hearth blessed, the committee read an ordinance.

Gold leaf on bread was forbidden in a hungry week. Seal of the Commons, ribbon of red. A woman of the Gallery had gilded the crust of her daughter's name-day loaf, three days into a hungry week. A crumb's worth of gold. They had the crust in a dish on the table to show it.

Clémence d'Aubrac.

I knew her before I knew her face. I had scrubbed her plates for eleven years. A child's plate, small, with a gold rim, and it always came down with the crust left on it. The child never ate the crust. Somebody upstairs never made her.

They brought her up onto the stage. She was not frightened the way the poor were frightened when the Gallery did this. She was offended. She looked at the long table as if the cloth were wrong.

She asked for her gloves. Her hands were cold, she said.

passages.heading: 4. The platter
passages.text:
It was not permitted.

The Commons used the Gallery's ceremony because it was the only ceremony there was. The cloches lifted along the table. The music, the same three fiddles. The bell. Her loaf was carried in through the south doors by the Aboyeur, who called her name once as it passed, and the Hearth received it.

Then the Hearth received her.

It was the first fire on the island anyone had ever blessed.

Afterward the committee sat down to the same supper the Gallery used to eat after, on the same silver, carried out by the same hands. Ours. I have scrubbed that silver. I scrubbed it that night.

But before the supper, a man of the committee stood and said the blessing had made them a church as well as a council, and a church must count its souls. The dish pit was registered. All of it. In thanks.

passages.heading: 4. The platter
passages.text:
They gave me a platter. Tin, not silver, at the far end of the Hall where the steam does not reach. A loaf on it with a seal pressed in. The Aboyeur walked the row and called each new loaf by its owner's name, the way he calls the Gallery's.

He called mine. In the Hall. Out loud. The first time anyone had said it above the pit.

I will not write it. It sounded like the Abbot's.

passages.heading: 5. Crumb
passages.text:
Dawn. The Great Proofing Bell struck six, and everyone with a platter cracked the loaf sitting on it.

I had never cracked a loaf of my own. I had cleaned up after ten thousand.

I broke it with my thumbs, the way I had seen them do it from the stair.

The crumb was threaded green. Fine lines, like veins in the back of a hand.

I looked up. Along the floor of the Hall, from the foot of my platter, there were footprints. Green. Glowing in the grey light under the cloches, faint, the way a wet stone holds the moon. They went from my platter down the Hall and out to the threshold of the pit stair, and on the threshold there was a round green mark, like a seal stamped into the stone.

I knew the feet. Wide in the heel, the left turned in. I had knelt beside those feet for twenty years.

passages.heading: 5. Crumb
passages.text:
The old man who scrubbed beside me. Thirty years in the pit. The Abbot had said his name thirty times, once a year, on his knees beside him. He walked the thresholds now, spore on his soles. The Spore-Caller. He did not look at me when I came down. He looked pleased.

They had registered us. I had thought that was a name.

It was a mark. A line in a book for a church that counts its souls.

They had not given me a name. They had given me a number.

passages.heading: 6. Kelp
passages.text:
I followed the prints.

Not the ones to the pit. There were others, older and fainter, that came in at the foot of my platter from the other side. They went out by the side door of the Hall, down the Wharf steps, and along the edge of the Salt-Flats. They started at my platter. Whatever had marked my bread had come from the Flats to do it.

Low tide. The Flats go grey and flat and wet, and the kelp lies in heaps like wash.

The prints stopped at one heap.

I pulled the kelp off with my hands. I am used to my hands in cold wet things.

The Abbot.

In his undershirt. No burlap. Bare feet, white, the soles cracked the way they were always cracked. His hose was patched at the knee, a square of brown, the same patch as the cowl's, because he wore through both in the same place. Kneeling. In our pit. Forty years.

passages.heading: 6. Kelp
passages.text:
His belt was empty where the bowl hung.

His face was turned to the side. His mouth a little open, as if he had been about to say a name and had been stopped on the first letter. There was sand in his eyebrows. His thumb was grey with ash.

"Dom Ambroise," I said. Once. Nobody calls an Abbot by his name. I had heard it from the old man, years ago, the way you hear the name of a saint.

Every child in the pit knows the saying. What a dead man wears will walk until someone tells the Bailiff where he lies. I had always thought it was about thieves selling the clothes off the drowned.

It was not about thieves.

The cowl was walking because he was lying here. He was lying here because nobody had told. And I was the only one who knew where.

He had been here since before he blessed me.

passages.heading: 7. Sails
passages.text:
I put the kelp back over him. I don't know why. Then I climbed.

The Wharf steps, the lane, the corner of the Square. The Bailiff kept his iron staff by the committee's door now, the Commons having taken the Guild's law along with the Gallery's stage. I could see the staff from the corner. Twenty steps.

Then the sails stopped.

Everyone on the island feels it. The Windmill Cliffs are behind everything, turning, and you stop seeing them, the way you stop hearing your own heart. Then they stop, and everyone in the Square looked up at once, the way a room looks at a door.

The Groat-Master. A miller's apprentice I had seen once at the flour carts. He had been blessed at the Square at dawn. He was up there now with the brake on, and the grinding stopped, and the island did what it does when the sails stop. It waited.

passages.heading: 7. Sails
passages.text:
By noon there was a new ordinance on the bulletin board. Seal and ribbon. Until the mill turns, flour to the blessed only.

I read it standing at the board. I worked it out with my fingers, like plates.

Tell the Bailiff, and the body is found. Find the body, and the cowl comes off. Take the cowl off, and every blessing it gave is void. The committee's. The Hearth's. Ours. The pit's platters are struck. The pit's flour stops.

The old man. The two girls who came down last winter. The boy with the bad hand. The whole pit. Hungry, in a week with no flour, with no platter, with no name.

I turned round on the steps of the Square.

I went back down. I told myself the stair was too steep.

passages.heading: 8. Bread
passages.text:
Tomorrow.

The tide would be low again tomorrow. The mill would turn tomorrow, or the day after, and there would be bread, and then I would tell. It was only a day. He had already waited a night and a day under the kelp. One more was not a sin. It was arithmetic.

That night there was a loaf on my platter. Mine. A seal in it, cut on the top with a cross, the way the Abbey marks its bread. The first bread in my life that nobody had eaten from first.

I did not crack it at the Hearth. I took it down to the pit and ate it on the Champignon seal, on my knees, in the dark.

There was green in it. I ate around it. Then I ate it.

It was good bread. That is the worst thing I know.

passages.heading: 9. Gone
passages.text:
Next low tide I went back to the Salt-Flats. The tomorrow I had promised myself.

The heap of kelp was there. I lifted it.

Sand. A dent in the sand the shape of a man, filling slowly with water from underneath. Nothing else.

No drag marks. Not one. No heel lines, no furrow, no broken kelp. As if he had stood up and walked, or as if something had carried him that did not touch the ground.

I stood there until the water came over my feet.

Now there was nothing to tell. I could say to the Bailiff, *I saw him*. I could say, *under the kelp, by the third post*. The Bailiff would go and lift the kelp and find sand. A Plongeur's word against an empty beach. Tomorrow was spent. I had spent it on bread.

That night the cowl came down the dish-pit stair again.

Not the eve. Not a feast. An ordinary night with the dusk loaf already set upstairs. It came along the row and the others knelt, so I knelt.

passages.heading: 9. Gone
passages.text:
It stopped at me.

The thumb. Salt. Cold. It pressed, and held, longer than the first time.

And it said my name.

Not the Aboyeur's way, loud, for the Hall. The Abbot's way. Low, the first letter soft, as if the name were something that could be bruised.

Nobody alive should have had it like that. The Aboyeur had it from a ledger. The committee had it from the register. The way it was said, only one man had it, and that man had said it down here once a year and nowhere else.

He had given it away. Before he died. Somebody asked him who he blessed, and he told them. Maybe he thought it would save us. Maybe he thought it would save him.

He had told it who I was.

passages.heading: 10. Key
passages.text:
The second blessing took.

I don't know how else to say it. The first was a smear on my brow. The second went in. I knelt there with the cowl's thumb on my face and I knew where he was. Not by the prints. Not by sense. I knew the way you know where your own hand is in the dark.

The cowl put something in my palm. Iron. Cold. A key with the cold pantry's mark on the bow.

The cold pantry is the coolest room in the Sacred Kitchen, and the only one with a lock on the outside.

He was in there. On the stone shelf where the Garde Manger keeps what is kept. Somebody had laid him straight. Somebody with no feet, or feet that leave nothing.

I was the somebody now. I would move him when he needed moving. I would leave no trail; I already knew I would leave no trail, the way I knew I would breathe. The Cellar-Ghoul, they call it. The one who keeps the body.

passages.heading: 10. Key
passages.text:
I sat with him all night. When I went out for water I locked him in behind me, from the outside, the way that door is made, and the key went back on its string round my neck.

The green had come up on him too. On the backs of his hands, at his temples, in the cracks of his soles. I did not wipe it off him either. It was his, now. It was ours.

His hose had ridden up. I pulled it down over his knees.

I kept his knees covered. He had knelt for us enough.

passages.heading: 11. Ink
passages.text:
The Inquisitor came down the stair in the afternoon.

Flour-white sleeves, a Guild man, young. The kind they set to learning. He had the Magnesium Powder Kit on a strap and white dust to his elbows, and he came along the row looking at feet.

He had been on the Salt-Flats. He had dusted the sand round the third post, and the powder had lifted prints out of the old green. Bare feet. A Plongeur's feet, because nobody else on the island goes barefoot on the Flats. Coming and going.

He stopped in front of me. He looked at my feet. Then my brow.

"Where is the Abbot?" he said.

passages.heading: I go for kelp. For the scouring.
passages.text:
He looked at me a long time. He had nothing in his kit for a body that was not where the prints led. He had sand and a dent in it.

He opened his ledger and wrote it down. *Plongeur. States: Abbot upstairs, blessing.* He blotted it. He climbed back up because he could not prove otherwise, and the committee would not thank a Guild man who said their blessings were void.

Now it was in a book. In ink. In the Guild's hand, with my mark of the pit beside it.

He wrote down what I said. That made it true enough to hold.

passages.heading: 12. Fifteen
passages.text:
Five thresholds were marked by then. The Windmill door. The Tavern. The Counting-House. The Apothecary. The south doors of the Hall, last, a green ring on the old stone where the Commons' stage met the Gallery's floor. The pit stair was marked too, but it did not count. The pit is not a building. It is a hole under one.

On the last night they went down.

They passed me in the kitchen on the way to the sub-basement door. The Spore-Caller first, the old man, his feet glowing. The Groat-Master, flour still in his hair from the brake. The Arch-Fermenter, a dockhand, in a leather apron his wife had mended twice at the same corner. I saw the two rows of stitches. Small. Even. A careful woman. Then the others, whose names I knew from their plates, with their eyes open and nothing behind them.

Six at the altar, and the Arch-Fermenter to lead them. Ninety-one steps down. The cowl went last, and did not look at me, because it did not need to.

passages.heading: 12. Fifteen
passages.text:
I did not go down. I had my door.

I sat on the floor of the kitchen with my back against the cold pantry, the key on its string, and his knees covered on the other side of the wood.

The chant came up. Through the ninety-one steps, through the stone, through the floor and into my legs, where the Champignon seal has lived for twenty years. Not loud. Steady, like a mill.

I have always counted plates. Gold-leaf plates in their own tub. Tin plates. Children's plates with the crust left on.

I counted the chant instead. One. Two. Three. As long as a held breath. Eleven. Twelve.

I do not know what it did to the Mother. I do not know what is in her glass now. That is not mine to tell. I was at my door.

Fourteen. Fifteen.

They will have my office in their book, one day. The Cellar-Ghoul. The Council always writes the office down. It does not write the name.

passages.heading: 12. Fifteen
passages.text:
That is all right. The name was never theirs.

Once a year the Abbot came down the dish-pit stair and said our names.

Now the cowl comes every night, and says one.

works.title: Three Fires and a Ferry
works.blurb: 20–24 September 1789: the Pyre-Master, Maître Lescop called Rassis, and his apprentice Fanch blow the Guild boilers, rupture the gas-lines and seal the windmill blades; a night stoker dies, a candle-boy is burned for the dark, the Grand Inspector-General lands with the news from Paris and dies in the fog, and the boy presses the Crown's seal into Madame de Montaury's gilded loaf, so that the Gallery's own Chancellor gives her to the Hearth and the Commons eat the Gallery's supper.

passages.text:
At dusk the Aboyeur set a loaf on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal.

Then the night began.

Fanch watched it from the gallery stair with the master's tool bag on his shoulder. Every soul on the rock had seen it done every dusk of their lives, and nobody looked anymore. He looked. An Apprenti is the one who watches. That is the whole of the office. Its disgrace is speaking.

passages.heading: The master touched his elbow. "Come.
passages.text:
They went down the Counting-House steps in the last of the light, to the Guild boiler-house under them, where the mountain's steam was taken in iron and made to work the Guild's presses and warm the Guild's rooms.

The door was not locked. The master had built the lock.

Inside: heat. Iron. A hiss in the pipes like a breath let out slow. Three boilers in a row, black and sweating. A coat on a nail. A tin plate on the floor, scraped clean.

"Lamp lower," the master said. "Look at the floor."

The boy held the lamp lower and looked at the floor. He heard the master's hands on iron, then a light tap, like someone knocking politely at a door. He did not look up. He was not asked to understand. He was asked to hold the light.

passages.heading: Nobody's in here at night?
passages.text:
He had not meant to say it. It came out of him in the heat.

"Empty as a church on market day," the master said. "Out."

They were on the cliff path when the boilers went.

First the ground. Then the sound, one flat blow, like a door the size of the town slammed shut. Then a white column standing up out of the Counting-House steps into the dark, and every window of the Guild Hall lit at once from underneath, and then none of them.

His knees had gone. He was sitting on the path. He did not remember sitting.

He took his father's plumb-bob out of his shirt and let it hang from his fist on its cord. The ground was still shaking. The bob hung true. A line that hangs true is the one thing on the rock nobody can argue with.

The boiler-house had been empty. The master had said so. The boy believed the boiler-house was empty, and the bob hung true, and that made two things.

At the bell they carried Pol out under sailcloth.

He knew the shape before the cloth slipped. Everyone on the Wharf knew Pol: the night stoker, no platter, no bed, Unregistered since before the boy was born. He played a tin whistle at the Tavern door for coppers. He played it badly, and people paid him to stop, and he knew it and played anyway. He slept against the boilers because the boilers were warm and nothing else on the rock was.

Nobody had told the boy that. He told himself he had not known it.

The sailcloth was too short. Pol's boots stuck out the end, and one had no lace. When the Iron-Wardens tipped the stretcher to clear the rubble, the whistle slid out of the cloth and dropped into the ash. Nobody picked it up.

The master stood at the edge of the crowd with his hat in his hands. His face was grey. He looked like a man who had lost something.

An accident, then. Nobody could have known an old man slept there. Not the master, who had said empty. Not the boy, who had held the light low and looked at the floor. An accident nobody could have known.

He waited until the stretcher was gone and the crowd had gone after it. Then he went into the ash and picked up the whistle. It was still warm.

He did not play it.

The second night the master talked.

He did that sometimes on a long walk, warmly, like a teacher, with his hand on the back of the boy's neck. The gas-lines ran from the vents to the Hall lamps under the Hall's east wall, and it was a long way round by the dark lanes, and the master talked the whole way.

passages.heading: Pol," he said. "You liked Pol.
passages.text:
The boy nodded.

"He slept there every night. Fifteen winters. The Guild knew. The Ledger-Clerk knew. It saved the Guild the price of a bed." The hand was warm. "Now the Guild has to bury him. In front of the Commons. And every soul on the Salt-Flats will stand at that grave and ask who let an old man sleep in a boiler-house."

The boy walked.

The accident went out of him like heat out of a loaf. The master had known. The master had counted Pol in, the way you count the eggs before you crack them.

He found something else to stand on. It came quickly; it had to. The island was asleep. It had been asleep four hundred years, eating off its silver plates. You do not wake a sleeper by asking. Pol was the price of waking the island. One old man with no bed. A price. Prices get paid.

passages.heading: Pol," he said. "You liked Pol.
passages.text:
At the east wall he did not wait to be told. He took the bag off his own shoulder and went down into the culvert first, and held the light, and handed up whatever was asked for.

When they came up, the lamps of the Hall of Platters were going out.

One. Then the next. Then the next, down the long room, until the Hall was dark but for the Hearth.

The Hearth is never let go out.

From the lane he could see it through the great south doors: the red mouth of it, the gilded platters nearest it catching the light, and on the empty platter the dusk loaf, lit from one side.

Only the Hearth, and the loaf beside it.

In the dark, someone had taken a candle-end.

That was the charge. The Iron-Wardens found it at first light on the Salt-Flats, burned down to a stub, in the fist of a boy called Gwenaël. He had taken it off a sconce in the black Hall to see his mother home along the Wharf. He was about the Apprenti's age. He whistled through a gap in his front teeth, and the dish-pit women threw rinds at him for it, and he whistled at them too.

It was the last morning of summer.

Morning Judgment was held in Gallows Square, before the Hall's south doors, so that the whole Square could see into the Hearth. The Gallery came down for it. They always came down for it.

Earlier that month a dockhand had gone to the Hearth for a fine he could not pay. The boy had not watched that one. He watched this one.

The musicians first. Then the bell. Then the cloches, carried out on silver and set in a row on the long table, gilded nearest the Chancellor, red crust at the far end. Under one of them was Gwenaël's Wake Loaf.

The High Chancellor read the sentence from a card. It took less time than the music had.

*One candle-end, property of the Council. Taken in darkness. Trial by Fire in the Great Hearth.*

In the gallery above the doors a table had been laid. White cloth. Glasses. The supper after.

The Aboyeur lifted the cloche, took up the loaf and carried it down toward the Hearth, calling the name as it passed. The Square was quiet enough to hear the surf on the reef.

The Hearth received the loaf, and then the one the loaf named.

The boy did not look at the Hearth. He looked up at the gallery, the way you look at anything else when you cannot look at the thing. Madame de Montaury had her napkin in her lap. She was old and very upright, and she had asked for the heel; she always asked for the heel. A footman bent to her. She tasted the sauce and gave the dish back to him with two fingers on its rim.

It had gone cold. That was all. It had gone cold while they waited.

He stood in the Square with Pol's whistle in his apron and the smell of the lampless night still in his clothes, and he understood one thing very clearly. The island had not woken. It had turned over in its sleep and burned a Commons boy for the master's dark.

No. Not the master's. The master had not lit the Hearth. The master had not written the card. The candle-end was the Council's property, the sentence was the Council's, and the sauce was Madame de Montaury's. It was the Gallery's sin, not the master's.

He held on to that all the way home.

The supper was venison. He could smell it from the Square.

The third night he went first.

He climbed the Windmill Cliffs in the wind, ahead of the master, with the bag and the coil of rope and the second bag the master would have carried. More than his share. For Gwenaël, he told himself. For the gap in Gwenaël's teeth.

At the top the sails were turning, great and slow and creaking in the dark, the way they had turned every night of his life.

The master's work took an hour. The boy's work was carrying, and holding, and keeping his mouth shut against the wind.

Then the sails stopped.

Not all at once. They slowed. They groaned. They stood.

In fog the fishermen told the hour by those sails. Now the hour had stopped.

No wind in the canvas. No grain under the stones. No flour on the rock by morning, except what the Gallery had in store.

They came down the cliff path by feel. Halfway down the boy heard wings over his head, going out to sea, and the master stopped to listen, and smiled.

"Council pigeon," he said. "That's the Council's pigeon gone for the Crown."

Three works done: the boilers, the lamps, the sails. The island crippled three ways, and the Council crying to the King across the water.

Nothing moved on the rock all night. Not a sail.

The Morning Ferry came in on the twenty-third with the Grand Inspector-General aboard, come to put the island back in order.

And the news.

The news came up the Wharf before he did. The dockhands had it off the deckhands before the gangplank was down, and it went up through the Salt-Flats and the fish lanes faster than any coach. The boy heard it at the Wharf rail in pieces, from five mouths:

passages.heading: They put the governor's head—
passages.text:
That one was a sailor's boast, and nobody finished it.

The Inspector came off last, grey, with a hand on the rail. He had been sick on the crossing and he did not hide it. He wiped his mouth with a handkerchief and folded it away. Nobody had come down to meet him but the Iron-Wardens. The Gallery had sent a coach, and it went up the hill slower than the news.

By noon the Commons were in Gallows Square.

There was no judgment that day. They came anyway, and stood: red crust, dish-pit grey, fish scale, in the space before the south doors where the gallery's servants used to stand holding the coats. Nobody told them to go.

Someone had chalked a red line across the Square's stones, from the Hall doors to the gallows step. Nobody scrubbed it out.

That afternoon the master sent him to the Counting-House with the plans of the boiler-house. The Crown's man had asked for them.

The boy had expected a wig, a sword and the Gallery's own face. What he found was a tired man at the Ledger-Clerk's long table with his coat off. On the table among the ledgers stood a little set of brass scales of his own, the kind the Inspecteur Sanitaire carried in the old days to weigh a loaf against its stamp.

He took the plans. He did not look at them.

"The stoker," he said to the Clerk. "The man in the boiler-house. What was his name?"

The Clerk did not know. Someone behind him said it.

passages.heading: Pol.
passages.text:
The Inspector wrote it in his file. The boy watched the pen. A dead man's name, first, before the damage, before any rank, written down by a man who did not have to.

"And the boy. The candle." He turned a page. "Bring me the verdict. I'll review it."

"He's burned, monsieur," the Clerk said.

passages.heading: Then I'll review it.
passages.text:
The boy went out into the lane with his hands empty. The master was waiting by the wall. The boy looked at him and made a sign with his hands, the one for *good*, the one for *kind*. The Crown's man is kind.

The master watched his hands. Then he said, without any heat, the way he said *lamp lower*:

passages.heading: The Crown's man dies in the fog tonight.
passages.text:
The boy's hands stopped.

The one man on the rock who was reviewing the Gallery's sin. The one man who had asked Pol's name.

He had one place left to stand, and it was as narrow as a step. The master had built the lock on the boiler-house. The master had built the Hall's flue, and been called Rassis for it, and had borne it. The master could see what the boy couldn't: the whole drawing, every course of brick. The master knew better.

It was not much to stand on. He stood on it.

The fog came in after the second bell.

It came off the water and put the harbour lamps out, nearest first. The lighthouse beam went to a smear, then to nothing, and the Witching Hour shut over the Wharf like a lid.

The master put him at the head of the Wharf steps with a lantern.

"The Gallery's giving the Crown's man his supper," he said. "He'll come down this way to his lodging. When you hear him pass, put it out."

The boy held the lantern. The fog beaded on the glass. He heard the party a long way off: boots, the Iron-Wardens' staves on the cobbles, a laugh that stopped. The Inspector's cough. Then closer, a voice saying something about Rouen, about a letter, about whether the ferry took the post.

They passed within arm's length. He could not see them. He could see the lantern.

He put the lantern out with his own hand.

The master went past him down the steps into the fog, and the fog closed behind him.

The boy stood in the dark. He heard the sea. He heard the boots go on, and stop, and someone call a name that was not his. He heard nothing he could name.

No lamps. No voices. No ferry till morning. Nothing.

Then the master came up the steps. His sleeves were wet to the elbow and he was breathing like a man who had climbed. In his right hand he had a seal, heavy and gilt, with the Crown's arms on it: the kind that hangs on a chain and sets the King's will in wax.

Then the bell.

The Iron-Wardens' alarm, three and three and three, and lanterns coming down the hill. They found the Inspector at the foot of the Wharf steps, on his back, with the tide over his shoes. His coat was buttoned. His little brass scales were still in its pocket, with the letter to his wife, folded, its last line unfinished.

The boy saw that much. Everyone did. They laid him on the stones under a lantern and left him there while they argued.

The Inquisitor came down with his powder. On the bottom step, where the fog had wetted the flour-dust from somebody's boots, he lifted a print: a builder's boot, square-toed, hobnailed at the heel.

The High Chancellor's word came down the hill at a run. An emergency tribunal at dawn. Every cloche in the Hall to be lifted and every loaf cracked until the Crown's seal was found. Whoever's loaf held it was the one.

In the lane behind the fish sheds the master took the boy's apron in one hand, opened the pocket with the other, and put the seal in.

It was heavy. It dragged the apron down on one side.

"Any gilded platter," the master said. "They'll never burn one of their own."

The Hall was dark but for the Hearth.

The boy went in by the kitchen stair, the Commis way, up past the shaping bench, with the Crown's seal in his apron and Pol's whistle beside it. Nobody stopped him. Nobody stops an Apprenti. An Apprenti is furniture that watches.

The platters ran down the long room in their rows, cloche after cloche, each one faintly red on its Hearth side.

He went past the empty platter nearest the Hearth with the dusk loaf on it, which nobody touches.

Past the Vane platters, their silver gone gold at the rims from the heat, the feeding hand's loaf under the largest cloche of all.

Past the flour-white of the Guild, and the master's own platter among them, his loaf still stamped with the Rassis mark. Past the red crust. Past the Unregistered, the bare ones, at the far end by the door.

The Proof-Reader's scales stood dark in their alcove. With the gas-lines out, nobody had weighed a loaf since the lamps went.

*Any gilded platter*, the master had said.

He chose.

He went back up the row to Madame de Montaury's and lifted the cloche. It was heavier than he had thought, and cold inside. Her Wake Loaf sat there round and pale, the heel already scored where she liked it. He pressed the Crown's seal up into the crumb from underneath, deep, closed the crust over it with his thumb the way his mother closed a pie, and set the cloche down again without a sound.

Then he stood there and told himself what every child on the rock knows.

The Gallery never burns its own.

She would be shamed. She would pay a Guild Fine out of the snuffbox money and hate the Commons for it. The master would walk free. Nobody would burn. Nobody at all.

He took out the plumb-bob and let it hang.

It did not hang true. His hand was shaking.

The Great Proofing Bell struck six.

The Square was full before the third stroke, and not with the gallery's servants. The Commons stood there, red crust and fish scale all the way back to the chalk line and over it, where they had stood since the ferry came in, and the news stood with them.

The gallery came down anyway. More slowly. Closer together.

The cloches were lifted to music, as they always are. The loaves were cracked one by one, platter by platter, the Aboyeur calling each name as each crust broke. Flour-white. Red crust. Unregistered. The master's own loaf, with nothing in it but bread.

At the long table the stenographer had the docket open. The boy could see it from where he stood. The verdict against the master's name was already written, *Trial by Fire*, to save time.

Then the gilded row.

Madame de Montaury's heel broke open on gold.

The Aboyeur held it up: the Crown's seal, crumb on it, catching the Hearth.

The noise from the Square was not a cheer. It was lower than that.

The High Chancellor looked at the Square. Then he looked for a long moment at his own platter, gilded, in the same row. Then he read from a card he had not had time to write.

*Trial by Fire, in the Great Hearth. The Hearth is for every platter alike.*

By his order, before the ink was dry, the master's verdict in the docket was struck through.

So Madame de Montaury was sentenced to the Hearth, and the master's verdict was struck, and the Gallery gave one gilded platter to the fire to keep the rest.

She did not look at the Square. She took a small thing out of her sleeve, a tortoiseshell snuffbox, and opened it. The boy was near enough to see the pressed violet inside. She looked at it. She closed it.

passages.heading: May I keep it?
passages.text:
It was not permitted.

The same cloches. The same musicians. The same bell. The Aboyeur carried her loaf down toward the Hearth and called her name as it passed, the whole of it, three titles long. The Commons stood where the gallery had always stood, and the gallery stood at the back, by the chalk, where the Commons had.

The Hearth received the loaf, and then the one the loaf named.

Then the supper. It had been laid in the gallery for the gallery, as always. The High Chancellor looked at it, and looked at the Square, and ordered it carried down.

So the footmen carried it down the stair and set it on the long table in the Square, and the Commons ate the Gallery's supper with their hands, standing up.

The boy did not speak. He was an Apprenti.

He ate.

It was venison again.

passages.heading: Coda
passages.text:
On the twenty-fourth, at the afternoon bell, Maître Lescop was registered a Guild Citizen.

The Ledger-Clerk did it at the long table where the Inspector had sat. The Rassis mark was scraped off the master's platter and a flour-white seal set in its place, and the Council gave him a commission, under seal, to rebuild the Guild boilers to his own code. The Inspector's file went into a drawer.

Fanch was set to clean Madame de Montaury's platter before it was given out again.

He scraped the gold leaf off with a blade: the face of it, the rim, the old crest. It came away in curls. He kept at it until the silver showed through, plain, the same as anyone's.

Pol's whistle was in his apron, in the pocket where the seal had been. It did not drag the apron down. It weighed nothing at all.

The fog came in off the water again.

passages.heading: Coda
passages.text:
At dusk the Aboyeur set a loaf on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal.

Then the night began.

works.title: What the Wolves Were Blamed For
works.blurb: Walt the sawyer is saved from the wolves by Albert the smith's lantern on 30 November 1893 and swears to walk the planks beside him every dusk; on 12 December he bars his door, hears the scream and does not get up; at the den he counts what does not fit on his fingers (a full lantern turned down, a drag smear, Mallory's *knife*, a Prussian-blue Thread his scarf's colour), learns from the Lamplighter that someone in his look walked into the wood while he was behind his door, and swears at the Bell that it was wolves, keeping the Thread.

passages.heading: Six seconds
passages.text:
Thursday, the thirtieth of November. Twilight. In HollowMere twilight lasts a quarter of an hour, and then it is gone.

I was coming back from the mill's timber stack at the wood's edge with no light. A lantern costs scrip, and scrip is rent. I had counted the stack, forty-one lengths, on the hand that has five. I was thinking of nothing but the number.

Then the footsteps.

They were behind me on the planks. Boot on board, boot on board, on the tarred planks that give a little under a man. I stopped, and they stopped. I went on, and they came on.

I turned round. There was nobody on the planks.

Mere-rot does that. Everybody knows it does. You hear footsteps where nobody walks. I knew it, and I ran anyway, and I ran the wrong way: off the planks, into the pines, into the mud that takes your boot and keeps it.

passages.heading: Six seconds
passages.text:
I had been gored at the wood's edge in October, by a boar, in daylight. I walked to Mallory's step on it, counting my own drips. Boars wound, and I had thought that was the worst the wood did.

I lost the planks. I lost the edge post. I lost the town. I found the den.

I did not know it was the den until they stood up.

Their eyes came first, then the rest of them. Grey in the grey. Four. Five. I counted them, because I count.

They say in town that the wolves hunt the edge of the light and never cross it. There was no light, so the whole wood was edge.

I had my back to a pine. One of them came in low with its head down, as if it were ashamed of what it was about to do.

Then a light came up from the clamp side, swinging through the trees. A man with a sack on his shoulder held a lantern out in front of him at arm's length, the way you hold a lantern when you mean it.

passages.heading: Six seconds
passages.text:
They broke like water off a hot plate. Every one of them went back from the flame, back past where the light reached, into the dark.

Except one. It had my smell. It came round the rim of the light and ran at me, and I ran, and I counted.

One, on the thumb. Two. Three. Four. Five, and the good hand was a fist. The sixth went on the other hand, the hand with three, on the stub where a finger used to be.

On six it stopped. It was not tired. It stopped the way a dog stops when it is called in. It turned round and trotted home to the den with its tail down, and did not look back.

The man with the lantern came up beside me. I knew him by his hands. He was the smith from the railyard bench, the one who rings every spike against the anvil and throws back the ones that sound wrong. He laughed once, not unkindly. He put the lantern in my hand to carry and took the sack back up on his shoulder.

passages.heading: The planks
passages.text:
I owed him my life, and I had nothing else he could use.

So I gave him what a sawyer has: my back, and my evenings.

From the next dusk I met him at the edge post as the Lamplighter lit it. She would touch the wick, the glass would go gold, and she would be off toward the manor gate before we had taken the first plank. I carried the sack and he carried the lantern. Every dusk we walked the planks out to Mother Moll's clamp in the Fenwood and back. The Company coal came up short for his forge, and the clamp's charcoal ran hotter. He said so, and I didn't know enough to argue.

He told me about the spikes. That was his talk. Not the weather, not the rent: how many he had rung that day and how many he had thrown back. Three. None. Seven, on a Tuesday, and he was cross about the seven all the way to the clamp. Under his breath he hummed the note a good spike gives. I never caught it, but he could hum it on a dark plank with his mouth shut.

passages.heading: The planks
passages.text:
His lantern was always full, and he topped it up before we turned for home. A man who listens to iron does not trust the dark to tell him anything.

I said it on the second night, and on most nights after: if it ever came to the Bell, I would stand for him.

He said nobody would ever need to.

I said it anyway.

Around us the town went on dying in its order. The Undertaker's cart went up and down. Vera went on the Saturday. On Monday the eleventh the Undertaker stood his cart at Rose's door on Pump Row in the middle of the day, where the Row could see it. Her geranium was out on the sill. By the morning they said she had gone.

I walked the planks with him that Monday night with my scarf up over my mouth.

Eleven dusks. I ran out of fingers on the fourth of them, and started again.

passages.heading: The scream
passages.text:
Tuesday, the twelfth of December. I didn't go.

I will say why, plainly, and I will not dress it. I was afraid. There was the cart at Rose's door. There was the stone up at the churchyard, which carries a name every morning; I did not ask Agnes whose it was, because I did not want to have it. There were my two fingers, already gone to the Panic. And the dark came down at four.

I barred my door. I told myself that he had the lantern. He was the one with the lantern. It was me that needed him, not him me.

At Curfew, when the lanes go empty, one scream came out of the wood.

It was the long one. Everybody in HollowMere knows that sound. It is the sound the whole town goes to its door for and does not open it. After it, the wolves.

passages.heading: The scream
passages.text:
I lay on my back and counted it out. I did not get up.

No bell. No boots in the lane. No light in the window across. Nothing.

passages.heading: One. The lantern
passages.text:
I went at Station Rush, before the whistle and before anyone. I took my own lantern, bought on the first of the month with rent and never lit, because I had always walked inside his.

I went because of the scream. I had heard it and lain there.

He was at the den mouth.

I will say it once and plainly, because he would have. They had been at him.

The left side of his face was gone to the bone. His throat was open. His coat was open, and what was under the coat was opened too, and there were his ribs. His right hand was gone at the wrist: the hammer hand, the hand that rang the spikes. I looked for it and did not find it.

There was fur round him in the mud, grey, in tufts. Down the near pine were claw marks, fresh and pale under the bark. There were no footprints. Wolves leave none, and the mud round the den was all paw, and the drag of bellies.

passages.heading: One. The lantern
passages.text:
The sack lay beside him, still tied, and the charcoal inside it was dry.

His lantern lay in the mud a yard off. It was dark, and the glass was whole.

I said it to myself the way you would say it at the Bell: the lantern went out, and they took him, the way they nearly took me. A lantern goes out, and then the whole wood is edge.

I put my thumb on the first finger.

One.

passages.heading: Two. The wick
passages.text:
I picked the lantern up. It was heavy. It was full to the brim, because he always filled it before he turned for home.

The wick was turned down, all the way down into the brass, to nothing.

A lantern that goes out by itself is empty, or it is broken. This one was neither. A hand had put it out.

I had that one on a shelf before I set the lantern down. He turned it down himself, to pass the den quiet. Dark is quieter; they say it at the Lantern. The Gamekeeper says it too, going past the den at dusk to count them. A man might do it.

He wouldn't. I knew he wouldn't. I put it on the shelf anyway.

Two.

passages.heading: Three. The smear
passages.text:
I walked back from the den toward the planks, the way a wolf would never have brought anyone. A wolf doesn't bring you anywhere. It leaves you where you fall.

There was a smear in the mud as wide as a man's shoulders, with two grooves in it where the heels had gone, all the way from the end of the planks to the den mouth. Forty yards. I counted them.

Somebody had brought him.

He had not fallen at the den. He had fallen at the planks and been carried home: their home, where they would be.

My third shelf was the oldest thing the town says about them: mere-rot makes them bold. The fog gets into them the way it gets into us, and they do what they don't do. They drag a man. Why not?

It was thin. I could see through it.

I ran back over the planks to the square and rang the Bell. The town came out past me and down the planks at a run: half of Mill Row, the platform crew, and the Constable last of all, buttoning his coat. By the time he reached the den the smear was under all of them, boot on boot, worked back into mud.

passages.heading: Three. The smear
passages.text: Three. And nobody had a finger on it but me.

passages.heading: The town's entry
passages.text:
The Gamekeeper crouched by him a long while. He rubbed the fur between his fingers and laid his hand flat on the claw marks on the pine, as if he were measuring them.

"Wolves," he said. There was no question in it.

He was right about the teeth.

The Constable wrote it in his book, standing up. Somebody behind me said it the way you would say the fog was in: blame the wolves. Nobody laughed, because the wolves do it. Everybody knew of a box that had gone down the Line for the wolves.

The Undertaker came with the cart and his boy in the shafts. He unlocked the box under the seat and opened his book on the lid, and over his arm I saw the page. At the head of the last column a word had a line ruled through it: ~~Cause~~. There was nowhere in that book to put what I knew.

passages.heading: The town's entry
passages.text:
I said nothing about the wick and nothing about the smear. When the Gamekeeper said wolves, I said yes. It was easy, because it was half true.

In the Constable's book it said wolves, and you can't hang a wolf.

passages.heading: Four. The knife
passages.text:
Nobody lifts a body until the Doc has been. The Undertaker waited with his cap off.

Mallory came at noon and knelt in the mud longer than anyone kneels in mud. Then the Doc spoke to the Constable, low. I heard it because I was standing where I should not have been: one wound, under the ribs, made before. The wolves had come to a dead man.

By the time the cart was on the planks there was a paper on the notice board by the Bell, in Mallory's hand, under the word *Verified*:

passages.heading: Knife. Before Curfew. The teeth after.
passages.text:
The Constable's word came down, and so did my last shelf, because mere-rot doesn't carry a knife.

I stood at the board with my hands in my pockets and counted without moving my fingers.

Four. The fourth finger is the one that shakes.

passages.heading: Five. The thread
passages.text:
Late in the afternoon, before her round, I went back out with my lantern lit and held up high in the last of the daylight. A knife means a man, and a man walks on planks.

On the third plank from the end, where the smear had begun, a nail head stood proud of the wood. Something was caught on it: a Thread of wool, a few inches long, Prussian blue.

The Company Store had that blue in October, two scarves of it. I bought one. I had not been wearing it that morning; I left it on its peg when I ran out at Station Rush.

I went home at a run and took it off the peg. It was whole. I turned it end to end twice and found no pull.

Then I put the Thread in my pocket, and not on the board. That was the first thing I hid.

passages.heading: Five. The thread
passages.text:
"There's more than one blue in the world," I said, to the peg.

Five. The good hand was full.

passages.heading: The edge post
passages.text:
At dusk the Lamplighter was at the pump with her ladder, starting her round. She stopped beside me and spoke low, so the pump would not hear.

"I lit the post last night, and you went by me."

I said nothing.

"Your scarf. Your walk. Into the wood, a bit after him. I thought it was the two of you, the same as always."

Last night I had been behind my barred door, on my back, counting a scream.

So it was not just more than one blue. It was my blue, my walk, near enough my height, past her post at dusk on the one night I wasn't there. Somebody had worn me into the wood, and she had seen it. Or something had. The threes walk the lanes unlit now and say they see well enough together. The fog makes footsteps where nobody walks; it might make a man where nobody walks. I didn't know, and she didn't ask me which.

passages.heading: The edge post
passages.text:
I counted what the town would have if the Thread went up on the board: my scarf, her word, Mallory's hour. The gallows is at the Bell.

She lit the post and went on. She did not look back to see whether I followed.

passages.heading: Six. The Bell
passages.text:
They met at the Bell after her round, the whole square in the cold, with the four lanterns lit and the fourth one last.

The Detective kept time at the railyard before the Constable made him what he is. He knew the smith's anvil by its sound; he told me once he could have set the yard clock by it. He stood the Constable's book open beside Mallory's paper on the board, *wolves* beside *knife*, and asked it plainly.

passages.heading: Who walked the planks with him at dusk?
passages.text:
Everybody knew. Eleven dusks, at the edge post, where the Lamplighter lights it.

I had said I would stand for him at the Bell, and I stood.

"Albert," I said. It was the first time I had said his name out loud in the open air, and I said it to the whole square.

"I walked with him," I said. "Not last night. Last night he went alone, and I heard it. It was the wolves."

The square was quiet.

"A wolf gives you six seconds," I said. "Then it goes home. I've been run. I counted. Last night they didn't go home."

I said it well. I believed it while I was saying it. The Thread was in my pocket, against the hand with three.

The Lamplighter looked at me across the square and said nothing.

Mallory's paper stayed on the board. Nobody took it down, and nobody read it again.

passages.heading: Who walked the planks with him at dusk?
passages.text:
The vote went the way the town had wanted it to go before it started: wolves. The town has spoken.

No suspect. No Tribunal. No rope. No blue.

passages.heading: Station Rush
passages.text:
In the morning I did not go to the Company Store to ask who had bought the other blue. I knew the Clerk would have it in a book. I didn't go.

I fed my scarf to the stove. Wool stinks when it burns, and it burns slowly. I kept the Thread.

The morning train came in with a private car behind it and dogs, and down on the boards there was a bigger death than ours. The crowd on the platform turned all at once, like a field in a wind, and the word went round the square. By noon nobody in HollowMere was asking about the smith.

At the pump a child, one of the Row's, small, with a pail, looked up at me.

passages.heading: What took the smith?
passages.text:
"Wolves," I said, before she had finished asking.

I had it ready. I will have it ready for the next one.

I counted it out for her on my fingers, the way he did for me: five on the one hand, and the sixth on the stub.

"They give you six," I said.

works.title: The Tin Gallery
works.blurb: Saturday 16 December 1893, the fourth night of fog: Norman the tinner follows his partner Reg under the hill with the only lit lantern, past bats and rats running out of the gallery and a drag smear going down into the risen water; he finds Reg carried and laid down below the VANE TIN CO crate, bitten twice, and the boards over the lower drift lifted and stacked by a hand that carried no light; the Beast comes up out of the water toward his lantern, shown plainly and never named, and bites him once; he leaves the lantern burning beside Reg, climbs out in the dark, and tells the square Reg was lost in the workings.

passages.text:
Saturday, 16 December 1893. The fourth night the fog did not lift.

The cough was on the Row. You could hear it from the mouth of the Gallery, door after door, as if one chest were going down the street and stopping at each house. The wolves had come down to the fence at noon. Noon. Mere-rot makes them bold, and everybody knew it, and everybody had stopped saying it.

Norman sat on the timber at the Gallery mouth with Reg.

They were the shut mine's two hands. The Company had issued each of them a lantern, a watch, chalk and rope, so they would have something to hold now that there was nothing to dig. Norman held his watch. He looked at it the way he always did, against nothing. There was nowhere either of them had to be.

Reg cracked his knuckles. Little finger first, then up the hand: the adit, the first level, the second, the long drift, the wet level, the bottom. Top to bottom. The old levels, in order. He did it the way other men whistle.

"I heard it again," Reg said.

Norman did not ask what.

"Two," Reg said. "Under the hill. Last night and tonight, about the curfew. Two, and then nothing." He laid his hand flat on the timber and struck it twice with the heel of the other. The way you strike a plug. The way the plug had been struck.

"Stone settles," Norman said.

passages.heading: Two.
passages.text:
"Water works on stone. It's had a lake on it."

Reg looked into the mouth. Cold air came out of it, with the smell it had always had: stone that has had water on the far side of it for a long time.

Norman took his hat off and put it on his knee.

"Stone settles," Norman said.

Reg didn't crack the last knuckle.

The Curfew bell. Dusk, or what the fog let pass for it.

Reg's lantern was on its nail in the tinners' shed, cold. His coat was gone. His pipe was gone. Reg was not there.

Norman stood in the door of the shed a long time.

Reg knew the Gallery in the dark. He had always said so. He knew it by his knuckles, level by level, and he would have gone down without a light because a light was oil and oil was scrip and Reg had never had scrip to spare. He had heard two knocks under the hill and he had gone down to answer them.

On the path between the shed and the mouth the wolves were already out. Norman could see their eyes at the bottom of the fog, low, patient, moving when he moved.

A pair goes down together. A pair comes up together.

He had gone down with Jory Kitto. He had come up. Jory had not.

He chalked two strokes on the mouth timber, the old way, so anyone passing would know: two down. Then he lit his lantern and turned it up, and walked into the light it made. The wolves held at the edge of it, the way they hold, and did not cross.

The only lit lantern under the hill was his.

Past the mouth the Gallery was dark and wet. Water on the rail bed. Water off the roof.

On the path the light had kept everything off him. He had walked inside it like a man inside a house.

Then the bats.

They came off the roof in one sheet. Not away. To it. At the glass, at his face, at the hand that held the lantern. Wings like wet leather, little teeth. One opened the back of his hand. One took a nick out of his ear. He swung the lantern and they came back to it.

Then the rats.

Up the rail bed toward him, out of the dark below, in a long grey run. He braced for them and they did not stop for him. They did not stop for the light. They went over his boots and round his ankles and on up past him, out of the mouth, out into the fog, toward the wolves.

Rats do not run toward wolves.

He stood with blood on the back of his hand, dripping off his knuckles, and watched the last of them go.

They were not running from him.

The pump beam stood where it had stood since the plug, rusted at its pivot, over the place where the water began.

On Sunday he had come down this far, as he did some Sundays, and looked. On Sunday the water had stood to the ankle, where it always stood. There was a mark on the timber leg of the beam where the wet stopped.

Tonight the water stood over the mark. A hand over it.

So that was it.

The mere keeps a tide with no sea. Everybody in HollowMere knew that. The water had come back once before, all of it, a whole lake into the hill in one night. It was coming back again, a little, the way the mere came and went. Rats run from water. Any tinner knows that. Rats leave a working before the water does.

The water was coming back. The rats ran from water.

He said it twice.

"Reg," he said, once, down the Gallery.

The Gallery took it.

The water was coming back. That was all.

Below the pump beam the rail ran on into the water. On the stone beside it, the smear.

It was wide. Wide as a man's shoulders. It came up out of the water onto the rail bed, and went along the bed a little way, and turned, and went back down into the water again.

Water comes in. Water goes out. It does not climb out of itself, drag across the stone, and go home.

There was something in the smear that was not water. Darker. Thicker. Where it ran down into the edge of the water it lay on top and would not mix, the way lamp oil lies on a puddle, but it was not oil. He put his lantern near it. It shone. It smelled of tin.

In the middle of the smear lay Reg's pipe.

Clay, short-stemmed, the bowl cold. Reg never lit it below ground. He said a pipe underground was a light, and the old hands said you don't carry more light than you need. He carried it anyway. He bit on the stem when he was frightened, and the stem was bitten through.

Norman picked it up.

Reg never dropped that pipe.

Reg had slipped.

That was all. Reg had come down in the dark, the fool, by his knuckles, and the wet had taken his feet, and he had gone down hard and hurt himself. And then he had crawled. Down. Toward the knocking. Because Reg was a fool for a knock, and two knocks was a man asking, and Reg would not leave a man asking.

Hurt. Crawling. Dragging himself. That was the smear.

Norman went down after it.

Past the ore cart, lying on its side where it had lain since the plug. Past the crate on its two planks above the water, VANE TIN CO on the lid, the lid pried up and left, the way the whole town knew it was left. The smear went past the crate and down.

He held the lantern up. All the way up, the wick turned high, the way Jory had kept his. Jory had paid for his own oil so he would never be in the dark down here. Norman had laughed at him for it, once.

passages.heading: Reg," he said. "Reg. It's me. Reg.
passages.text:
He looked at his watch. It said a time. It meant nothing down here.

He held the lantern up, the way Jory did, so Reg would see.

Reg was below the crate, on a dry shelf of stone above the water.

He was on his back. His arms were at his sides. He had not crawled there. A crawling man ends on his face, reaching. Reg had been put down, the way you put down something you have carried and mean to come back to.

"Reg," Norman said, because he was still saying it.

Two bites.

One had taken the shoulder and the side of the neck, all of it, down to where the collarbone should have been and was not. One had opened him low on the left side, and what had been inside was partly beside him and partly not anywhere. The dark stuff that would not mix was on him, on his shirt and in his hair. Round him the grit was scored with drag marks, long, in pairs, going away toward the water and coming back.

His right hand was whole.

It lay by his hip, palm down, knuckles up. Broad, scarred, the little finger bent from an old fall. Norman would have known that hand anywhere. He had watched it crack its way top to bottom every day since the mine shut.

He knelt. He did not touch it. He did not crack his own knuckles, though his hand wanted to.

Reg had made it to the bottom of his knuckles.

"Wolves," Norman said.

He said it to the dark, aloud, so it would be said.

There was no fur on Reg. Not a hair. There were no claw marks on the stone, none on Reg, nothing raked. A wolf does not come into a cave. A wolf does not come into the light of a lit lantern; it holds at the edge, and it does not cross. Norman had walked through them an hour ago with this lantern and watched them hold.

Two bites. A wolf does not take a shoulder in one.

The town would say wolves. The town always said wolves. Wolves were what the town had.

"Wolves," he said again, so he would have said it twice.

The word went down the Gallery and did not come back.

Below the shelf where Reg lay, the lower drift went under.

The level Jory had been working. The level of the plug. Since the night the lake went into the hill, there had been boards laid over the mouth of that drift, heavy, spiked down, so no one would walk into it in the dark and go where Jory went.

The boards were up.

They were not broken. They were not floated off. They lay stacked beside the drift, dry, on the dry stone, one on another, square, the edges true. The way you stack timber you mean to put back.

Wolves do not stack boards. Water does not.

In the grit by the stack there were prints. One pair. Going in to the edge of the drift, and coming back out. Dry boots over the wet. And nowhere over them, on the low roof, any black from a lamp, and nowhere on the stone a drop of oil. Whoever had stood here had come down without a light, and taken up the boards, and stood at the edge of the open drift, and gone back up.

Someone had opened the way down.

Norman did not try to think who. He found he could not get his mind to go up the Gallery after them. It stayed where it was, at the open drift, at his feet.

Someone had come down here in the dark, and gone home.

Two knocks.

From the drift. Close. Under his feet, nearly.

Then the water in the open drift rose. No splash. It rose the way water rises in a jug, smooth, and something came up out of it, and the water ran off it, and it came on up onto the stone.

Big. The size of the ore cart. Bigger.

Long and low. The grey of wet slate, and shining like the stuff in the smear.

A mouth at the front. Nothing round the mouth he would call a face.

It did not look at him. It did not look at Reg. It came toward the lantern.

He did not decide anything. His arm put the lantern behind him, and the thing came round for it, and he was in the way.

The first hit took his left forearm. He heard it before he felt it. Then he saw it: the sleeve gone, the meat of the arm gone with it to the bone in one long bite, the white of the bone in the lamplight, the lamp swinging on its handle in his other hand. He was on his knees. He did not remember going down.

It drew back.

Two strikes on a plug, and the plug goes. Every tinner knows the second one. He knew it now.

It wanted the light.

One more.

He could see it in the edge of the light, waiting at the lantern's reach as the wolves had waited at the edge of it outside. Not looking at him. Looking at the light.

If he put it out, he would be in the dark with it. If he kept it, it would come for the light and he was holding the light.

The crate stood above him on its two planks, a few yards up the bed from where Reg lay. VANE TIN CO.

He got up. He did not know how. He climbed the shelf on his knees and one hand, holding the lantern by the bail, and he set it on the lid of the crate and turned the wick all the way up. As high as Jory would have. Higher. The light stood up off the crate, bright, and ran down the stone and lay on Reg's whole hand.

Then he backed out of it. Into the dark.

He went up the Gallery the way Reg went down it. By the levels. The bottom, the wet level, the long drift, the second, the first, the adit. Bottom to top. He counted them on the knuckles of the hand that still worked, one by one, and the dark did not get any lighter.

Behind him the light stayed lit.

He heard it reach the light. He heard it reach Reg.

He did not turn.

A pair goes down together.

He came up.

The mouth, with no light in it. The fog outside. Grey on black.

He did not go out. The wolves were at the edge of the path, and he had no edge to give them now; the lantern going out is the town's dread, and his was on a crate below the hill. He sat inside the mouth on the timber, out of their reach and out of the reach of the light he could no longer see, and bled. It went from his arm down his fingers in drips onto the stone. He listened to it. He listened below it, for anything coming up.

Nothing came up.

He held his hat on his knee with his good hand. He looked at his watch, against nothing, and could not see it.

The Station Rush. The whistle, far off, out of the pines. The fog going thin and grey.

Someone was standing at the mouth.

No lantern. Just standing, in the thin fog, at the place where the two chalk strokes were. Looking in at him.

Norman looked back.

Neither of them said anything.

Then the someone turned, and walked back down the path toward the town, and the fog took them.

They asked him on the square. Where was Reg.

Reg went down alone, he said. In the dark. Lost in the workings.

He said nothing about the boards. He said nothing about the prints, or the smear, or the thing that came up out of the water, or the lantern burning on the crate below the hill, if it was burning still. They were the Company's words, *lost in the workings*. The Company had written them once already, about Jory. Now he gave them to Reg.

The town nodded. The town said wolves, after, among itself. He let it.

"Stone settles," he said.
He came up.

works.title: Dead Weight
works.pov: first person (an unnamed carrier, the Minion)
works.blurb: from 18 to 29 December 1893 an unnamed carrier, paid by the crate and docked for a scuff, keeps the Vicar's body from being found at the robes' word: the chapel loft, the coach road that the storm has taken, a whiskey case and a barrel in the Lantern's back room, a pine thicket where a pink candle stub holds off the wolves and the Undertaker says "Not yet", and a pocket of the cave where he winds the dead man's watch each dawn; on 29 December he carries a second roll of lead off the first train through while a man with the Vicar's face sets a watch at the Telegraph Room counter.

passages.heading: Dead Weight
passages.text:
A dragged crate is a docked crate.

That is the first thing you learn carrying off the morning train in HollowMere, and the only thing anybody bothers to tell you. The Company pays by the crate. The Company docks by the scuff. A sack that leaves a furrow on the boards is a sack that cost you, so you take it up on the shoulder, the whole weight of it, and you walk. You never drag. Not a crate, not a sack, not your own heel.

I know every door in this town by its count from the platform. Crumb's back step is two hundred and twelve. The Lantern's yard door, a hundred and eighty. The Bell is three hundred and some from the Lantern, depending on the mud. I had never needed to count to the Bell.

---

passages.heading: 1. Monday, 18 December
passages.text:
In his first week a crate of tonics went over on the platform steps, mine, and the Vicar took the other end of it before I could swear. Nobody of rank in this town has ever taken the other end of anything. He carried it up to the Morgue door with me, two hundred and forty steps, and halfway he said my name. I don't know where he got it. Nobody up here uses it.

After that I walked with the threes. I was entered L. I took my tea black at the Lantern because he did.

Sunday the stone said he was dead. Monday at dusk the robes preached.

I went in after. The box was warm from the one before me. Through the grille the voice was his voice, the cadence, the open hands, and it said my name. The second time anybody in HollowMere had said it. The same voice. I knelt there and could not think of one thing I had done.

passages.heading: 1. Monday, 18 December
passages.text:
I went in with the parish. I came out with nothing in me at all, except one thing, set down the way you set a crate on a shelf.

*There's a weight in the loft. Keep it off the floor.*

The hands came through the grille to bless me. I have carried for those hands. I could not have told you when.

The loft ladder is behind the vestry. Twenty-one rungs. I climbed them with no lamp.

He was on the boards under the eaves with his hands in his coat. As if he were cold, or waiting for somebody. A watch was going in his waistcoat, loud in that little room. Not the one on the chain he came up with in October. An older one. Brass gone brown.

I sat down beside him because my legs did.

I had heard the end of Sunday's sermon, or the pump tells me I did. The strength of ten in the next life. I worked it out sitting there, the way you work out a load: what's heavy, what isn't, where it goes. A man who goes on to ten lives steps out of the one. What's left on the boards is what he stepped out of. A shell. And you keep a shell for the one who left it, the way you'd hold a man's coat while he's in the river.

passages.heading: 1. Monday, 18 December
passages.text:
So I would keep it. Not in the loft, where the parish might trip on it. Off the Grant. Down the coach road before light, into the ground somewhere past the last Company post, where nobody's rent was owed.

I got my shoulder under him.

He was lighter than a sack of flour, and he wouldn't split, and I lifted him as if he might.

---

passages.heading: 2. Tuesday, 19 December, before light
passages.text:
Down the slope, past the old plots, onto the road. I counted. Three hundred. Four hundred. Past the last count I know, out where I keep no counts because nothing of mine is that far.

His heels did not touch. I made sure.

At something over a mile the road wasn't there.

Wind. Water where the ruts should be. The dark, and the noise of the dark moving. The storm had come over the ridge in the night and taken the coach road in its mouth. I stood at the edge of it with a dead man on my shoulder and the water going past my boots, carrying off bits of the road I'd walked on.

Nothing off the Grant now but the Train.

The Train counts the crate, not the contents. It's on the board on the platform, Rule 2; I read it every morning. But a crate goes through the Clerk's book, and a box goes through the Undertaker's, and I had neither.

passages.heading: 2. Tuesday, 19 December, before light
passages.text:
So I carried him back. Up the slope, past the plots, in by the vestry door, up the twenty-one rungs. Laid him under the eaves where he'd been. Found the chapel's spare sacking, folded on a pew-end against the floods, and drew it over him to the chin. Not the face. I couldn't do the face.

Then I went down to the platform for the Station Rush, as on any morning, because a man who isn't at his crates gets asked why. The loft would have to hold. Lofts do. Nobody climbs a ladder in a chapel.

I had carried a dead man two miles for nothing, and I was not tired.

---

passages.heading: 3. Tuesday, Station Rush
passages.text:
The parish bag comes off the train with the post. It's mine to carry to the Telegraph Room counter, a hundred and four steps, and it was the Vicar's to come and take.

The robes came. With the voice, thanking the Clerk. They stood where he always stood, at the rail, and took the bag.

And didn't ask the time.

Every morning since October he had asked the Clerk the time by the telegraph clock, and set his watch to it, and said thank you as if he'd been given something. The whole platform knew it. You could set the platform by it.

The Clerk stood with his hand on the clock-case. Waiting. I stood in the door with the crate strap in my fist. Waiting.

The robes went out with the bag.

Up in the loft, under the sacking, an old brown watch was going.

I turned that over, standing there, the way you turn a crate to find the stencil. A man of ten lives has no use for one hour. That's all it was. Why would he ask. He was past asking.

passages.heading: 3. Tuesday, Station Rush
passages.text:
I put it on the shelf with the shell, and carried the next crate.

The clock on the wall kept going. So did the one in the loft.

---

passages.heading: 4. Tuesday, dusk, and after Curfew
passages.text:
I sat at the back for the dusk sermon. I always sat at the back. The threes don't sit together inside.

It was a good sermon. Debts, and the weight of them. I didn't hear much of it.

Halfway, up in the roof, a sound. Bone on bone. Once. A small dry knock like chimes in a wind, and no wind, and nothing hung up there to make it. I hadn't hung anything. In the box I'd been told I would hear when. I hadn't known what that meant.

Three pews in front of me the Detective lifted his head off his case file and looked up at the loft door.

He did not get up. He sat through the hymn with the file shut on his knee and his eyes on that door. The robes led the hymn. I knew every word of it. I did not open my mouth.

passages.heading: 4. Tuesday, dusk, and after Curfew
passages.text:
The Detective had looked up. He would go up. Not tonight, with the parish all round him, but by light.

After Curfew I came back with a whiskey case, empty, one I'd carried up to the Lantern full that morning. It is the right length if a man's knees are bent. I did not think about that while I did it. I thought about the stencil, which side up.

Down the twenty-one rungs. Across the square in the dark, the case on my shoulder, eighty steps from the chapel to the Lantern yard, every one of them lifted clean. In by the yard door. The back room: the oil barrel on its chock with the funnel hung on its string, the whiskey cases stacked, two empty barrels against the wall waiting for the dray. I put him in the far one and set the lid on.

In the morning the pump had it. The Detective went up the loft ladder at first light with a lamp. He found the place, and nothing in it but the place.

passages.heading: 4. Tuesday, dusk, and after Curfew
passages.text:
No smear on the rungs. No furrow in the mud. Nothing follows a carry. A drag is what talks.

The mud had nothing to say about me.

---

passages.heading: 5. Wednesday, 20 December, Midday
passages.text:
The escort drink at the Lantern now. They have since the Baron, standing, in their long coats, waiting to be told something by somebody.

They brought the dogs in.

One of the dogs left them. It walked across the boards between the tables, past the bar, and lay down across the back-room door. Put its nose to the gap at the bottom. Breathed.

They whistled. It didn't come.

It didn't bark. Those dogs bark at a man who runs, or a man who's armed. I was neither. I was at the end of the bar with tea, black. It whined, a thin sound through its nose, at the gap.

One of the escort took it by the collar, and it lay flat and let itself be pulled six inches, and crawled back.

Bar looked at the dog. Then at me. He did not reach under the counter. He wiped a glass that was already dry.

passages.heading: 5. Wednesday, 20 December, Midday
passages.text:
Nobody in the Lantern would look at the back-room door except the dog.

---

passages.heading: 6. Wednesday, dusk
passages.text:
I was still there at dusk. Leaving would have been a thing a man does.

Bar set a Liquid Courage down in front of me. I hadn't asked. I hadn't the scrip for it.

"Paid," he said.

He didn't say by whom. The Vicar used to stand them for men who couldn't run to one, and sit with each of them a while. That was his line in Mrs Grieves's book, every time. Paid.

I drank it.

They say at the Lantern it keeps a man proof against any prayer for about two minutes. I can tell you what it is like inside the two minutes. It's like setting down a load you didn't know you were carrying, and standing up straight, and hearing your back go.

The man in the barrel was dead because somebody had killed him.

Not stepped out. Not risen. Killed, on Sunday, at dusk, and carried up a ladder by somebody before ever I went near it.

passages.heading: 6. Wednesday, dusk
passages.text:
And the robes were not him. A risen man has no use for the hour, I'd told myself. He'd have asked. Risen or dead or any way you like, he'd have asked. It was the one thing he could not have stopped himself doing.
