I was out the door before the glass was down.

Two minutes is about two hundred of my steps. The Bell is three hundred and some from the Lantern. I counted. I always count. Fifty. Ninety. A hundred and forty, past the pump trough, the square opening out ahead, the Bell up on its frame against the last of the light. A hundred and eighty.

At the pump the count ran out.

Not the steps. The other thing. The load came back down on me the way a sack comes down when the man on the other end lets go. I stood on the stones by the pump with my hand out at nothing, reaching, at the height a bell rope would be if the Bell were twenty yards nearer.

passages.heading: 6. Wednesday, dusk
passages.text:
I knew. That stayed. The drink went, and the knowing didn't go with it.

I walked back.

I had known for two minutes. Knowing didn't need the drink, it turned out. Only the walking did.

---

passages.heading: 7. Wednesday, night
passages.text:
The dog was still across the back-room door when they closed. They had to carry it out in the end, two of them, and it didn't fight, only looked back over the escort's arm all the way to the street.

It would be there tomorrow. And the Bell was behind me. I had walked back from it. You can't carry a thing back to a place you've already walked away from.

So it was the yard door again. No lamp. A lamp is a man saying *here I am* to every window in the Row. I got the barrel up on the shoulder, which is a bad carry, and the Vicar in it, which made it a worse one, and I went out the back of town.

Past Crumb's. Past where the lane goes to planks. The Lamplighter had been round: her post at the Gallows Wood edge was lit, the last lantern on the Grant. I went by it on the dark side, over the planks, tarred and warped, and into the pines.

passages.heading: 7. Wednesday, night
passages.text:
A thicket, twenty yards in. I tipped the barrel and took him out as gently as I have ever taken anything out of anything, and laid him under the low branches with the needles under his head.

This was the first carry I had made knowing what it was. I noticed I'd made it just as well.

Past the last lamp there's no count. So I stopped counting.

---

passages.heading: 8. The same night
passages.text:
I heard them before anything. Not a howl. Feet, a lot of them, soft, and breath.

A wolf doesn't run at the dead. It doesn't run at what's hidden. Every child on the Row can tell you. It runs at a living man it can see.

A living man, unlit, alone in its wood, kneeling over something.

I found it in his coat pocket while I was looking for nothing: a stub of candle. Pink. The one for the third Sunday. He said once, at the service, that it was the one for joy and he had always thought it the wrong colour for it. He must have pocketed the end of it. I had the Lantern's matches in my vest, as I always do, for the back-room lamp.

It took three. My hands.

Then it was lit, small and pink and the wrong colour, and I held it out at the length of my arm.

passages.heading: 8. The same night
passages.text:
They came their six seconds. You can count them. Everybody does. Eyes, low down, the shine. Then they stopped, all of them, wherever they were, like men who hear their names, and went back into the dark. Home, the Row says. As if called.

I stood there with it burning.

A light at the Gallows Wood edge, past the last post, where no lamp is meant to be. The whole town can see that edge from its windows.

It was the wrong colour for it, he said. It was what I had.

---

## 9. The same night, and Thursday, 21 December, Station Rush

The chimes went in the pines. Bone. Once. Nothing hung.

Then a lantern on the planks. Low, swinging on its pole. A cart lantern. The boy at the shafts, and the Undertaker walking beside him with his hat down.

I didn't run. I didn't put the candle out. I don't know why. I think I wanted somebody to see it, and then I think that's a lie.

passages.heading: 8. The same night
passages.text:
He stopped at the edge of the thicket. He looked at me. He looked at the candle. Then he looked down under the branches at the length of the man there, a long while, the way he must look at every one of them before the box. The boy kept his eyes on the shafts.

The Undertaker has seen the body, I thought. It's done.

"Not yet," he said.

It's the word his book gives the living. Everybody on the Grant knows it; he carries the book to the Midday Rent on Saturdays. He turned the cart on the planks, the boy hauling, and went back toward the lamps.

He rang nothing. Nobody came.

In the morning, the incoming manifest was on the platform board, as on any morning. Flour, tonics, whiskey. And in a hand I knew, a requisition. Lead, sheet. Officer of the Dead.

I'd carried his first one. On the ninth, off that same train, a roll he unrolled the end of right there on the boards and stood looking at. Longer than any of his forty, the crew said. He signed for it, and I took it up on my shoulder to his shed and leaned it on the back wall where he'd cleared the trestles. Heavy as a man. Heavier.

passages.heading: 8. The same night
passages.text:
He had one. He'd asked for more.

I didn't try to know why. I've carried coffins and I know nothing about what goes into their walls. What I knew was this: when the lead came, the Undertaker would take him. Sealed. And whatever I was keeping him for would be finished, and nobody would need a man with a shoulder. I would wait on the lead.

I'd carried his lining. I would carry the rest of it.

---

passages.heading: 10. Thursday, the pump
passages.text:
The pump says things the way it says the weather. Nobody's mouth. Just said.

That morning it said where the Vicar's body had been.

The chapel loft. A barrel in a saloon back room. A pine thicket at the Gallows Wood edge.

The cave.

I had my bucket under the spout. The water ran over the lip and onto my boots.

Nobody saw the loft. Nobody saw the barrel. The Undertaker saw the thicket and nobody else did, and the Undertaker doesn't come to the pump. Three true. Nothing follows a carry, I'd said, and the pump had followed every one.

And the fourth. I hadn't been to the cave. I hadn't thought of the cave.

"Who says?" I said.

Nobody said. It was only said. A woman from Mill Row looked at me as if I'd asked who says it's raining.

On the Constable's corner of the board in the square the notices were up, the four of them, reissued Saturday. Before Sunday. Before any of it. I'd walked past them every day. I read one now.

passages.heading: 10. Thursday, the pump
passages.text:
> **The Minion.** Keeps a body from being found.

Before Sunday. Before Monday's box. Somebody had written the work down and pinned it up, and then come and found the man for it.

The town was a carry ahead of me.

---

passages.heading: 11. Thursday, night
passages.text:
I went to the box first. I hadn't been back since Monday. I knelt and said, the cave?

"Yes," the voice said.

Nothing else. I waited for something else. I could hear breathing on the other side of the grille, slow, the way you breathe when you've been carrying.

So I went out past the post in the dark and got him up out of the thicket, and the wolves did not come, because I wasn't hiding him now, only taking him somewhere. Down through the pines to where the forest goes into the hill. In, a long way, with my free hand on the wall.

There's a passage in there that runs down toward the Gallery, the way the Entranced go. Off it, in the dark, a pocket. A room the size of a bunk, dry, with a lip of stone you have to step over. I laid him there.

passages.heading: 11. Thursday, night
passages.text:
The air is bad. It catches in your chest and you want to cough and you mustn't, because a cough goes on and on in the stone. And there are feet in it. Steps behind you, ahead of you, that stop when you stop. Mere-rot makes false footsteps. Everybody knows it. I knew it, and I stood with my back to the wall a long time anyway, till they stopped.

At dawn, if it was dawn, I couldn't see, I took the old brown watch out of his waistcoat by feel. It had stopped. I don't know when. Sometime in the barrel, or the pines. I wound it, and it went.

The first of the mornings.

Down here there was nobody. Not the dog, not the Detective, not the Undertaker with his not yet. Down here the keeping was mine alone, and the pump could say what it liked.

I wound it full. A man should have the hour, whether he wants it or not.

passages.heading: 12. Saturday, 23 December
passages.text:
Friday at dawn Agnes called a name up the Row, the way she calls them all. Somebody who paid at the Company Store in exact coppers, counted twice. I heard the name. I won't write it. It isn't mine to carry.

Saturday the last train in came in the morning, out of the weather. I unloaded it. Flour. Whiskey. Tonics, a crate. Post.

No lead.

I looked twice. I went through it a third time, every crate and every sack, the way you look for a thing you've already been told isn't there. The requisition went unfilled. Nobody entered it so. Nobody enters anything now.

At dusk the train stood at the platform with steam up to go out, the last one, and after it nothing till Friday the twenty-ninth, the storm willing. Everyone on the platform knew it. You could see it in how they held their bags.

I had my crate money in my boot. Enough for a one-way fare. I had counted it on Tuesday night, after the road. I had counted it every night since.

passages.heading: 12. Saturday, 23 December
passages.text:
Several were leaving. I carried their things aboard: a trunk with a broken strap, two carpet bags, a hatbox, a crate of somebody's whole kitchen, tin by tin. I am good at it. Nothing scuffed. One passenger had a heavy case and would not let me take it, would not even let it go up on the rack. I know the carry of a weight a man wants to look lighter than it is. I said nothing. I took the next bag.

The back car went past me at the rail when she pulled out. Car 3. The coffins ride in Car 3, and nobody opens them in transit, for any reason. It was empty of what I could have put in it.

I stood on the boards with the money in my boot.

The train went at dusk and did not wait. It never has.

---

passages.heading: 13. Monday, 25 December
passages.text:
Christmas. The Company doesn't keep it. Rent was due, as on any Monday.

I had taken to being in the pocket at Dusk as well as at dawn. Sitting by him. Not winding, only sitting. I had a lantern by then, a small one, turned so low it was hardly more than a coal, for the step over the lip.

That night they came down the passage.

The Entranced. No lanterns. No sound but their feet, and their feet in step, one behind another, going down toward the Gallery. Shapes at the edge of what light I had. Twenty, maybe. I knew some of them. I've carried for most of them. A woman from Pump Row who used to give me the heel of a loaf. A man off the crew. Not one of them turned a head toward the pocket.

I put my hand over the coal and waited, and they went past, and down.

passages.heading: 13. Monday, 25 December
passages.text:
When I took my hand away there was a candle at his feet.

It hadn't been there at dawn. A long one, white, a church candle, unlit, standing upright on the stone between his boots. I knew it. It had stood in its stick by the pulpit at St Brannock's since October, and he had lit it every evening before he spoke.

I hadn't set it there. I hadn't heard anybody step over the lip.

Someone had come into the pocket and stood at his feet in the dark, a yard from me, and set it down, and gone on with the others.

I was not keeping him. I was only one of the ones keeping him.

---

passages.heading: 14. Tuesday, 26 December
passages.text:
The chimes went in the passage, at what I had for Midday. Bone. Once.

Then light. A lantern, properly lit, coming down from the forest mouth. Boots. One man, careful, a case file under one arm and the lantern held out ahead of him at the end of the other.

Going past. Down toward the Gallery, where, the pump said after, black candles stood on the old tin crate like an altar. He had come for that. Not for me.

But he would pass the pocket going down, and pass it again coming up.

The candle at the Vicar's feet was white. White wax catches a lantern. I had watched it catch my own coal.

I lay down on it. On the stone between the lip and his boots, my body between the passage and him, my hand closed round the candle so not a thread of it showed. Face down. The air sat in my chest and wanted out of me as a cough, and I held it, and held it, until it wasn't air any more, only a stone I had swallowed.

passages.heading: 14. Tuesday, 26 December
passages.text:
The light came along the passage wall. Into the mouth of the pocket. Across the lip, the length of my arm from my head.

It went down.

I lay. I don't know how long. The feet in the stone came and went, false ones and maybe true ones. Then the real light again, coming up, slower, the way a man walks who has seen something he must tell somebody. Across the lip. Within reach.

It went up.

The dead man didn't need to hold his breath. I held it for the both of us.

---

passages.heading: 15. Friday, 29 December, Station Rush
passages.text:
Five days nothing had come. Not a train, not a wire, not a sack of flour. The pump got thin on it.

Friday the first train through came in out of the fog, as though it had been waiting at the edge of the weather to be let in.

The freight first. That's my work. Flour. Post. And down the length of the car, a roll of sheet lead, long, tied at three places with cord. A tag: *Officer of the Dead*. No sender.

I got it up on my shoulder. I know a man's weight. This was more.

Then the private car. Conductor Pruett in the door of it with his punch out and ready, and then not using it, his hand coming down slowly to his side.

A man stepped down into the fog.

He had the dead man's face.

Light stood on him. Not lamplight. The way low sun stands on still water, too level, too bright. The fog drew off it all round in a ring, a clean edge on the boards. People inside the ring went still. People outside it stepped in, some of them, and I watched their faces change.

passages.heading: 15. Friday, 29 December, Station Rush
passages.text:
I stood outside the ring by the length of the roll on my shoulder.

He had a crosier, black iron, plain, as tall as he was. He crossed the platform to the Telegraph Room with it, and the crowd went back from him, and he put one hand on the rail inside, and I heard him through the glass. He asked the Clerk the time.

Then he took out a watch. Opened it, set it to the clock on the wall, shut it, and thanked the Clerk as though he'd been given something.

The same watch, or its twin. From where I stood I couldn't tell you. I can't now.

I had wound the one in the cave at dawn. By feel, in the dark, the old brown one, full. It would be going now in his waistcoat, down there under the hill.

There were two watches in HollowMere, and I had wound one of them.

passages.heading: 16. Friday, Midday and dusk
passages.text:
I carried the lead to the Undertaker's shed. Lifted every step.

The first roll was where I'd leaned it on the ninth, against the back wall. I laid the second beside it. Two lengths. Nobody on his forty that long.

He came out of the back and signed the tag where I held it. *Officer of the Dead.* His hand was steady.

"Is it for him?" I said.

"Not yet," he said.

He didn't say for whom. He didn't look at me when he said it, or away from me. He looked at the lead.

At dusk the robes preached on the chapel step, as they had every evening, the open hands, the voice. And the man with the light was somewhere in the lanes. You could tell where by the people coming over, a whole lane at a time, and the lamps not needed. Two of him, in the one town.

passages.heading: 16. Friday, Midday and dusk
passages.text:
I went down to the cave, as on every evening. Past the post. Into the hill. Over the lip.

The candle stood at his feet where I'd set it back after the Detective. The old brown watch was going. I knelt and took it out by feel and wound it, though I'd wound it at dawn, and counted the turns. Four. It had hardly run.

The pump hasn't said where he goes next. It will. The town is a carry ahead of me, and I mean to be ready when it says.

I got my shoulder under him.

On the shoulder. Never dragged.

A dragged crate is a docked crate.

works.title: The Redemption Vote
works.blurb: Thursday 14 to Saturday 16 December 1893: Gert, Indebted since the gallows pine, lets her lean-to to a woman from the railyard; the Baron falls on the platform while Gert is watching her boy, her lodger washes black water out of her hands in Gert's basin, and at the Bell, with Clem reading Article X's "by whatever means", a voice asks who sleeps in Gert's lean-to; she says nobody, the vote carries no name, and by the Articles the lodger is restored to the rolls; the Clerk takes rent on "every bed that should have been" in a narrow hand, and the reissued notice still wants her.

passages.heading: Station Rush. Thursday, 14 December 1893.
passages.text:
I scrub my step every morning. The mud is back by noon. I scrub it anyway, because it is mine to scrub, and there is not much on the Grant that is.

I had done it that morning in the dark, with the brush and the last of the hot water, and the boy held the lamp for me. Then we took the empty basket down to the platform for the bunks' washing, as we do every morning but Sunday. He carries the basket. He is eight, and he carries it in front of him in both arms, so that it walks ahead of him down the Row.

The train was in. Behind the engine there was a car I had never seen on the Line, with curtains in the windows. Dogs came out of it first, two and then two more, on chains. Then men in long coats.

The boy wanted the engine. He always wants the engine. He stood at the edge of the boards with the basket on his hip and looked up at the wheels and the steam, and I looked at him, because the edge of the boards is the edge of the boards.

passages.heading: Station Rush. Thursday, 14 December 1893.
passages.text:
Then a sound. Not loud.

The whole platform turned at once, the way a room turns when a plate goes.

When I looked, there was a man down on the boards by the curtained car, in a good coat, and the dogs were out.

I did not see it. If anyone ever writes this down, I want that in. I had my eyes on my boy. I always have my eyes on my boy.

passages.heading: Station Rush, after.
passages.text:
The dogs went through us.

Through the crew, through the mailbags, through the Rows standing about with their crates. They pulled their men along on the chains, noses down, and stopped at a boot here and a hem there, and went on, and settled on nobody. The men in long coats turned the cars out one by one. The mail car. The passenger car. Car 3 at the back, where the boxes ride. They found the boxes. They found nobody.

By then everyone was saying who the man on the boards was. The Baron. I had never seen his face. Now I had seen the back of his coat.

"Who did it?" the boy said.

"Somebody off the train," I said. "Somebody who came up with him. He'll be in the pines by now."

passages.heading: The dogs don't go past the fence.
passages.text:
I said it to him as a fact, and he took it as one, and so did I. A stranger off the train. That was where I put it, and it fit there. Everything bad in HollowMere comes up the Line sooner or later, and goes back down it in a box.

Nobody had thought to stop the washing. We took up the bunks' bundle and carried the basket home full, a handle each.

passages.heading: The Shift.
passages.text:
She came to my door on the Monday after they hanged him, with a bundle and a shawl, and asked after the lean-to. A bed and her supper. She had been turned out of somewhere, she said, and did not say where. She hauls in the railyard. I said yes before she had finished asking, because an Indebted house takes what knocks.

She has paid every Saturday since. She folds her scrip into small hard squares, like letters she means to send, and sets them by my plate without being asked. I do not count them until she has gone back out.

I know her name. She told it me on the step that Monday. I will come to that.

That morning at breakfast she had said she would be in the yard until the Shift. She said it the way she says everything, as if she had thought about it first.

passages.heading: The Shift.
passages.text:
When the boy and I came up Pump Row with the basket she was at my table with her sleeves up, washing her hands in my basin.

You can hear the yard from Pump Row. The hammers on the workbench. The cars being shunted. I could hear them then, through the open door, over the water.

"You're early," I said.

passages.heading: They stopped us.
passages.text:
The hammers went on.

The water in the basin was black. Not grey, the way a mill hand's goes. Black from the bottom up.

She dried her hands on her own skirt, not my cloth, and went out to the lean-to. She shut the door the way he used to, with the latch held up so it would not knock.

I stood and looked at the basin.

No stranger. No pines. No train.

My table. My basin. The black water in my own basin.

passages.heading: The Shift, still.
passages.text:
Then I thought about it, which I should not have done, because thinking is how I got the pine.

Powder comes up on the Train every morning. The yard unloads it with their hands, and it goes under the nails and stays there. I wash for the bunks. Every cuff in that basket had black on it, and I have scrubbed black out of a hundred cuffs since Michaelmas. A yard hand washes at noon and the water goes black. That is what water does in this town.

So I put it there instead. Every yard hand's powder. It was a smaller shelf than the first one, and I had to push to make it hold.

I took the basin to the step and tipped it into the mud. I scrubbed the basin out with sand and set it upside down on the table to dry, the way I have set every basin of my life.

passages.heading: The Shift, still.
passages.text: The mud takes everything by noon. I had only brought this a little forward.

passages.heading: The Bell.
passages.text:
Somebody paid the ten scrip and rang it in the last of the afternoon.

By the Articles I keep curfew twice over: from Dusk, and from the hour of my entry, which was a Tuesday noon. Nobody has ever come to see whether I keep it. I went down to the square with the boy.

The square was full. The men in long coats stood along the bank side with their dogs sitting at their boots. They looked up at the bank windows, where the Baron had been carried, and waited to be told something. Nobody told them anything.

Clem got up on the kit chest by the pump. He had the town's copy of the Articles, the one with the corners gone soft. He reads them aloud at the Lantern, the parts nobody asks for. Nobody had asked now either.

passages.heading: Article Ten," he said. "Section four. Restoration.
passages.text:
He read it slowly, with his finger under it.

"Any person who spoke against the Company during Public Unrest, and who remains within the Grant upon the President's departure, by whatever means, shall be restored to the rolls as Townsfolk."

Somebody at the back laughed once. "He's departed, all right."

"By whatever means," Clem said, and read the rest. "Their speech shall be struck from the record, and their account shall not."

The square took it a word at a time, the way the Row takes the stone's name off Agnes at dawn. Whoever she was, the woman off the soapbox in November, the Company's own book said she was forgiven if she was still on the Grant when the President left it. He had left it. If nobody stood her up before the Dusk train went out, the Articles would do the rest.

She was at my shoulder. She had come out of the lean-to behind us, and she stood with her hand on my boy's cap, the way you steady a child in a crowd. I looked at her only because she was close.

passages.heading: Article Ten," he said. "Section four. Restoration.
passages.text:
Her lips were moving.

Not much. A woman at her prayers in a back pew. But it was not a prayer. It was the clause. She had it a word ahead of Clem. "Remains" before he got to remains. "Whatever" before whatever. He stumbled on "Restoration" and she did not.

Every yard hand has the powder. Not every yard hand has the clause by heart.

"We'll have a vote," somebody said. "Before the train."

That meant the last of the light. The Dusk train goes when it goes.

passages.heading: The sum.
passages.text:
I do every sum in washing. A sheet is so much. A shirt is so much. A week of the bunks' cuffs is so much, and Saturday's rent is so many weeks of cuffs.

The reward on the November notice never would come to washing. There were too many sheets in it. It would clear my line. It would clear his pine, which the Company had billed to my household and was still billing. It would buy the boy a winter.

On the other side was Article Eleven. I do not need Clem for that one. I learned it the Tuesday they hanged him. The account survives the man. It passes first to the household. A man who sleeps in your lean-to is your household when the pine comes. If they stood her up and hanged her, the pine for her would come up Pump Row to the fourth door, the same as his had. A second rope on a line that had not finished paying for the first.

passages.heading: The sum.
passages.text:
And at noon, before the Bell, she had come in from the lean-to and set two weeks by my plate. Small hard squares. On a Thursday. She pays on Saturdays.

I did not know if it was rent or something else. I did not know what else there was in this town but rent.

I did the sum twice, standing in the square with my hands under my shawl. It came out near even. It always does here.

passages.heading: Hands.
passages.text:
The names went round.

A dozen voices, the way they go round the pump: a Row name, a mill name, a yard name, one I might have said myself that morning if anyone had asked me. For each one a few hands went up. Then the one named would say where they had been at the Rush, and a voice would say, "With me," and the hands would come down. None carried.

The light was going. Down at the platform the engine let off steam and stood.

Then a voice from the back. I never saw whose.

passages.heading: Who's in Gert's lean-to now?
passages.text:
The square turned round to me.

They were the same faces that stood under this Bell the Tuesday the Judge struck my word. Not one of them had asked me anything at the Bell since. I had not been let answer anything. The Indebted may not bear witness. But this was not the Tribunal, and no Judge was sitting, and at a vote anyone may say anything.

Her hand stayed on the boy's cap. It did not tighten. That was the worst of it: it did not have to.

I had not finished the sum. I want that in, too.

passages.heading: Nobody," I said. "Not since him.
passages.text:
I said it loud, louder than I had ever said anything under that Bell. Louder than I had said eleven, and twelve, and one, to the Judge, before they struck it.

I thought of him then, at my table on that Sunday night, with the boy's boot and his last, by my one candle. How he held the boot up to the light when it was done and turned it over, and whistled two notes, up and down, the way you call a dog you are fond of. The boy wore that boot to the Rush this morning. He was wearing it in the square.

passages.heading: Hands, the last round.
passages.text:
The square looked away from me.

All at once, the way it had turned. I knew why. They had hanged the last man who slept in that lean-to, after my word was struck, and they had stood here and watched it, and his pine was on my line. Not one of them was going to ask me twice what slept in my lean-to. They owed me that much. It was the first thing anybody in HollowMere ever owed me that got paid.

There was one more round. Nobody's name. No hands.

A man by the pump said, "The Town has spoken," the way the Judge says it, though there was no Judge. Nobody laughed this time.

The Dusk whistle went. The train pulled out. The men in long coats watched it go and stayed where they were.

That was all a vote is. By Clem's book she was restored. She was Townsfolk now, the same as me.

passages.heading: Hands, the last round.
passages.text:
She walked home behind me with the boy's hand in hers. I had soup and the heel of a wake loaf. She ate my bread at my table and said it was good bread, and thanked me for it, and the boy talked about the engine until he was asleep on his arms.

After curfew I sat up with the one candle.

Through the window I could see the lean-to. The door was open. She was standing in it.

A long while. Not moving. A darker piece of the dark against the wash-house wall. I could not see her face, or whether she was looking at my window or at the square, or at nothing.

She did not go in.

I put out the candle first.

passages.heading: Midday Rent. Friday, 15 December.
passages.text:
The Clerk comes up Pump Row in person every day at the Shift, with a man behind him carrying the roll. Two years I have watched him do it. He has never once spoken at a door. He holds out his hand. You put the scrip in it. The man with the roll writes.

On Friday he spoke.

"Two beds," he said.

He had a voice. I had not known he had one.

"One," I said. "Mine and the boy's. The lean-to's empty. I said so at the Bell."

He looked at the lean-to. Not for long.

"Rent is due on every bed slept in," he said, "and on every bed that should have been."

The Articles' words. He did not need the book for them.

He did not ask who slept there. He did not need to know. The Company does not count people. It counts beds, and a bed that should have been slept in costs the same as one that was.

passages.heading: Midday Rent. Friday, 15 December.
passages.text:
I paid him in her squares. He took them folded and did not open them. Then he took the pen from the man with the roll and entered it himself, on my line, in a narrow hand, small and leaning, which I had never seen him write in before.

I cannot read much. I know a hand the way I know a stain, by the shape of it and where it sits.

What I said at the Bell, I said to the square, and the square let it stand. On the roll it stood nowhere. Two beds, paid. It changed nothing on the roll at all.

Her debt was paid. Clem had read it out. Her account was not. Clem had read that out too.

passages.heading: Station Rush. Saturday, 16 December.
passages.text: The Constable had pasted a new one up on the board by the pump, face out, four tacks. Clem read it to the square over the water.

passages.heading: Wanted. The Activist. Reissued.
passages.text:
He read the Baron's name and the platform and the Thursday. He read the mill loft, and the four sticks under the last mile, and the soapbox. Then he slowed.

"If she is taken, or gives herself up, the Town will vote at the Bell on her Redemption."

passages.heading: He stopped there. Somebody said, "We've voted.
passages.text:
Nobody told the Company. Nobody is going to.

"Reward," Clem said. "Five hundred scrip. Payable at the Company Bank, at the Midday Rent, by order of the Heir to the Baron."

"What heir?" somebody said, and nobody answered.

There was writing below the stamp. Clem put his finger on it and said it was not the Constable's. I went up close, as if to see the print. It was narrow, small and leaning. It sat where it sat on my line the day before.

Across the square, under the Bell, the Clerk was nailing up a paper of his own. When it was up he stood beside it, which I had never known him do.

Five hundred. I did the sum again, in washing, and it would not come to washing at all. I did it against a household that has already paid for one rope. I kept my hand under my shawl.

passages.heading: He stopped there. Somebody said, "We've voted.
passages.text:
She was on the boards with the yard hands, going down to the crates. Her shawl was up and her nails were black already, and nobody looked at her, because nobody looks at a yard hand at the Rush. The boy waved. She waved back.

I know her name. She told it me on my step. I have not said it at the Bell or at the pump or to the Clerk's hand, and I will not write it here, on the back of anything.

I scrubbed my step this morning, before the Rush, in the dark.

The mud will be back by noon.

works.title: The Express Safe
works.blurb: the Bandit's last two scores, 18 to 23 December 1893, kept as an account: a round for every living soul and every man of the law, and a gold coin for every score; the storm cuts the week to four days, the bank vault opens in one line, and that night a round is gone with no shot heard; a name on the stone balances the count, and an upright .45 casing, the Bandit's own sign, stands over the hidden case; on the last train out the safe opens in transit, and the count by lamplight comes to one round more than the souls the Bandit can count, as the brakes take for a light at Gallows Wood Siding.

passages.heading: The count
passages.text:
Monday, the eighteenth of December. Station Rush.

The board by the pump. My notice had been turned again.

The Constable pastes them face out. By the next Rush somebody has taken them down, written on the back and put them up face in. That morning the back was the baker's, in pencil, with flour in the creases.

Three coins behind her crock. Two prints in her flour that would not agree. Then the last of it, at the bottom, pressed hard:

passages.heading: A thief who pays is keeping an account.
passages.text:
I read it twice. I liked it. Nobody had ever put it about me so well.

I turned the sheet face out again myself, with the four tacks, and read the front. The front I knew. The ovens. The plate. Then:

*3. The Company Bank, the vault. Not yet.*
*4. The Daily Train, the express safe. Not yet.*

passages.heading: Height: short, by the bootprint. Scarf: grey wool.
passages.text:
A man at my elbow said they'd never catch him, a short man in grey in a mill town. The woman beside him said that was half the town, and they both laughed. I had my scarf on. I keep one end tucked inside my coat. I always have.

Then the stone.

Agnes is first up every morning, so she can tell the Row before it asks. Her arm was still bound in its sling from the wolf. She came down calling a name to every door. I stood in the crowd at the pump, put my hand inside my coat lining, and took one round out of the sock.

That is my arithmetic. I'll set it down once, plainly.

A round for every living soul in HollowMere, and one for every man of the law. Not one more. A gun loaded for everyone isn't loaded for anyone in particular. That's a courtesy too, the way I see it. Nobody in this town is singled out by me.

passages.heading: Height: short, by the bootprint. Scarf: grey wool.
passages.text:
When the stone takes a name, I take a round. That evening I dropped it in the mere off the end of the planks, where the water is black and gives nothing back.

And a gold coin for every score, polished on the scarf first. The baker got hers on the hearth-lip and on the counter. God got brass.

Two scores to go. The safe goes out on the Train. I had a week to do the vault first, and a week is a long time in a town that can't leave.

I have never carried a round for the dead.

passages.heading: The road
passages.text:
Tuesday, the nineteenth.

The storm came down off the hills in the night, and by the Midday Shift the coach road was gone. Not closed. Gone. A carter turned back at the first bend with snow to his horse's chest, and said so at the Bell.

So it went round the square, the way things go round it. The Train is the only way in. The Train is the only way out. The last train out goes at dusk on Saturday. After that the Line shuts for the storm, and nothing comes.

My week was four days now.

I counted them on the hand inside my coat. Wednesday. Thursday. Friday. Saturday. The safe would have to go on that last train, somewhere between here and wherever it got to. So the vault had to go before it.

No coach. No horse that would go. No road. The Train.

passages.heading: The vault
passages.text:
Thursday, the twenty-first. After Curfew.

The guard's stool at the bank door was empty, with the cushion on it, the way it always is. One of the escort's dogs lay along the step. It lifted its head when I came and looked at me. Then it put its head down on its paws again. I don't know what it saw. Something it had decided was not its business.

The vault came open. That is all I will say about the vault.

The gold went into the case, a plain case and heavy now. I took the coin from my pocket and rubbed it on the scarf until it caught the lantern. Then I set it on the shelf where the gold had been. The Company would find it in the morning and enter it, and somewhere in the Eastern Office a clerk would wonder.

I never drew the gun. Not one round was fired.

passages.heading: The vault
passages.text:
Out in the lane the fog had come in off the mere. I walked with my hand in my coat, counting the sock by touch, the way I do. Other people say their prayers walking home.

They say it's the one bank that can't fail, because the town can't leave it. It hadn't needed a single round.

passages.heading: Short one
passages.text:
The same night. Under the station boards.

There's a dry place under the boards at the platform's end, where the crew throw their ash. I keep the case there. Some nights I keep myself there too.

I counted before sleep, as every night. The cylinder first. Then the sock, round by round, between finger and thumb.

One short.

I counted again by a match. One short.

There was no casing. The cylinder smelled of oil and nothing else. I would have heard a shot. After Curfew I hear everything in this town: the crew's shovel, the planks at the wood edge, the mere at the dock. Nobody fired anything that night. Not me.

So I'd dropped it. In the vault, in the dark, taking the sock out to get at the coin. That was all. It would be lying on the floor by the shelf. The Company would find it with my coin and know the calibre, which it knew already.

passages.heading: Short one
passages.text: I lay with my hand on the sock. Five fingers on it, and the sock was wrong.

passages.heading: The name
passages.text:
Friday, the twenty-second.

I went to the board before the Rush, before it was light, to see what the Company had found.

The Constable had been. There was new paste on my notice, with the score written in:

passages.heading: 3. The Company Bank, the vault. Entered.
passages.text:
Under it was the sum, which I won't put here. Then the traces: *a gold coin, on the vault shelf.*

Nothing else. No round on any floor.

So it wasn't in the vault. In the lane, then. In the fog on the way home, when I had the sock out counting. A round in the mud of the bank lane. Somebody's child would find it in the spring.

Then came the Rush, and the crowd at the pump, and Agnes down the Row with her arm in the sling, calling a name to every door before anyone asked.

I knew the face that went with it. Somebody who paid at the Company Store in exact coppers and counted them out twice on the counter before letting go. I stood behind them in the line once and counted along under my breath. We got to the end at the same time.

passages.heading: 3. The Company Bank, the vault. Entered.
passages.text:
Nobody said how. Nobody asks how now. The Undertaker's book stopped asking some time ago.

I put my hand into my coat to take a round out for the name.

The count was right.

I counted again with my back to the pump. Right. A round for every living soul and every man of the law, and not one more. I hadn't taken anything out. A round lost in the fog would have left me short, and I wasn't short. I was even.

One round gone in the night, one soul gone in the night. The sum came out the same as if I'd done it with my own hand at the stone. That's arithmetic. Only arithmetic: two things that come to the same number.

I had a round for that name. I will not write it.

passages.heading: Upright
passages.text:
Friday night.

The hoods were out after Curfew, for the first time. Flour sacks with the eyes cut out, and torches, going up the Rise after anyone who walked in threes.

I walk alone. I went the other way, down to the platform, to move the case somewhere better.

The case was where I'd left it. I opened it by feel. The gold was all there, still in the bank's own paper. Nobody had touched it.

On the beam above it, in the dark, at the height of my eyes, a casing stood on its end.

I struck a match to be sure. Brass, a .45, spent. It was stood on its base, upright, the way you'd set one down if you wanted it found standing.

I stood one like that at St Brannock's, on the plate, where the coins had been. I know how it looks. It's mine. It's what I leave.

passages.heading: Upright
passages.text:
I didn't leave this one.

Arithmetic doesn't leave signs. A number doesn't come down under the station boards in the night and stand a shell on a beam over your case. Somebody does.

At the end of the platform lane one torch had stopped. Just stopped, the way a man stops when he's heard something. It lit the snow round it and the fence and nothing else. I couldn't see anybody under it. I watched it until the match burned my fingers. When I looked again it was going on up the Rise with the others.

Somebody in HollowMere knew me: my face, or my walk, or the place a hand can go. They had been at my case and taken nothing. They were keeping my account.

Someone had tipped me.

passages.heading: The last train
passages.text:
Saturday, the twenty-third.

I kept away from Harold's sale. At the Midday Shift I saw the square from a doorway. Everybody was standing on their own, nobody in threes, and the long coats stood along the bank front looking at the bank. They'd been looking at it since the Baron fell. Since Thursday night they'd had a reason.

At dusk I went down to the platform with the case.

The last train was in, breathing, its lamps lit along its length. The snow came sideways under the roof.

The ones leaving weren't many. A drummer with his tonic trunk. A Mill Row family a fare short, the mother arguing it at the step. A man who wouldn't tell the Conductor where he was going and paid to the end of the line. And me: one passenger with a heavy case.

I bought one-way at the window, in scrip. Pruett took the ticket at the step, and his crescent came down on it once. He looked at the case, not at me.

passages.heading: The last train
passages.text:
The Company counts the crate. I was counting too.

If somebody in HollowMere was keeping my account, I'd leave it square. I wouldn't go owing the town a thing. I stood on the car step as the train took the strain, and I counted the souls aboard I could see. Pruett at the step. The driver and the fireman, up front in the glow. The drummer. The family, every one of them, the smallest on a lap. The man who wouldn't say. I didn't count myself. I never have.

I kept that many rounds.

The rest belonged to the town: a round for every soul back there, and for the law. We went out onto the last mile over the drained lake. I put my hand in the sock and dropped them off the step one at a time into the dark, the way I did at the mere. The snow took them before they landed.

passages.heading: The last train
passages.text:
Under the last mile, the talk goes, there are four sticks that never went off. We went over them. They didn't.

Punched once. Counted out.

passages.heading: The safe
passages.text:
Saturday, dusk. Moving.

I went forward to the express car. That's as much as I'll say about the going.

The lamp in there swung on its hook. Crates. The mail. The safe at the end.

The safe came open. That's all I'll say about the safe.

The Company's sealed sacks went into the case, on top of the bank's gold. I took out the last coin, rubbed it on the scarf until it caught the lamp, and set it on the safe's empty floor.

Four scores, four tips: the ovens, the plate, the bank, the Train. The account was closed.

Behind us, HollowMere was going out like a lamp. Ahead lay Thorne Junction, with the storm in between. The Line would shut behind us, and nothing would come up it for five days. Nothing could come after.

The Company counts the crate, not the contents.

passages.heading: One over
passages.text:
The same car.

I counted by touch, as every night. The cylinder, then the sock.

One more than I'd kept.

I turned the lamp up and laid them out in a row on the lid of the safe, in the light. I counted them with a finger on each.

One more.

I counted the train again, the only way I could from in there: by what I'd seen at the step. Pruett. The driver. The fireman. The drummer. The family. The man who wouldn't say. Car 3 behind us held the week's boxes, and I don't count the dead.

One round more than I can count souls for.

*A passenger booked in is a passenger counted out.* That's the Company's own rule, in the Rules of Carriage. Pruett counted me in, and Pruett will count me out. If I count myself, the sum comes right. I have never counted myself.

passages.heading: One over
passages.text:
Or there's somebody on this train who is on nobody's count.

No step in the car. No light in the gap between the crates. The lamp swinging, and stopping, and swinging. One over.

passages.heading: The siding
passages.text:
The brakes take.

I feel it in the floor before I hear it. The crates lean. The lamp swings out on its hook and stays out.

Through the slats the snow is going past slower, and pines, and in the pines a light. Swinging, low. This is Gallows Wood Siding, and the Siding stops on signal only. Somebody is signalling. A lantern, or something that knows how a lantern moves.

The train slows. It doesn't stop. We're still moving.

My hand is on the row on the lid of the safe.

In the next car there's a step. It comes down the aisle toward the express car door, unhurried: the step of a man with a punch in his hand and a count to make.

I have never carried a round for the dead.

I count again. One over.

works.title: Whoever Is Here
works.pov: second person (the hand that did not burn the letter)
works.blurb: from 7 to 16 December 1893 "you", who has met the mail every morning for four winters with nothing coming, is handed a black-wax letter with your name on the outside and, under the Baron's line, the name of the man you sit beside on the platform bench; you keep a list of reasons on the back of an old envelope and strike each one, until the Postmaster's guide says it "comes for whoever is here"; before curfew ends on the 12th you sit down beside him and later stand up, let the Dusk train go, take his place on the bench, and on the 16th watch the wax go into the hand in front of yours.

passages.heading: Whoever Is Here
passages.text:
The platform an hour before the Rush. Fog on the boards. One lantern.

He is on the bench already. He always is. He has the lantern end, and when you come up the steps he moves his elbow off the dark end without looking. That is the whole of what passes between you most mornings, and it is more than passes between you and anyone else.

He came up the Line on the eleventh of October. Railyard bunks. Powder under his nails, like all of them. He keeps his scrip in a sock, and a one-way ticket in his hatband.

He breathes on the lantern glass, and with a fingertip writes a number in the fog. He looks at it. He wipes it off before anyone else comes up the steps. You have never asked what it counts. You think it is days.

You come for the bag. You watch it come off the train, and you follow it across the lane to the window, and you stand at the window until the Postmaster has sorted it. Then you go home. Nobody has written to you in four winters.

passages.heading: Whoever Is Here
passages.text:
You keep the last one in your coat. What it says is not much: a house is sold, and the name at the bottom used to be yours too. You do not keep it for that. You keep it for the outside, where your name is written in somebody's hand, in ink, as if it were worth the ink.

On the back of that envelope, in pencil, you have started a list. You did not mean it to be a list. It has a heading.

passages.heading: Reasons.
passages.text:
The train comes at the Rush. Nothing has ever come for you on it.

---

passages.heading: 1. Because someone wrote your name
passages.text:
Thursday, 7 December. The Rush.

The Postmaster puts it into your hand at the window. He does not look at it. He does not write anything down. He is already looking past you at the next one.

Black wax. No sender.

Your name on the outside, in a hand.

You walk home without running, which takes everything you have.

In your room you sit on the bed with it on your knees and do not open it for a long time. You just read the outside. Your name. Somebody sat down and wrote it, letter by letter, and sealed something to it. After four winters.

Then you open it.

One line, printed.

*Burn the Letter & Keep Your Mundane Life, OR Accept the Baron's Contract.*

Under the line, a name.

You know the name. You have sat at the dark end of the bench beside it every morning since October.

passages.heading: 1. Because someone wrote your name
passages.text:
The stove is lit. The door of it is open. It would take one movement.

You put the letter under the four-winters one, in your coat, against your ribs. You take the pencil and write the first reason on the back of the old envelope, because it is true and you want to see it:

passages.heading: Because someone wrote your name.
passages.text:
Out of everyone in the Grant, at all the rents on all the Rows, it came to you. It picked you out.

The stove burns down without being fed.

Out of the whole Grant.

---

passages.heading: 2. Because the others burned it
passages.text:
Friday, 8 December.

You go to the window with nothing to post and buy a stamp you do not need, so that you have a reason to stand there.

The Postmaster counts your change into your hand. Then he looks up.

Only his eyes. He holds your eyes for one breath, and he seems to like holding it.

passages.heading: In that breath you read one word. *Again.
passages.text:
He has seen this name before. Under another seal, to another hand. In November, maybe. That hand did not come back to the window looking like you look. That hand burned it.

He says nothing. He drops his eyes. You take the stamp.

So it did not choose you first.

On the walk back you stop in the lane and take the envelope out and look at the first reason. It still holds, you think, if you turn it a little. It went to someone who would burn it, and they burned it, and it came on. It went past them. It kept coming until it found the one who would not.

You cross out the first reason, because it is not quite right, and write the right one under it.

~~*Because someone wrote your name.*~~

passages.heading: Because the others burned it.
passages.text:
Not chosen first. Chosen last, which is better.

---

passages.heading: 3. Because you could
passages.text:
Saturday, 9 December.

If it came on until it found the one who would not burn it, then you have to be that one. Otherwise it was a mistake to come to you, and you could not bear that.

So you answer it.

That is all there is to say about how.

Saturday's bag has something in it for you. The Postmaster puts it into your hand at the window and does not look at it. Small, in brown paper and string. No sender. Small enough for a coat.

You do not unwrap it in daylight. You do not unwrap it at all. It goes into the coat, beside the letter, beside the four-winters letter, and the coat hangs differently on you now.

You do your chores in pairs that afternoon, the way everyone not important enough to do them alone does them. Your pair talks. You answer. Your pair says you are quiet today, and you say you slept badly, which is true.

passages.heading: 3. Because you could
passages.text: On the back of the envelope, under the struck line and the line that stands, you write a third:

passages.heading: Because you could.
passages.text:
It weighs less than the letter did.

---

passages.heading: 4. Because it would lapse
passages.text:
Sunday, 10 December. Before the Rush.

You go up the steps with it in your coat.

He is there. Of course he is. He moves his elbow off the dark end.

You sit.

He takes his hat off, which he has never done, and works the ticket out of the band to show you, as if you had not seen its corner every morning since October. One way. Thorne Junction and on. January. He says it the way people here say "back east": as if it were a place, and you could already see it from the platform if the fog would lift.

"January," he says.

He puts the ticket back. He puts the hat back. He breathes on the glass and writes *28*. He looks at it. He wipes it off.

He has powder under his nails and nothing else. No secret in the sock but scrip. Nothing in his face that the Company could want. He looks at the rails the way you look at the bag.

passages.heading: 4. Because it would lapse
passages.text:
Your hand is in your coat.

You do nothing.

The train comes. He stands for it, the way he always stands, though he is not getting on. You walk behind the bag across the lane to the window and stand there, and the Postmaster sorts it, and there is nothing for you, as always.

At home you take out the envelope and cross out the third reason.

~~*Because you could.*~~

You could not. It is that simple, and you are glad. Some of you is glad.

Then you think it through at the table, slowly, and you find that there is a way out after all. If you do nothing, nothing happens. The letter waits in your coat. The days go. Whatever it wanted lapses. It goes to nobody, and nobody finishes anything, and he gets on in January.

You write it down. It is a thinner reason than the others. You write it anyway.

passages.heading: Because it would lapse.
passages.text:
No train early. No letter. No hand. Nothing.

You let it lapse. That is a thing you can do.

---

## 5. Because it comes for whoever is here

Monday, 11 December.

At the window the Postmaster has a stack of something printed. He is handing copies across the sorting table to the ones who came off the morning train: a drummer, a woman with a carpet bag.

*Who to Ask in HollowMere. For the Use of Persons Arriving by the Daily Train.*

You have not arrived anywhere in four winters.

He hands you one anyway, because you are standing there.

You read it in the lane. Who to ask, and where to find them, and what not to say. A list of rules on the first page, numbered. *Ask in pairs. The town counts alibis in twos, and so should you.* *Don't miss the train.*

On the last page, in the Postmaster's own words:

passages.heading: Because it would lapse.
passages.text:
*If a letter comes for you sealed in black wax, I did not open it. I could not have told you whose it was before it came. It comes in the bag like the rest, and it comes for whoever is here.*

And under it, in the margin, in a narrower hand: *Nor could I. — Clk.*

You read it until the words come apart.

It comes for whoever is here.

It did not pick you out. It did not pass the others over to find you. It came to the window, and you were at the window. It would have come to anyone standing where you stand, at the hour you stand there, every morning, for four winters.

And it does not lapse. That is the rest of it. Somebody burned it in November, and it came again in December with the same name under the line. If you do nothing, it comes again in a week, or two, to the next hand, and the next. It comes on with his name until a hand finishes it.

passages.heading: Because it would lapse.
passages.text:
It comes for whoever is here.

There is one other person on that platform every morning before the Rush.

The next letter might have your name under the line, and his on the outside.

At home you do not cross out the fourth reason. You write the fifth under it, and you do not cross that out either. There is nothing to cross it out with.

passages.heading: Because it comes for whoever is here.
passages.text:
It wrote your name because you were there to write it to.

---

The night of Monday the eleventh. Before curfew ends.

There is no reason written under this number. You write the number and leave the line empty.

You go up to the platform in the dark. The lane is black. The platform lantern burns, as it does all night.

He is there. An hour before the Rush, and then some. Early, in case.

The fog is on the lantern glass, and there is a number in it: *26*.

He moves his elbow.

You sit down beside him.

Later you stand up.

That is all of it that will ever be written down.

His hat is on the boards. The ticket is in the band. The sock is where it is. You touch none of it. You take only the mark.

You open the little door of the platform lantern and feed the letter to it. It is the only thing you have ever burned of your own. The paper goes. The seal comes away in your fingers, broken, and you let it go, and you do not hear it land.

You do not wipe the glass.

You leave the number.

---

passages.heading: 7. The notice
passages.text:
Tuesday, 12 December. The Rush.

You meet your pair in the lane, as on any chore day, and you come up to the platform together. For the first time in four winters you are not early. Nobody notices. Nobody has ever noticed when you came.

Then the shouting. Then the crowd. Then the space the crowd makes round the bench.

You do not go near. You stand with your pair at the back, and your pair says *God* and *who* and *the bench, the poor sod, the bench*, and you say nothing, and that is allowed. The town counts alibis in twos. You are two.

By noon the Constable has pasted it up in his corner of the board, with four tacks and flour paste.

You read it in the crowd, over a shoulder.

*For the death of ____________, a man of the railyard bunks who came up the Line in October.*

passages.heading: 7. The notice
passages.text:
A needle, it says, or a small-bore pistol. The Doctor puts it before curfew ended. A seal of black wax, broken, on the boards beside him. No letter found.

The Company's three particulars. *Height: unknown. No print on the boards. Scarf: none.*

passages.heading: Hat: felt, brown, common.
passages.text:
It is his hat. It was his hat on the boards, with the ticket in the band. And the Company has written it down as yours.

You look at it for a long time. The Company does not know who you are. So it has described you with whatever was lying there. It describes whoever is here with whatever is near them.

Further down: *He will be on the Dusk train. So will others.*

You do your chores in pairs. Your pair talks about the bench all afternoon. The lantern. The hour. Who sits on a platform in the dark before the Rush. Some lunatic. Some poor sod with a ticket.

It has written you onto the Dusk train.

---

passages.heading: 8. The Dusk train
passages.text:
Tuesday, 12 December. Dusk.

The train is the way out. It always was. *Don't miss the train,* the little book says, rule seven.

You go up to the platform. The bench is empty. Somebody has scrubbed the boards in front of it, and the wet has dried paler than the rest.

The Constable stands at the car step and looks at every face that boards. A drummer. A woman with a basket. A railyard hand with his collar up, whom the Constable stops and turns to the light, and then lets go.

passages.heading: So will others.
passages.text:
The others are looked at, every one of them.

There is no fare in your coat. The only fare you know of is in a hatband, and the hatband is with the hat, and the hat is wherever the Constable keeps what is lying around.

You stand at the back of the platform with your hands in your pockets.

You do not move.

The Conductor punches the last fare. The doors go. The train does not wait; it has never waited; the Rules of Carriage say so. The Lamplighter lights the platform post as the last car clears, and the light comes down over the empty bench, and over you.

It goes. You are still here.

---

passages.heading: 9. Because the Baron wanted it
passages.text:
Wednesday, 13 December, to Thursday, 14 December.

You are still here, and the only thing you know how to do with a morning is be early.

So on Wednesday you go up an hour before the Rush. The bench is there. The lantern is there. The dark end is yours.

You cannot sit at the dark end. It is wrong now. The elbow does not move off it.

You sit at the lantern end, where he sat.

The fog comes onto the glass. You do not write in it.

On Thursday the train comes in with a private car and dogs. The whole platform turns to look at the train, the way everybody looks at the train. You are looking at it too. You hear it and you do not see it. Then there is a hat on the boards, and the Pinkertons have the dogs out, and nobody in the town is looking at anybody.

passages.heading: 9. Because the Baron wanted it
passages.text:
By noon the platform has it. The Baron is dead. The Baron is dead on the same boards.

And they say the contract was his. All of it. The black wax was the Baron's, and the Baron is dead.

You take out the envelope that evening. You write it slowly. It is the thinnest reason yet, and you know that, and you write it:

passages.heading: Because the Baron wanted it.
passages.text:
The hand that sent it is gone. So the wax has stopped. Whatever comes in the bag now is only mail. What you did was the end of it.

The last of it.

---

Saturday, 16 December. The Rush.

On the board in the square the Hitman notice has been turned face-in. Someone has written on the back of it.

Ink, from a bottle nearly dry. Small writing, to fit. You do not read it all. You do not know the hand. You read the end:

*The Train comes at the Rush, and the bag comes with it. Check yours.*

You go up the steps. You are early. You take the lantern end.

The fog on the glass. The fog on the boards. Nobody comes up the steps for a long time, and then the train comes.

The bag comes off it.

You follow it across the lane, the way you always have. You stand at the window. The Postmaster sorts. There is someone in front of you.

The Postmaster puts a letter into the hand in front of yours and does not look at it. Black wax. No sender.

You do not look at the face. You look at the hand, which closes on it.

Then it is your turn, and there is nothing for you, and you go back out and up the steps to the bench.

Under the struck lines on the old envelope there is the one you never struck. You find it with your thumb.

passages.heading: Because it comes for whoever is here.
passages.text:
The hand from the window is opening it now, somewhere, in a room like yours. Under the line there will be a name. The hand will know it. They will know it because it is someone who is always there, early, in the same place, every morning, in case.

No name. No sender. No reason. Only the bench, and the hour before.

You move your elbow off the dark end for nobody.

It comes for whoever is here. You are here.

works.title: The Road Is Closed
works.blurb: Gert's second week, 19 to 29 December 1893: the storm takes the coach road and with it the boy's seat; Harold buys him a ticket the Indebted may not buy, the wire says no service after Saturday, and the Mill keeps her at the wheel while the last train goes out by the dark; with no whistle the square in law never opens, the robes knock and name her debt to the penny, a half-step-flat whistle in the night lies, and on the first train through the boy follows the man in the light up the square, the ticket still sewn in his coat; from the wheel she hears the train go out a second time and does not know whether he is on it.

passages.heading: Tuesday, 19 December
passages.text:
Keep to the light, and don't miss the train.

I say it to the boy every morning on the step while I scrub it, and he says it back with the basket on his arm. Every mother in HollowMere says it. None of us made it up.

That morning Clem said something else. He had the paper from the Telegraph Room in his hand at the pump, and he read it twice, the way he reads everything: once for us, and once for the parts nobody asked for. The storm had come down off the hills in the night. Trees were down across the coach road at the Cut, and past them the drifts stood as high as a horse's chest. There would be no coach till the thaw.

The tin sits on the shelf behind the copper. In it is my washing money, saved a penny at a time. In it is Harold's money for my grandmother's brooch, paid out of his own drawer when the brooch went off his shelf. And in it is what was left of the lodger's rent, in the small hard squares she folds it into, like letters she means to send.

passages.heading: Tuesday, 19 December
passages.text:
That tin was the boy's seat. The New Year coach goes out over the road to the junction with the carrier's mail, the mail that does not go by the Company. I was to pay the carrier on the day. A coach is not the Company's, and a seat on it is not a ticket. The Articles say that whoever leaves the Grant by any way but the Train stays on the Grant in law, and their rent goes on falling due. I had done that sum at the copper more nights than one. Let it fall. Let it fall on me.

Now the road was under the snow. The Train was the only way out, and the Train sells no ticket to the Indebted. I have been Indebted since the pine.

"Roads come back," I said.

The boy asked when.

Roads come back.

passages.heading: Wednesday, 20 December
passages.text:
No ticket shall be sold to the Indebted. Clem has read us that line often enough. The Articles never say who may ride on one.

I took the tin to Harold's step with the boy behind me, carrying the empty basket so the Row would think we were going for washing. Harold looked at the tin and then at the boy, and he did not ask. He has four terms. The fourth is that he does not ask.

He put on his coat, walked down to the platform window, and bought it with my money: one way, HollowMere to the junction, for a boy of eight. He brought it back and laid it on his counter face up, with his hand flat beside it, the way he lays down everything.

"Keeps," he said.

I would keep to the coach's day, after the New Year. That gave us one more Christmas at the fourth door. I had earned one.

passages.heading: Wednesday, 20 December
passages.text: The sale was his. The boy was mine.

passages.heading: Thursday, 21 December
passages.text:
At the Station Rush there was a wire pasted on the platform window. The flour paste was already curling in the wet. Clem read it, then read it again, slower.

NO SERVICE AFTER SATURDAY DUSK STOP UNTIL WEATHER ALLOWS STOP

The crowd read it over my shoulder: the ones who can read, out loud, for the ones who can't. *Weather allows.* Nobody on that platform could have told you how many days that was.

So there was no after the New Year any more. There was Saturday.

I changed my mind right there on the boards, with my hand round the boy's wrist and the engine breathing at my back. I did not tell him. He knew by my hand.

Saturday, then.

passages.heading: Friday, 22 December
passages.text:
At the pump Agnes called the stone, her arm still bound up from the wolf. Behind me someone said who it was: the one who paid at the Company Store in exact coppers, and counted them twice before letting go. I will not say the name. It is not mine to say.

The Mill takes the Indebted at Midday and gives us back at Dusk; that is the Schedule. So I could not sit with him in a car through the afternoon. And I would not put him in one alone, a boy of eight on a cold seat, with the long coats standing along the bank front watching the square and nobody to stand between.

So I sat up with his coat. I unpicked a hand's width of the lining at the hem. In went the ticket, and with it a paper in my own hand, which does not write much: his name, where he came from, and *Please*. I had nothing else to put. I sewed it shut with the small stitch, the one that does not show on a collar.

passages.heading: Friday, 22 December
passages.text:
He was to wait at the Mill door with the basket, as he always has. If you lose me, I have always told him, wait at the Mill door. I would leave the wheel at the Dusk bell. I would see the crescent go through his ticket with my own eyes and put his hand into the Conductor's.

That night torches went past the gap under the door. Hoods, flour sacks with holes cut in them. I put my hand over the boy's mouth, though he was not making a sound.

The bell, then the door, then the train.

passages.heading: Saturday, 23 December
passages.text: The sale was at Midday, at Harold's step. The list was on a board, and I read down it till I found my grandmother's brooch.

passages.heading: Gone.
passages.text:
I looked at the word. I had known it would be there, and it was there.

Then the Mill. The wheel goes round on the mere's tide, and we go round with it. By the middle of the afternoon the storm had taken the light. The windows went brown, then grey, then nothing, and the lamps were lit at three. I kept my eyes on the door. The bell would ring Dusk at its hour, and I would go.

The whistle went.

Not the bell. The whistle: one long, two short. Pruett takes his train out by the dark and not by anybody's bell, and the storm had brought the dark early.

I let go of the bar and ran. Somebody shouted my line after me. The boy was at the Mill door with the basket, where I had told him to be. I pulled the basket off him and dropped it, and took his hand, and we ran the square with the snow coming sideways and every lamp a smear.

passages.heading: Gone.
passages.text:
The platform was bare boards. Down the line, going away, were the lit windows, four, five, yellow in the snow, and the red lamp behind them. In one window a passenger sat with a case held on the knees in both arms, the way you hold a thing that is heavy. Then the snow took the windows, and then it took the red lamp.

The Rules of Carriage say it does not wait. It does not.

Then the Dusk bell rang at its proper hour, over nobody.

The bell rang Dusk for a train that had gone.

passages.heading: Sunday, 24 December
passages.text:
There is no Sunday service. There never has been. So nothing was wrong yet, and I told him so, and I told myself. Monday.

At first light Agnes came down the Row with her arm in its sling and called the stone at every door before anyone could ask. She called it at ours too. I heard it through the wood. It was not ours. I will not put it down here.

I kept him in his coat all day, buttoned over the lining, and he slept in it. I sat with my hand on the hem, over the stitches.

Monday.

passages.heading: Monday, 25 December
passages.text:
No whistle at dawn.

I stood behind the door with the boy and listened. The only thing I heard was Clem at the pump, reading Schedule B to whoever came out, though nobody was meant to come out.

*Station Rush. Dawn, on the Train's whistle. The square opens. The platform opens.*

passages.heading: No whistle," Clem said. "So.
passages.text:
He did not finish it. He read it again.

So the square had not opened, not since Saturday's Dusk. In law it was still Saturday night out there.

And still the Clerk came up the Row at Midday with his box, because rent is due on a Monday and the Company does not keep Christmas. He did not knock at the doors where the stoves were cold. He stood at them with his pencil and wrote something against each one. The boy said afterwards it was *forfeit*. He had seen the shape of the word.

Then the Mill took me. The Shift keeps its hour even when the Station Rush keeps none.

Our Christmas was a heel of bread. Peg had it off a loaf at Crumb's back door when Tamsin turned round, and the boy brought it to the Mill in the basket. Between turns I came out, and we ate it on the wheel-house step, half each, his half bigger. He asked if it was Christmas at the junction. I said it was Christmas everywhere. I did not know if that was true.

passages.heading: No whistle," Clem said. "So.
passages.text: The square had not opened, and still the Mill took me.

passages.heading: Tuesday, 26 December
passages.text:
The rule keeps the door. That much I had. If the square has not opened, the Indebted keep in, and I keep in twice over. It is the Company's rule, and it had kept me this far.

So I stayed behind the door until the Mill. And I did not scrub my step. I have scrubbed it every morning since I have had a step, through the cough, through the pine. But it is outside the door, and outside had not opened.

The lean-to door stayed shut all that week. I did not knock on it.

At Dusk I watched through the gap. They came past the pump without lanterns, one and then another a hand's length behind, and nobody spoke. They went off the end of the Row toward the Fenwood and the Gallery mouth. Next door's stove went out, and nobody lit it again.

The Row, by morning:

passages.heading: Tuesday, 26 December
passages.text:
Third door, step not swept.
Fifth door, step not swept.
Seventh door, open, and the stove cold.
Mine.

The mud came up over my step, and I let it.

passages.heading: Wednesday, 27 December
passages.text:
Agnes told it at the pump that morning: what the sermons on the chapel step had turned into. Debts were not forgiven any more. They were called in.

At Dusk something in the Vicar's robes came down Pump Row. I watched it through the gap: a black hem, wet to the knee, going door to door. It knocked, stood, and knocked again.

It knocked at mine.

I put my back to the wood. The boy held the basket in both arms, the empty basket, as if I had told him we were going for washing.

Through the door it told me my debt. The pine, so many feet at the rate, with the rope separate. It gave the sum to the penny, the Company's own sum, the one on my line in the Clerk's hand, the one I work in my head at the copper every night because I can't afford the paper. It said it kindly, the way you would give out a hymn number.

passages.heading: Wednesday, 27 December
passages.text:
I did not answer. The hem stayed in the gap under the door a long time. Then it went on to the fifth door.

It knew the sum. Only the Clerk knows the sum.

passages.heading: Wednesday, 27 December, late
passages.text:
The rule did not keep the door. The law was never going to open this square for me, not ever, not for the Indebted.

So it would be the first whistle, at whatever hour it came, Mill or no Mill, curfew or none. At the first whistle we would go. If the long coats wanted me, they could have me on the platform once he was aboard.

We lay down in our coats against the door, the boy inside my arm. I told him: at the first whistle you get up, and you go.

Before I lay down, I went one step's width out into the dark with the brush and the cold water and scrubbed the step. Just once, but properly. I wanted it clean when we left it.

I left it clean.

passages.heading: Thursday, 28 December
passages.text:
The whistle came in the night.

It was half a step flat, long and flat, the way Arthur used to whistle the Dusk out every night on the platform until his brother told him to quit. Arthur was buried last winter.

I was asleep. I had told the boy the first whistle. He was up and gone before my eyes were open, and the door stood wide on the black.

I went after him across the square, the square that had not opened. There were no lamps but the Lamplighter's. Snow lay on everything, and his prints went through it, small and straight, to the platform.

He stood at the edge of the boards under the one lit post, with the basket on his arm. There was no train. The rails went off into the dark, filling up with snow.

Past where the light reached, along the line, something was standing. It was as tall as a man, or taller, and as still as a post that is not a post. I did not look at it long enough to say what it was. I have never been sorry for that.

passages.heading: Thursday, 28 December
passages.text:
I picked him up. He is too big to carry. I carried him.

A whistle can lie. I had told him it could not.

passages.heading: Friday, 29 December
passages.text:
The real whistle came at first light, far off and then not far: one long, two short, and in tune.

I had his hand before I had my shawl, and I did not let go of it from my door to the platform, not once. Behind us the Row came out, the ones who were left.

The train pulls into the station. That is what you say here, and it did. The engine came in, then the cars, then the private car at the back, with the snow sliding off its roof in sheets.

I had it worked out. I would put him aboard now, at the Rush, with the ticket in his lining, and sit with him in the cold car with my hand on his until the Midday bell. Then the Mill. I would not see it go, because the Indebted never do. But I would have seen him on it.

passages.heading: Friday, 29 December
passages.text: I had his hand.

passages.heading: The same morning
passages.text:
Pruett stood in the door of the private car with his punch in his hand. He did not use it. He stood aside.

A man stepped down into the fog. He had the Vicar's face, the dead Vicar's; everyone in HollowMere knows that face. He carried a staff of black iron, crooked at the top like a shepherd's and taller than he was.

The light on him lay flat, like the last of the sun lying on a pail of water, and there was too much of it. The fog went back off him all round, the way steam goes back off a pan when you lift the lid.

I do not know what my hand did. I know what the boy's did. It went out of mine. He did not pull or tug. It was in mine, and then it was not, the way water goes out of a cloth.

passages.heading: The same morning
passages.text:
He went up the square after the light. They all did: the crew, the Row, the ones who had sat with their hands in their laps since the Monday before, all walking after it in the snow. The ticket was still sewn in his coat.

I called his name, once.

I went after him and could not get through. It was all backs and shoulders, everyone facing the one way. The light went in at the Telegraph Room door, to the Clerk's counter, and the crowd pushed in behind it as far as it could and stood. I lost him there. I saw a cap, and then I didn't.

He did not look back. He was looking at the light.

passages.heading: Midday to Dusk
passages.text:
He knows it: if you lose me, the Mill door.

So at the Midday bell I went where the Mill takes the Indebted, because that was where he would be.

He was not at the door. There was no basket.

I went in and took the bar, and I watched the door all afternoon. Each time it opened, it was someone else.

Dusk came at its hour. There was no storm. For the first time in ten days the sky was clear at the edges, a strip of green-white over the pines.

The whistle went: one long, two short, in tune.

From the wheel, for the second time, I heard the train go out. I do not know if he was on it. The ticket is in his coat, and the coat is on him, or on a peg somewhere in the light. Nobody punched it that I saw. Nobody would tell me if they had.

passages.heading: Midday to Dusk
passages.text:
The bell rang Dusk.

Keep to the light, I told him, every morning of his life. And don't miss the train.

works.title: The Last Dance at the Hall
