works.blurb: Lady Day, Monday 25 March 1793: the Committee of the Common Loaf orders the Gallery's ball kept "as anciently used", with the south doors open on Gallows Square and every dance card already filled in red; Isaure de Lanvaux, seventeen, of a cadet line, dances to her absent brother's empty place, reads the same twelfth line on every card ("The last dance. Beside the Hearth. At the ferry."), learns that the Hall is seated at dawn from the platters, nearest the Hearth first, and moves her own platter past kind Thibault Lormeau's; at dawn she dances the last dance with him while the Razor is put together beside the Hearth.

passages.heading: The Notice
passages.text:
The notice went up at noon on Lady Day, in red.

Isaure read it in Gallows Square on her father's arm. The fog was coming off the stones in strips. The board was the old board, with the old nails, and the hand on it was the Committee's.

> *The Ball of the Gallery, on the night of Lady Day, is retained, as anciently used. The consort to play from the gallery stair. The great south doors of the Hall to stand open on Gallows Square, so that the Square may see. The attendance of the Gallery is required, and counted.*
>
> *For the Committee of the Common Loaf.*

Under it, in the same red, smaller:

> *On the Morning Ferry: a crate, for the Committee.*

She knew the words *required, and counted*. When she was small they were printed on the Council's notice for a Fire, about the Commons, every time there was one. She had learned to read partly from that notice.

passages.heading: The Notice
passages.text:
The words were turned round now. She thought that was the whole point of them.

A truce, then. They had taken the Hall, and the leaf off the rims, and the chairs. They had taken the old order of the platters and stood it on its head. Now they wanted to see the Gallery dance, and the Gallery would dance, and the Square would watch, and nobody gets hurt by being watched. It was a way of saying the thing was over.

The crate would be type for the press, or chairs, or one of the Committee's new bells. They would not have the money for anything else.

Her father read it twice. He had gout in both feet and leaned on her more than he meant to.

"Anciently used," he said, and laughed, and did not stop.

passages.heading: I to III
passages.text:
At dusk the Aboyeur carried a loaf down the Hall and set it on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal. He called no name. The ball was reckoned from it, as every night is.

The Gallery came in at the cold end.

That was where the gilded platters stood now, by the great south doors, a row of silver with the rims scraped bare. The leaf had come off in the dish pit and gone to the Counting-House by weight. Each platter still had its loaf on it under its cloche, for the morning. The Gallery stood among them in its good clothes. There were no chairs. Her father found the wall and put his back to it.

She counted the candles. She always did. On fog nights as a child she had counted them to know how long the light would last, and she had never stopped.

passages.heading: I to III
passages.text:
Sixty-one.

By the door a clerk had chalked a slate: *Candles, 61.* Issued by count. Enough for one night and not a stub more.

The same clerk gave out the cards.

They were the old cards, cream, with a pencil on a silk cord. The pencils had been cut off. The cords hung down with nothing on them.

The cards were already full.

Every dance, I to XII, and against every number a partner, in red. Her first three were men she had known all her life, written in a hand that did not know them. Across the foot of the card:

passages.heading: Not to be amended.
passages.text:
All right, she thought. A truce does not write your partners in for you. So this was not a truce.

It was humiliation, though, not harm. For two hundred years the Gallery had put the Commons in a rope pen beyond the doors. Now the Commons put the Gallery on a card. A card was paper. It had never hurt anyone.

So she would dance it well.

If they wanted to watch the Gallery, she would show them what they had been looking at all those years. She stood up straight. The consort struck up on the gallery stair, hautboys and a viol, the same consort that had always played, and the set formed.

The first went cleanly. The second. The third.

The south doors were open, and the Square stood beyond them in the fog. It did not make a sound. She could see faces at the edge of the light, and the shoulders of the ones behind, and the dark past them that was the rest of the island.

passages.heading: Not to be amended.
passages.text:
At the end of the third she turned and curtsied to the doors. The old Order had the accused bow to the gallery, once, lower than to the Hearth.

Nobody told her to.

passages.heading: IV. A minuet. Aymeric de Lanvaux, in absence.
passages.text:
Her brother.

He had taken the ferry in the autumn of '89, a week after the news came, without telling her, because she was thirteen and would have told their father. The Committee judged the platter, since it could not judge the man. His Wake Loaf went to the Hearth in his place, and the Aboyeur called his name as it passed. She had been in the Square for it. Required, and counted.

The set formed for the minuet, and it had holes in it.

Six. Wherever a card named someone who had taken the ferry, or someone the Hearth had already had, there was a space on the floor the width of a person. The dancer opposite the space danced to it.

She danced to hers.

She bowed to nothing and rose. At the turn she gave her hand to the air at the height of his hand. She went down the set beside nobody and kept the distance a partner keeps.

passages.heading: IV. A minuet. Aymeric de Lanvaux, in absence.
passages.text:
The Square laughed.

It was not cruel laughter, or not only. It sounded surprised, like people who have never seen a thing and find it funny. Then, at the end, it applauded. Applause had always belonged between courses, at the Gallery's suppers with the doors open, and the Square had been at enough of those to learn when to clap.

She could not dance well. Nobody can dance a figure well with a hole in it. Grace needs someone to be graceful toward. The Square could see that, and that was what it had come to see.

Still, she thought. It was mockery of the dead. Aymeric was wherever the ferry had taken him. In law he was ash already, and the dead cannot be hurt. The cards were about the past. They were the Committee's way of reading out the Gallery's debts.

She put her hand flat on her bodice. Under the silk was her first card, from Lady Day of '89, with one dance filled in, in his hand, because nobody else had asked her and he would not let her stand out.

passages.heading: IV. A minuet. Aymeric de Lanvaux, in absence.
passages.text: She found she had kept time for two.

passages.heading: V to VI
passages.text:
Thibault Lormeau was not in absence.

He was her partner for the sixth. He was older than her father had been at her birth, unhurried, and slightly behind the beat in a way that made the beat seem wrong. He smelled of the bread he never finished. Everyone knew he did not eat his crusts. He kept them for the gulls.

Between figures he showed her his card. Then he took hers, gently, and turned it over to the last line.

They were the same. He had checked others. Every card in the Gallery had the same twelfth line.

*XII. The last dance. Beside the Hearth. At the ferry.*

No partner.

She looked past him to the Hearth.

Two Guild carpenters were kneeling on the flags beside it. One had chalk. The other had the brass finger-breadth from the Counting-House, the High Chancellor's measure, the one the Committee kept. They were marking out a square.

passages.heading: V to VI
passages.text:
So the cards were not about the past. The last dance was for the living. The crate was not type or chairs. It was for that square.

Everyone on the rock knew what had been done in Paris in January. The ferry had brought that too.

She found the one shelf left.

It would be for the great houses. For the platters that had stood nearest the Hearth for four hundred years, and the houses of the first rank, four finger-breadths of rim. The Committee would want those first, and loudly. Not a cadet line. Not two finger-breadths, scraped.

The carpenters measured the square twice, and wrote the number down.

passages.heading: Supper
passages.text:
At midnight the supper went out.

It came down from the gallery the way it always had, course by course, on the Gallery's own plate, and then it went on past the Gallery, through the south doors and into the Square. The Square ate it standing. She could hear the silver on the cobbles when someone set a dish down.

The Gallery got one loaf on a board. Red crust. Bread of the Committee's bake.

Thibault broke the crust off his share and put it in his coat.

passages.heading: For the gulls," he said. "In the morning.
passages.text:
She went to the stenographer's desk.

It was below the gallery rail, where it had always been. The stenographer had always been there. At every Fire of her childhood the same head bent over the same book, and nobody looked at it, because nobody looks at the person who writes things down.

She spoke loudly enough for the doors to hear. If the Square heard it said, it would be true.

"The cards are by precedence. The great houses first."

The stenographer did not look up.

"Who wrote them?" she said.

passages.heading: By precedence.
passages.text:
"As the platters stand. Nearest the Hearth first. As the cloches were always lifted."

That was all.

She knew how the platters stood. Everyone did. The Committee had moved them in its first spring, reading out each step from the Ordinances in red. The gilded platters were now at the cold end, in the order of their old nearness, turned round: what had been nearest the Hearth was farthest. The Vane platter stood right by the doors, last of all, because the Mother has no other hand. The cadet lines, which had always been at the far end of the gold, stood now on the Hearth side of it.

Nearest the Hearth first.

"And the Hall is seated again at dawn," the stenographer said, to the book. "From the platters."

She went back to the cold end and counted the platters between hers and the Hearth, the way she counted candles.

passages.heading: By precedence.
passages.text: Three.

passages.heading: VII to IX
passages.text:
She danced the seventh and the eighth by the card and did not hear them.

The ninth ended. The Square applauded, and every head at the doors turned to its hands to clap. The polisher had just gone past, a Commons woman, one of the Hall's polishers now. She went down the row with her cloth and breathed on each scraped rim as she passed, because the Committee had written that she could. She was at the far end.

Isaure picked up her own platter.

Silver, her loaf on it, the cloche over the loaf. It was heavier than it looked and lighter than it should have been. She carried it one platter's length toward the south doors, past the platter of the house of Lormeau, and set it down on the other side.

Silver on stone. Very quietly.

It was the oldest crime in the Ordinances, a platter moved. For the Commons it had been one copper and a night's tokens the finger-breadth. She had moved hers the other way, toward the cold, toward the fog and the Square, away from the fire.

passages.heading: VII to IX
passages.text:
She told herself he was kind and would have offered.

She told herself he was older and had had more of it.

She did not tell herself anything about the gulls.

She looked down at the platter where she had put it. By her own hand. Two finger-breadths of rim, scraped, and still a little warm from her palms.

passages.heading: X to XI
passages.text:
Thibault had seen.

She knew it from the tenth, from how carefully he took her hand when the figure brought them together, as if it might be hurt. He did not go to the row. He did not move the platter back. He did not look at it again.

At the end of the eleventh he bowed to her.

"The twelfth has no partner," he said. "May I?"

The old etiquette lets a gentleman ask for any dance left unfilled. Nobody had ever asked her for one.

She could not say no to him now. So she said yes.

She was counting on the ferry. *At the ferry*, the card said. The ball ended when the ferry came. If the boat came in before the twelfth was called, the twelfth would never be danced, and she would never have to stand opposite him beside the Hearth.

She had three candles left by her count.

passages.heading: X to XI
passages.text: The ferry had never once been early.

passages.heading: XII
passages.text:
It was not early. It was on time.

Grey came into the doorway first, and then the bell from the Wharf, and then a sound from the Square like a crowd taking one breath. Through the south doors she watched the crate come up from the water. Four dockhands carried it on their shoulders through the Square and in at the doors, past the dancers, the stencil on its side turned to the room: *for the Committee*. They set it down beside the chalked square. The carpenters were already there with their tools.

Nobody ended the ball.

Nobody told the consort to stop.

At the sixth bell the Iron-Wardens let one man off the floor. Évariste Vane had not danced all night. He crossed the Hall to the sub-basement door, holding his feeding hand a little away from his coat, and went through it, and down the ninety-one steps to the Mother. She has no other hand. The door closed behind him.

passages.heading: XII
passages.text:
The rest of them were kept.

The twelfth was called.

She danced it with Thibault beside the chalked square.

Behind him the carpenters took the crate apart. Boards came off. They stood the uprights up and made them fast. Something went across the top. Something heavy was lifted with a rope and a word from the older carpenter. With each figure the thing beside the Hearth stood a little taller, and the Hearth's light lay along one side of it.

The Razor.

The viol played in a major key. By the old article the consort played nothing in a minor key before a sentence, and nobody had read a sentence.

The Square applauded between figures. It had learned that too.

Her last counted candle went out at the turn. After that the only light was the Hearth, and the fog coming grey through the doors, and the two together made no shadows.

passages.heading: XII
passages.text: At the last turn Thibault pressed something into her glove. The crust from his coat.

passages.heading: For the gulls," he said. "In case.
passages.text:
No candles. No chairs. No one to say stop.

Music.

passages.heading: Coda
passages.text:
At dusk the Aboyeur carried a loaf down the Hall and set it on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal. He called no name. The night was reckoned from it.

The stenographer had seated the Hall again at dawn, walking the row with the plan while the carpenters finished. At dusk the ushers followed the paper. They read the gilded platters off as they stood, nearest the Hearth first.

passages.heading: Lanvaux.
passages.text:
Thibault's name went before hers because his platter now stood nearer the Hearth than hers. She had put it there one place ahead of her, a platter's length, by her own hand, and nothing on the paper said a platter had been moved.

She lifted her own cloche. Under it was her loaf, cold, for the morning. She took the card from her bodice, cream, Lady Day of '89, one dance filled in her brother's hand. She laid it on the loaf and set the cloche back over both.

The thing beside the Hearth had been finished at noon. The consort was gone from the stair.

She still had Thibault's crust in her glove. She had not gone to the window with it. She did not know what the gulls ate when no one fed them.

The next night had begun, and the platters stood where she had put them.

works.title: Three Heirlooms, Low Tide
works.pov: first person (Cyril and Nora's daughter, about thirteen), in her father's tide book
works.blurb: the V1.5 Thief, seen by Cyril and Nora's daughter, who keeps her drowned father's tide book and checks his marks against the water at the ferry post: a dark coat with its thumb on the door notch nobody outside the family knows, Gert's brooch and Agnes's ring gone at the low waters, a lie to the Detective to keep the book, the coat at her window asking for it, the two heirlooms left on her sill on Christmas morning; at the first door low she reads the hour aloud and hands over all three grandmothers' things, and on the 27th finds a stranger's blue thumb on the notch.

passages.heading: Three Heirlooms, Low Tide
passages.text:
*Wednesday 13 December. Low water 10.15, night. Father's mark: short.*

My grandmother started the book the first winter the mere kept a tide. Her hand is on the first pages, in ink, small and leaning. After that it's my father's, in pencil, because pencil doesn't run when the book gets wet. Mine comes in after the twenty-ninth of November.

I don't write tides in it. I check them. At every low he marked I take the book and the lantern down to the ferry post and see whether he was right. When he was, I write *true* in the margin.

He has been right every time.

That night my mother was on the dock behind me with the nets, whistling the two notes. High, then low. Then the wait, where his used to come.

The ferry post has the tar line on it, where Tuck ties up. Everybody knows the tar line. A hand's breadth below it my father cut a notch with his knife, and nobody knows the notch. It's ours. If the water stops above it, the book says *short*. If it goes under, the book says *under*, and on the furthest nights of all it says *door*.

passages.heading: Three Heirlooms, Low Tide
passages.text:
Somebody was at the post.

It was a dark coat, at the edge of my light. Not in the light, just where it gives out. Its thumb was on the notch.

I stopped on the boards. The coat didn't take its thumb away. It was watching the water the way my father watched it, not the way Tuck does. Tuck looks at the tar line. This was looking lower.

The water went down slowly, as if it was thinking about it. It stopped a hand short of the notch. Short, the way the book said.

The coat took its thumb off and went along the bank toward the cave side, not hurrying. It never looked at my light. That was how I knew it had seen it.

When I got to the post there was blue on the tar, right on the notch. It was a smear, the kind a thumb leaves when it has been leaning on the chart at the Lantern, where the circle never seems to be dry.

passages.heading: Three Heirlooms, Low Tide
passages.text:
Pell, I thought. Pell checks his skiff at low water, and Pell leans on the Lantern wall like everybody does.

I wrote *true* against the hour, and under it, *Pell*.

---

*Thursday 14 December. Low water 11.05, night. Father's mark: short.*

At the pump in the morning it was Harold's shelf.

Gert's brooch was gone off it in the night. That was the jet one, with her grandfather's hair plaited under the glass, and it had been her grandmother's. Nothing else was touched, not the ring beside it.

Gert came down the Row with her boy behind her carrying the empty basket. She had scrubbed her step already. She went and stood at Harold's window and looked at the place where it had been.

The Row had it settled before my bucket was full. The Killer takes keepsakes now, they said. It takes something off you so it can remember you.

passages.heading: Three Heirlooms, Low Tide
passages.text:
At the dock I asked Tuck whether Pell had been out at the low.

"Pell?" Tuck said. "Pell's been abed since Sunday with his chest. I took him his water."

I put my thumb on the notch. There was no blue on it now. The damp had had it in the night.

So it wasn't Pell. I had written *Pell* in my father's book and it was wrong, and I rubbed it out. Whoever it was knew the notch, and stood at it the same low water Gert's brooch went.

The coat at the notch took Gert's brooch. I knew it the way you know a net is torn before you find the tear.

The town has a word ready for anything that goes in the night. I didn't have the word. What I had was a coat.

---

*Friday 15 December. Low water 11.55, morning. Father's mark: short.*

So I read the book back, and not for the hours this time. I was looking for why anybody would want the notch.

passages.heading: Three Heirlooms, Low Tide
passages.text:
It's in my father's pencil. Twice a moon there's one word beside two nights of the big low: *door*. Never more than two nights. It's always the second night of the run and the fourth. I'd always read it as his word for the furthest under. I never thought it was a door to anything.

I turned forward. The next run starts on Christmas Eve. *Door* stands against Christmas night, and *door* against Wednesday the twenty-seventh.

At the morning low I walked the bank, out along the channel past where the boats are drawn up, to the cave mouth, where the old iron gate is chained across. Through the bars, at the back, is the place where the mere goes in under the rock. The town calls it the sea door. There's no sea. There are boards nailed across where the water runs in under the stone. Nobody goes near it, because of the cave.

passages.heading: Three Heirlooms, Low Tide
passages.text:
The water was down, and from the bars I could see the boards all the way to the bottom one. The bottom two hung wrong. Somebody had loosed them and set them back. That was all there was to see, and you'd have had to be looking.

On Saturday night Reg didn't come out of the Tin Gallery. The cave takes people. That's all I'll say about the cave.

On Saturday Harold paid Gert what the brooch was worth out of his own drawer, and the Row knew it by noon.

I sat on my bed with the book and worked it out the way my mother works a net, one hole at a time. It was a thief. A thief that took a brooch already pawned, and now paid for besides, so Gert had her money and nobody was hurt. A thief who takes only what is already lost, and goes out by the sea door on Christmas night, and is gone.

passages.heading: Three Heirlooms, Low Tide
passages.text:
A thief that goes is a thief gone. I wrote that in the back of the book as well.

---

*Tuesday 19 December. Low water 3.15, morning. Father's mark: short. Storm.*

The storm came in on Monday night and shut the coach road. I didn't go down to the post. You couldn't stand on the boards. I lay listening to the water, and it never went down. The storm held it up against the boards. It was the first time the book was wrong, and it wasn't my father's fault.

At first light Agnes came down the Row with her arm still bound up from the wolf. She called the stone at every door, the way she does, before anyone could ask. Then she called something else.

passages.heading: My grandmother's ring.
passages.text:
She said it the way she said the stone's name.

It had hung on a nail over her bed, she said, because she couldn't get it over her knuckle any more. In the night it went. She had been asleep. Nothing else in the room was touched. Her shawl was still on the chair and her scrip was still in the jug.

It had stood over her. It had wanted only the ring.

By noon the Row had barred its doors. The Killer comes in now, they said. It stands over your bed, takes a keepsake and leaves you. Nobody said why it leaves you. Nobody wanted to.

I sat with the book open at the page where I'd written *a thief who takes only what is already lost*. Agnes's ring hadn't been lost. Nobody had pawned it, and nobody had paid her for it. It was taken from a sleeping house, at the low water, the one night the book was wrong.

passages.heading: My grandmother's ring.
passages.text:
I didn't rub that line out. I left it there, so I'd have to look at it.

---

*Wednesday 20 December. Low water 4.30, afternoon. Father's mark: short.*

I took the book up to the Constable's under my shawl. I was going to tell. I had it all ready: the coat, the notch, the boards, the two nights.

The Constable was out. The Detective was at the desk, the one there is now, who kept time at the railyard once and still carries the watch. On the blotter there was a stamp, inked, and a file with nothing in it.

"What's that?" he said.

passages.heading: Can I see it?
passages.text:
He held out his hand. There was blue down the side of his thumb, the chart's blue. Anybody who leans on the Lantern wall gets it.

"I'd want to keep it a while," he said. "Check it against the chart. You'd have it back."

I looked at the stamp. I looked at the file with nothing in it. My father's book would go into that file. Somebody would check it against the chart at the Lantern, where my father went out at the circle on the twenty-ninth, and they'd write a word on it. The word would be short.

"Does anything move on the water," he said, "at the circle?"

passages.heading: No.
passages.text:
He wrote it down.

I took the book home under my shawl. I'd lied to the Detective to keep it, and now nobody in HollowMere knew the door lows except me and the coat.

He wrote down *no* the way my father wrote *true*.

---

*Sunday 24 December. Low water 7.50, night. Father's mark: under. First night of the run.*

The last train went out at dusk on Saturday with several people on it. I didn't go to see who. The long coats stood along the platform and looked at anybody carrying anything. The coat wasn't on the train. I knew that without going. A thing that wants a door doesn't take a train.

Two of the long coats had been carried down from the cave side since Thursday. The second one was Saturday, at the low. The pump didn't say how.

At the sale on Saturday my mother bought Ivy Cotter's lantern off Harold's list for the dock. She paid three times what was lent. So he can see where I am, she said. On Christmas Eve she sat out on the dock with it lit and the nets across her knees, and whistled.

passages.heading: No.
passages.text:
I was at the window with the book. Out there the water was going under the notch. The book said *under* for tonight: under, but not far enough. Not *door*. Not yet.

The coat came up out of the dark at the edge of her light, where the light stops. My mother didn't turn round. She was whistling.

It came and stood at my window. I couldn't see a face, only the coat, and a sack with something in the bottom of it.

"You told him no," it said.

I didn't say anything.

"Three things that were somebody's grandmother's," it said. "And the sea door, at low water."

It said it like a list it had said before, to somebody else.

passages.heading: I have two.
passages.text: It looked past me at the table, at the book.

passages.heading: That one was your grandmother's.
passages.text:
The window was open a crack for the lamp smoke. It could have had the book off the table before I turned round. It didn't reach for it.

"No," I said, and shut the window.

On the other side of the glass it waited exactly as long as the water waits at the bottom of a low before it turns. Then it went.

---

*Monday 25 December. Low water 8.40, night. Father's mark: door.*

On Christmas morning there was a twist of paper on the sill, outside the shut window.

It smelled of saltpetre and match-heads. I opened it on the table.

Inside was a jet brooch with a plait of grey-brown hair under the glass. There was a ring too, thin, worn flat on one side where a hand had worked in it.

Gert's. Agnes's.

My first thought was to carry them back. Up the Row, and knock.

But every door on the Row was barred against a Killer who takes keepsakes. Anybody knocking on Christmas morning with Gert's grandmother's brooch in her hand would be the Killer. That's how the Row would count it. It's how I would have counted it.

passages.heading: That one was your grandmother's.
passages.text:
I had told it no, and now my no was lying on the table in a twist of paper.

I put them in the net locker, under the spare floats at the bottom, where my mother doesn't go any more. The brooch and the ring were hidden in our house now. My no couldn't keep me out of it.

Two grandmothers in our house, and mine in the book on the table.

---

passages.heading: Later.
passages.text:
At eight my mother came in off the dock, hung the lantern on its hook and sat down by the fire with her hands in her lap. I took the lantern down again. She didn't ask. She hasn't asked anything since the twenty-ninth.

I had the book under my arm. The brooch and the ring were in the twist, in my fist. I'd been the one keeping them hidden in our house all day, and I couldn't keep them there another night.

The coat was at the post, at the edge of the light.

I opened the book to the page, my father's pencil. *Door*, and the hour.

"Twenty to nine," I said.

That was all. It nodded. We both watched the water.

It went past the tar line, then past the notch, and it kept going. I had never seen it so far down. The channel stones came up out of it black.

passages.heading: Later.
passages.text:
I held out the twist and it took it. Then I held out the book.

That was where I chose. Nobody made me. The brooch and the ring had gone out of my hands the minute I let them into the house. But the book was mine, and I held it out.

It put all three in the sack. Three grandmothers' things.

"Nobody's hero," it said. Or that's what I remember it saying.

It had the book now. It had the hour as well. The hour was the only thing I gave it that it couldn't have taken.

---

"Put that out," it said, meaning the lantern.

So I put it out. That was Ivy Cotter's lantern. It had sat unlit on Harold's shelf since October, and my mother had lit it every night since Saturday. I put it out on the boards.

It was dark. Then my eyes came.

passages.heading: Later.
passages.text:
The coat went along the bank toward the cave side. For a little while I could hear it on the stones, and then I couldn't.

Far round the water the Company's lamp hung at the Gate, where it has hung for a week now. I didn't look at it long.

Out on the marsh there were lights that aren't steady. I didn't follow them.

I stood at the post with my thumb on the notch. The water came back over my thumb and over the notch, and then over the tar line. Nothing came back along the bank.

Behind me the cottage door opened. My mother whistled the two notes from the dock, in the dark, because I had her lantern and it was out. High, then low. I didn't answer. I have never answered. They aren't mine to answer.

The water was over the door notch again, with the coat behind the sea door, and whatever is behind it was behind it.

passages.heading: Wednesday 27 December.
passages.text:
There's no heading for tonight. I haven't got the book.

I didn't need it. I've read his pencil on that page so many times I could see it on the ceiling. The fourth night, the second door, at twenty past ten.

My mother let me take the lantern. She lit it for me first.

The water went under the notch at twenty past ten, right on time. I was right without the book, and my father was right without me.

On the notch, under the lantern, there was a thumb. It was fresh and wet, with blue in it.

It wasn't mine. Mine were in my pockets.

Somebody had read the door notch tonight. It could have been the coat, come back for something it forgot. It could have been whoever circles the chart at the Lantern, because that's still circled every morning, coat or no coat. It could have been a man with a watch and blue down the side of his thumb, or anybody at all who leans on the Lantern wall. I've thought about it all night, and I can't make it come to one.

passages.heading: Wednesday 27 December.
passages.text:
I put my thumb on the notch beside it, so there were two. Then I went home and didn't tell anyone.

Tomorrow at the pump Agnes will call the stone. Somebody will say the Killer took Gert's brooch and Agnes's ring, and I'll fill my bucket. My mother let *drowned* stand. I can let *Killer* stand. It's a short word, and it's the one the town has.

The door lows come round again in a moon, the second night and the fourth. I know where they fall without the book, and whoever owns that thumb will want to know.

I wrote the hour on the back of my hand in pencil. Under it I wrote the one word of his I've got left.

works.title: The Cave Gate
works.blurb: the V2 Cave Gate from the town's side, 18 to 28 December 1893: the Clerk's slip adds a seventh post to the Lamplighter's round, a lantern on the iron gate across the cave mouth, VANE TIN CO in its crossbar; the lantern is found inside the bars with its glass black, an escort man is laid down dead against the gate where the water never came, a second is taken from the middle of nine lit lanterns, and her trade's one rule (a flame near at hand keeps you) turns over, until on the fourth night the padlock hangs open and she lights the Gate high, leaves the square's fourth lantern dark, and does not turn from the one who walks down to it.

passages.text:
Monday, 18 December 1893. Midday.

The slip was on her nail, under the hook where the oil can hung. It was Company paper in the Clerk's hand, pencil, with no fold in it.

*Post 7. The Cave Gate, below the fisher cottage. One lantern. Lit with the rest. Half again.*

The slip gave no reason, and she did not ask for one. She had never asked why a window was lit and never reported one, and she did not ask why a lantern was wanted. A lantern lit was scrip. A lantern dark was docked. That was the whole of her contract, and she understood it better than most people in the town understood theirs.

She read it twice. Then she counted on her fingers, because the slip had done a thing to her round without saying so. Platform, one. The square, two, three, four. The Gallows Wood edge, five. The manor gatepost, six. Then the Gate, seven. Then up the hill again to the fourth lantern of the square, over the chalk and the well, the one she always left for last.

The last lantern was the eighth now. The slip had not said that either.

At dusk the train stood at the platform with steam up. She filled the can at the barrel in the Lantern's back room, to the seam and no further, took the wick-pole and the short ladder, and went out to see the train go. It went, the way it always went, into the pines. *One.* Touch. Light. Touch. The square, the wood's edge, the manor gate. Then, for the first time, she went down past the tavern alley onto the shingle.

The town called it the sea cave. There was no sea. There was the mere, which kept a tide with no sea to keep it, and the hill, and the hole where the mere went into the hill. Everybody called the stones in front of it the shingle, as if a sea had left them there.

The Gate stood across the mouth.

It was iron, salt-bloomed, though there was no salt. The bars were set into the rock top and bottom. VANE TIN CO was cast into the crossbar in letters the size of a hand, and an old chain was wound twice through the bars and the post. A hook was already set at lantern height. Somebody had put it there before anyone wrote the slip.

Behind the bars the cave ran back into the dark. Cold air came out of it. It smelled of stone that has had water on the far side of it for a long time.

She hung the lantern on the hook. *Seven.* Touch. Light. Touch.

Across the water, low on the far edge of the mere, the new light came on, the Company's. She had heard at the pump that it would be lit tonight. There were two of them now. Neither was hers.

Up on the bank the fisher cottage had its shutters across. Nora's girl kept a book in there. Every morning she wrote down where the water stood. The whole shore knew it.

She went back up the hill to the eighth.

Seven posts. Half again for the seventh.

Tuesday, 19 December. Dawn.

The storm had held the water up all night. It was over the shingle to the foot of the Gate and in through the bars. At the pump they were saying the coach road was shut, which meant snow on the pass, which meant the road would stay shut.

She came down for her dawn round to trim the wicks and count.

The hook was empty.

The lantern was inside the bars. It lay on its side on a ledge of stone above the water, a body's length back from the Gate. It was whole. The glass had not cracked.

The glass was black.

Not soot. Something on it. Something dark and thick that lay on the glass and ran down it, and where it had run into the water below the ledge it sat on top of the water and would not mix, the way lamp oil lies on a puddle. It was not oil. She leaned in to the bars. It smelled of tin.

The bars were wide enough to let a lantern through.

She did not finish that thought.

She put the wick-pole through and hooked the bail, and drew it back along the ledge and through the bars. It came heavy and slow, and left a line in the dark stuff as it came.

She turned it in her hands. The wick was burned to the collar. The well was dry.

It had not spilled. It had burned down where it lay.

Tuesday, 19 December. Dusk.

The mere keeps a tide with no sea. Everybody in HollowMere knows that. There is a chart on the wall by the Lantern's door, an island chart, with the low water circled in ink. Some say the mere keeps to it and some say it only seems to, and she read the circle every dusk with her thumb under it either way.

Last night it had not been low water. Last night the storm had held the water up over the shingle and in through the bars.

So the water had come in. And the water had brought the leak with it. Everybody knew about the leak, too. The flooded gallery under the hill bled mere-rot into the marsh, and the mere-rot made the wolves bold, and it was black, everybody said so, black and stinking. The water had come up, and lifted the lantern off its hook, and floated it in, and set it down on the ledge, and the black had come up with the water and stuck to the glass.

The water moved it. The water blacked it.

She said it twice, under her breath, the way she said the posts.

She cleaned a second lantern at the barrel. At the Gate she found the wrack line from the storm, a line of weed and rot along the stones, the highest the water had come. She took the wire from her coat and hung the lantern from the crossbar on it, a hand above the wrack. Higher than any water in the town's memory had come.

*Seven.* Touch. Light. Touch.

The water, then.

Thursday, 21 December. Dawn. Low water.

The escort had a man on the Gate that night. She did not know whose idea it was. The Baron's long coats had been standing about the town since the Baron fell, nine of them and four dogs, waiting at the Clerk's counter to be told something. Somebody had told one of them something, or he had told himself. When she came down at dusk on Wednesday he was on the shingle with his own lantern and a dog, a big man in the long coat, standing where he could see both the Gate and the alley.

He nodded to her. She nodded back. She lit the seventh and went up.

At dawn the water was out. The shingle ran clean to the bars and past them, wet stones and pools.

The wire on the crossbar was wrung round on itself like a rag, and the lantern was gone off it. It was inside again. She could see it farther back this time, past the ledge, black.

He was against the bars.

On the outside. On his back, with his arms at his sides. Not fallen. A fallen man ends on his face. He had been put down, the way you put down a thing you mean to come back for. His own lantern stood upright beside his hand. Its glass was black. The black was on his coat, on the long coat, and on the stones round him.

From the bars to where he lay, and back, the shingle was scored. Drag marks. Long, in pairs.

The shingle there was dry. It was above the wrack line. She had stood on that spot on Tuesday to hang the wire.

The dog was at the top of the shingle where the planks began. It lay flat and would not come down. Another of the long coats came along the alley at a run, and stopped, and called to the dog, and the dog did not come. He called it by name.

It was a woman's name. Annie.

He went down to the man at the bars, and knelt, and said "Kearney," once, and nothing after it.

The water had never come up that far. She had hung the wire there herself.

Thursday, 21 December.

The boy brought the cart down with his shoulders in the shafts, and the Undertaker walked beside it with his hat off. They lifted Kearney. The long coat walked behind. The dog came as far as the top of the planks and then it came the rest of the way, close to the wheel.

She followed them up to the shed. She did not know why. Then she did: she wanted the word. Every thing in HollowMere had a word. Somebody would give her the word for this, and she would go home with it.

Doris had the water warm. She washed him. She always told the dead the news while she worked, the rate and the weather and who was barred. She did not tell him anything. She washed his face and his hands and said nothing at all.

The Undertaker unlocked the box under the cart seat and opened his book on the lid. She looked over his arm. The last column had a word at the head of it with a line ruled through. Under it, for the dead above, there was nothing.

"Two wounds," the Undertaker said, to nobody. That was all he said.

He did not write it.

At the pump by noon the town had its word without him. Wolves. The wolves had been bold all December. The mere-rot made them bold. A man alone on the shingle at night. Wolves.

She knew wolves better than anyone at that pump. She had walked among them every dusk for years. They came to the edge of the light and held there, and did not cross. She had stood still with her lantern lit and watched them go round her like water round a stone. A flame near at hand. That was the whole of the rule, and she had never seen it broken.

Kearney had had his lantern. It had been standing upright beside his hand.

She said nothing at the pump. She filled her bucket and went home.

It was the town's word. The town had no other, and neither did she. She let it stand.

Saturday, 23 December.

The last train went out at dusk. There were several people on it, and the town stood on the boards and watched them go. She stood with the pole up and lit the platform post as the last car cleared. Then there was only the sound of it going into the pines. Then not that.

The square would not open again until a train came back.

Low water was circled on the chart that night. The long coats knew it. They had been in the Lantern all afternoon, standing, the way they drank. When she came for the oil they were waiting by the barrel.

There were eight of them. They were going in after the wolf. They would go in at low water, when the floor was bare, and they would have it out of there or know why. They wanted light, a lantern each, and only hers were lawful after the train. They paid her for eight on top of her own, out of their own pockets, coin and not scrip.

Nine lanterns. She had never lit so many at once in one place.

On the square they stopped Norman, who was sitting on the pump step with his arm bound to his chest. Somebody said he was a tinner, he knew the hill, he could take them under.

Norman looked at the lanterns. He looked at her.

"Lost in the workings," he said.

He did not get up.

On the shingle the eight stood round the Gate with their lanterns raised, and one of them put a bar through the old chain and twisted it until a link gave. The chain came down off the bars in a heap. The Gate swung in a little way on its own weight and stopped, and they pushed it back to the rock.

They went in. She went in with them, because the lanterns were hers. A lantern lit was scrip, and nobody had said a word about a lantern carried.

At low water the floor of the cave was bare, wet rock and pools, running back and down. The light went before them on the walls. The dogs had not come. The long coats had left them at the planks.

They looked for fur. There was none. They looked for claw marks on the rock, the scoring a wolf leaves where it scrambles. There were none. There were the drag marks, long, in pairs, in the grit between the pools, and the black stuff in them, all of them going the same way. Back.

At the back of the cave was the sea door. The town called it that, though there was no sea for three hundred miles. It was boards, old, heavy, nailed across where the cave went on, and the water went out under them at low water through a gap at the foot.

The drag marks went to the boards and stopped at the foot of them.

The long coats stood there with their lanterns up and argued, low, about whether to take a bar to the boards.

One of them went off to the side, round a rock where the wall bellied out, to look. She heard him counting under his breath as he went. Cartridges. He did it with his thumb on the loops of his belt. Six, seven, eight. She knew that kind of count. She had one of her own.

The count stopped.

Two knocks. Dull, heavy, the way a man strikes a door with the heel of his hand. Two, and then nothing.

They went round the rock with nine lanterns and he was not there. His lantern was there, on its side, black.

They found him at the foot of the boards. They could not have missed him going round. He was on his back, arms at his sides, laid down. The black was on him.

Nobody said wolf.

They picked him up between four of them and ran with him, and she ran with them, ahead, with the light, because they could not run in the dark and the light was hers. Out through the Gate. Up the shingle. The Gate hung open behind them with its chain in a heap, and nobody went back to close it.

There had been nine lanterns in that cave, and no wolf.

Monday, 25 December.

No whistle at dawn. There was no train to whistle.

The Clerk went up the Row at Midday with his box all the same, because rent falls on a Monday and the Company does not keep Christmas. She heard about it at the pump. She did not see it.

By Sunday noon a new chain had come down from the Company stores with a new padlock on it, and the Gate was shut on the outfall again. The slip on her nail had not changed. *Post 7.*

She had thought about it all of Sunday, with her hands round a cup, and she had got it to lie down.

He had gone round the rock. He had stepped out of the others' light. One man with one lantern, alone, past the bulge of the wall, where the eight could not see him and he could not see them. And the eight who had stayed together, in the light of each other's lanterns, had come out. She had come out.

A flame near at hand. Not one flame. All of them, together.

It was the rule. It was only the rule, said bigger. The light kept the others. It had kept her.

At dusk she lit the platform with no train to light it for. On the square she turned every wick up as far as it would go, and stood at each post longer than she needed, with her hand on the iron after the second touch. The Gallows Wood edge, the manor gate. She went down to the Gate and turned the seventh up so high the flame stood in the glass like a finger. She did not look past it into the cave. She did not look at the back of the cave at all. She hung it and touched the post and went up.

The light kept the eight.

Tuesday, 26 December. Dawn.

She did her dawn count the way she always did, post by post, and wrote nothing down, because there was nothing to write on.

The Gate post. Lantern on its hook, glass clean, burned down. At the foot of the post, black. Smeared up the iron a hand's height.

The shingle. Drag marks, in pairs, out of the Gate and up the stones.

The planks at the top of the shingle. The black on the planks, in a line, going up.

The platform post, at the east end, the one nearest the water. Black at its foot.

The tavern alley. Doors dark all night. Nothing.

Pell's dock, dark all night. Nothing.

The square. Nothing. The fence. Nothing.

She stood at the platform post with her hand on the iron for a long time.

Two posts lit nearest the water, and the black at the foot of both. Not one dark door touched, not one dark step. Whatever came up off the shingle in the night had not wandered. It had gone from light to light.

She remembered then. It had been at the Lantern, weeks back, one of those things the town says that she had let go by her like the rest. That something sleeps in the cave. That it comes to a light and not away from one. She had heard it and thought nothing of it, because it was said the way the town said everything.

The wolves' rule, turned over.

Kearney with his lantern. The man round the rock with his lantern. Herself, with the wire.

She took her hand off the post.

Her posts were the light.

Tuesday, 26 December. Midday.

The Clerk's counter. The long coats were not at it. Seven of them stood out on the square now, in pairs, with the dogs.

She said she wanted the Gate post dark.

He did not ask why. He took the slip out of a drawer, the copy, the same hand as hers, and laid it on the counter, and laid the Schedule beside it.

"Only the Lamplighter's lanterns may be lit," he said. "Schedule B." He put his finger on the slip. "Post seven is on the schedule. A lantern left dark is docked."

passages.heading: Then dock it.
passages.text:
"Docked, at the rate. Half again." He wrote the sum in pencil on the edge of the slip and turned it round so she could read it. "Or you may resign the round. Anyone may."

The road was shut. There was no train. There was no work on the Grant that paid in anything but scrip, and her scrip went on oil, and on the rent, and on the line in his book with her name on it.

She looked at the sum.

He put the slip back in the drawer. That was all there was to it.

At dusk she lit the round, the Gate with it.

Lit or docked.

Wednesday, 27 December. Dusk. Low water, circled.

The fourth night since the last train. She had counted them without meaning to. Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, and this was the fourth dark since, coming on.

She went down the shingle with the can and the pole and the lantern.

The new chain hung straight down from the bars.

The padlock was open. It hung on the last link with its shackle up. She put her hand on it. Not broken. Not forced. Not cut. Turned. A key had turned it, or something had that did what a key does.

The Gate stood a hand open.

Inside, the pools were still. Nothing on them. Nothing moved on the walls. The cold came out of the cave the way it always did, and the smell of tin with it, stronger.

She stood with the lantern unlit in her hand.

It did not matter now what the Clerk would dock. There was nothing between the cave and the town but whatever she chose to light. Whatever she lit tonight, the Gate or the square or the platform, it would come to.

Wednesday, 27 December. Night.

She thought it through once, standing there, and then she did not think it again.

If she lit the town, it would come up to the town. Up the planks. To the platform. To the square. To the fourth lantern, over the chalk where the children played hopscotch, and over the well.

If she lit the Gate, it would come here.

She hung the lantern on its hook. She turned the wick all the way up, higher than the schedule asked, higher than she had ever turned a wick, until the flame stood tall and white in the glass and the light ran off the bars and out over the shingle and the water.

*Seven.* Touch. Light. Touch.

Then she went up. The platform, the square, the wood's edge, the manor gate, in their order. Up the hill to the fourth lantern, over the chalk and the well.

She stood under it with the pole.

She did not light it.

She had always come back to it last. She had come back to it every night she had ever kept the round. She stood under it with the pole up and the wick dark, and then she lowered the pole, and put her hand on the post once, and took it off.

She went back down to look at the Gate from the top of the shingle. She did not mean to go further than that.

Someone was coming down.

No lantern. Just walking, in the dark, down the planks from the alley and onto the stones, unhurried, the way you walk to a place you have been asked to. Toward the Gate. Toward the light.

They passed her close enough to touch. Neither of them said anything.

She did not turn.

She went up the planks, and up the alley, and she did not turn, and the light at her back threw her shadow up the alley ahead of her, long and thin.

Behind her, after a while: two knocks.

She did not turn.

Thursday, 28 December.

At dawn the Undertaker's cart was on the shingle. The boy was in the shafts. The Undertaker had his hat off. There was a box on the cart, nailed, and Doris walking beside it with her hand on the lid, telling it the news. The rate. The weather. The road still shut.

She did not look into the box. She did not ask the name. She went past on the planks with the can and did her count and came back up.

At Midday the Clerk counted her scrip out on the counter, to the penny. The platform, the square, the wood's edge, the manor gate. The Gate post, lit, half again. The fourth lantern of the square, dark, docked.

She counted it twice.

At dusk she filled the can at the barrel, to the seam and no further, for eight posts. The chart was on the wall by the door. She found the next circle with her thumb under it.

The square's lamps went on that night, one after another, in their order. The last of them was the fourth, over the chalk and the well.

Then she went down to the shingle.

The chain hung straight down. The Gate stood a hand open. She did not touch it. She hung the lantern on the hook and turned the wick up.

works.title: What the Lab Made
works.pov: close on the subject (Sawmill No. 3), as a cinematic treatment
works.blurb: the Project Man Eater special ending as a cinematic treatment, unlocked by a scientist's victory or the Secret Agent's enlistment: Sawmill No. 3, the man who asked every Friday whether the train had brought mail and thanked the clerk for looking, hears a low sound once on 18 November and walks toward it; in the lab under a house that is never named he fails a trial, eats the tray, grows long in the cold readings, wakes to his own hand tagged on a bench, says his name once and his word becomes the sound; at 0310 on 11 December he stands, a hand types WINDIGO on the blank form, and the film ends on a door too tall being hung in the North Dakota woods.

passages.heading: A treatment.
passages.text:
`SPECIAL ENDING — plays on: a scientist's victory. Or: the Secret Agent's enlistment, completed.`

---

passages.heading: COLD OPEN
passages.text:
Black.

`READING — ROOM: BELOW FREEZING. MAINTAIN.`

A pencil on camp paper, the grey furry kind that drinks the lead. Scratch. Scratch. Stop.

Cut.

---

**1. INT. COMPANY OFFICE — FRIDAY 14 NOVEMBER 1952 — 0700**

The counter. Two hands on it. The knuckles white, the skin across them tight and shiny as a drumhead.

The stove is lit behind the duty hand. Sawmill No. 3's breath shows anyway.

passages.heading: No.
passages.text:
He nods. He doesn't go. He stands with his hands on the wood like a man who has walked into a room and forgotten what for. His shirt hangs on him. Under it, the ribs. Crate slats under a sheet.

*The ration,* he thinks. *That's all it is. Measured. Nothing outside issue. A man gets thin on measured.*

passages.heading: And Fridays are slow. It's only late.
passages.text:
He finds what he came for. Nothing. "Thank you for looking."

The duty hand did not look. We see that he didn't.

At the door it comes up in him, the thing since the ration started. He ate at six. He is hungrier now than before he ate.

He puts that down to the ration too.

---

**2. INT. BUNKHOUSE, THE SAWMILL CREW'S ROW — TUESDAY 18 NOVEMBER — AFTER THE MIDNIGHT WHISTLE**

Dark. The count done. Ten men flat on ten boards. The morning's dust fire is still in the planks, in the blankets, in his hair.

Then, far off. Past the kilns, past the ridge, somewhere he has never been.

Once.

Low. Long. Breath drawn across the mouth of a bottle.

For one breath he is not afraid. It is the first breath in weeks that he hasn't been.

Then the hunger, and not the ration's. The ration's hunger sits in the belly and complains. This one stands up. It came after the sound, the way a dog's head lifts at a step it knows.

passages.heading: And Fridays are slow. It's only late.
passages.text:
So it was never the ration.

*Kiln wind,* he tells himself. *Wind in a flue.*

He lies on his side facing the wall the sound came through, and does not sleep.

*It called,* he thinks. He is ashamed of how glad that makes him.

---

**3. EXT. THE YARD / THE POND — THURSDAY 20 NOVEMBER — 2358**

Boots on, laced in the dark. Nobody wakes. Men here sleep shallow and all at once, and it is not yet the whistle.

Past the rack: his billet, 3, burned in pine. Past the pump. Out toward the pond and the broken trestle and the ridge, toward where it came from on Tuesday. Nothing is sounding tonight. He goes anyway. He was called once, and that is enough for the legs.

The whistle starts behind him.

It doesn't begin. It's there.

He counts it out of habit, walking away from it. One. Two. Three.

passages.heading: And Fridays are slow. It's only late.
passages.text:
The arc-light swings off the Foundry roof and comes down over the pond. It lies on the black water and waits.

Seven. Eight.

Hands. Out of the dark, from both sides. No face. No mask. No word.

Fourteen.

Black on fifteen.

---

passages.heading: 4. INT. THE LAB — LATE NOVEMBER
passages.text:
Cold.

Not yard cold. A cold that has been kept.

He is on his back on a cot. Above him are pine joists with planks across them: a house's floor, seen from underneath. Frost lies furred along the grain.

He sits up. He stands. There is a hand's width between his head and the joists.

Concrete. A bench. A ladder to a hatch. A door.

`READING — ROOM: BELOW FREEZING. MAINTAIN.`

A typed card lies on the cot where his chest was.

`A SUBJECT WHO WAKES IS OFFERED THREE TRIALS.`

He reads it twice. He is a sawyer. He reads a board twice before he cuts it.

He goes for the door.

Cut.

He wakes on the cot. The same joists, the same frost.

`TRIAL 1 — FAILED. RETURNED TO FIRST.`

Nobody tells him the rest. He works it out on the edge of the cot with his hands between his knees. Fail once and you start again. Fail twice in a row and there is no again.

passages.heading: 4. INT. THE LAB — LATE NOVEMBER
passages.text:
He doesn't say thank you. There is no one yet to say it to.

---

passages.heading: 5. INT. THE LAB — THE FRIDAYS
passages.text:
The tray comes down the ladder. Gloves bring it, grey rubber to the elbow. That is all we ever see of anyone who comes: gloves.

Meat. Dark. Cut thick. Not the mess hall's grey boil. Not anything he has had.

He knows what he means to do. One more try at the door is all he has before the closing, so it has to be the right one. Save it. Eat nothing he doesn't know. Keep his legs.

He doesn't ask whose it is. Nobody would say.

He eats it.

All of it, standing, with his fingers. The tray is clean, and he is hungrier than before he started. Hungrier after. Always after.

`RATION: TAKEN. RESPONSE: SEEKS MORE.`

Then, up through the ground, through the soles of his feet and into the planks overhead: the payroll train coming in. 0610.

Friday.

The gloves come back for the tray.

passages.heading: Mail?
passages.text: Nothing.

passages.heading: Thank you for looking.
passages.text:
The next Friday he doesn't look at the door. He looks at the hatch the tray comes down through.

---

**6. INT. THE LAB — READINGS — LATE NOVEMBER INTO DECEMBER**

The strips stack up, one over the next, none of them staying.

`WEIGHT — 104 LB (CAMP SHEET, LAST).`
`WEIGHT — DOWN.`
`LENGTH — UP.`
`TEMPERATURE — DOWN.`

What the strips mean:

Ribs, every one of them, through the skin.
Forearms longer than they were. Shins too.
On the cot his feet find the wall, so he lies with his knees up.
He stoops to sit. Then he stoops to stand.
Fingertips black. Not with dirt.
A rubber tube taped into the crook of his arm. The tape goes grey. Nobody changes it.
Lips thinned and drawn back. The teeth show at rest.
Knuckles like knots in a rope.

At night he writes the letter in his head, the way he used to write it on the back of a ration sheet with the carpenter's pencil from behind his ear.

passages.heading: Dear —,
passages.text:
*The food is better here. More of it, nearly. I am growing, if you can believe it, at my age. It's the cold does it. Cold sets a man long, same as a board left out in the frost. You've seen a board do that.*

He has seen boards warp and boards shrink. He has never seen one grow. He doesn't think about that part.

He believes the board.

---

**7. INT. THE LAB — FRIDAY 5 DECEMBER — 0610**

The train, through the ground.

He wakes to it and reaches for the edge of the cot to sit up. The left arm reaches, and there is nothing at the end of it to take hold.

The arm ends, wrapped. The wrap has gone brown.

On the bench, on an enamel tray, lies a hand.

His. He knows it by the nail he split on the head saw in October. Fingers black to the second joint. Skin drawn tight to the bone. Nails grown out long and yellow, longer than he ever let them grow. Tied round the wrist on string is a tag.

passages.heading: Dear —,
passages.text:
`SAWMILL 3.`

The gloves lift the tray, carry it to the ladder and take it up, out of frame.

`SPECIMEN — HAND, LEFT. TO COLD CABINET (INFIRMARY).`

So it was never the cold. The cold doesn't tie on a tag with a man's number.

*Dear —,* he starts, out of habit, in the dark of his head.

Then he looks at the stump. There is no hand to write it with.

---

passages.heading: 8. INT. THE LAB — THE NIGHTS AFTER
passages.text:
So he says it.

Out loud, to the joists, since there is nothing to write on and nothing to write with.

passages.heading: Dear —
passages.text:
The words come out wet and short. His mouth is wrong for them now; the lips don't meet where words want them to. "The food —" He loses it. He starts again and loses it again.

He tries something smaller. Something that is his.

passages.heading: Emmett.
passages.text:
His own name, said to the planks once, to keep it. It sounds like somebody else's.

Then the other thing that is his: the word. In October he had the duty hand write it down at the counter, so it would be written somewhere. The hand got it close. He never said what it meant.

He says it now.

It doesn't come out as a word.

It comes out low and long. Breath across the mouth of a bottle.

It is the sound from Tuesday the eighteenth, the one that called him. It has been coming up in him since the bunks.

He stops with his mouth open. He knows it.

He doesn't say his name again.

---

**9. INT. THE LAB — THURSDAY 11 DECEMBER — 0310**

He sounds it once more, all of it, full.

And stands.

No one is in the room. No gloves, no instrument, nobody's hand on him. It happens in the body, the way a tree comes down: a long time, then all at once.

passages.heading: Emmett.
passages.text:
The back unbends past where the joists are.
His head meets the planks, then presses against them.
His breath goes onto the underside of the floor, and frost spreads out from it, white, across the grain, plank to plank.
The length: arms past the knee, shins like rails.
The skin stretched thin and white as tallow over all of it.
Bone showing at the knuckles and elbows, where the skin has given up.
The stump held to his chest like something he is carrying.
The mouth.

The strips fall.

`TEMPERATURE — DOWN.`
`TEMPERATURE — DOWN.`
`TEMPERATURE — BELOW`
`READING —`

The last one is never finished.

passages.heading: INSERT. INT. COMPANY OFFICE — 0310
passages.text:
The dead telephone rings once.
A hand lifts the receiver.
The line is open. No voice comes down it.
Frost on the earpiece. The stove lit.

passages.heading: BACK TO THE LAB.
passages.text:
He is not cold.

It is the last thing he notices the way a man would. The cold isn't on him any more. It is his. It comes off him the way heat comes off a stove.

He isn't afraid.

The rest goes quietly, in order: the thanks, the letter, the Fridays, the board left out in the frost.

What is left wants one thing.

Hunger, standing up.

---

**10. INT. THE LAB — BEFORE DAWN, FRIDAY 12 DECEMBER**

The hatch. The gloves come down the ladder with the reading board.

They are warm. He can smell how warm: the rubber, and what is under the rubber.

He turns to them the way he turned to the tray.

But across the room, at a bench he has never looked at, a hand is at a typewriter. In the platen is a form, every line of it blank. *Former name*, empty. *Billet*, empty.

passages.heading: BACK TO THE LAB.
passages.text:
On the line marked *designation*, the keys come down one letter at a time.

`W`
`I`
`N`
`D`
`I`
`G`
`O`

Under it, the transfer line: `TRANSFER OF` — and the frame cuts before the rest.

(On the Agent's road, one more shot: a stamp comes down under the transfer line, `DEPT.` and a black bar where the name should be. Nothing else.)

The steel case on the bench. The lid comes down and the seal goes on. Stencilled on its side: `MAINTAIN BELOW FREEZING.` Frost creeps along the seam.

He turns away from the warm gloves. He turns his whole height, bent under the joists, and follows the cold case with it, the way the hunger in the bunks followed the sound.

The stump comes up an inch off his chest, toward the gloves, toward the case, toward nothing. It is the way a man lifts his hand at a counter to say thank you for looking.

passages.heading: BACK TO THE LAB.
passages.text:
The body still knows how. There is nobody left in it to mean it.

`OBSERVATION: KEPT LIKE AN ANIMAL IN A ZOO.`

---

passages.heading: 11. INT. UNDER THE RESIDENCE — DAY
passages.text:
Planks overhead. Joists. Earth below.

No stair. No room. No bench, no cot, no case. Nothing of anyone, not a button.

Only frost on the underside of the planks, in one long white shape, and nothing under here that could have made it.

`SITE ███, N. DAK.`

passages.heading: EXT. WOODS AND MOUNTAINS, NORTH DAKOTA — WINTER
passages.text:
Snow. Pines to the ridgeline. In a clearing a building is going up, concrete and steel and armoured, and the armour faces in.

Inside the frame are halls four feet wide and fifteen high. Men on ladders work at the tops of the walls.

A door, far too tall, is being hung on hinges set a man's height apart.

On the wall at the end of the hall hangs a clock. A man on a ladder sets its hands.

Nobody who works here needs a door that tall.

The frame is built to a height.

FADE OUT on the empty door. Nobody has come through it yet.

works.title: Behind the Peephole
works.blurb: A hotel-set thriller told only through guests' returns from unseen missions.

passages.heading: Behind the Peephole
passages.text:
Book Scripts

Behind the Peephole: A Thriller Told in the Quiet Aftermath

Most thrillers show you the danger.  
Behind the Peephole shows you what happens after.

This upcoming novel takes place inside a single hotel — a crossroads for people who live on the edge. Mercenaries. Whistleblowers. Art thieves. Undercover journalists. Hackers. Activists. People whose lives burn fast and bright, but whose secrets only surface when they think no one is watching.

The twist is simple and devastating:

You never see their missions.  
You only see their return.

Each chapter opens with a guest slipping back into their room late at night. The story unfolds through the smallest details:

• A smear of dirt on a collar  
• A phone call cut short  
• A trembling hand holding a keycard  
• A suitcase that wasn’t there yesterday  
• A stranger knocking at 2:14 AM  
• A TV channel chosen for comfort or for cover  
• A ritual repeated with obsessive precision

passages.heading: Behind the Peephole
passages.text:
The reader becomes the detective, piecing together the invisible lives of people who risk everything outside the hotel walls.

And the peephole — that tiny circle of glass — becomes the book’s central metaphor.  
A threshold.  
A surveillance device.  
A confession booth.  
A trap.

Because the more you watch these guests, the more you realize something is wrong. Their stories overlap. Their secrets rhyme. Their patterns converge.

They’re not here by accident.  
They’re not alone.  
And someone is watching them all.

Behind the Peephole is a slow-burn, atmospheric mystery built from negative space — a story that invites readers to lean in, observe, and assemble the truth from the fragments left behind.

If you love thrillers that reward attention, tension built from silence, and mysteries that unfold like a mosaic, this is a book that will stay with you long after you close the door.

works.title: Missing Campsites
works.blurb: A campground quietly erases itself around a group nobody else notices is missing.

passages.heading: Missing Campsites
passages.text:
Missing Campsites: A Slow-Burn Horror Mystery About Vanishing Reality

Imagine arriving at a remote campground only to discover something is… off.

Not dangerous.  
Not dramatic.  
Just wrong.

In Missing Campsites, a group of campers pulls into a national forest expecting a quiet weekend. But the first few campsites — the ones that should be right there at the entrance — simply aren’t. Not destroyed. Not taped off. Not overgrown.

They just don’t exist.

The map shows them.  
The signs point to them.  
But the land is empty.

The campers are unsettled, but everyone else — rangers, families, hikers — acts like nothing is missing.

The next morning, more campsites have vanished.

No one notices.  
No one cares.  
No one even remembers they were there.

Except the campers.

By the end of the second day, the entire campground has been erased from reality — all except the last five sites, the ones where the campers are staying. They’re now the only fixed points in a landscape that’s quietly unraveling.

passages.heading: Missing Campsites
passages.text:
And then comes the final morning.

They wake up to find the forest transformed.  
The sky is wrong.  
The air feels heavier.  
The trees are arranged in patterns that shouldn’t exist.  
Their phones show no signal, no time, no date.

They haven’t just lost the campsites.

They’ve slipped into a different dimension — one that has been pulling them in, piece by piece, since the moment they arrived.

Missing Campsites is a creeping, atmospheric horror story about unnoticed disappearances, the fragility of shared reality, and the terrifying moment when you realize the world has been quietly rewriting itself around you.

works.title: Beetles for Brains
works.blurb: Boot-camp recruits' mandatory sleep cycles may be letting something crawl into their minds.

passages.heading: Beetles for Brains
passages.text:
Beetles for Brains: A Psychological Horror About Sleep, Control, and the Things That Crawl in the Dark

In this world, sleep isn’t rest — it’s exposure.

Beetles for Brains follows a group of recruits entering an elite, secretive boot camp known for producing the toughest soldiers on the planet. What no one tells them is the real reason for the camp’s brutal schedule: mandatory, unnaturally long sleep cycles.

At first, it seems like a strange training method.  
Then the symptoms begin.

Recruits wake up disoriented.  
Their thoughts feel foggy.  
Memories slip.  
Reflexes dull.  
Personalities shift in subtle, unsettling ways.

Rumors spread about “the bugs” — tiny organisms that supposedly enter the body during sleep and slowly interfere with neural pathways. No one knows if they’re real, a myth, or a psychological tactic used by the instructors.

passages.heading: Beetles for Brains
passages.text:
But the longer the recruits sleep, the worse the effects become.

Some start hearing faint clicking sounds when they close their eyes.  
Some feel phantom sensations under their skin.  
Some swear they can sense something moving in the quiet spaces of their minds.

The camp insists everything is normal.  
The recruits know something is wrong.  
And the truth is far more disturbing than any of them imagined.

Beetles for Brains is a slow-burn psychological horror about control, paranoia, and the terrifying idea that the most vulnerable moment in your life — sleep — might be the moment something else takes hold.

works.title: The Bloody Alarm Clock
works.blurb: An inherited clock that consumes its owner's time through inescapable nightmares, then moves on.

passages.heading: The Bloody Alarm Clock
passages.text:
The Bloody Alarm Clock: A Horror Story About a Timepiece That Won’t Let You Wake

Some cursed objects announce themselves.  
This one just… ticks.

The Bloody Alarm Clock follows an ordinary person who inherits an old bedside clock with a strange quirk: it never rings out loud, yet every night it plays inside their head. The sound isn’t a tone or a melody — it’s a pressure, a pulse, a presence that drags them into vivid, terrifying dreams.

At first, the dreams are just unsettling.  
Then they become unbearable.

Each night brings a new nightmare: running out of time, suffering mysterious internal pain, drowning, collapsing, or meeting some unseen fate. And every morning, the victim wakes with real‑world echoes of what they dreamed:

• Waking soaked after dreaming of drowning  
• Feeling faint after dreaming of losing blood  
• Hearing phantom ticking long after opening their eyes

passages.heading: The Bloody Alarm Clock
passages.text:
Worst of all, their ears begin to bleed when they wake — a quiet, chilling sign that the clock is doing something far more dangerous than disturbing their sleep.

The victim tries everything to get rid of it.  
Throwing it away.  
Smashing it.  
Leaving it behind.

But the clock always returns — sometimes on the nightstand, sometimes in a dream, sometimes in a place they don’t remember putting it. It’s as if the clock is choosing them, not the other way around.

As sleep becomes a threat, the victim starts avoiding it entirely. Exhaustion leads to waking hallucinations — daydreams that feel just as real and terrifying as the nightmares. The line between dream and reality dissolves, and the ticking becomes constant, inescapable.

Eventually, the victim realizes the truth:

The clock doesn’t measure time.  
It consumes it.

And when it finally takes the last of theirs, the clock quietly moves on — appearing in the home of its next unsuspecting owner, ready to begin the cycle again.

passages.heading: The Bloody Alarm Clock
passages.text: The Bloody Alarm Clock is a psychological horror story about dread, inevitability, and the terrifying idea that something as harmless as a bedside clock could be counting down to your end.

works.title: Chasing Cold Clues

passages.heading: Chasing Cold Clues
passages.text:
Chasing Cold Clues

Character design:

Main character:

passages.heading: Dr. Sterling Vanguard
passages.text:
Bio:

Dr. Sterling Vanguard is a renowned cryptozoologist and esteemed explorer with a deep passion for unraveling the mysteries of the natural world. With a PHd in zoology and a wealth of knowledge in the field, Dr. Vanguard has dedicated his life to studying and documenting elusive and undiscovered creatures. His expertise in cryptozoology, combined with his extensive experience as a versed adventurer, has led him to remote and unexplored corners of the globe in search of rare and mythical creatures.

First story plot line:

Opening Scene:  
The scene opens with a high-energy chase through the bustling marketplace. Dr. Vanguard, a seasoned adventurer and scholar, is in pursuit of a mysterious boy weaving through the crowded streets. The chase intensifies as Dr. Vanguard tries to catch up, his determination fueled by the sense that something important is at stake.

Rising Action:  
During the chase, Dr. Vanguard manages to catch the boy, who reveals a cryptic clue that leads him on an unexpected and thrilling journey. Intrigued by the enigma before him, Dr. Vanguard delves deeper into the mystery, uncovering fragments of a forgotten history that could change the course of knowledge forever. He realizes that he is up against powerful adversaries who will stop at nothing to obtain the secrets he's stumbled upon.

passages.heading: Dr. Sterling Vanguard
