passages.heading: Ledger.
passages.text:
The Vicar is entered under his own roof. He asked to be.

**Wired east.** LIGHT 19 STOP ASH NIL STOP RENT IN FULL STOP

passages.heading: Monday 20 November
passages.text:
**Of the Light.** Maud went out in the back car at Dusk. The Vicar walked behind it as far as the end of the platform and stood there until the car was out of the lamp's reach. Mrs Grieves's book has him paying for a Liquid Courage for Len the same night.

Bar's Liquid Courage is the one thing in town that keeps a man proof against any prayer, the Vicar's or anyone's, for about two minutes by my clock. The Vicar buys it for others. I have never known what to enter for that.

He sits with whoever cannot pay. He takes his tea black, because milk costs scrip and he will not run a line at the Ovens. He asks me the time whenever he passes, and sets his watch, and I have stopped thinking it strange.

**Of the Ash.** The first *lapsed*. A Pump Row name I had entered as L in October did not come to the line this week, or last. I asked nothing. I moved the mark. The Company's own codes for this are three words, *sown*, *doubt*, *lapsed*, and I have begun to use them because they fit in a wire.

passages.heading: Thursday 7 December
passages.text:
**Of the Light.** The Gazette came in sealed and was opened here as always. Its notice reads: "The Vicar preaches at dusk." I went, the first time I have gone. It was him. The watch, the open hands, a voice that did not need to be raised. He spoke about debts forgiven, and I could not tell whether he was looking at me. Afterward he came by the counter for the time and set the watch. He said the door of the confessional was open. He said it the way you say the weather.

I did not confess.

**Of the Ash.** The Undertaker's book has taken four since Maud: Elsie on the 25th, Mabel on the 27th, Cyril on the 29th, Hattie on the 2nd. I do not count the dead. I note them, because their roofs change. The Watchman has been fined and stood down since Hattie. Nobody walks the lanes at night now but the threes.

passages.heading: Thursday 7 December
passages.text:
**Wired east.** LIGHT 34 STOP DECEASED REMOVED FROM COUNT STOP

---

passages.heading: Wednesday 13 December
passages.text: The wire came at noon: MR THORNE ARRIVING 14TH STOP. I aired the study above the bank, as I am told to. The town says that whoever airs that room knows first, and is not saying. I have never said.

passages.heading: Thursday 14 December
passages.text:
The Baron came on the morning train, private car, dogs first and his escort after, *Not counted (Rule 6)*. He stepped down onto the platform at the Station Rush, in the press of the crew and the mailbags and the dogs, and there on the boards the Baron fell.

I was at this window. I will not enter how. The Constable has entered *person unknown*. The town has entered a dozen names in a dozen voices at the pump, and I enter none of them. There is talk at the bell of a vote on whoever did it, if whoever did it is ever stood up. The crepe for Vane is still on the rail. They have put another length beside it.

He was carried up to the study I had aired. His escort did not go back on the train. They stand on the square in their long coats and look at the bank, and wait to be told something.

passages.heading: Thursday 14 December
passages.text:
**Of the Light.** The Vicar went up to the study with his candle and sat there an hour. He came down and asked me the time.

**Of the Ash.** Nothing entered. I had no room in me today for the Ash.

passages.heading: Friday 15 December
passages.text:
The bag came at the Station Rush. In it was one envelope addressed to me by my full name, which the Company has not written since it hired me. The seal is the Company's, in red. Inside is a writ from the Eastern Office, concerning the estate of the late Mr C. Thorne, and a key with a brass tag.

I have read it three times. It uses a word for me that my mother never once said aloud, though she had reason to. It is in my drawer, under the rent schedule.

passages.heading: Reply.** AWAITING YOUR INSTRUCTIONS STOP
passages.text:
The Eastern Office has never before awaited anything of mine.

*Margin, pencil:* The tag is for the study door.

passages.heading: Sunday 17 December
passages.text:
The third Sunday of Advent. The telegraph room is shut on a Sunday. I was here regardless, at the drawer.

The stone that morning carried no name. It carried a title: THE VICAR. Agnes read it to the Row at dawn as she reads them all, and the Row went to its doors and looked up the slope at the chapel. I entered it under *Stone*. I do not enter whether the stone cuts the name or only knows it first. Nobody has watched it cut.

At four he knocked on the glass. He had seen my lamp. He asked me the time, for the evening service, and set his watch, and said the pink candle was the one for joy, and that he had always thought it the wrong colour for it. Then he went up the slope in the last of the light with his hands in his coat.

passages.heading: Sunday 17 December
passages.text: That was the last time. I know the hour because I was here on a Sunday, reading a writ, and for no better reason.

passages.heading: Tuesday 19 December
passages.text:
**Of the Light.** The Vicar has preached both evenings since, as advertised. This morning he came to the counter for the parish bag and stood where he always stands, in the robes he always wears, with his voice. He did not ask the time. I waited with my hand on the clock-case, and he did not ask. He took the bag and went.

The town has ruled the stone wrong. It named the Vicar and the Vicar is preaching. Agnes says it is the first time. I have entered the ruling as the town's, not mine.

**Of the Ash.** *Sown.* I do not know what else to write.

passages.heading: Wednesday 20 December
passages.text:
In the night of the 17th, more than one roof dreamt the same thing and told it at the pump in the morning as though it were weather. They dreamt a lavender field on wind-bent hills. They dreamt a lone orange tree, near, standing over it. Behind it there was a sky so blue it hurt to tell. Nobody in the Territory has seen lavender. Nobody in HollowMere has seen a blue sky since the fog came off the mere.

On Monday morning a paper was handed across my counter by someone who would not sign for it and whom I did not look at, because I was reading the writ. On it, in a plain hand:

> "In the end I sought nothing else but to serve God. And serve him I did. With this death's last breath I pray this prayer: may the Almighty grant me the strength of ten in the next life. And in return, tenfold my own."

passages.heading: Wednesday 20 December
passages.text:
A second copy, word for word, was in the mailbag when the Postmaster cut it open. The bag had come sealed from the east.

Some say these were the end of his last sermon, at Sunday dusk. Some say they were his last breath, and not in the chapel. I enter both, and the Vicar is still preaching.

passages.heading: Thursday 21 December
passages.text:
**Of the Light, falling.** I went to the dusk sermon again. It had the same cadence and the same open hands, and every promise was turned inside out like a coat pocket. Debts were not forgiven; they were called in. I did not confess. I was not asked to.

Since Monday the confessional has given back less than it takes. People go in entered L and come out with nothing in them, blank, sitting on the chapel step with their hands in their laps. I have moved eleven marks this week, name by name, and each one cost me the ink of a single stroke. One man from Pump Row, prayed for by both sides inside a week, came out of it snapped. He carries a rusted pitchfork now and both faiths cross the square to keep clear of him.

**Of the Ash: the keeper.** The town has done what the Constable would not, and said it: the Vicar is dead, and what walks in his robes walks only as long as the body is not found. So the body is not found. Where it has been is a catalogue the pump keeps for me without my asking. The chapel loft. A barrel in a saloon back room. A pine thicket at the Gallows Wood edge. The cave. Mrs Grieves's book has her oil barrel a gallon short in riot week, and I note it here only because the pump does, and because that was before.

passages.heading: Thursday 21 December
passages.text:
Bone chimes ring where nothing hangs. The Detective walks toward them with his case file under his arm, and they ring once before he reaches the place, and there is nothing there but the place. Whoever keeps the body leaves no drag in the mud. In this town that is the strangest thing I have entered.

**The lead.** The Undertaker's requisition for sheet lead is on the incoming manifest, in his hand. *Filled / Unfilled:* not entered.

passages.heading: Ledger.
passages.text:
| Roof | L | A | — | ? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mill Row | 4 | ? | 3 | 5 |
| Pump Row | 2 | ? | 3 | 4 |
| The platform crew | 1 | ? | 3 | 1 |
| Hale Barn | 0 | ? | 0 | 2 |

The A column will not take a number. The Ash does not come to a line.

---

passages.heading: Friday 22 December. The collector
passages.text:
Rent day. I went out at the Midday Shift with the cashbox and the keys, and was cornered three times.

At Crumb's Ovens a man stood in the doorway, and Tamsin Crumb paid twice: once into my box and once into his hand. At the Lantern Bar did not reach under the counter. He looked at the man and then at me and poured nothing. In the lane behind the bank, the man took me by the coat. Brass across the knuckles knocked the Company's keys out of my hand into the mud. For the length of a held breath I could not open my own cashbox. I stood there with my hands on it like a man at a locked door in his own house. I entered the sum taken before I entered the bruise.

The mobs began that night. They are men with torches and hoods made of flour sacks, and they go out after Curfew to find the ones who walk in threes. Walking together was what let the faithful see in the dark. Now it is what marks them. By Saturday they had stopped walking together.

passages.heading: Friday 22 December. The collector
passages.text:
A witness was taken by the collar on the square. That night there was cause to ring the bell, and it was not rung, and nobody who could have rung it will say what the cause was.

One the mob found was a woman of Mill Row who minds the mill hands' children through the Shift. She had come over to the Light because the threes walked her home past the Gallows Wood edge, and she had not been walked home by anyone in years. She is alive. She keeps her door now. She still sets out three cups at Dusk, and I am told she washes all three in the morning, though only one has been used.

**Wired east.** ESCORT REMAINS IN TOWN STOP AWAIT INSTRUCTION STOP

**Reply.** COMPANY TAKES NO POSITION ON MATTERS OF FAITH STOP ESCORT IS YOURS TO INSTRUCT SIR STOP

I have not instructed them. They stand at my counter in the mornings now, and wait.

passages.heading: Monday 25 December
passages.text:
Rent due, as on every Monday. The Company does not keep Christmas. I went out with the box. Nobody tried my coat. Where a roof was empty, a roof of the Ash whose sleepers walk at Dusk and do not pay, I wrote *forfeit*, as the schedule allows and as I have never before written. The schedule allowed it before. Nobody had been minded to.

### Sunday 24 December. The herald *(entered out of order, the 26th)*

passages.heading: Ledger of Marks.
passages.text:
| Building | First seen | By whom | Scrubbed | Back by morning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| The Chapel | 18 Dec | not entered | Y | Y |
| The Bank | 20 Dec | not entered | Y | Y |
| The Bakery | 21 Dec | not entered | Y | Y |
| The Mill | 23 Dec | not entered | N | — |
| The Station | 24 Dec | not entered | Y | Y |

The Station's mark is on my own wall, beside the door I come in by. It is ash and something darker, a sign I have no word for, and it was there on Christmas Eve when I came down to the drawer. I scrubbed it with lye. By morning it was there again, with the brush marks of my own scrubbing showing under it.

passages.heading: Ledger of Marks.
passages.text:
The tracts come in the mailbags. They come into this room, where the Postmaster holds envelopes over the kettle every morning and I sit six feet away at the key, and I cannot say which hand slips them in. They come in the crates of flour that go up to Crumb's. I will not copy one into this book. A tract is a page that reads like a promise and is shaped like a debt.

The ones the tracts take are the Entranced. They pay no rent and sleep by day. At Dusk they walk out without lanterns, silent, into the Fenwood past the drowned lantern, which is lit — by whom, not entered — or down the Tin Gallery mouth to the Flooded Gallery. Each one brings another the next night. I watch them from this window and count them as they pass the pump, and the count is only what is gone: empty bunks, unswept steps, a cold stove on Pump Row.

passages.heading: Ledger of Marks.
passages.text: The A column has numbers in it at last, and every one of them is a subtraction.

passages.heading: Tuesday 26 December. The shepherd
passages.text:
Nobody has seen this one. The pump calls them *the one who will carry on*.

Black candles stand on the VANE TIN CO crate in the Flooded Gallery, set out as on an altar. The Detective has been down and come up and said so to the Constable, and the Constable to me, because I keep the wire. At St Brannock's the pulpit has been fouled. The hymn board's cards are gone, the alms dish is gone, and the Vicar's candle is gone from its stick.

The law the pump whispers is this. If the robes fall, the shepherd keeps the power to turn souls. The Ash has insured itself, as the Company insures a train.

**Wired east.** MARKS FIVE OF FIVE STOP REQUIRE SIX STOP SIX WHAT STOP

*Margin, pencil:* gathered.

The Eastern Office forwards a Harrow wire, unasked. The camp at BlackPine reports its Chaplain *not at work for reasons of religion*. By the time it was in my hand it had been read aloud at the pump, and I cannot say who carried it there, or whether it was ever a wire at all.

passages.heading: Friday 29 December
passages.text:
The morning train. Conductor Pruett in the door of the private car, punch in hand, and then not using it: *Not counted (Rule 6)*. A man stepped down into the fog of the Station Rush with the dead Vicar's face. The light stood on him the way low sun stands on still water, too level and too bright, and the fog drew back from it in a ring. He carried a crosier of plain black iron, as tall as himself.

He crossed the square to this counter, and put one hand on the rail, and asked me the time.

I told him. My pen hand would not hold the nib. He took out a watch, the same watch or its twin, and set it to my clock, and thanked me as if I had given him something, and went out.

There are two Vicars in HollowMere. One wears the robes and preaches at dusk. One wears the light. I entered both under St Brannock's, and struck one, and restored it. The column cannot say which. Neither can I.

passages.heading: Friday 29 December
passages.text:
**Tenfold.** He does not hear confessions one at a time. He stands in a lane and the lane comes over. Mill Row went over in an afternoon: wash-house, wheel-house, every door down to the mere. The row I had entered at noon as *1 L* I entered again at three as *10 L*. The pencil in the margin was there before me each time.

**The crosier.** The wing doors at the manor stood locked under Horace's ring. He struck them once and they stood open, and Horace stood beside them holding keys that had no more work to do. The Undercroft door the same. A torch-mob came at him across the square at Curfew and broke, as a wave does on a post, and went back into the lanes, and nobody was hurt. I enter that too.

passages.heading: Saturday 30 December, Dusk
passages.text:
It can be done once. The pump knew that before I did.

The man in the robes was on the chapel step at dusk, hands open, and the square filled to hear him. The man in the light came up from the platform with the crosier. He did not speak. He raised it.

The light came down on the square in a pillar from nowhere I could see. It was white as the inside of a lamp-glass and as wide as the pump. It was not on him. It was on the step. The robes went off the man standing there as if a wind had taken them, and went over the rail and down the slope empty.

Under them was a face, and the face was borrowed.

It was a face from this town. I have taken its rent. The one it belongs to was standing beside me at the window, come in from the cold to watch, and made a sound I will not enter.

passages.heading: Saturday 30 December, Dusk
passages.text:
I enter no name. The face's owner did nothing. Whoever wore it went down the step into the crowd and the crowd let go of them, and the fog took them before the pillar went out.

The body has still not been reported. The pump has the rule ready: once the robes have fallen, the shepherd's power stays. Robes were seen at the Gallery mouth an hour after Curfew. I cannot say they were the same robes. I cannot say how many robes there are.

---

passages.heading: Sunday 31 December 1893
passages.text: The Company closes its books at midnight on the year. I write this in the study above the bank, at a desk nobody sat at, by the key with the brass tag. The chair faced the window on the line. There is a second window, on the square. I have turned the chair to it.

passages.heading: Ledger, year's end.
passages.text:
| Roof | L | A | — | ? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| St Brannock's | 2 | ? | 0 | 1 |
| The Drowned Lantern | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Crumb's Ovens | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Mallory Apothecary | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Vane Manor | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Widow Vane's parlour | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Hale Barn | 0 | ? | 0 | 1 |
| Mill Row | 11 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Pump Row | 4 | 5 | 0 | 0 |
| The platform crew | 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Post Office & Telegraph Room | 0 | 0 | ~~1~~ | 1 |
| The marsh dock | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Fennick's light | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| The study above the bank | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |

passages.heading: Ledger, year's end.
passages.text:
*Margin, pencil:* moved.

There is one *—* left in HollowMere, and it is under this roof. Both faiths have come to my door, the one with an open hand and the one with brass across it. So has the Company. The Light cannot say it holds every roof while one is entered as neither. I know what that makes me tonight. I do not write it.

On the desk is a form printed back east for a time like this one. It locks every house door in HollowMere at Curfew, by order, the escort to see it kept. It wants a signature and a date. It would keep the Entranced in their beds. It would keep the faithful off the square. It has my signature. The date is not entered.

Dusk. Below, the faithful are gathering on the scorched stones where the pillar stood, close, shoulder to shoulder, carrying no lanterns. Along the far side of the square the Entranced are walking toward the Gallery mouth, without a sound, one behind another. From this window I count them as they pass the pump.

passages.heading: Ledger, year's end.
passages.text:
One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

The fog has come off the mere and taken the end of the line. I cannot see a sixth. I cannot see that there is no sixth.

I am a man of columns. The columns are mine now; I have not said so and will not. The column your name is in at dawn is who you are.

The bell has begun.

**Wired east.** BELL RINGING STOP CANNOT SAY WHICH BELL STOP CANNOT SAY WHICH WAY STOP SKY

*Margin, pencil, over the count of walkers: a single numeral, smudged, that could be a 5 or a 6.*

works.title: Intake
works.blurb: the released-in-part intake packet of detainee 99-0417, an interpreter received by payroll train on 17 October 1952: Form G99-1 and the eight Rules of the Camp filled in and initialled with his number, a Counter Intelligence requisition that takes him hooded down to the cold room where the pier man is kept, and the rack slip that makes him the new Workings No. 7.

passages.heading: Intake
passages.text:
**RELEASED IN PART**
EXEMPTIONS (b)(1) (b)(3) (b)(6) · RELEASE DATE ████████████

---

passages.heading: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE ██████
passages.text:
TO: ██████████████
FROM: ██████████████
SUBJECT: PROGRAM **ANOMALY UNKNOWN**. DETAINEE INTAKE, FORM G99-1. ONE (1) PACKET, COMPLETED.
SITE: **GROUNDS 99** (site formerly designated BLACKPINE; redesignated 1952)
SPONSORING OFFICE: ██████████████████

1. The enclosed is the intake packet of detainee 99-0417. He was received by payroll train on Friday 17 October 1952 and entered on the Workings rack on Tuesday 21 October 1952.
2. The packet is forwarded complete, as kept by the camp. No portion has been removed at the site.
3. Form G99-1 is printed on stock held over at the site. Earlier matter showing through the overprint is of no relevance to the Program and has not been redacted.

DISTRIBUTION: ████████ / ████████ / ████████: SEALED / File (camp).

*[Release note: pencil annotations appear throughout the margins, in one hand. Under the heading of Part I, earlier print shows faintly through the overprint: "…TIMBER & COAL SYND…" and, below it, "CONTRACT OF ENGAGE…".]*

passages.heading: I. Form G99-1: Processing
passages.text:
**GROUNDS 99 · PROGRAM ██████ · FORM G99-1 (REV. 1952)**
**TO BE COMPLETED BY THE DETAINEE, IN PENCIL. WRITE INSIDE THE FIELDS.**

**1. DATE AND MEANS OF ARRIVAL.**
*Fri 17 Oct 52. Payroll train.*

> *The payroll rode in the front car and we rode behind it. At the platform they counted the strongbox first, then us. Eleven. They took the box down with two men and gloves. They took us down with dogs.*

**2. NAME.** NOT REQUIRED. A NUMBER WILL BE ISSUED.
*[blank]*

> *I had it ready. For nine years I have said my name first, so the other man knows whose words are coming. The clerk kept his thumb on the field until I lifted the pencil.*

**3. NUMBER.** COPY THE NUMBER STAMPED ABOVE.
[STAMP: 99-0417]
*99-0417*

> *Twice now. It gets easier. That is what it is for.*

**4. CLASSIFICATION.** TICK ONE.
□ PRISONER OF WAR  □ ENEMY OF THE STATE  □ OTHER (SPECIFY) ________
CLASSIFICATION IS ENTERED BY THE DETAINEE AND CONFIRMED BY THE OFFICE.
*☒ OTHER (SPECIFY): interpreter*
[STAMP: RECLASSIFIED. SEE ANNEX ██]
*[Release note: Annex ██, a FEDERAL BUREAU OF ███████████ referral, is withheld in full.]*

passages.heading: I. Form G99-1: Processing
passages.text:
> *Other / whichever they need. I asked the clerk which box. He said, whichever you can live with. I have been an interpreter for nine years, German and Swedish and part of a third, and I have no word for that in any of them. I ticked the one that was true. The stamp came down before the pencil was off the paper.*

**5. TRADE ASSIGNED.** STAMPED BY THE OFFICE. COPY.
[STAMP: WORKINGS. FACE.]
*Workings. Face.*

**6. BILLET WOOD.** FOLLOWS TRADE. OAK: WORKINGS. FIR: BOILERS. PINE: TALLY.
*Oak.*

> *Oak is the heaviest. I asked whether a man who can read might be pine. The clerk said reading is not a trade.*

**7. RACK SLOT.** PENDING VACANCY. EACH CREW KEEPS A RACK OF TEN. DETAINEES ARE ENTERED AS SLOTS BECOME AVAILABLE. DO NOT ENTER A SLOT UNTIL ONE IS ISSUED.
*[blank]*

> *Available / empty. Empty / someone. Ten places to a rack, eleven of us off the train, and no rack short a man that I could see. I have done the sum. So has everyone in the bunkhouse. That is why they will not look at us.*

passages.heading: I. Form G99-1: Processing
passages.text:
**8. BASELINE, RESPIRATORY.** BREATH HELD (SECONDS) ____.
LUNG-ROT IS MEASURED ON ARRIVAL AND MONTHLY. RESULTS ARE THE PROPERTY OF THE PROGRAM.
*41*

> *The orderly had a stopwatch, the only watch I have seen since the train.*
>
> *The man ahead of me at the table told me, while we waited, that as a boy he dived off the town pier for pennies, and that he could still stay under longer than anyone. He said it as if it would help.*
>
> *He went past a minute. The orderly stopped looking at the watch and looked at him instead. He was taken aside.*
>
> *I let my breath go at forty-one because I was frightened. I do not know yet whether that was the cleverest thing I have done here or only the first.*

**9. EFFECTS SURRENDERED.** LIST.
*Photograph (my mother, 1931). Pocket dictionary, Swedish–English. Wristwatch, steel. Letter, one, unopened.*
EFFECTS RETAINED: NONE.

passages.heading: I. Form G99-1: Processing
passages.text:
> *None / one. I am writing with it.*
>
> *The letter was from Hanne. I was keeping it for the train, for when I knew where I was going, so I could read it knowing. They took it at the platform. Now I know she wrote. I will not know what.*

**10. NEXT OF KIN.** WILL NOT BE NOTIFIED. ENTER FOR THE RECORD.
*Hanne (sister).*

> *She hums when she irons and stops when you come into the room, as if humming were owed to nobody.*

---

passages.heading: II. Rules of the Camp
passages.text:
**GROUNDS 99 · RULES OF THE CAMP**
**READ AND INITIAL EACH RULE. DETAINEES INITIAL WITH THE NUMBER.**

**RULE ONE. THE SHIFT-WHISTLE.**
The Shift-Whistle is the camp's clock. Shifts begin on it and end on it. Detainees do not carry time.
READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417*

> *The watch is in field 9. I count now. Eins, zwei. My mother's counting. I catch myself at it and go on anyway.*

**RULE TWO. THE RATION.**
Detainees eat the mess ration and nothing else. No food is to be taken outside the mess, and no food from outside the mess is to be eaten. The ration is set by the Program and is not to be traded, saved or refused.
READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417*

> *Not refused. That is the word they underlined.*
>
> *Grey meat in the evening, cut small. I could not name the animal in any of my three languages. I ate it all and was hungrier when the plate was clean than when it was full. They gave us bread after, to fill the space. The men who have been here since the first roll eat fast, with their elbows out, and their wrists are thinner than Hanne's.*

passages.heading: II. Rules of the Camp
passages.text:
**RULE THREE. THE MIDNIGHT ROLL CALL.**
At the whistle, the detainee has fifteen seconds to stand beside his assigned bunk. A bunk without a detainee at the end of fifteen seconds is lit. Equipment for the Roll: searchlights; Order Enforcement Agents, masked; dogs. Detainees not in place are recovered.
READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417*

> *Recovered / brought back. Or found. I have not stood one yet. The man in the next bunk said, sleep in your boots. It is all he has said to me.*
>
> *After the Roll the mess hall hums through the wall, one note, all of them. One man told me not to join in. Later another told me to.*

**RULE FOUR. THE QUOTA.**
Production is entered against the number daily. A shortfall is debited in scrip. A repeated shortfall goes before the Tribunal for Scrip Forfeiture.

> **UNITED STATES SECRET ██████**
> Scrip is the property of the Office. Possession of altered or counterfeit scrip is an offence against ████████████ and will be referred.

passages.heading: READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417
passages.text:
> *Quota / the price of tomorrow. The scrip carries a seal, as if it were money. It is only paper that tells you how far behind you are.*

**RULE FIVE. LUNG-ROT AND THE TONIC.**
A detainee who coughs on shift is to be reported by the detainees beside him. The oxygen tonic is issued at the Infirmary and debited against quota.
READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417*

> *So the cure is billed to the cough, and the cough is reported by the man next to you. I have started listening to my own breathing at night. So, I think, has he.*

**RULE SIX. THE BLADE.**
Sentences of the Tribunal are carried out at the head-saw platform at dawn. The camp refers to this as the Blade. Detainees will use the camp's term.
READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417*

> *The Blade / ——. I looked for the plain word. On the train I had it in three languages. Here I could not write it down. They have made it so that I won't.*

passages.heading: READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417
passages.text:
**RULE SEVEN. RELIGIOUS OBSERVANCE.**
The camp chapel hut. The Reverend E. Moss. Sundays, by permission of the Office.
READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417*

> *He was at the gate when we came through, thumbing resin onto every brow and saying the same words each time. Nobody stopped him. It is still on mine. It smells of the woods we are going to cut.*

**RULE EIGHT. THE RACK.**
Every detainee is a billet on his crew's rack. The rack is checked at dawn. The log on your rack at dawn is who you are.
READ AND UNDERSTOOD: *99-0417*

> *The only rule they wrote as if it were a hymn.*

---

passages.heading: III. Acknowledgement
passages.text:
THE DETAINEE HAS PASSED UNDER THE GATE AND HAS READ THE MOTTO:

> **PRODUCTION IS OBLIGATION.**

COPY THE FOLLOWING IN YOUR OWN HAND. PENMANSHIP AND LITERACY ARE ASSESSED.

> YOU'RE EITHER FEEDING THE FURNACE OR YOU'RE FUEL.

passages.heading: You're either feeding the furnace or you're fuel.
passages.text:
> *The clerk read it out as he gave me back the pencil, the way you read a man his rights, so that later nobody can say he was not told. He did not look up at "fuel".*
>
> *Fuel / *

NUMBER: *99-0417*

passages.heading: IV. Requisition for Language Services
passages.text: *[Release note: a half-sheet, folded into the packet after Part III.]*

passages.heading: COUNTER INTELLIGENCE ██████ ████
passages.text:
REQUISITION. DETAINEE 99-0417 IS TO BE RELEASED FROM SHIFT TO PROVIDE LANGUAGE SERVICES.
DATE: SUN 19 OCT 52
SUBJECT TO BE INTERVIEWED: ███-████
LANGUAGE: ██████
QUESTIONS (ASK IN ORDER. RECORD ANSWERS ONLY.)
1. Do you know your number?
2. Are you cold?
3. Are you hungry?
THE DETAINEE IS NOT TO DESCRIBE THE ROUTE, THE ROOM OR THE SUBJECT. ANSWERS ARE THE PROPERTY OF THE PROGRAM.
ANSWERS RECORDED: *1. —  2. —  3. Yes.*

> *A sack over my head from the yard. Stairs, more than I counted, and I count everything now. Then cold. Not October. Cold that came out of the walls, so I saw my breath indoors and it hung there.*
>
> *It was the pier man. Two days.*
>
> *Skin drawn tight on him like wet paper dried on a frame. Ribs standing out, every one, as if something inside were pushing to get out between them. Knuckles white. Fingertips black. A tube taped into the crook of one arm.*
>
> *On the table by the wall, under a cloth that did not cover all of it, the rest of two fingers, and a foot, each with a tag. A man in a white coat was writing on the tags. He did not look up either.*
>
> *I asked the first question. Nothing. The second. Nothing. He was watching my mouth the way the dogs at the platform watched the strongbox. At the third his head came round, all at once, and he made a sound that was not yes in any language, and the man in the white coat wrote "yes".*
>
> *I said the word for pier. That is not one of the questions. Something went over his face and was gone, like a coin going down in green water. I do not know whether he heard it. I wanted him to have heard it.*
>
> *Going back up I counted the stairs again and got a different number. The cold stayed down there. I was in the yard before I stopped seeing my breath.*

passages.heading: V. Rack Entry
passages.text:
*[Release note: a slip, stapled inside the back cover.]*

**GROUNDS 99 · RACK ENTRY · WORKINGS CREW**
DATE: TUE 21 OCT 52
VACANCY: SLOT 7
PREVIOUS HOLDER: ██████ ██████ (WORKINGS NO. 7)
DATE VACATED: ██ OCT 52
DISPOSITION: ████████████
BILLET: OAK. PLANED AND RE-BRANDED.
ISSUED TO: 99-0417. ENTER SLOT AT FIELD 7, FORM G99-1.

*[Release note: field 7 of Form G99-1 now reads, in the same hand: "7".]*

> *They gave me the billet at dawn. Oak, as promised. It is worn smooth at the two places where a hand takes it down from the rack and puts it back. Someone did that every morning, with a wider grip than mine. My number is burned in fresh. Under it the old brand is planed nearly out. I could read only that it was not mine.*
>
> *They moved me to his bunk. There is a black band on the post, and a dent in the straw on the left side, so he slept facing the wall. On the slat by the dent he scratched a few words in the third language, the one I have only part of. I know enough of it to know they are a children's counting rhyme, and not enough to know how it ends. I sleep on my left now, so the dent does not change.*
>
> *I asked the man in the next bunk where No. 7 went. He said the word the Office uses, and I will not write it, because I know now what it means here.*
>
> *He has said a third thing, too. Down in the Workings there is a board where the crew is chalked on and off each shift, and there is a name on it that nobody chalks off. He said it the way you say weather. I go down on Monday.*
>
> *The log on my rack at dawn is who I am. It was someone first.*
>
> *I have written my name nowhere in this packet. Field 2 would not take it. So, small, here, so that it is somewhere: ████████ ██████████.*
>
> *If they hand you this form after me, with my number planed off the oak: the pencil is in the ash box of the stove, at the back, on the left. Eat what they give you; you will not be able to stop. Write small. They do not ████ ███ ███████.*

works.title: The Last Shift's Tally Board
works.blurb: Ned Corwin, a payroll clerk turned Workings No. 4, keeps the ore chamber's tally board from 6 October to 20 December 1952 and learns that the smudged old name in the DOWN column, A_T_N K_SS__R, takes a man whenever it is washed out: Wrona, then Danny Fitch, until he writes "transferred" himself and goes down with the last shift, having chalked the name back in.

passages.heading: 1. Custody
passages.text:
Clean slate each shift.

That was the rule. It was painted along the top of the frame in white letters gone yellow, where nobody looking at the board could miss it. Foreman Hask read it out anyway. Hask read everything out.

"Clean slate each shift," he said. "Down on the left. Up on the right. Sign."

Monday, 6 October 1952. The ore chamber of the Blackpine Workings. A slate in a timber frame, nailed to the rock. A row of nails under it for the brass lamp checks. A bucket, a rag, a stub of chalk, a custody chit.

passages.heading: Transferred," Hask said. "Sign.
passages.text:
Ned Corwin had been a payroll clerk at a foundry in Pittsburgh for eleven years. Then he signed a union petition, and in the camp's words he became an enemy of the state, and in the Workings crew's words he became Four. Hask had looked down the crew's numbers that morning and stopped at his. *You. Four. You were a clerk.*

A keeper does not go down. He knew that before he knew anything else about the job. He signed with his number.

The DOWN column was not empty.

High up, above where any of the crew would be chalked, was one entry in older chalk and a rounder hand than any hand in the crew:

`A_T_N  K_SS__R`

It was not struck through. It had never come up.

He did the sum on his trouser seam with his thumbnail, the way he had done sums on the foundry's ledgers when the adding machine jammed. Nine men down. Nine men up. And one.

passages.heading: Transferred," Hask said. "Sign.
passages.text:
"From today," Hask said, "the count is yours to close."

It would not close. He knew that before the first shift went down.

passages.heading: 2. Short count
passages.text:
> G99-T · SHIFT TALLY RECONCILIATION · WORKINGS · TUE 7 OCT 52 · DAY · KEEPER 4 · DOWN 10 · UP 9 · RESIDUAL 1 · DISPOSITION —

Every shift came out the same. Nine men down and nine men up, all of them struck through. And the old name, which was not.

Residual one.

The camp had a rule for that, and the rule had a rhyme, which is how you knew it was old. Short count, short ration. Hask read it out at the bread line on Wednesday with the sheet held up to the lamp.

passages.heading: Workings. Residual one. Keeper four.
passages.text: Ten men. Nine loaves.

passages.heading: Your keeper's count is.
passages.text:
He did not answer them. He kept his daughter's arithmetic folded in the lining of his cap: long division, forty-seven by five. She had written *9 R 2* at the bottom, very carefully, and he had taught her that the remainder is not a mistake. It is only what is left over. Under it she had written one line of her own, and the camp censor had put a black bar through it before the letter reached him. He never found out what she had written.

Residual one, every shift, and Hask's pencil going down the sheet.

The crew ate short for his count, and every man in the crew knew whose count it was.

passages.heading: 3. Washed out
passages.text: On Sunday, 12 October, Hask came down with a paper folded once.

passages.heading: It isn't mine.
passages.text:
"Office asked. Office got an answer." He read it. He read everything. "Do not carry."

So Four read the frame again. *Clean slate each shift.* He read it the way a clerk reads a rule, looking for the word that gives permission. It was there. *Clean.*

He filled the bucket at the drip. He wet the rag. The slate went black and shining under it, then slowly back to grey. The rounder hand came off the way any chalk comes off. There was nothing in it that held on.

Old chalk in the grain, washed out. That was all it had ever been.

Monday's sheet: down nine, up nine, residual nought. The bread came back.

Tadeusz Wrona, Seven, a coal man out of Silesia by way of Scranton, hummed through his teeth at the bread line. He had been carving a bird whistle out of a pine offcut since the first week, a little more every night. That night it had a mouthpiece. He blew one note at Four across the table, for the bread. It was flat, and everybody laughed.

passages.heading: 4. Payroll Friday
passages.text:
> G99-T · WORKINGS · FRI 17 OCT 52 · DAY · KEEPER 4 · DOWN 9 · UP 8 · RESIDUAL 1 · DISPOSITION —

The payroll train whistled in the yard at noon. Up in the camp men were standing in a line for scrip. Down here Four chalked the shift down: one, two, three, all of them, and 7 for Wrona, who went by humming toward the old stope with the whistle in his shirt pocket.

At the end of the shift they came up. He struck them through one at a time. Eight.

He waited for the ninth.

He looked at the board.

Seven was not on it. He had chalked it himself that morning, and now there was no 7, struck or unstruck, anywhere on the slate. In the place where his chalk had been, in the rounder hand, was the old name.

He had washed it out. Old chalk, washed out. He had watched the slate go grey.

passages.heading: 4. Payroll Friday
passages.text:
Residual one. The same as the first week. A count the office already knew, and already docked bread for, and had already told him not to carry.

Nothing on the board showed that a man was missing.

The board balanced the way it had balanced the first week: one below, and the one was not Seven.

passages.heading: 5. Transferred
passages.text:
On Monday, 20 October, he went up to the office in his shift clothes and reported a man missing.

Hask turned the Friday sheet round on the desk so Four could read his own hand.

passages.heading: Residual's your name.
passages.text:
"It isn't my name. Seven went down. I chalked him."

"Not on your board." Hask tapped the sheet. "Board doesn't show him."

The office could not log a missing man the board did not show. There was no box on any form for it. Four had kept a payroll's books for eleven years, and he understood that before Hask said another word. Hask took his pen and wrote, in the office's hand, in the Disposition field against slot 7:

passages.heading: Transferred.
passages.text:
There was a requisition on the spike by Hask's elbow, and Four read it upside down because he was a clerk: LAMP OIL, DEEP LEVEL REFUGE, 1 QT, WEEKLY. He did not know why the Deep Level needed a lamp. He did not ask.

Walking back down the adit, he worked it out. He had been tired. He had chalked a wrong number, or washed one he should have kept. The office had corrected him. That was what offices were for.

On Tuesday a new man stood at the board. He had a pencil behind his ear and slot 7's new billet number on his shirt, and he counted the nails under his breath in German, *eins, zwei, drei*, the way a man counts in the language he first learned to count in.

passages.heading: 6. The check
passages.text:
At the end of October the winze boards came off twice for something the office called a recovery detail. A man with a clipboard took a number down each time. Neither went on the board. The detail officer kept his own count, and it was not the keeper's count. Four told himself that, and kept his own.

On Wednesday, 5 November, the last of the shift came up, and he struck them through, and he went to hang the rag on its nail.

Wrona's brass lamp check was hanging beside the old name.

A brass disc stamped 7. It was wet, and cold enough to sting, and there was a ring of water on the floor under it the colour of the stope water, as if it had been carried up from there and hung, and had dripped. Caught round the nail with it was a thread of something white that he took for string until he touched it. It was skin. A long curl of it, soft as wet paper, the whorls of a fingertip still on it.

passages.heading: 6. The check
passages.text:
Transferred men take their checks with them. They hand them in at the gate with their boots and their spoons. That was the rule, and he had seen it done.

He went down the winze gallery with his own lamp, as far as the boards over the ladder shaft, and put his eye to the gap between two of them.

A long way down there was a light: small and yellow, steady, in the refuge, where nobody had been sent that day. One quart, weekly. Somebody carried it down.

Under the light, the water. Black, flat, and then not flat. It rose a finger's width up the ladder and went back, slow, the way a chest goes. The crew called it the Mother's water. He had thought that was a joke.

At its edge something sat with its head on one side, the way Wrona sat at the bread line.

passages.heading: 6. The check
passages.text:
White. Not pale: white, like bread left in the rain. The skin drawn so tight over the skull that the teeth showed through the cheeks. The ribs standing out like the rungs of the ladder. The fingers gone soft and long, the nails gone, the ends of them split. The eyes open under a skin of water that did not run off.

It was not breathing.

He counted on his trouser seam. Sixty. A hundred. A hundred and eighty.

At two hundred and twelve the chest let go, all at once, a long wet sigh that came up the shaft to him. Then the mouth closed and the count began again.

It was humming. No tune. Just the hum, through the teeth, the way Wrona had hummed when he was carving.

He stood there until his lamp needed trimming. Then he went back and put Wrona's check in his own pocket, and did not hang the rag.

passages.heading: 6. The check
passages.text: Transferred men take their checks with them, and Seven had not.

passages.heading: 7. The trade
passages.text:
He did it on his trouser seam, with his thumbnail, the way he did every sum.

He washed the name on the twelfth. On the seventeenth the board had Seven instead, and the name came back. The board did not keep a residual. It kept a man below. If the old name was not the man, the board found one.

Wash the name, and the board takes a man to balance it.

So he left it up.

> G99-T · WORKINGS · MON 10 NOV 52 · DAY · KEEPER 4 · DOWN 10 · UP 9 · RESIDUAL 1 · DISPOSITION —

Residual one, shift after shift. Short count, short ration. On Tuesday, 18 November, the seam dust went up in the far heading, and the adit was shut for forty hours, and the office carried the quota forward against labour. So the crew was hungry twice over, and both times it was his number on the sheet.

passages.heading: 7. The trade
passages.text:
Every man came up. Every shift. He struck each of them through and watched each one take his check off its nail.

The crew turned on him by the second week.

passages.heading: My kid brother could wash a board.
passages.text:
Danny Fitch was loudest. He was nineteen, Two, off the Baltimore docks. He played solitaire every night with a deck that had lost its queen of hearts, and he said he would win without her. At the bread line he said it to Four's face:

"You like it up there. Nice and dry. You like keeping us short."

Four could not tell them the sum. Said aloud, it was a report, and a report gets read out at the office. He kept Wrona's check in his pocket and his daughter's remainder in his cap, and he ate short with the rest of them.

The new Seven counted the men up in German every evening, under his breath, standing by Wrona's nail. Once he stood in front of the old name for a long time, reading it the way a man reads a word in a language he knows. He said nothing about it.

passages.heading: My kid brother could wash a board.
passages.text: Left up, the name took no one. Nobody went down for it. Everybody went hungry for it.

passages.heading: 8. Audit notice
passages.text:
On Monday, 1 December, the notice went up on the board in the yard, and Hask brought a copy down to the ore chamber and read it out.

The Inspector-General was coming on Friday's payroll train. Every board in the camp would be reconciled by then. An unreconciled board was the keeper's fault.

"Clean by Friday," Hask said. "Or your billet goes down the winze with the next shift."

"No," Four said.

He said it out loud. It was the first time in the camp he had said it to anyone.

Hask wrote something. The bread was cut again, for the whole crew, by a third.

That night, in the yard, Four went to the Workings rack and looked at his own billet for the first time: slot 4, oak, his number burned in. Just under the number was a knot in the grain, round and dark, like a thumbprint.

passages.heading: 8. Audit notice
passages.text: His own billet, set against a clean board.

passages.heading: 9. Closed count
passages.text:
He washed it on Thursday night.

Nobody was in the chamber. The bucket, the drip, the rag. The rounder hand came off the way it had the first time, as if it had never been anything but chalk. He told himself it might be a different man this time, or no man at all. He told himself the Inspector-General's signature might be worth something, even down here.

> G99-T · WORKINGS · THU 4–FRI 5 DEC 52 · NIGHT · KEEPER 4 · DOWN 9 · UP 9 · RESIDUAL 0 · DISPOSITION — · SIGNED: ███████, INSPECTOR-GENERAL (PROGRAM)

On Friday morning the Inspector-General came down the adit with Hask and a man carrying a lamp in front of him. From the far end of the chamber he was a coat and a pen. He did not look at the board. He looked at the sheet, and signed it, and went back up into the daylight.

passages.heading: 9. Closed count
passages.text:
Danny went down on the first shift under that signature. He went past the board with his deck in his shirt pocket and did not look at Four.

He did not come up.

At the end of the shift the old name was back in the DOWN column, in Danny's place, in the rounder hand. Two was nowhere on the board.

On the nail beside the name hung Wrona's whistle, on a length of string. It was finished: the finger holes cut, the mouthpiece rounded. Somebody had done the last of the work below.

Four did not blow it.

Danny's deck was on his bunk that night, squared up. Fifty-one cards, and still no queen.

passages.heading: 10. In his own hand
passages.text:
> G99-T · WORKINGS · SAT 6 DEC 52 · DAY · KEEPER 4 · DOWN 9 · UP 8 · RESIDUAL 1 · DISPOSITION 2 — TRANSFERRED

He wrote it before Hask asked. Slot 2, transferred, in his own hand, in the field where the office had written it for Seven. It took no longer than any other word.

Then, because the board still read residual one and the bread would be cut again, he wrote it a second time, on the same line, against the old name. *Transferred.*

The office took it. The sheet closed. The bread came back.

The next two Fridays were single lines.

Friday, 12 December: payroll on time. At the platform the guards took a man, a scientist, the men said, in a good coat. After that nothing was found that had been his. No room, no papers, nobody he had been working on. Nothing at all. *It's almost like they had help,* somebody said at the bread line, and nobody asked who.

passages.heading: 10. In his own hand
passages.text:
Friday, 19 December: the steam went off all over the camp, and the arc-lights with it, and in the morning the Inspector-General was not accounted for.

Four heard both and did not follow either. He had a count to keep. Down, up, residual one, transferred. His sheets closed clean every shift.

The word was easy once it was his.

passages.heading: 11. Last shift
passages.text: On Saturday, 20 December, the last shift of the season, Hask came down with all of Four's sheets in a stack and read them out, the way he read everything.

passages.heading: Clean," he said. "Clean. Clean. Good sheets, Four.
passages.text: Then: "Keeper rotates. The new Two keeps the board from Monday. You go down with the last shift."

passages.heading: The keeper before me.
passages.text:
"Transferred," Hask said.

Writing the word had not kept him above. He had thought it would, in some sum he had never quite finished on his trouser seam.

Hask chalked nothing. He never did. Keeping the board was the keeper's job. Four took the stub of chalk and wrote 4 in the DOWN column, under the old name, in his own hand.

He left the residual field empty, for somebody else to fill.

passages.heading: 12. Clean slate
passages.text:
The new Two was a big, quiet boy with his billet still pale from the brand. He held the custody chit in both hands as if it might tear.

Four taught him the board in four sentences.

"Down on the left. Up on the right. Close it every shift."

Then the fourth.

passages.heading: Don't wash that one.
passages.text:
The old name had gone thin over the weeks, from the drip and the damp and men's shoulders brushing it. Some of the gaps had spread. Four went over it with the chalk, letter by letter where there were letters, and he left the gaps where they had always been. The hand that came out was rounder than his own. He looked at it for a while. It was the hand he had found on the first day.

He put the chalk in the boy's palm and closed the boy's fingers on it.

He kept Wrona's check in his pocket and his daughter's remainder in his cap. He left the whistle on its nail. Then he went down with the last shift.

The ladder was wet below the boards. The cold came up it like a hand.

The light in the refuge. The water under it, rising and going back.

passages.heading: Don't wash that one.
passages.text:
At its edge they were sitting in a row, the way the crew sat at the bread line. Eight of them, nine. White. The skin pulled tight round bone and split at the knuckles. Ribs. Mouths shut on a breath held so long the cheeks had sunk to the teeth. One had a flat of pine on its knee and was working at it with nails that were not there. One, the smallest, held a single playing card face down against its chest, very carefully, the way a boy holds the card he means to win with.

None of them looked up. They were counting. He could see it in the throats.

Above him, small and far off, he heard the new keeper read the frame aloud, slowly, the way Hask did, the way a man reads a rule he has been told is his now.

works.title: Ordinances of the Sovereign Sourdough Council
works.pov: none (printed law), with a 1793 committee's margin in red
works.blurb: the Council's printed law of 1787 (the Letters Patent of the Crown, then Titles I–VIII: rank and the platters, the Wake Loaf and its seal, the yeast-tax and registration, crimes against the bread, the Dawn Judgment and the Hearth, the offices, the Abbey and its heresies, and Dusk), revised in red in 1793 by the Committee of the Common Loaf, which keeps almost every article and turns it round, leaves Title VIII alone, and signs "We are the Council".

passages.heading: Ordinances of the Sovereign Sourdough Council
passages.text:
*Of Port-au-Levain, with the Letters Patent of the Crown. Printed at the press of the Counting-House in the year 1787, by order, and to be read aloud in the Hall of Platters once in every year, at the first bell after Candlemas.*

[PROPERTY OF THE COUNTING-HOUSE]

*[red, 1793: Read aloud this year at the first bell after Candlemas, as directed, by the committee. We have kept the day.]*

---

passages.heading: The Letters Patent
passages.text:
His Majesty, by the grace of God King of France and of Navarre, to all who shall see these present letters, greeting.

Our well-beloved the Master Bakers of Our island of Port-au-Levain, beyond the reef and in the fog of Our seas of New France, have shown Us that from time out of mind they have kept upon that rock a Hearth that has not gone out, a Hall of Platters in which every soul of the island has its place, and a living leaven they name the Mother of Mothers. They have shown Us that by these three they are governed, fed and numbered, and that the order of it is kept by a Council of their oldest houses.

Wishing that so old an order not fall into dispute for want of Our hand, We confirm to the Guild of Port-au-Levain and to its Council their privileges as anciently used: the keeping of the Hearth and of the Hall; the guard of the Mother of Mothers in her Vault; the nightly tariff in Guild Copper and in Yeast Tokens; the three verdicts of their Dawn Judgment; and the ordinances that follow, which We have caused to be read to Us and find to be in order.

passages.heading: The Letters Patent
passages.text:
We permit the said Council to style itself ~~Sovereign, by Our grace,~~ Sovereign, it being understood that the word signifies the bread and not the rock.

*[red, 1793: The grace is withdrawn. The word stands.]*

Given at Versailles, in the month of March, in the year of grace one thousand seven hundred and eighty-seven, and of Our reign the thirteenth.

passages.heading: By the King.
passages.text:
*[red, 1793: The hand that signed this has been dead since January. The patent is not struck. It is not needed.]*

Registered in the Council, read in the Hall and entered at the Counting-House, the fourteenth of May, 1787.

---

passages.heading: Title I: Of Rank and the Platters
passages.text:
**Art. 1. Of the order of the Hall.** Every soul upon the rock has a silver platter in the Hall of Platters, and no soul has two. The platters stand in order of their distance from the Great Hearth. The gilded platters of the Gallery stand nearest. The platters of the Guild stand after them, the platters of the Commons after the Guild, and the platters of the Abbey of the Crust along the north wall, where the heat does not reach and is not asked for.

*[red, 1793: Retained. Order reversed. The gilded platters are moved to the cold end of the Hall, by the great south doors and the Square. They stand there in the order of their former nearness, the nearest now the farthest, measured by the finger-breadth of Art. 4. Excepted: the empty platter nearest the Hearth, which is not moved. See Title VIII.]*

**Art. 2. Of gold leaf.** The rim of a Gallery platter carries gold leaf according to rank: for a house of the first rank, four finger-breadths of rim; of the second, three; for a cadet line, two; for a widow, what her house allows. The leaf is renewed on each quarter-day by the Council's gilder, and never by a hand that has been in the dish pit since the bell before.

passages.heading: Title I: Of Rank and the Platters
passages.text:
*[red, 1793: The leaf is to be scraped, by the dish pit, and entered at the Counting-House by weight. Entered: eleven ounces and some grains. The gilder asked to keep his office. Granted. He scrapes.]*

**Art. 3. Of the colours of rank.** A Gallery loaf is gilt at the seal. A Guild loaf is dusted flour-white before the calling. A Commons loaf is baked at the Hearth's mouth, the cheaper heat, and comes out red in the crust. An Abbey loaf is wrapped in burlap and is not looked at. No loaf shall wear the colour of a rank not its holder's. A Commons loaf found dusted shall be read as false.

*[red, 1793: Retained. All loaves red. The Abbey's burlap retained: it is no rank, it is a cloth.]*

**Art. 4. Of platters moved.** No platter shall be moved nearer the Hearth than its rank allows. For every finger-breadth a platter is found moved, a Guild holder shall pay one Guild Copper, and a Commons holder one Guild Copper and one night's tokens. A Gallery platter is not found moved. The finger-breadth is the High Chancellor's, and a measure of it in brass is kept at the Counting-House.

passages.heading: Title I: Of Rank and the Platters
passages.text:
*[red, 1793: Applied to the Gallery from the printing of this book, for every finger-breadth the gilded platters stood nearer the fire than the platters of the Commons. Computed by the brass measure, which we have kept.]*

**Art. 5. Of polishing.** A Commons platter shall be polished by its holder and by no other, before the proofing bell, with ash and not with flour. A Gallery platter shall be polished by the Hall's polishers, who are ~~of the Commons~~ of the Gallery, and who shall not breathe upon the gilt.

*[red, 1793: And who may breathe as they please.]*

---

## Title II: Of the Wake Loaf and its Seal

**Art. 6. Of the shaping.** Each Wake Loaf is shaped at the shaping bench from the leaven of its holder's house, and sealed by Le Boulanger with its holder's guild seal before it is proved. A holder without a house is given the leaven of the Hall, which is the cheapest, and the seal of the Commons, which is a plain ring.

passages.heading: Title I: Of Rank and the Platters
passages.text:
*[red, 1793: Retained. All seals a plain ring. The Gallery's seals are at the Counting-House, in a box, counted.]*

**Art. 7. Of the calling.** At the expediter, L'Aboyeur calls each loaf by its holder's name as it passes. He calls the Gallery first, by precedence; the Guild next, by office; the Commons last, in a single breath where the hour is late.

*[red, 1793: Retained. Call the Gallery last, and in one breath.]*

**Art. 8. Of the reading of the platter.** The loaf upon a platter at dawn is read as that platter's holder. A loaf found at dawn upon a platter not its own is read as the holder of the platter on which it sits. The Council presumes the platter and not the person, for a platter is entered in the census and a person is only entered on it.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained. It has served us.]
passages.text:
**Art. 9. Of the seal smudged.** A seal found smudged at dawn shall be read against its holder, no hand but the holder's being presumed to have touched it. ~~A Gallery seal found smudged shall be re-impressed by Le Boulanger at the Council's charge, and the smudge not entered.~~

*[red, 1793: Struck. Under this article, in the spring of 1788: Ondine Leroux, of the dish pit, whose right thumb was not once dry in eleven years at the basins. She pressed her own seal at the shaping bench every morning to see that it sat straight. It was her thumb that smudged it. Entered here, so that it is entered.]*

---

## Title III: Of the Yeast-Tax and of Registration

**Art. 10. Of the tariff.** Every platter owes a tariff each night. It is paid at the proofing bell, at the Ledger-Clerk's tariff desk in the Counting-House, in Guild Copper and in Yeast Tokens, and in no other coin.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained.]
passages.text:
**Art. 11. Of the tariff by rank.**
- A Commons platter: two Guild Copper and one Yeast Token, nightly.
- A Guild platter: one Yeast Token, nightly.
- A Gallery platter: one Yeast Token on the first night of each quarter, or as the house shall see fit. It is excused on feast nights, on the nights of a Trial, and on any night the house dines.

*[red, 1793: The Gallery's excused nights are computed, every house, to the token, from the printing of this book to the night of this mark. They are entered at folio 212 of the Counting-House ledger and underlined twice. A house that dines every night has been excused every night. They dined every night.]*

**Art. 12. Of the stamp.** A platter whose tariff is unpaid at the bell is stamped [UNREGISTERED]. L'Aboyeur shall not call it. Its holder shall not be heard at the Dawn Judgment, neither in accusation nor in answer. Its loaf shall be covered with the Iron Cloche, which is of iron and not of silver, so that no officer need look upon it.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained.]
passages.text:
*[red, 1793: Retained. Apply to the gilded platters, beginning with the arrears of Art. 11. The Iron Cloches have been cleaned. There were more of them in the Counting-House than the Commons ever had platters. We have counted them.]*

**Art. 13. Of arrears.** A holder in arrears may not inherit Yeast Tokens, which pass to the Counting-House. Copper rings, buckles and the like may be given at the tariff desk in place of coin, at the Counting-House's valuation, which is not disputed.

*[red, 1793: Under Arts. 12 and 13, in June of 1789: Hervé Morel, dockhand of the Wharf, a widower. He would not give in his wife's copper ring at the Counting-House's valuation, and wore it on a cord at his neck. His platter went Unregistered three nights. On the third it was a crime (Art. 15). The ring was valued after.]*

---

passages.heading: Title IV: Of Crimes Against the Bread
passages.text:
*The following are crimes against the Mother and the Hall. They are set down with their definitions, so that no one may say he did not know what a crumb was.*

**Art. 14. A crumb ~~taken~~ withheld.** A crumb is a portion of crust or of crumb not exceeding, in its greatest length, the nail of the High Chancellor's smallest finger, the said nail being measured at Michaelmas and entered. A portion larger is a loaf, and its taking is theft of a loaf. The crumbs that fall from the gallery to the floor of the Hall ~~belong to the floor~~ were withheld from the floor. They shall not be taken up by any hand, but swept at dawn into the Hearth by the Plongeur.

*[red, 1793: The definition is retained to the word, and the nail with it; the High Chancellor's is in our keeping. For "taken" read "withheld".]*

passages.heading: Title IV: Of Crimes Against the Bread
passages.text:
*[red, 1793: Under this article as printed, in the autumn of 1787: Jehanne Coquart, a net-mender's daughter of fourteen. She counted the gulls off the Wharf every morning and told her mother the number. She took up one crumb from under the gallery rail. It was within the nail.]*

*[red, 1793: Under this article as amended, in April of 1793: Thibault Lormeau, of the house of Lormeau. In all his life he did not eat the crust of his own Wake Loaf. He kept the crusts in a drawer of his writing table and fed them to the gulls from the gallery window. Withheld from the floor. Within the nail.]*

**Art. 15. A platter unpaid.** A platter Unregistered three nights together (Art. 12) is a crime on the third night.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained. The Gallery's quarter has come.]
passages.text: **Art. 16. A seal smudged.** As at Art. 9.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: See Art. 9. Entered there.]
passages.text:
**Art. 17. A loaf eaten before dawn.** This includes the holder's own, for the Wake Loaf is not the holder's to eat but the Hall's to read.

*[red, 1793: Retained. Hunger is no plea. It was none before.]*

**Art. 18. Speaking below the gallery during the calling.** This is the old disgrace of L'Apprenti, extended to all of the Commons, the calling being the Council's hour.

*[red, 1793: Retained. Extended to the gallery, which shall be silent while it is called.]*

**Art. 19. Kneeling off the seal.** Le Plongeur kneels at the basins upon the seal of the abolished office of Le Champignon, which is ground into the floor of the dish pit, and upon no other part of that floor.

*[red, 1793: Retained. The Gallery's widows kneel there now. They have asked for cushions. The article does not provide for cushions.]*

**Art. 20. Carrying from the Mother.** Le Commis carries flour, water and ash down to the Mother of Mothers, and carries nothing up from her.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: See Art. 9. Entered there.]
passages.text:
The verdicts for this Title are in the Schedule, save that of Art. 20.

---

## Title V: Of the Dawn Judgment and of the Hearth

**Art. 21. Of the law.** The Inquisitor asks. The Guild Bailiff takes. The High Chancellor decides, from the gallery, and does not come down. There are three verdicts: Acquittal; a Guild Fine; Trial by Fire in the Great Hearth.

*[red, 1793: Retained. The President of the committee decides, from the floor, and does not go up.]*

**Art. 22. Of the ceremony of a Trial by Fire.**
- The Great Proofing Bell strikes six, and not before.
- The great south doors of the Hall are opened onto Gallows Square.
- The cloches are lifted in the order of rank, the Gallery first.
- The Council's consort plays from the gallery stair: hautboys and a viol, and nothing in a minor key before the sentence.
- The sentence is read twice: once by the High Chancellor, and once by a member of the Gallery chosen by lot at supper the evening before, who shall be thanked.
- The places in the Square: the first three rows to the Gallery, seated, with cushions; the Guild behind them, standing; the Commons behind the Guild, standing. The attendance of the Commons is required, and counted.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: See Art. 9. Entered there.]
passages.text:
*[red, 1793: Retained in every particular. The lot is drawn at the committee's supper. The Gallery shall attend, standing, and be counted. The cushions are entered at the Counting-House.]*

**Art. 23. Of the hour.** No sentence of Fire shall be carried out within the hour before the Council's supper, nor in any way that delays it. Where the hour of a sentence and the hour of a supper fall together, the sentence shall be moved. The Council sups in the gallery afterward, the doors to the Square being closed.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained. The committee also eats.]
passages.text:
**Art. 24. Of the manner.** The manner of the Hearth is not set down in this book.

*[red, 1793: Beside the Hearth, since the ferry of the spring: the National Razor, which came in crates and was put together there by Guild carpenters. Its manner is not set down either. The consort played while it was put together. No one had told them to stop.]*

*[red, 1793: Under Arts. 21 to 24: the dowager of the house of Belcourt. Every morning of her life she carried her linnet's cage to the gallery window, so that the bird could see the harbour. She heard her sentence read twice, and thanked the second reader, as the article requires.]*

**Art. 25. Of judgment in absence.** Where the accused is beyond the reef or under the water, the Council judges the platter. The accused's Wake Loaf is given to the Hearth in the accused's place, and L'Aboyeur calls the name as it passes.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained. The committee also eats.]
passages.text:
*[red, 1793: Retained. Applied since the autumn of 1789 to the gilded platters of those who took the ferry. The ferry is watched now.]*

---

passages.heading: Title VI: Of the Offices
passages.text:
**Art. 26. Of the Old Brigade.** These are the kitchen's ranks, which are older than the Council:
- Le Boulanger, the bake.
- Le Levain, the feeding hand (Art. 27).
- Le Commis, the carrying hands (Art. 20).
- L'Apprenti, who watches, and does not speak.
- Le Rat de Cave, the cellar door.
- Le Champignon, abolished; its seal is in the floor of the dish pit.
- Le Chef de Cuisine and Le Sous-Chef, ~~now the Council and its clerks~~ now the committee and its clerks.
- L'Aboyeur, the calling.
- Le Tourrier, the folds.
- Le Plongeur, the dish pit, by sentence or by birth.
- Le Garde Manger, the cold pantry and its lock.
- L'Inspecteur Sanitaire, the hygiene room.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: The clerks are the same clerks.]
passages.text:
**Art. 27. Of Le Levain.** The office of the feeding hand is held by the eldest line of the house of Vane, as it has always been held. No hand of any other house shall touch the Mother of Mothers, nor be in the Vault at the feeding hour.

*[red, 1793: This article is suspended, not struck, the feeding hand being before the tribunal.]*

**Art. 28. Of Le Critique Gastronomique.** The office is vacant. Its chair at the front of house is dusted daily, and sat in by no one, so that it stays empty.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained.]
passages.text:
**Art. 29. Of Le Croissant Rassis.** This is not an office but a style. A holder of the Gallery who is disgraced is styled Le Croissant Rassis, and keeps his platter, his gilt and his seat. A holder of the Commons who is disgraced goes to the dish pit and is styled nothing.

*[red, 1793: Every gilded platter is styled Croissant Rassis, and keeps nothing.]*

**Art. 30. Of the Guild offices and of the Crown's officer.** The Master Proof-Reader weighs. The Spice-Master keeps the Apothecary and its register. The Tide-Watcher keeps the lighthouse and the Wharf's tally. The Hearth-Warden keeps the peace of the Tavern. The Ledger-Clerk keeps the tariff desk and the deadbolts. The Iron-Wardens enforce. When the Crown sends a Grand Inspector-General, successor to L'Inspecteur Sanitaire, the Council shall receive him at the Wharf, seat him at the gallery's table, and show him what it shows.

*[red, 1793: The Guild offices are retained, their holders having chosen. The Crown's man came, in the autumn of 1789. This article is answered.]*

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained.]
passages.text:
## Title VII: Of the Abbey and of the Heresies

**Art. 31. Of the blessing.** The Abbot of the Crust walks the island and blesses the flour with the Apostolic Starter. The Council attends the blessing on the first day of each month, in burlap over its gilt.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained as to the burlap.]
passages.text:
**Art. 32. Of the Four Sour-Practices.** These are charged against the Mother, and named here by practice and not by any person.
- *The Leaven-Rot*, which would sour the Mother on purpose; against the Abbot. ~~Heresy. Trial by Fire.~~
- *The Pyre-Master's practice*, which holds that the Hearth belongs to the island and not to the Council. Trial by Fire.
- *The Smuggler-Blackguard's practice*: the pocket-mortar at the Wharf, and loaves lifted from one platter to another under the cloche. A Guild Fine, then the Square.
- *The Black-Crust Contract*: a commission rolled in a cylinder sealed in black wax and brought by pigeon. Trial by Fire for the one who accepts it, and for the one who bought it, if a buyer is found.

*[red, 1793: The Leaven-Rot: heresy no longer. See the Rite. The Pyre-Master's: the island holds it. The Smuggler-Blackguard's: retained; it is no one's. The Black-Crust Contract: retained. No buyer has been found.]*

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained as to the burlap.]
passages.text: **Art. 33. Of black wax.** Every cylinder sealed in black wax found on the rock shall be delivered unopened to the Counting-House. No pigeon shall be kept but in the Council's loft.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained. The committee keeps the loft.]
passages.text: **Art. 34. Of the glaze.** No apothecary shall keep the Nightshade Glaze, in the register or out of it, and the word shall not be written on any label.

passages.heading: [red, 1793: Retained.]
passages.text:
**Art. 35. Of rumour.** Rumour off the Morning Ferry, whether it runs inland or comes from there, shall be posted on the board in Gallows Square only by order of the Council, and in the Council's hand.

*[red, 1793: Retained. It was by the ferry that we heard, in the September of '89. We post it in our hand.]*

---

passages.heading: Title VIII: Of Dusk
passages.text:
**Art. 36.** At dusk, when the Morning Ferry is gone and the harbour lamps are lit, L'Aboyeur shall carry a Wake Loaf down the Hall of Platters, calling no name, and set it upon the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal. The watches of the night are counted from the setting down of that loaf, and the rounds of the Iron-Wardens begin from it. It is taken up at dawn and not eaten. Its tariff is not entered.

---

passages.heading: Schedule of Fines and Sentences
passages.text:
*Carrying from the Mother (Art. 20) is not scheduled. Its verdict is the Hearth, for any hand.*

*[red, 1793: The headings are exchanged. No cell is altered.]*

These Ordinances shall not be amended save by the Council.

Printed at the press of the Counting-House, 1787, in the Counting-House type, by order.

[SEALED: SOVEREIGN SOURDOUGH COUNCIL]

*[red, 1793: We are the Council. For the Committee of the Common Loaf, in the week of the tribunal.]*

works.title: The Lighthouse Sweep
works.pov: the Tide-Watcher's sweep-book (third person on Perrine Goulet between sweeps)
works.blurb: the Tide-Watcher's sweep-book for the night of 2–3 December 1788: four landward turns of the lighthouse beam, as the Council's ordinance requires, over Smuggler's Wharf, the Counting-House, the Tavern, the Hall and its ten kitchen vents, Gallows Square, the Yeast Vault, the Abbey, the Apothecary, the Drowners on the Flats, the Windmill Cliffs and the gilded houses, each bearing given what she logged and what she did not, until the last "Not logged" is left empty.

passages.heading: The Lighthouse Sweep
passages.text:
*The Sweep-Book of the Tower on the Reef. Kept by the Tide-Watcher of the Guild, under the Council's Ordinance of the Landward Turn. The night of the second to the third of December, 1788. Tide-Watcher: P. Goulet.*

> *Of the Landward Turn.* The lamp keeps the reef. At each of the four watches of the night the Tide-Watcher shall turn it landward and sweep the town once, from east to west. Any soul the beam finds abroad after the proofing bell without a registered seal shall be logged, and the Iron-Wardens shall attend to the log.
> *Rider.* Bearings three hundred to three hundred and twenty, being the houses of the cliff road, are dipped by subscription.
> — Ordinances of the Sovereign Sourdough Council, as painted inside the tower door

---

passages.heading: Of the Tower
passages.text:
**The Tower.** It stands on the reef point, south of the town, on the last rock that is still the island. Its work is the reef. Ships come in by the light and the drowned go out by it. Four times a night, by ordinance, it turns its back on the sea and looks at the people instead.

**The Lamp.** Oil, burned in a row of wicks before copper mirrors, polished every watch. A clockwork turns the frame so that the light walks round the reef. A weight on a chain drives the clockwork, and the weight is wound by hand. For the Landward Turn the clockwork is unlatched and the frame is cranked round by the keeper's own arm, slowly, east to west, at the pace the ordinance calls *a walking pace for the eye*.

**The Office.** The Tide-Watcher is a Guild office, flour-white. It keeps the beacon, the customs ledger of incoming cargo, and the ferry tally of who leaves. It is paid in Guild Copper by the night, less the yeast-tax on the keeper's own platter in the Hall. The Council's registers note that the office *may become, under the Council's need*, one of two other things. One is the **Wreck-Looter**, who knows what the fog does to a manifest. The other is the **Harbor Master**, who holds the gangplank and deputizes dockhands when the Crown's man comes. No Tide-Watcher chooses which. The need chooses.

passages.heading: Of the Tower
passages.text:
**The Predecessor.** The keeper before this one let the light fail on a wreck night. He was made Croissant Rassis, the stale one, and his seal on the tower door was scratched through with a nail and left there, so that the next keeper would have to pass it every time she came up the stair. She has not missed a turn in eleven years.

**The Colours under the Beam.** From the tower no face can be read at any distance, but rank can.

| Colour | Whose | What the beam does with it |
|---|---|---|
| gold leaf | the Gallery | throws it back; the tower sees a second light |
| flour-white | the Guild | glows |
| red crust | the Commons | shows black |
| burlap | the Abbey of the Crust | drinks it, gives nothing back |

The island can be read entire from the reef point without one name in it. The Council considers this the beam's chief virtue.

passages.heading: The First Sweep: Dusk, the Seating
passages.text: *The Morning Ferry is long gone. The fog has not come. The beam is long and clean.*

passages.heading: Bearing 075: Smuggler's Wharf & the Salt-Flats
passages.text: The wharf is where things come ashore that the Counting-House did not count. The Flats are the Council's, and the salt raked from them is the Council's, less what the rakers are let keep, which is what sticks to their hands. In the customs shed there is a crate with a lid that has never been nailed. A silver piece is left on it, some nights, for the Master Proof-Reader. It is a custom. Whose hand keeps the custom is not entered. The dockhands say it is a way of telling the Hall that it is watched both ways.

passages.heading: Logged:** *Counting-House lit within. Lawful.
passages.text: The Counting-House holds the archive, the Guild Copper and the yeast tokens. The tariff falls due every night at the proofing bell. A platter that does not pay is stamped UNREGISTERED, and an Unregistered loaf is a soul the Council has stopped feeding. The Debtor has been Unregistered since the spring. He still comes to the steps.

passages.heading: Logged:** *Tavern. One at the pillar.
passages.text:
Here rumour is weighed before the Council weighs it. Its weights are lighter. The Hearth-Warden keeps the rum cellar under the floor, and the rum cellar is a cellar.

**Bearing 010: the Great Hearth & Hall of Platters (by the high windows)**

**Held by:** the Gallery, on the gilded platters nearest the Hearth; the Guild, in the middle rows, flour-white; the Commons, at the far end by the doors, where the draught is.

**In the beam:** The Hall from outside is a field of small lights. Nearest the fire the Gallery's platters throw the beam straight back at the tower, so that for a moment the keeper is looking into her own lamp. The middle rows glow. The far rows are dull. Several have no cloche, and the beam picks out the stamp on the silver where a cloche should be. The platters of the house of Vane sit nearest of all, their silver gone faintly gold from the heat. The Master Proof-Reader is at the scales with a loaf in each pan. Down the length of the Hall the Aboyeur carries one loaf in both hands. He calls no name. He sets it on the empty platter nearest the Hearth and steps back from it.

passages.heading: Logged:** *Tavern. One at the pillar.
passages.text:
The Hearth is the oldest fire on the rock and has never been let go out. The Hall around it holds a silver platter for every soul on the island, and on every platter a Wake Loaf stamped with its owner's guild seal. A soul without a platter has no name in law. The words for the dusk loaf are the Aboyeur's own. The Tide-Watcher copies them into the book every night, as her predecessor did, and his did, and as the first book in the tower does on its first page. The book does not say what the name is. Nobody she has ever asked has known.

On the rock it is said that you are the loaf on your platter when the cloche comes off at dawn. It is said to children as a comfort.

passages.heading: Between Sweeps
passages.text:
She latched the frame back to the reef and wound the weight. The chain went up through her hands, cold, link by link, and the clockwork took the lamp out of her keeping and walked it round the water again.
