**Tag.** MABEL. Opened at the Morgue on Monday, 27 November. Doc Mallory: between eleven on Sunday night and one on Monday morning. "Not before eleven. Not after one."

**Cross-filed.** The account of the witness Gert, Pump Row, 4th door. It covered the hour from eleven to one: the defendant sat at her table by her one candle and resoled her boy's boot. It was struck at the Third Sitting under Article V §3, the witness having been entered Indebted at Midday. Struck, and legible, the way the Company likes a strike made.

*[The hour was the case. Not the knife, and not the voices. I have kept the strike here exactly as I made it at the bench, the line through it and every word under the line. I have not added a word to it. I would have liked to. — R.]*

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
**J. SILHOUETTE.**
*Shows:* height and scarf. *Read by:* the Child, as "The Child saw it." *Held:* not held. The Child's word would be entered, Verified, at the next sitting.

**Tag.** None this season. The card is blank.

*[The Constable asked the girl of about nine, the one who counts. Everybody knows she counts things: the planks on the platform, the hands that go up at the Bell. She told him she counts feet. She does not look up at faces.*

*The press has asked. Children are about. — R.]*

---

**K. LEDGER.**
*Shows:* the last house each living soul entered this cycle. House only, no hour. *Read by:* the Butler. *Held:* a leaf, lodged.

**Tag.** A leaf from the household day-book of Vane Manor, in the hand of Horace, Butler for twenty-two years. It is headed Sunday, 26 November, was lodged at the Clerk's Office on the Monday, and was not called at the Tribunal.

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
Against the defendant, the line reads in full: *the widow's, Pump Row, 4th door.*

*[House only, no hour. It would not have helped him. The hour was the case.*

*The leaf is in one ink from heading to foot, without a blot. The Undertaker says Horace writes the round down before he walks it. I have entered that as the Undertaker did, as a habit. — R.]*

---

**L. DROPPED ITEMS.**
*Shows:* what the dead carried, except what belonged to an office; an office keeps its own. *Read by:* anyone. *Held:* not by the form. These came in by the Constable's hand.

**Tag.** EDITH. See G.
- A letter to a sister back east, folded once, not finished.
- A postage stamp, two cents, bought at the Post Office with money kept back from the scrip. It was lying loose on top, not stuck down.

**The life.** She did washing for the manor and the mill office and was two weeks behind. The Undertaker writes that she said "two weeks" "as if, said carefully enough, it might come to one." Her sister had written to her twice. Edith had not finished writing back.

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
*[The press has not stuck the stamp down. Once it is stuck down the letter has to go, and nobody here knows where to. — R.]*

---

**M. FUR.**
*Shows:* wolf. Wolf kills leave fur, never footprints. *Read by:* anyone. *Held:* yes. *May be laid by a hand:* no.

**Tag.** A MAN NOT OF THE GRANT. Saturday, 21 October, the rail bed below Gallows Wood Siding. He got off the down train at the Siding and walked in along the bed at dusk with a carpet bag. The platform crew found him at the Station Rush. Entered by the Constable. Name not entered: he was the Line's, not the Company's town, and the Line did not send one.

**Found.**
- On his back on the ballast, the bag still in his left hand.
- The throat open. The coat off the shoulder in strips, and the shoulder under it.
- The right arm gone at the elbow. It was found two days later, forty yards up the bed, without the hand.
- The face left alone.
- Grey fur in the wounds. No prints round him but his own, coming in from the Siding.

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
**Autopsy.** On the printed line, *wolf* is struck. Verified.

**The life.** In the carpet bag, wrapped in a Gazette: a pair of child's boots, new, the laces still tied together through the eyes. Nobody in HollowMere has asked for them. They lie in the drawer under the fur.

*[The Undertaker carried three that day, and Car 3 went out with four. This is the fourth. He was not one of the forty, so he was not the Undertaker's, so he is the press's.*

*The form and the town agreed this once. The Autopsy said wolf, the square said wolf, and it was a wolf. That is why the town can say it of the others. — R.]*

---

**N. CLAW MARKS.**
*Shows:* wolf. Wolf kills leave claw marks. *Read by:* anyone. *Held:* a tracing on Company paper. *May be laid by a hand:* no.

**Tag.** No body. The lantern post at the Gallows Wood edge, on the Lamplighter's round. The marks are below the lamp, at a child's height, and the wood above them is scored the way bark goes when something climbs it in a hurry.

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
The chalk under the fourth lantern says Sid "chased his shadow to where the light stops". At the Gallows Wood edge the light stops at this post. The Lamplighter lit it at her hour. The wolves hunt the edge of the light and never cross it. In the morning the tracing was taken, and there was a child's cap on the fence beside the post. The Row says it is Sid's.

*[Whether a child came down off that post, the tracing does not say. His mother says he is about. Children are about. I have entered the cap as seen, not held: it is still on the fence.*

*On the morning of his Tribunal the Watchman asked for this tracing to be read. There was a cry at the fence, he said, and wolves in the square, and he went, because that is what the lantern is for. It was not read. The post is a quarter mile from the wash-house, and the marks are older than his night. — R.]*

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
**O. DRIP TRAIL.**
*Shows:* wounded. *Read by:* anyone. *Held:* never; it is gone by the next rain. *May be laid by a hand:* no.

**Tag.** WALT, sawyer at the mill. Thursday, 12 October, after Dusk. The trail ran from the wood's edge above the mill race to Mallory's step. He was gored in the thigh by a boar at the wood's edge. Boars wound and do not kill. Salts and a bandage at Mallory's. Living.

The Constable's man followed the drips by lantern from the edge of the wood, expecting a killer at the end of them. At the end of them was Walt, sitting on the step with his trouser leg cut away, counting.

**The life.** Short two fingers from before the Panic, he counts on the hand that has five. He had counted the drips back toward the wood as far as he could see them, and he got to forty, and said that was about right for a pig.

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
*[The form has a line for wounded and none for living. I wrote it in the margin: living. It is the only word of its kind in the press. — R.]*

---

**P. GLOWING FOOTPRINTS.**
*Shows:* hunger, and the walker's own height, on the ground the walker crosses until a stroke is made; then they stop. *Read by:* anyone. *Held:* never; they are gone by the Station Rush. *May be laid by a hand:* no.

**Tag.** ROSE. Pump Row, the night of Monday, 11 December.

A line of prints, faint and green, lit from inside like a coal under ash, came up the Row from the square end. No lantern reaches that end, because the Lamplighter's round does not come that way. The prints stop at Rose's door.

**The life.** She kept a geranium in a tin on her sill, the only flower on Pump Row, and carried it in at curfew the way you would carry in a child. That night it stayed out.

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
**Witness.** GERT, Pump Row, 4th door. *Indebted; not a witness.* Entered by order, and struck:

> ~~They came up past my step. I saw them through the crack of the door. They were the size of anybody's. They went to Rose's and they did not go on.~~

*[Struck, and legible. She is Indebted and may not bear witness, so the Company keeps what she saw and has the line put through it, so that the east can see what was taken out.*

*Tuck, who poles the marsh, says the island has prints like these. He says it the way the town says the weather. Nobody has asked him more. I have not asked him either.*

*The form calls it a kind. Somebody back east set type for it and gave it a letter. So it has happened before, somewhere the form was printed for. — R.]*

---

**Q. LANDING FOOTPRINTS.**
*Shows:* height, at the foot of a drop that does not go back up. *Read by:* anyone. *Held:* a tracing. *May be laid by a hand:* no.

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
**Tag.** Monday, 4 December, the platform. At the foot of the drop from the platform edge to the rail bed: a trail, short in the stride. It goes east along the bed a few yards and is lost in the ballast. Nothing climbs back up.

**The day.** Mill Row says Ada Brook lost her grey scarf that Monday, between the pump and the platform. It was her mother's, darned in red at one end. On the Tuesday she paid Crumb's ahead for ten wake loaves for Mill Row.

*[I have not laid her beside the tracing. I do not know her height. The Undertaker's line for her reads neither, and I have made the press's line read the same. A few yards, and then the ballast. — R.]*

---

**R. LONG-STRIDE FOOTPRINTS.**
*Shows:* height. *Read by:* anyone. *Held:* not from any case. *May be laid by a hand:* no.

**Tag.** Specimen. The print beside the well on the square, older than the books. The Constable's office keeps a card of it so new hands learn the reading before they are sent out. The card says, in print: *Footprints, long stride: Tall.*

passages.heading: Match.
passages.text:
**Cross-filed.** Crumb's Ovens. In October, on a Wednesday or a Thursday night, the till was emptied and there was "a boot in the flour dust, long in the stride". On the fourth of December the print was short. The baker stood in both in her own flour and wrote on her notice: "I fit neither, and I fit both, depending on how I walk."

*[I went out at the Midday Rent with the roll under my arm and stood in the specimen. I fit it. Then I walked the way I walk when I am carrying the roll, and I did not. — R.]*

---

passages.heading: Last leaf, under the eighteenth line.
passages.text:
*[Eighteen kinds, A to R. Height, scarf and hat. The hour. The house. Wolf, wounded, hunger. The Detective said it at the bench and I wrote it down: "Verified clues narrow the board. They don't name." The press has a drawer for every kind of thing a hand leaves. It has none for a name. The defendant's name is a blank in the bench's book, and it is a blank in mine.*

*Exhibit R and I share a letter. I have signed under it anyway, as the form wants, and blotted it. Nobody east will need to know the difference.*

works.title: Arrivals
works.pov: the platform book (Clem's entries and margins)
works.blurb: the Thorne & Expanse Line's arrivals and departures book at HollowMere, 2 October to 29 December 1893, kept by Clem of the platform crew: one page a week of who came off at Day and who got on at Dusk, with the Company's exclusions (freight, Car 3, persons of rank, men on the ties) and Clem's margins; Calloway, the Vicar and his trunk, Ivy Cotter not counted out at the Junction, the bench man's blank name, the Baron counted only by his dogs, the road closed, eleven on the last train out with one heavy case, five pages of No train, and the first train through, where Clem breaks Rule 6 once and counts the man off the private car.

passages.heading: Arrivals
passages.text:
**THORNE & EXPANSE LINE**
**HOLLOWMERE SPUR**
**ARRIVALS AND DEPARTURES**

*To be kept at the platform by a servant of the Company who can write. No Sunday service.*

passages.heading: Head note
passages.text:
This is a new book, because the timetable is new. It is in force from 2 October 1893. The old book, if there was one, went down the Line, or nobody handed it to me. This one begins on the 2nd. Whoever went before the 2nd went in some other book, and that includes Father Bray. I am writing down that I noticed.

I am on this book because I am the one on the boards who can fill in a form. I am also the one who reads it back to them. They let me, because it passes the cold. Len says a thing read out weighs less. He has never lifted a word.

This book counts who comes off at Day and who gets on at Dusk.

It does not count these:

- **Freight.** Freight is the Conductor's manifest. Rule 2: "The Company counts the crate, not the contents."
- **Car 3.** Car 3 is the Undertaker's. When a box goes out I write that it went. The count is his.
- **Persons of rank.** Rule 6: "Persons of rank and their escorts travel in the private car and are not entered on the passenger count." So when the private car comes, I count the dogs. The form has no rule against dogs.
- **Anyone walking the ties.** They do not come off the train, so they are not in this book.

passages.heading: Head note
passages.text:
The law of this book is Rule 9. I read it aloud the first morning to Len and Ernie and the frost: "A passenger booked in is a passenger counted out."

Counted out where, Ernie asked. At the Junction. I have never seen the Junction send a count back.

I came up the Line once myself, smaller than Ernie. I don't remember the train. That is the one arrival this book will not have.

---

## Week I. Monday 2 October to Saturday 7 October

| Day | Off, at Day | On, at Dusk | Remarks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon 2 Oct | 2. A lady, for the lean-to behind Fennick's light, with a bag and a flat case for drawings. 1 for the railyard. | 1, east. | Timetable in force. |
| Tue 3 Oct | 1, railyard. | — | |
| Wed 4 Oct | — | 2, east. | |
| Thu 5 Oct | — | — | Crew only. |
| Fri 6 Oct | 3, railyard. | 1, east. | |
| Sat 7 Oct | — | — | Crew only. |

passages.text:

works.title: The South-East Light
works.pov: first person (Abel Penhallow, keeper of the Company's marsh light), his log
works.blurb: the V1.5 coast as a keeper's log, 18 to 31 December 1893: the Company's second marsh light at the south-east edge of the mere (there is no lighthouse at HollowMere, and still no sea), kept by an ex-signalman who has never set foot in the town and knows it only by its lights, the six lawful ones in their order, the unlawful ones he does not report, Fennick's, the Gate lantern at the boards, Nora's two unanswered notes; through the storm, the escort's lanterns going into the cave, a carried light put out on Christmas night, five lights on the 27th, "the Train?" on the 29th, a white light standing over the town on the 30th, and the last oil.

passages.heading: The South-East Light
passages.text:
**THORNE & EXPANSE LINE**
**SOUTH-EAST LIGHT · MARSH EDGE**
**KEEPER'S LOG**

*To be returned to the Company by the Train.*

passages.heading: Printed inside the cover.
passages.text:
1. The light is lit at Dusk and put out at Day. Dusk and Day are kept by the Train. On Sunday, by the keeper's watch.
2. The keeper logs what the light shows. The log is returned to the Company by the Train.
3. Oil is issued by the gallon and docked by the gallon.
4. The keeper does not leave the light between Dusk and Day.

*Folded inside the cover: the order of appointment, one sheet, under a red Company seal. It is signed for the Company in a hand I do not know. The name under the signature has been ruled through, neatly, with a rule. Whoever did that owns a rule.*

---

passages.heading: Head note
passages.text:
My trade was lamps. Eleven years in a signal box at a junction back east, until the Panic shut the junction and the box with it. A signalman learns one thing before any other. You log what you saw and nothing you did not, because a man who logs what he did not see is how two trains meet. I took this post because it was a lamp and it was paid. I have not been told more than that, and I have not asked.

I came out in November by the ferry. The boy who poles it is Tuck. He brought the post in sections and the lamp in a crate, and the crate came up the Line with the Company's chalk on it and the lid nailed. The Company counts the crate. I counted what was in it.

The light stands on the south-east edge of the mere. A Company post, iron, with rungs, and a lamp at the top in a glass house the size of a bread oven. It throws a steady light. It does not go round. Tuck says there is a light out on the island that goes round, sweeping, all night. He says it the way he says the weather. I have written it down because he said it, and that is all I know of it.

passages.heading: Head note
passages.text:
West across the mere, at the far edge, there is another steady light. That one is old. Tuck says it is Fennick's and has been Fennick's since there was a lake. The Company calls mine a light. Tuck says the town will call it Fennick's other one. I expect the town is right. Towns usually are, about names.

Tuck says the town's paper allows one kind of light after the train has gone. "Only the Lamplighter's lanterns may be lit." I asked him whether mine is one of hers. He said it is the Company's. I take that as the same answer.

I have never been into the town. I know it by its lights. That is what this log is for.

---

passages.heading: The post and the hut
passages.text:
The Company built a hut of field stone beside the post, one room, with the door to the water. I give it in the form the junction taught me: what is kept there, and what can be seen from it.

**The post.**
*Kept:* the lamp, the glass, the trimming scissors on a string. Fourteen rungs. My knees count them for me on the way down.
*Seen from it:* everything in this book.

**The table at the window.**
*Kept:* this log, the pen, the ink in a cup so the frost does not split the bottle. A drawer.
*Seen from it:* the cottage across the south water, on the shore below an alley's mouth. One window.

**The stove corner.**
*Kept:* the stove, the cot, my watch on a nail where it can be read from the cot. The watch was set by the train in November. It has been right since, because I wind it.
*Seen from it:* nothing. The window is on the other wall. I chose it so.

passages.heading: The post and the hut
passages.text:
**The oil corner.**
*Kept:* the Company's oil, by the gallon, in its cans. On the wall above them, a tally in chalk: a stroke for every can come, a cross for every can burned.
*Seen from it:* the tally.

---

passages.heading: Written the first night, and kept to.
passages.text:
- **Six lights, lawful, after the train goes.** They always come on in the same order. First, one low and alone, by the rails. Then three close together on what must be a square. Then a wait, while whoever carries the flame goes somewhere I cannot see. Then one up a rise, at what may be a gate. Last, a fourth on the square, after the others, and after the wait. It is always last. I do not know why. I do not need to.
- **Lights that are not the Company's.** A window high in one house, burning green. A candle at an upstairs glass that does not move. A lit window near the square, past the hour, most nights. I enter them as *not lawful, not mine to report*. I do not report them.
- **Fennick's, out west.** Steady, at the same height every night. On Saturdays it stands unattended for an hour. Tuck says the old man goes down to fill his can.
- **Low lights over the fen that are not steady.** They are never twice in one place. Entered as *unknown*.
- **The cottage.** One window lamp, lit at the low-water hour. Someone stands in it with a paper and looks at the water, then at the paper.
- **The light at the boards.** Below the cottage, across the south water, at the hill's foot, there is a black mouth with boards across it, low on the shingle. A lantern hangs there. It was lit at dusk on my first night, the same dusk as mine. Tuck calls the mouth the sea door. There is no sea. There is the mere, and it keeps a tide, and nobody here will say why.

passages.heading: Page One
passages.text:
*FIRST NIGHT to FOURTH NIGHT. The "Boards clear" box is printed on the second and fourth nights only.*

| Night | Lit at | Flame | Lights seen | Boards clear | Extinguished at |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| First | ~~—~~ | ~~—~~ | ~~—~~ | | ~~—~~ |
| Second | ~~—~~ | ~~—~~ | ~~—~~ | ~~—~~ | ~~—~~ |
| Third. Mon 18 Dec | Dusk. | Full. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. | | Day. |
| Fourth. Tue 19 Dec | Dusk. | Full. | Two, then none. Fennick's. The boards. | No. | Day. |

> *The first two nights were ruled through in the Company's ink before the book came out to me. The Company began its count on Saturday. I began mine on Monday. I note that the Company's page and mine do not start together.*

> *Monday. Tuck at Day with the issue and a loaf. A gull came out over the fen with the ferry and stood on the hut roof when he went. It is there now.*
> *At Dusk the train's lamp went up the line into the pines. I climbed. "Clear." I said it to nobody. I said it eleven years to nobody in the box, and I am too old to stop.*
> *From the cottage side, after dark, two notes whistled. High, then low. Then a wait, as long as it takes to answer. Then the same two again. Nobody answered them. I logged it as a signal sent with no reply.*

passages.heading: Page One
passages.text:
> *Tuesday. The box for the boards is printed on this night and not on the one before. I looked at the next page. Second and fourth, every page. I do not know how a printer back east knows the nights the water will go down at a mere he has never seen. I rule nothing. I fill in the box.*
> *Wind off the ridge from noon. At Dusk the water stood up against it and did not go down. Boards under. I wrote No in the box, the first time the box has been wrong, and that was the wind's doing, not the printer's.*
> *In the gusts the town's lights went out one at a time. The rise first. Then two on the square. Then the one by the rails. Fennick's held. The boards held, low down, under the hill. Mine held. For most of an hour those were the only steady lights I could see, and mine was the only one on the Company's paper. I have written it down because it was so. It means nothing to me.*
> *The cottage window stayed lit through it.*
> *The two notes. Nobody.*

passages.heading: Page Two
passages.text:
| Night | Lit at | Flame | Lights seen | Boards clear | Extinguished at |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| First. Wed 20 Dec | Dusk. | Full. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. | | Day. |
| Second. Thu 21 Dec | Dusk. | Full. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. | Yes. | Day. |
| Third. Fri 22 Dec | Dusk. | Full. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. | | Day. |
| Fourth. Sat 23 Dec | Dusk. | Full. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. Lanterns at the boards; fewer back. | Yes. | My watch. Sunday. |

> *Wednesday. Tuck at Day. I asked him about the wind. He said the coach road is shut below the ridge, and from now on the train is the only road. He said nothing else, and poled back.*
> *At night the crows went up off the roofs over the square, all at once, black against the lit fog, and settled again. Tuck told me in November that they go up when somebody runs under them. Somebody ran. That is the whole entry.*

passages.heading: Page Two
passages.text:
> *Thursday. At Day, when I came down the rungs, the light at the boards was not there. I did not see it put out. It was burning at the last hour I logged, and at Day it was gone, and the boards were black. I log the fact.*
> *At Dusk it was lit again, in the same place.*
> *Low water at the hour. Boards clear, as printed. My light reaches them across the water when the water is down. Boards whole. Spiked. Shut.*
> *Late, the lamp went dim over my head with oil in it and my hand on the table. I counted on the watch. Five. Then it came back. I had not touched it. Out west, at the same five, Fennick's went too, and came back too. Two lamps, a mile apart, and the same five. I logged both.*

> *Friday. Tuck at Day. A second gull came with him and stayed with the first. I asked him why they come out and do not go back. He said they follow the pole, not the boat. I have not seen one leave the roof.*
> *He said it was rent day in town. He did not say it as news.*

passages.heading: Page Two
passages.text:
> *Saturday. Tuck at Day with the last of the issue, and the wire off the station window, which he made me read back to him because he cannot read it himself:*
> *LINE CLOSED FROM 24TH STOP.*
> *So no train after tonight's, and no oil after this.*
> *Tally on the wall: five nights at full flame, and a little over.*
> *Snow by afternoon. At Dusk the train went up the line into the pines with its windows lit. I could not count who was in them. A lit window is not a person, and I log lights.*
> *Saturday, so Fennick's stood alone for its hour.*
> *Low water late. Boards clear, as printed. At the hour, lanterns came down onto the shingle under the cottage, one after another, and gathered at the boards around the light that hangs there. They stood close together for a long while, and then they went in past it, and for a long while there was only the one light at the boards. When they came out they came at a run. Fewer went back up the shingle than came down, and closer together.*
> *I have written only what the light showed. I did not count them. I know how it reads.*
> *The two notes. Nobody.*

passages.heading: Page Three
passages.text:
| Night | Lit at | Flame | Lights seen | Boards clear | Extinguished at |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| First. Sun 24 Dec | Dusk, my watch. | Full. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. | | My watch. Against Rule 1. |
| Second. Mon 25 Dec | Dusk, my watch. | Half. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. One carried, put out. | Yes. | My watch. Against Rule 1. |
| Third. Tue 26 Dec | Dusk, my watch. | Half. | Six, late. Fennick's. The boards. | | My watch. Against Rule 1. |
| Fourth. Wed 27 Dec | Dusk, my watch. | Half. | Five. Fennick's. The boards, high. Lanterns in pairs. | Yes. | My watch. Against Rule 1. |

> *Sunday. No Sunday train in any week, so the rule gave me my own watch for the day, and I took it. At Dusk I lit by the watch.*

passages.heading: Page Three
passages.text:
> *Monday. At first light: no train. Rule 1 says the light goes out at Day, and Day is kept by the Train. There is no Train. By the Company's paper it is still night, and it will be night until the Company sends a Day up the Line. To keep the rule I should burn day and night until the oil is gone, and then the light goes out for good, lawfully.*
> *I put it out at first light by my watch. I wrote "Against Rule 1" in the column, in full, so that nobody reading this will think I did not know.*
> *The Articles of the Line, which Tuck has by heart from hearing them read at the tavern: "Every clock within the Grant shall be set by the Train." Mine is set by me. I am within the Grant. I log it.*
> *Flame to half from tonight. The tally will not carry full.*
> *Christmas, by the calendar. I remembered at noon. Nobody came.*
> *Low water. Boards clear, as printed. Late, a small light came down from the cottage, carried low, a child's height or a stooping one. It went along the shingle to the post at the water's edge below the cottage. It stopped there for the length of a breath. Then it was put out.*
> *I did not see it again, and I did not see it go back up. A lantern, not lawful, put out. I do not know whose, and I have not written whose.*
> *The window lamp in the cottage burned until Day.*

passages.heading: Page Three
passages.text:
> *Tuesday. The six came on later than they have. Whoever carries the flame had no train to start from either. Same order: the rails, three on the square, the wait, the rise, the fourth on the square last.*

> *Wednesday. Low water. Boards clear, as printed.*
> *Five lights, not six. The rails. Three on the square. The rise. Then the wait, and after the wait nothing. The fourth on the square did not come on. I waited for it until the cottage lamp was lit, and then I wrote Five.*
> *The light at the boards burned high tonight, higher than I have seen it. Whoever trims it turned it all the way up.*
> *On the rise, lanterns in pairs, walking, with dogs barking under them. I counted the pairs and the stray ones until they were behind the houses. The crows did not go up. They do not go up for men who walk.*
> *The two notes. Nobody.*

passages.heading: Page Four
passages.text:
| Night | Lit at | Flame | Lights seen | Boards clear | Extinguished at |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| First. Thu 28 Dec | Dusk, my watch. | Half. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. | | My watch. Against Rule 1. |
| Second. Fri 29 Dec | Dusk, my watch. | Half. | The Train? Six. Fennick's. The boards. | Yes. | By the Train. |
| Third. Sat 30 Dec | Dusk, my watch. | Half. | One. Six. Fennick's. The boards. | | My watch. |
| Fourth. Sun 31 Dec | Dusk, my watch. | Half. | Six. Fennick's. The boards. | Yes. | |

> *Thursday. Six again. The fourth on the square came on last, after the wait, as before. I do not know why it was dark last night, and I do not know why it is lit tonight.*
> *The loaf was finished at noon. I broke the heel for the gulls, and something hard went against my thumb: a crumb of wax, pressed with a mark, baked into the bread. Tuck brought that loaf on Saturday and said nothing about it. I do not know the custom here. I have not thrown it away. It is in the table drawer. It looks like it was meant for someone.*

passages.heading: Page Four
passages.text:
> *Friday. At Day, fog. Up the line, beyond the town, a smudge of light, yellow, low, moving slowly from the east. Then it stopped, about where the first light by the rails stands.*
> *I wrote "the Train?" in the column. It is the only question mark in this book. I am not sure enough to leave it off.*
> *I put the lamp out at that Day and wrote "By the Train", the first time since Saturday that the column and the rule agree.*
> *Tuck did not come. No oil, no word, no bread.*
> *At Dusk I could not see whether the smudge went back into the pines. I did not see it go. I lit by my watch.*
> *Low water. Boards clear, as printed. Nothing at them but their own light.*

> *Saturday. A light I have no column for.*
> *After Dusk, over the town: white, standing straight up out of the ground into the cloud. No fire under it that I could see, no smoke, no flicker. It did not move and it did not spread. It stood.*
> *I wrote "One" in the column, because it was one light, and I log lights. I have written nothing in the Remarks for it. I do not have a word the Company would accept, and I will not log a word I do not have.*
> *The six came on under it, in their order, as on any night.*
> *Saturday, so Fennick's stood alone for its hour, under it.*
> *The gulls faced the town all night.*

passages.heading: Page Four
passages.text:
> *Sunday.*
> *Tally on the wall: one night at half, and the measure says not all of that.*
> *Dusk by my watch. Fourteen rungs. "Clear."*
> *The rails. Three on the square. The wait. The rise. The fourth on the square. Six.*
> *Fennick's, out west, steady.*
> *The light at the boards.*
> *The cottage window, at the low-water hour, and someone in it with the paper.*
> *Boards clear, as printed. Nothing at them.*
> *The two notes, from the cottage side, high and low.*
> *I tried them once, after. I cannot whistle. I had the first and could not hold the second, and it came out as breath. I do not think it carried. Nobody answered it. I did not expect anyone to.*
> *Extinguished at:*

works.title: Standing Orders
works.pov: three printed orders with margins in many hands; a binder's notes
works.blurb: the three orders of enforcers bound into one board by a binder who adds nothing but sewing, a blind-stamped spine and three ribbons: the Pinkertons' card-book (HollowMere, 1893), written in by the town on the Lantern's bar; the Iron-Wardens' Rule (Port-au-Levain, 1789), nailed inside the cold pantry door and scratched by those held there until 1793; and the OEAs' mimeographed roll-call orders (Grounds 99, 1952), pencilled by detainees; each says when and on whom and never how, and each ribbon lies at the night its own order could not be carried out.

passages.heading: Standing Orders
passages.text:
*[Binding note: three books of different sizes, trimmed to the smallest and sewn on three cords into plain grey boards. The spine is stamped blind, without ink: STANDING ORDERS. No imprint, no binder's ticket, no date. Three silk ribbons, one sewn into the gathering of each book. The endpapers are blank.]*

---

passages.heading: Book I
passages.text:
**GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS TO OPERATIVES ON DETAIL**
*to the Thorne & Expanse Line, Coldwater Territory*

*Issued by the Agency, back east. To be carried on the person. Not to be shown.*

Operative No. *6*
Detail: *Mr C. Thorne*
Strength: Operatives *9*. Dogs *4*.

*[Binding note: a card-book in an oilcloth cover, the corners worn round. The blanks are filled in one ink. The margins are in pencil and in two other inks, in several hands, none signed. On the back board, the ring of a glass, twice.]*

---

passages.heading: Order 1. Of the Principal
passages.text:
1. The detail travels in the private car with the Principal. It is not entered on the passenger count of the Line.
2. At every platform the dogs go down first, the operatives after them, and the Principal last.
3. The detail does not carry the Principal's bags. Bags are for the platform crew.
4. The detail does not speak to the town. The town is spoken to by the Constable.

> *I took off my hat. I took his bags. He gave me scrip for the carrying and I bowed at the hip, and the dog beside him watched me do it. I pay a glass every week on my brother's line here, that's closed since the cough. I paid it that night with the Baron's scrip. It didn't feel like paying.*

---

passages.heading: Dogs on strength: *Major. Bess. Turk. Jip.
passages.text:
1. The dogs do not maul unless provoked.
2. A dog gives voice at a man who runs, a man at a lock, and a man with a weapon out.
3. A dog that gives voice is answered by its operative. It is not hushed.
4. The dogs are not taken past the last lantern.

> *The wolf didn't bark. That's how I know the one from the other. I have the difference under the binding on my arm. I go up to the stone every dawn and read it to the Row, and these four watch me up and watch me down, and not one of them has made a sound at me. I'm not running. I've no lock and no knife. I've an arm I can't close.*

> *They whine at the fen edge. Every dog of the four. They stand where the lanterns stop and won't go a step past, and nobody had to read them this page.*

passages.heading: Order 3. Of Public Unrest
passages.text:
The Company's Clerk enters the temper of the town each day under one of four heads. The detail is governed by the head, as follows.

| Temper, as entered | The detail |
|---|---|
| Calm | Not deployed. |
| Panicked | Not deployed. The Principal is wired. |
| Rioting | Deployed by the first train. The square is cleared. The soapbox is removed and is not returned. |
| Entranced | Not provided for. |

> *Fri 20 Oct. Wed 15 Nov, the day after. Sat 18 Nov. Thu 14 Dec, and that time they stayed.*

---

passages.heading: Order 4. Of Answering the Armed
passages.text:
An unholstered weapon within the hearing of the dogs is answered. The baton answers first. The rifle answers after. The order of the answer is the Agency's.

The manner is not set down here.

*[Binding note: the margins of this leaf are clean on both sides.]*

---

passages.heading: Order 5. Of the Telegraph Curfew
passages.text:
1. Curfew is declared by the detail on receipt of a wire from the Company's key. The Company's key is worked by the Clerk alone.
2. From the declaration, only the Lamplighter's lanterns may be lit.
3. The detail keeps to the lit ground. The dark beyond the lantern is not warranted by the Company, and is not warranted by the Agency.

> *They wait at each post while I light it, and walk on when it's lit, two of them and a dog, as if I were lighting for them. I'm paid by the lantern. I don't light for anybody. I leave the one over the chalk and the well till last, the same as always. I don't tell them that.*

---

passages.heading: Order 6. Of Wages and Rations
passages.text:
The wages, rations, lodging and ammunition of the detail are charged by the Company against the accounts of the Grant. The peaceable are not excused.

> *Twine, ordered on account, for a man who drowned in water to his ankles. I mend the nets he'd have used and sell them to nobody. Now the same line carries a share of nine men's bread and four dogs' meat. I mend at the window here for the light. They drink standing. They don't look at my hands.*

---

### Order 7. Of the Death of the Principal

1. Should the Principal die within the Grant, the detail wires east, holds its post, and awaits instruction.
2. Until instruction comes, the detail answers to the Principal, or to such person as the Principal's writ names: ________________________.

*[Pasted in below, two telegraph slips, copied out in the ink of the blanks:]*

> **Wired east.** ESCORT REMAINS IN TOWN STOP AWAIT INSTRUCTION STOP
>
> **Reply.** COMPANY TAKES NO POSITION ON MATTERS OF FAITH STOP ESCORT IS YOURS TO INSTRUCT SIR STOP

passages.heading: Order 6. Of Wages and Rations
passages.text:
*[Binding note: the blank at 2 is not filled.]*

---

passages.heading: Order 8. Of Return
passages.text:
The detail returns by the first train after the Principal's departure, and not before.

> *The coach road shut Tuesday the 19th. The last train went down at dusk on Saturday the 23rd, and they weren't on it. Nothing has come up since. Mornings they stand at the Company counter. Afternoons they keep the square in their long coats, facing the bank, the way you'd wait on a door that might open. The dogs lie down when they stand still.*
>
> *Nine came. Seven stand.*
>
> *Two were at the Gate.*
>
> *Thurs. 28th.*

passages.heading: Book II
passages.text:
**RULE OF THE ROUNDS OF THE IRON-WARDENS OF THE GUILD**
*Of Port-au-Levain. Printed at the press of the Counting-House at Candlemas, in the year 1789, by order of the Council. To be read to every Warden at his taking of the staff, and kept.*

[PROPERTY OF THE COUNTING-HOUSE]

*[Binding note: a quarto gathering, stained along its lower edge by damp from a cold wall. Four nail holes at the head of the first leaf, each ringed with rust. The margins are scratched with a point that is not a pen, in several hands, except one pressed in flour and one in ink. The print is not altered on any leaf.]*

---

passages.heading: Title I. Of the Rounds
passages.text:
**Art. 1.** The watches of the night are counted from the dusk loaf, set by L'Aboyeur on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal. The rounds of the Wardens begin from it. A Warden does not ask whose.

**Art. 2.** There are four rounds, at the four watches. At each round a Warden passes the Hall, the Counting-House, the Wharf steps and Gallows Square, in that order, and back in the other.

---

passages.heading: Title II. Of the Habit
passages.text:
**Art. 3.** A Warden wears brass-plated leather, buckled to the Guild's pattern and kept bright at his own charge. He carries the shock-staff over the shoulder, and carries it so in the Hall as in the street.

**Art. 4.** The staff is laid on the Commons. It is shown to the Guild. In the presence of the Gallery it is neither raised nor lowered, but held still.

**Art. 5.** A holder of the Gallery is not hauled. He is accompanied, a pace behind, at his own pace. A holder of the Commons is hauled, at the Warden's.

The manner of either is not set down in this book.

---

### Title III. Of the Log from the Tower

**Art. 6.** After every proofing bell two Wardens go down the reef road for the Tide-Watcher's log, which is lowered to them through the hatch on its cord and drawn up again when read.

passages.heading: Title II. Of the Habit
passages.text:
**Art. 7.** A line struck through in the log is read. Wardens are taught to read through ink. A struck line is a line.

---

passages.heading: Title IV. Of the Hall at Midnight
passages.text:
**Art. 8.** At the midnight proofing bell the Hall is locked from outside, and the key goes on the round.

---

### Title V. Of the Cold Pantry and the Stool

**Art. 9.** The accused waits in the cold pantry, which is the only room of the Sacred Kitchen with its lock on the outside. This Rule shall be fixed inside its door, so that the accused may know what holds him.

**Art. 10.** At dawn the Wardens bring the accused up and set him on the stool. They turn out his coat onto the trial table, and touch nothing on it.

*[Beside Art. 10, a thumb pressed in flour. No letters.]*

---

passages.heading: Title VI. Of the Alarm
passages.text: **Art. 11.** The alarm of the Wardens is three strokes, and three, and three. Lanterns come down the hill on it, and every door that hears it is shut.

passages.heading: [Scratched, in capitals, the letters uneven:]
passages.text:
> *I TOOK IT OF THE SCONSE TO SEE MAMAN HOME ALONG THE WARF. IT WAS DARK. IT WAS ONLY THE END OF IT*

*[Beneath, three short strokes and one long, then three short again, as a tune might be written by someone who could not write one.]*

---

passages.heading: Title VII. Of Tariffs Unpaid
passages.text:
**Art. 12.** Where the yeast-tax goes unpaid in more than one quarter of the island on one night, the Wardens shut the gates of the Hall and of the Counting-House and cry the curfew from the Square.

**Art. 13.** A holder Unregistered three nights together is brought to the cold pantry on the third.

> *Her ring is on its cord at my neck. They may value it when I have done wearing it.*

---

passages.heading: Title VIII. Of the Crown's Man
passages.text:
**Art. 14.** When the Crown sends a Grand Inspector-General, the Council shall go down to the Wharf to receive him, and the Wardens shall stand at the Council's back, two paces behind, with staves shouldered.

> *Nobody went down to him but the Wardens.*

---

### Title IX. Of the Order of Rank in the Pantry

**Art. 15.** No holder of the Gallery shall be held in the cold pantry. A Gallery holder waits in his own house, at his own table, and is accompanied from it.

passages.heading: [In ink, a fine hand:]
passages.text:
> *The young man with the staff addresses me as "the accused". I have corrected him. Madame. He has not been taught to say it, and there is no time now to teach him.*
>
> *I have asked for the heel of the loaf. I have always had the heel. It has not come.*
>
> *I am held in a room the article says I am not held in. I shall tell the Chancellor that his article is wrong. I shall see him at six.*
>
> *the 24th*

---

passages.heading: Title X. Of Whose Hand
passages.text:
**Art. 16.** The Wardens serve the Council and the Hearth, and no other hand.

**Art. 17.** This Rule shall not be amended save by the Council.

*[Scratched, small, in an old woman's hand. Under it, the date 1793:]*

> *Who will carry the cage to the window? The bird must see the harbour every morning or it will not sing. I have asked the Warden. It is the same Warden who stood behind my chair at the ball, with the same staff, held still. He has chosen, he says, as they all chose. He says the committee has not provided for birds.*

*[Binding note: Ribbon II lies at this leaf. The print is the print of 1789 throughout.]*

---

passages.heading: Book III
passages.text:
**RELEASED IN PART**
EXEMPTIONS (b)(1) (b)(3) · RELEASE DATE ████████████

**GROUNDS 99 · ORDER ENFORCEMENT AGENTS**
**STANDING ORDERS · ROLL CALL DETAIL**
ISSUED MON 6 OCT 52 · REISSUED SAT 13 DEC 52 · CORRECTED FRI 19 DEC 52
SPONSORING OFFICE: ██████████████
POST IN GUARDROOM. NOT FOR DETAINEE CIRCULATION.

*[Binding note: two mimeographed sheets folded to a gathering of eight leaves, with staple holes and a drawing-pin hole at each corner. Pencil throughout, in the margins and between the typed lines. The hand is very small, and grows smaller toward the end. Several hands. Each is signed with a number, or not at all.]*

---

passages.heading: 1. THE ROLL.
passages.text:
1.1 AT THE WHISTLE THE DETAINEE HAS FIFTEEN SECONDS TO STAND BESIDE HIS ASSIGNED BUNK. A BUNK WITHOUT A DETAINEE AT THE END OF FIFTEEN SECONDS IS LIT.
1.2 AGENTS DO NOT SPEAK THE NUMBER. AGENTS LOOK AT IT.
1.3 DETAINEES NOT IN PLACE ARE RECOVERED. SEE 4.

> *Brown button, off the coat they took at the gate. In the cheek, so the teeth don't go. A man whose teeth go is saying something. — 4*

---

passages.heading: 2. EQUIPMENT.
passages.text:
2.1 MASK, PROTECTIVE. WORN ON DETAIL AT ALL TIMES.
2.2 MASKS FOR LABOUR NOT AUTHORIZED.
2.3 ARC-LIGHT, CARBON, 60 IN. TWO (2), FOUNDRY ROOF AND YARD.
2.4 DOGS. REPLACEMENTS AS REQUISITIONED.
2.5 GAS, AND RIOT SLUG-GUNS, ARE ISSUED ON THE WARDEN'S HORN AND RETURNED ON IT.
2.6 THE MANNER OF THEIR USE IS NOT SET DOWN HERE.

> *Masks for them, so they can breathe it. None for us, so they can measure us breathing it.*

---

passages.heading: 3. ABSENT AND SURPLUS.
passages.text:
3.1 A BILLET WITHOUT A BODY IS ENTERED ABSENT.
3.2 A BODY WITHOUT A BILLET IS ENTERED SURPLUS.
3.3 NEITHER IS ENTERED BY NAME.

> *Fri 10 Oct. Sawmill 3 asked at the counter whether the train had brought mail. Told no. He thanked the clerk for looking.*

> *Fri 21 Nov. Sawmill 3 not at his slot when the whistle stopped. Dogs out. Lights over the pond and the trestle. Nothing found. His billet still on the rack in the morning. Absent.*

---

passages.heading: 4. RECOVERY.
passages.text:
4.1 RECOVERED DETAINEES ARE DELIVERED TO ████████████ AND NOT TO THE INFIRMARY.
4.2 THE ROUTE IS NOT LOGGED.
4.3 AGENTS DO NOT DESCRIBE THE ROUTE, THE ROOM OR THE DETAINEE.

> *Tue 25 Nov, about two. Sawmill 8, across the yard in a sack between two masks, under the arc-light. Not heavy. You could see that from the way they carried him. His ribs through the burlap, every one, like a washboard. One hand out of the mouth of the sack. Fingers black to the second knuckle. No nails. The cold came off him in the light like steam off a horse.*
>
> *He sang bass at the bread line. He saved his sugar for the man in the next bunk, who has the cough. He told me once he had a boy in Duluth who'd be eight at Christmas.*
>
> *The hand moved. It opened and shut, slow, like it was counting.*
>
> *I am not describing the route.*

passages.heading: 5. THE MESS HALL AFTER ROLL.
passages.text:
5.1 AFTER ROLL CALL THE MESS HALL IS CLEARED OF STAFF.
5.2 A HUM IN THE MESS HALL IS NOT AN ASSEMBLY. AGENTS DO NOT ENTER.
5.3 GAS IS NOT TO BE USED IN THE MESS HALL.

> *They use it in the yard and never in the mess. Ask yourself why. I did, and I stopped humming, and then I heard I'd started again.*

---

passages.heading: 6. STEAM MAINS.
passages.text:
6.1 ON THE RUPTURE OF A STEAM MAIN THE DETAIL DEPLOYS AT ONCE, MASKED, WITH LIGHTS AND DOGS.
6.2 DETAINEES ARE HELD STANDING AT THEIR SLOTS UNTIL THE MAIN IS CLOSED.

> *Tue 11 Nov. The boiler main. Four hours at the slots. I counted to keep from sitting down. Eins, zwei. My mother's counting. I caught myself at it and went on. — 7*

> *Tue 18 Nov. The seam. The same four hours.*

---

passages.heading: 7. THE DEEP LEVEL.
passages.text:
7.1 OIL, LAMP, 1 QT. REFUGE, DEEP LEVEL. WEEKLY. STANDING.
7.2 THE DETAIL ESCORTS THE MAN WHO CARRIES IT TO THE WINZE, AND NO FARTHER.
7.3 WHO FILLS THE LAMP IS NOT LOGGED.

---

passages.heading: 8. REISSUE, SAT 13 DEC 52.
passages.text:
8.1 SEARCH OF CAMP PREMISES FOR ████████████ IS SUSPENDED BY ██████████████.
8.2 DO NOT ENTER IN LOG.
8.3 ORDERS 4.1 TO 4.3 STAND.
8.4 A DETAINEE PRESENTING ████ ████████ ████ ███ IS PASSED THROUGH THE GATE WITHOUT ENTRY.

> *Friday they took a man in a good coat off the payroll platform. Saturday the masks went through every hut, under every floor. By night they'd stopped, all at once, the way they stop when the whistle stops. Nothing found. Nobody's been down since. You would think somebody helped.*

---

**9. CORRECTION, FRI 19 DEC 52.** *(in ink, on the stencil)*

STEAM OUT, ALL MAINS. ARC-LIGHTS OUT. ROLL BY HAND LAMP.
1.1 CANNOT BE COMPLIED WITH.

*(in another ink, below)*
SAT 20 DEC, 0600. INSPECTOR-GENERAL NOT ACCOUNTED FOR. ROLL STANDS AS TAKEN.

> *Fri 19 Dec. No light. The whistle went, and nobody could be lit, so nobody was missing. We stood by the bunks in the dark. I put my hand out to the right, and there was a shoulder there. I don't know whose bunk it was. I don't know whose shoulder. I kept my hand on it till the dogs came back.*

passages.heading: [Binding note: Ribbon III lies at this leaf.]
passages.text: *[Binding note: The three ribbons lie, in the first book, at the Order of Return; in the second, at the last Title; in the third, at the correction of 19 December. The rear endpaper is blank. Nothing is pasted in. The cords are drawn so tight that the boards will not open flat, and each book has to be held open by hand to be read. Released, it closes of itself.]*

works.title: Grounds 99, Survey of 2626
works.pov: third person (Surveyor No. 30, of himself), field book
works.blurb: the future map as a registry surveyor's field book, 18 to 23 December 2626: the settlement its people call Ninety-Nine, poured concrete held by day and contested by wolves, boar, beavers, elk, crows, rats, bats and owls by night; eight stations walked under residents' names, a plugged adit, a light reported under the drowned mouth, a box stamped RETAIN UNTIL 2626 burned unread at the one kept fire, and an iron rack whose one unused slot carries a smudge no one will wipe, under which a girl entered as over count chalks her own number.

passages.heading: Grounds 99, Survey of 2626
passages.text:
**SURVEY OF 2626**
**Settlement:** GROUNDS 99. Called by its people Ninety-Nine.
**Registry file:** 99/R/41.
**Surveyor:** No. 30. Party of one.
**In the field:** Mon 18 Dec to Sat 23 Dec 2626.

---

passages.heading: 1. Commission and Datum
passages.text:
**Commission.** Re-fix the bounds. Take the census by heads. Dispose of any record whose retention has run.

The registry's file on the place was thin. A ring map with no names on it. A census from before the last one, water-stained. And one clause, copied forward from a file older than the registry, typed in capitals the clerk could not account for:

GROUNDS 99 DESIGNATION TO STAND THROUGH ANY EXCHANGE, AND AFTER.

"It has always been in the file," the clerk said. The registry kept it because it had been kept.

The people of Ninety-Nine call the war the Exchange. They say it the way one says the weather. The file does not say whether the clause meant that exchange, and the surveyor did not enter a guess.

**Datum.** He set it Monday at first light on the oldest slab in the settlement, which the people call the Yard. The concrete there is older than the concrete round it and thinner laid, cracked in a grid like river ice the morning after a hard frost. The surveyor cut a bench-mark at the north-west corner and entered it as BM 1.

passages.heading: 1. Commission and Datum
passages.text:
Counter at the bench-mark: within the registry's tolerance. At the pump: within. At the south road, where the water crosses it: within, high.

Soil core beside the slab, one arm deep: loam; needles; loam; one dark band, a finger thick; clay. The band was entered as a band.

The bench-mark is the only new mark the surveyor made in Ninety-Nine.

passages.heading: 2. Ground
passages.text:
Concrete over everything that was ever flat. A ring wall, shoulder high, poured in lifts you can count like the rings of a stump. Blocks of four storeys and blocks of two. Stairs that climb a wall and stop in air. Nobody living can say who poured it. The people say *the builders*, and leave it there.

At the ring wall's corners stand old light masts, with lamps hung at the height a man can reach and crows above the lamps.

Pines in every seam. They split the pours slowly, the way a fist opens in sleep.

To the south the Blackwater has come back over the road. Beaver dams lean on the broken piers of an old trestle: five piers, the sixth gone. South of the piers a rail grade runs off through the trees. Its ties have long since rotted to brown lines in the moss, and only animals use it now. The people say it ran to the end of a line. Which line, and to what end, nobody says. Entered as a saying.

passages.heading: 2. Ground
passages.text: **Contest.** By day the settlement holds the concrete. By night the ground holds itself. The animals did not leave when the people came, and the people stopped asking them to.

passages.heading: 3. Traverse
passages.text:
**Stn 1. The Yard.** BM 1. Slab, pump, bench-mark. An iron frame is set into the inner face of the ring wall on the north side: a rack of ten slots, each with an iron plate stamped with a numeral, 0 to 9. The concrete was poured round it, not over it, as if whoever poured had been told to leave it be. Each household of Ninety-Nine hangs a tag in its slot: a wooden peg, a bent spoon, a knot of wire, a child's shoe. Nine slots carry a tag. One slot not in use.

**Stn 2. The Long House.** A dormitory block of two storeys, poured round an older timber frame whose posts show through the walls like the bones in a fin. Downstairs, one room split by a half wall, with rats in the half wall. The residents sleep upstairs in two rows, by household number. At dark a mother on the east row counts her children aloud by their numbers, and stops when the count is right. If it is not right, she goes down to the Yard with a lamp. On the surveyor's two nights in the Long House it was right both times. Entered as a custom. The floor was not lifted.

passages.heading: 3. Traverse
passages.text:
**Stn 3. The Mill.** The concrete stops at the race, as if the pour had come to the water and decided not to argue. No wheel, only a stone sill where a wheel was. The beavers have the race. Some of the timbers in their dam are sawn planks, square-edged and grey as old teeth; the beavers used what they found. Contest: the water, which the beavers are winning.

**Stn 4. The Woods.** West and north of the ring wall. The felling slope has come back as pine, close as wheat. Elk stand on the old stumps at dawn, their breath hanging over them in the frost like smoke over a kiln. In a clearing are two brick domes, both fallen in, and owls nest in what is left. Wolves use the grade at dusk and the slope at night. The surveyor did not walk the woods after dark. Woods north of the domes, after dark: unsurveyed.

passages.heading: 3. Traverse
passages.text:
**Stn 5. The Workings.** An adit in the cliff north of the Yard, closed with a poured plug. The plug is older than the ring wall. A crack runs across its crown, and at dusk the bats go out and in through it like smoke drawn up a flue. The surveyor did not breach the plug. Interior: not surveyed.

**Stn 6. The low ground.** Under the Workings, the people say, there is more: a lower level, flooded. The only way to it is a drowned mouth west of the ford, where the river goes in under the hill. Water at the mouth: to the roof. Not entered.

There is one report, from a man of the Mill household who fishes the ford. Some nights there is a light under the water at the mouth, low and steady, "like a lamp somebody keeps filling." He did not say who. He did not want it entered. Entered: reported; not verified. The surveyor stood at the ford one night from dusk to the second hour and saw the river.

passages.heading: 3. Traverse
passages.text:
**Stn 7. The Office.** Walls faced with concrete, roof gone. A telephone body is bolted to the wall. Its wire has been gone so long that the bolt-holes have rusted shut round nothing. The children use it to call one another from across the room. Behind it is a records cell with a steel door that opened when leaned on.

Inside, one box. The paper had gone to pulp, and the pulp to a single grey brick. The label had weathered off except for one stamp in red, faded to the colour of a scraped knee:

RETAIN UNTIL 2626.

The surveyor did not open the brick, and there was no reading it without opening it. Entered by its stamp. See Records.

**Stn 8. The Forge.** A stone hearth in a low block by the Yard, the oldest stone in the settlement. The people of Ninety-Nine keep one fire, and this is it. They tend it in turns by household number, so it is never out. Wolves come to the edge of its light and no nearer. The surveyor warmed his hands at it on the first night. He had not expected to be glad of it, and was.

passages.heading: 4. Fauna
passages.text:
**Wolves — the grade.** They hold the grade at dusk and the slope by night. They give way to the forge light and to nothing else.
*Contest: the night.*

**Boar — the Yard.** They root at the seams and take the slab back a hand's width at a time.
*Contest: the pours.*

**Beavers — the race and the piers.** They build with whatever the river brings, planks included.
*Contest: the water.*

**Elk — the felling slope.** On the stumps at dawn. They do not move for a person; a person moves for them.
*Contest: the slope.*

**Crows — the light masts.** Above the lamps, on every mast. They watch who goes out after dark.
*Contest: the lamps.*

**Rats — the Long House.** In the half wall, and in the ration bins when a lid is left off.
*Contest: the half wall.*

**Bats — the plug.** Out of the crack at dusk, back at first light.
*Contest: the crack.*

passages.heading: 4. Fauna
passages.text:
**Owls — the brick domes.**
*Contest: none. They took what nobody wanted.*

passages.heading: 5. Inhabitants
passages.text:
Ten households, by slot, 0 to 9. Nine slots in use. Sixty heads, and one over count.

The people go by slot and place: Two-of-the-Yard, Six-of-the-Long-House, Five-of-the-Mill. The old say there used to be names as well as numbers, and that their grandparents had them. Asked which names, they shrug. The numbers were what got written down, and the numbers were what lasted.

**Nought.** Keeper of the rack, of household 0, eighty or near it. She drinks from a tin cup with a dent in its lip, and turns the dent away from her mouth without looking. Each dusk she walks the north face of the Yard and touches the plates one by one, 0 to 9, counting under her breath. At the unused slot her hand passes over without stopping, and her eyes do not go to it. She has done it, she says, since she was given the rack, and the woman who gave it to her did it the same way.

passages.heading: 5. Inhabitants
passages.text:
**The girl.** About ten. She came down the grade as a baby in a fish basket, the year every slot was full, and no household has room for her on the rack. On the registry's census she is entered as she was entered last time: over count. She keeps a stub of chalk, found in the ballast of the grade, in a pocket she sewed for it herself. She draws numbers on the slab, and the boar root them out. At dusk she sits on the edge of the Yard and watches Nought's hand pass the empty slot.

On the Wednesday she asked the surveyor, "Can a number be taken if nobody's got it?"

The surveyor entered her on the census as head 61, over count. He did not answer, because the commission did not say.

passages.heading: 6. Records
passages.text:
The commission is plain: a record whose retention has run is to be disposed of. The year on the stamp is this year. The box qualified.

Nought asked for it. The winter was long already, and paper burns, even pulp, even a brick of it, if you break it small. The surveyor allowed it.

They fed it to the forge over two nights, Wednesday and Thursday, a piece at a time on top of the wood. Nobody read it; it could not have been read. The stamp was on the last piece and went last, the red turning brown and then gone.

passages.heading: Entered: *Disposed of per retention. Contents: not read.
passages.text: Afterwards Nought warmed her cup at the fire and drank.

passages.heading: 7. The slot
passages.text:
The unused slot carries no tag. On its iron plate, where a tag would hang, there is a grey smudge worked into the grain of the iron, like old chalk that has been wiped and come back, or was never wiped. No letter can be read in it. The surveyor looked by daylight and by lamplight and made out none. He has set none down.

The people will not hang a tag there, and they will not wipe the plate. Asked whose slot it was, no one could say. Asked whose it is, Nought said, "It's taken," and that was all she said.

The registry has a rule: a slot with no known holder is to be reassigned from the census. There was a head over count, and the case was plain.

The surveyor entered the slot:

*Slot: one. Holder: none known. Mark: one, not legible. Retention: no schedule covers it.*

passages.heading: 7. The slot
passages.text:
He did not reassign it.

On the Saturday, at dusk, the girl went to the rack with her chalk. Nought was at the plates, and her hand passed over the empty slot as it always did. The girl reached up and wrote 61 on the iron below the smudge, small, not touching it. Then she sat down on the edge of the Yard where she always sat.

Nobody wiped it. That night Nought counted 0 to 9. Her hand passed the slot, stopped a moment lower down, and went on.

passages.heading: 8. Certificate
passages.text:
Bounds re-fixed to BM 1. Woods north of the domes, after dark: unsurveyed. Workings and the low ground: not surveyed. Designation stands, as filed. Records past retention: disposed of. Census: sixty heads, and one over count, now entered under a slot that is also held.

Surveyor No. 30. Sat 23 Dec 2626.

Entered as found.

works.title: Timetable of Stations Not Yet Built
works.pov: the Company's print, with a second hand and pasted slips
works.blurb: the closing codex: the Thorne & Expanse Line's timetable for 1894, printed at the Eastern Office in November 1893 before the winter happened, with its four stations in service and an Extension under survey (South-East Halt for the marsh light, the Cave Gate, the Fork, and Harrow, which may not be built), a second hand's ink margins on the closed line and the two out of the cave, 1952 slips for Grounds 99 and a sealed car to a site in North Dakota, a 2626 slip pasted half over them, and a last row with no name, where one January fare is held for the passenger.

passages.heading: Timetable of Stations Not Yet Built
passages.text:
**THORNE & EXPANSE LINE**
**HOLLOWMERE SPUR**
**Cornelius Thorne, Prop.**

*[A ruled line through the name, in ink, in a second hand. Beside it:]* Prop. ______

passages.heading: TIMETABLE FOR 1894
passages.text:
In force from Monday, 1 January 1894, until further notice.
Printed at the Eastern Office, November 1893.

No Sunday service.

Connections back east not guaranteed during the present financial disturbance.

passages.heading: [in a second hand]
passages.text:
> *Line closed from the 24th. Wire.*

---

passages.heading: I. STATIONS IN SERVICE
passages.text:
| Station | Down | Up | Remarks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thorne Junction | Day | Dusk | Main line. Connections back east. |
| Widow's Cut | Day | Dusk | Water only. |
| Gallows Wood Siding | — | — | Stops on signal only. |
| HollowMere | Day | Dusk | End of line.† |

† Until the opening of the Extension.

The Daily Train arrives at the start of each Day and departs at Dusk.

> *Thorne Junction. Counted out here.*

> *HollowMere, Up. It does not wait.*

---

passages.heading: UNDER SURVEY. TIMES TO BE ANNOUNCED.
passages.text:
| Station | Down | Up | Remarks |
|---|---|---|---|
| South-East Halt, for the marsh light | T.B.A. | T.B.A. | Low water only.\* |
| Tin Gallery, the Cave Gate | T.B.A. | T.B.A. | Lamp at the Gate only.§ |
| The Fork | T.B.A. | T.B.A. | Change here. Two roads.‖ |
| Harrow, for timber | — | — | Under survey; may not be built.¶ |
|  | — | — | Stops on signal only.‡ |

\* Passengers will consult the tide. The Company does not keep it.
§ The Company does not say why.
‖ A passenger at the Fork travels one road. The ticket reads both. The Company does not say which.
¶ Owner of record: Harrow.
‡ Name to be announced.

> *South-East Halt. Light lit at Dusk. Seen from the step.*

> *The Gate. Two out of the cave this month.*
> *Drag marks.*
> *Black on them. The Undertaker would not write it as blood.*
> *Ruled the cause through.*

passages.heading: UNDER SURVEY. TIMES TO BE ANNOUNCED.
passages.text: > *The Fork. Either road is in force. Neither is guaranteed.*

passages.heading: [Against Harrow, the second hand writes nothing.]
passages.text:
> *The last row.*
> *One fare, January, one-way. Booked. Not punched.*
> *He sat the bench an hour before the Rush. In case it came early.*
> *Held for the passenger.*

*[Pasted against the Harrow row, a little askew, typed:]*

1952. GROUNDS 99. PAYROLL TRAIN, FRIDAYS. PRODUCTION IS OBLIGATION.

passages.heading: [Beneath it, the same typewriter:]
passages.text:
SITE ███, N. DAK. SEALED CAR ONLY. NO RETURN WORKING.

*[Pasted half over the first slip, so that its type shows at the edge: a slip of some other stuff, not paper, faded, one corner gone:]*

2626. The same place. No train. The grade holds as far as where the trestle was. Numbers where names were.

---

passages.heading: III. RULES OF CARRIAGE, 1894
passages.text:
Passengers, consignees and servants of the Company will observe the following.

1. The Daily Train arrives at the start of each Day and departs at Dusk. It does not wait.
2. Freight is carried at the consignee's risk. The Company counts the crate, not the contents.
3. As 1893.
4. Coffins ride in Car 3, the back car, and are not opened in transit, by any person, for any reason.
5. As 1893.
6. Persons of rank and their escorts travel in the private car and are not entered on the passenger count.
7. Mail sealed in black wax is the property of the addressee and of the Company. The Conductor does not read it.
8. As 1893.
9. A passenger booked in is a passenger counted out.
10. As 1893.
11. As 1893.
12. Should the Conductor of record be unable to sign, the manifest is signed by whoever remains.

passages.heading: III. RULES OF CARRIAGE, 1894
passages.text:
> *6. Dogs: counted.*

> *7. The wax still comes.*

*[Against Rule 12, the second hand underlines "whoever remains" twice and writes nothing.]*

passages.heading: For the Extension:
passages.text:
13. South-East Halt is served at low water only. The Company does not keep the tide.
14. One lamp is shown at the Gate, and none between the Tin Gallery and the Gate. The Company is not answerable for what is lost on that section, in the cars or out of them.
15. At the Fork a passenger travels one road. Tickets are not exchanged.
16. Fares are not sold to stations under survey. A passenger for such a station travels as freight, at the consignee's risk.

> *16. Then who signs for them.*

By order,
The Thorne & Expanse Line

> *Conductor of record:*

‡ Name to be announced.

works.title: Cable Construction Circus
works.blurb: a narrative rap portraying a chaotic work site crew as a circus troupe.

passages.heading: Cable Construction Circus
passages.text:
Seven in the mornin’, sun barely risen,  
Locates all wrong like somebody wasn’t listenin’,  
Half the crew standin’ around like they lost in a vision,  
Boss pulled up and immediately started the bitchin’

——

Step right up, hard hat on, leave your pride at the gate,  
Best damn circus in the county, don’t you dare be late,  
Cable construction circus, everybody losin’ they mind,  
Clowns on the trencher, monkey one step behind,  
Boss breathin’ on our necks, dirt flyin’ every direction,  
Whole job site’s a shit show with a fiber optic connection,  
Roll up — big top sunk deep in the mud,  
Cable construction circus, runnin’ on coffee and blood

——  
(storytelling cadence, laid back, heavy)  
Now Rob’s in the hole complainin’ like the hole is the problem,  
Greg’s playin’ with himself, somebody really oughta stop him,  
Foreman’s on the phone screamin’ at the fuck who laid out —  
Third time this week, same lazy pout, same sorry mouth,  
Waterline got hit, boss man’s face went south,  
Veins in his neck like the cable comin’ out,  
Walker ringin’ my phone talkin’ ‘bout he needs it by four,  
Bore path ain’t marked, no locates, sun ain’t even sure,  
Paperwork from yesterday, locates by tonight —  
Sir we just got here, with respect, you ain’t right,  
Machine hit rock at nine, gas line right at noon,  
Should’ve known from the jump we’d be cryin’ pretty soon —

passages.heading: Cable Construction Circus
passages.text:
——

(beat drops out)  
JACOB.

JACOB WHAT THE FUCK ARE YOU DOING.

I SAID DRILL STRAIGHT YOU DUMB SON OF A BITCH.

WE TALKED ABOUT THIS.

WE TALKED ABOUT THIS YESTERDAY.

PUT THE DAMN PHONE DOWN AND LISTEN YOU STUPID BITCH.

EVERY SINGLE TIME.

EVERY GODDAMN TIME.

(beat rolls back in slow and heavy)  
Inspector pulled up, surveyed the scene, turned around and fled,  
Came back at noon after the worst of it was dead

Chaos is free but the overtime’ll cost ya,  
Best paid shit show in the Southeast — welcome, I’ll host ya

(darker, slower, almost amused)  
Now Greg — Lord Greg — rolled up with the strangest energy,  
Lawn chair in the shade like the job site’s his amenity,  
BlueChew in his pocket like it’s doing him a favor,  
Useless as the man, pill ain’t finding no savior,  
Looked at the driller’s legs, said it slow like it was normal —  
“Them legs gave me a hard on” — nothing about it formal,  
Every man on the crew just froze, stared, carried on,  
Couldn’t unhear it, couldn’t process, just moved along,  
Barkin’ out instructions he ain’t qualified to give,  
Soft-dick bastard telling hardworking men how to live,  
More excuses than the pill got listed on the label —  
Greg, sit your ass down and get up from the table

passages.heading: Cable Construction Circus
passages.text:
(drops to almost a whisper, deliberate)  
Then there’s Ethan —  
Only reason this whole circus ain’t burned to the ground,  
Fixin’ everybody’s disasters without makin’ a sound,  
You can see it in his eyes if you look long enough —  
Tired, worn, runnin’ thin, done with all of this stuff,  
Cleanin’ up behind Rob, cleanin’ up behind Greg,  
Jacob drillin’ crooked with his phone up to his head,  
Ethan’s the only sumbitch here who genuinely knows the trade,  
While the rest of us are circus clowns that somebody got paid,  
Somebody give that man a raise, a drink, a week of sleep —  
He’s carryin’ this whole damn show and it’s gettin’ way too deep

Cable construction circus, everybody losin’ they mind,  
Clowns runnin’ the trencher, monkey one step behind,  
Boss breathin’ fire, dirt flyin’ every direction,  
This whole job site’s a shit show with a fiber optic connection,  
Roll up — big top sunk deep in the mud,  
Cable construction circus, runnin’ on coffee and blood

passages.heading: Cable Construction Circus
passages.text:
(half spoken, fading slow like the beat’s dying)  
Step right up…  
Tickets free but your sanity’s gonna cost ya…  
Somebody pull Rob outta that hole…  
Tell limp dick Greg to sit his ass down…  
Jacob… put the goddamn phone away…  
And somebody get Ethan a drink…  
He earned it…  
We all did…  
…circus don’t close till the fiber’s lit

works.title: How i feel
works.blurb: a confessional song lyric on isolation, creative burnout, and disillusionment with time and fame.

passages.heading: How i feel
passages.text:
How i feel

I see your face in shadows so sweet  
Times replaced, emotion heaps  
Maybe I'm better left unseen  
Playing aloud within my own scene  
Feels like friends have left me all alone  
Walking corpses, not a word just a groan

Everyones hungry for new ideas  
Forgetting we're just kids  
selling us off like they got dibs  
Burning us out before we first sprout  
Never touched a pen till i got tinged  
from fake friends with minds unhinged  
Walking alone in silent dreams  
 just wondering what I might be

Trying to survive, never gonna fade inside  
in a world full of jump scares  
nightmares got me pulling out my hair  
Lost without a place to call found  
people be saying “is that all now”  
don’t worry i get your in a hurry  
ill make it quick fast forward to the hit

passages.heading: How i feel
passages.text:
Maybe my dreams are only my own  
Maybe I'm just trying to find my soul  
When did it become overrated to be outrageous  
am I outdated?

Before my time, before its line  
In a time that ain't even mine  
Yes, I'm tired of talk about time  
Because it only wastes what's mine

Every day I sit and rest  
Is another day I can't invest  
Every hour is a deadlines call  
because one day ill lose it all

When we all head to heaven  
Sit around eating bread unleaven  
we’ll see we were just living free  
Now we're living life's greatest luxury

works.title: Ballad of the Iron Beast
works.blurb: a HollowMere platform hand's work ballad for the Daily Train — the crew, the freight, the black wax, the back car — turning on the brother who stayed for him.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
*(no music; boots on frozen planks)*
Ten past five in the mornin', November, ninety-three,
Frost on the spur and the platform lantern still burnin' for me,
HOLLOWMERE — EST. BY THE RAILROAD EXPANSE, sign swingin' on its chain,
Town don't wake till the Beast clears its throat — then the whole town's waitin' on the train

——

Step on up, frost on the boards, keep your hat in your hand,
Barons own the mill and the bank and the dirt where you stand,
You want bread, you want news, you want somewhere to go —
Seven days' walk to a soul and the walk's mostly snow,
Here she comes round the black pines, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
HollowMere, end of the line, wash the mud off your name,
Whatever you do, boys — don't miss the train

——
(storytelling cadence, laid back, heavy)
Now Len's on the spikes singin' time to the maul,
Swears the rails go walkin' when nobody's watchin' at all,
Stan Pike on the switch with a cough like a saw,
Calls it a cold — been a cold since the thaw,
Jack Rudd liftin' whiskey, one bottle a load,
Calls it a tariff, says the Company owes,
Clem reads the manifests out loud, every word,
Only man on the platform who reads, so the loudest one heard,
And Ernie, twelve, with the bucket, askin' every train
Where she goes after us — and nobody's ever explained

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
Six o'clock, flour for Crumb's, sacks white as the frost,
Seven, the whiskey for the Lantern, I count what got lost,
Eight, tonics for the morgue — morgue orders ahead,
Nine, the gunpowder, the railyard, sign here for the lead,
I unload the flour. I unload the lead.
I unload whatever the Barons said.

——

Step on up, frost on the boards, keep your scrip in your hand,
Clerk comes at noon for the rent on the dirt where you stand,
Banks fallin' back east like the pines in a blow,
Seven days' walk to a soul and the walk's mostly snow,
Here she sits on the spur, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
Ticket out costs a year, and the year's in the Company's name —
Can't afford the train, boys — so don't miss the train

——
(sacks hit the boards)
Ten o'clock, mailbags, heavy as a man,
Gazette on the top, tossed down like contraband,
Prints yesterday's secrets, every sin that got proved,
Names nobody it can't — so the rest of us move,
Clem reads the headline, nobody looks at each other,
Every man on the platform real interested in his brother,
And down in the bag there's a letter sealed black,
Somebody's name on it, and nobody's lookin' back,
I sort around it slow like a snake in the flour,
Don't touch it, don't turn it, don't ask it the hour.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
Then I slip in my three, outbound, Ma's name in my hand,
Jack Rudd grins, "Arthur too rich now to write her? Too grand?"
"Arthur's busy gettin' rich," I say, and the whole crew roars,
And I laugh along, tie off the bag, and I heave it aboard.

What's a platform hand worth on a Panic year?
A dollar in scrip and a back that don't quit?
And who's countin' — the Clerk, or the man in the mirror?

——

(beat drops out)
WHO SIGNED FOR THE LEAD.

WHO SIGNED FOR THE LEAD.

CLEM. CLEM, PUT THE GAZETTE DOWN.

THAT CRATE IS BREATHING.

NOBODY OPENS THAT CRATE.

NOBODY TOUCHES THE BLACK WAX. NOBODY.

COFFINS TO THE BACK CAR.

THE BACK CAR.

EVERY DAY.

EVERY GODDAMN DAY.

(beat rolls back in slow and heavy)
Crate went quiet by one, and nobody asked why,
Freight is freight, and the Company don't ask, so don't I.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
——
(darker, slower)
Afternoon car, and the new Vicar steps down,
Father Bray died or ran, depends who's drinkin' in town,
Collar so white it hurts in the fog,
Shakes every hand like he's countin' a flock,
And they say every soul here confesses to him, sooner or later —
I carry his trunk up the hill, and I keep mine for later.

Town rioted Tuesday. Wednesday, the Baron,
Cornelius Thorne in a coat worth more than I'm earnin',
Pinkertons, dogs, and a rifle apiece,
Steps on the boards like the boards owe him peace,
Took off my hat. Took his bags. Took his scrip.
Hated myself, and I bowed at the hip.

And Stan Pike's switch is quiet — cough stopped Monday night,
Stan caught the Dusk train, back car, lid on tight,
Len sang him spike-time, Ernie held his cap,
I signed for Stan Pike like a sack, and I set him in back.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
And who loads the back car, if not the hand that's here?
Who's left to sign for a man?
Who'd carry them out, if I went?

——

Step on up, light's goin' down, take your hat off your head,
She brings the bread and the whiskey, the priest and the lead,
She brings the Baron and the dogs and the letter sealed black,
She takes the ones we can't keep, in a box, in the back,
Here she sits on the spur, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
Owns the clock, owns the town, owns the mud and the rain —
Don't miss the train, boys — she don't miss you, all the same

——
(drops to almost a whisper, deliberate)
But Arthur didn't miss the train.

Two springs back — two tickets, one for him, one for me,
Punched for a Tuesday, Dusk, out past the trees,
Arthur on the step with his hat in his hand,
Me on the boards like I'm bolted to the land,
Scrip debt for an excuse. Fear for a reason.
Clerk's rent for a story I could tell every season.
He looked at me once. He stepped back down.
He stayed for me. He stayed in this town.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
Called her the Iron Beast, like he did when we were boys,
To make me laugh — and it did — just a word, just a noise,
Whistled the Dusk whistle a half-step flat,
Every night on the platform, and I'd tell him quit that,
Then winter. The mere-rot. The same cough as Stan.
Then the back car.
I loaded the flour. I loaded the lead.
I loaded my brother.

And every week since, Ma, I write you in his hand —
*Doin' fine, Ma. Good wages. The West agrees with me, Ma* —
I sign it Arthur. I post it outbound.
I load the bag myself.
His ticket's in the hatband, never punched past Tuesday.
I wear the hat. I whistle flat.

So which of us missed it?
The one who never boarded —
or the one who boarded in a box?

——

Step on up, frost on the boards, keep your hat in your hand,
Barons own the mill and the bank and the dirt where you stand,
You want bread, you want news, you want somewhere to go —
Seven days' walk to a soul and the walk's mostly snow,
There she goes round the black pines, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast — that was Arthur's word — she don't wait, don't explain,
HollowMere, end of the line, wash the mud off your name,
Town says don't miss the train, boys — I never missed the train

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
——
(half-spoken, fading slow like the beat's dying)
Dusk whistle…
Somebody tell Ernie to get off the tracks…
Back car's full…
See you at five…
