Don't miss the train, they tell you. I never missed it once —
I just let it carry everyone I couldn't follow.

works.title: Tenfold
works.blurb: the new Vicar's last sermon at dusk on the third Sunday of Advent, 17 December 1893, a confession to his own congregation that ends on his last words verbatim, followed by the converts' hymn for what comes back, broken by a shouted capitals passage, WHO PREACHED AT DUSK TONIGHT.

passages.heading: Tenfold
passages.text:
*(no organ; the Company bell, once; the Dusk whistle going out through the pines)*
Third Sunday of Advent, ninety-three, seventeenth of December, dusk,
St Brannock's, under the bell the Company paid for,
Fourteen in the pews. Twenty-two last Sunday. Thirty the Sunday before.
I count you the way the Clerk counts rent.
I light the pink one. The candle for rejoicing.

——
(spoken, plain)
Everyone in HollowMere confesses to me sooner or later.
Tonight it's later. And it's me.

You know me. I came off the afternoon car on the seventeenth of October,
and a platform hand carried my trunk up the hill and said nothing the whole way.
I asked a child at the pump where the man before me had gone.
She told me.
I did not ask twice.

——

You told me things.

Maud told me one thing, at the Lantern, with her glass untouched.
I walked it behind the back car on the twentieth of November,
I carried it out of this town unopened,
and I will not open it here.

passages.heading: Tenfold
passages.text:
Three men at Mrs Grieves's bar told me things,
each one wanting a Liquid Courage he couldn't run to.
I bought three. I drank none.
One owed. One had a brother. One had a lie he'd told so long it had a room in his house.

And the town told me the rest without meaning to:
a baker halving the mourners' loaves to feed the dead,
a lamplighter who saves the fourth lantern for last,
a stone that goes up at dawn with a name on it, and Agnes reading it to the Row.
A town that lost its master on the platform Thursday,
and had a writ from the next one before the boards were swept.

And who hears the one who hears?
Who does the confessor kneel to, at the end of the line?

Tonight, you do.

——
(slower)
Every night I learn where one soul stands.
That's the gift, or the work, or the curse. I have called it all three.
Every night I choose how much to say.

passages.heading: Tenfold
passages.text:
I have known where one of you stands since November.
I chose how much to say.
I said nothing.

You are in this room.
Somebody has been taking my candles, one at a time, from the third pew.
Somebody has measured my robes with their eyes, collar to hem.
And the one beside you will swear you were somewhere else.

Why didn't I say?
Because I have seen what this town does with a name.
It takes it to the Bell. It tries it. It drops it through the floor.
Because the man before me rang that bell till his gloves wore through, they say —
and they say a lot.
Because I would rather this town lose a priest than hang a guess.

Is that mercy?
Or is it pride, wearing my collar?

This morning the stone went up. You've all read the name.
I read it too.

——
*(a draught up the Undercroft stair; the pink candle; the bell rope moves with no hand on it)*

passages.heading: Tenfold
passages.text:
(in the dark, slow)
"In the end I sought nothing else but to serve God.
And serve him I did.
With this death's last breath I pray this prayer: may the Almighty grant me the strength of ten in the next life.
And in return, tenfold my own."

passages.heading: (no bell)
passages.text:
*(Monday, dusk: the robes come out of the vestry and climb the pulpit, and preach. Nobody reports anything.)*

——
(the pews sing; one voice under the rest)
Where he's gone there's a lavender field,
and an orange tree, just the one,
and a sky that's blue — they swear it's blue —
though none of us here has seen one.

I told him the worst thing I ever did.
He kept it. It's his now,
wherever he is. In the lavender.
Or under the floor.

Ten for one, he said, ten for one,
strength of ten when the night is done,
light the lamp and hold the pew —
come down, come down, come down.

——

Five doors on the square had ash by morning,
ash and something darker, drawn by a careful hand,
and men went door to door by lantern, asking
which of us he'd made believe.
The pews went thin. The pews went thinner.
And up from the Undercroft, through the boards,
a second hymn, to our tune, in our time,
and not one word of it ours.

passages.heading: (no bell)
passages.text:
How many does it take to make a town believe?
Six, they say.
We counted.
We stopped counting at —

——
(the tune drops out)
KEEP SINGING.

DON'T LOOK AT THE PULPIT.

THE VICAR PREACHED AT DUSK TONIGHT.

WHO PREACHED AT DUSK TONIGHT.

NOBODY GOES DOWN THE STAIR.

NOBODY REPORTS ANYTHING.

SING.

(the tune comes back, lower)
Ten for one, he said — ten of what?
Tenfold my own — his own what?
His blood? His silence? Mine?
Come down, come down, come down.

——

They say the Friday morning train came in with a man on it
nobody sold a ticket to.
They say an iron crosier rang on the platform boards.
They say on Saturday a pillar of light stood over St Brannock's,
and he was ten of himself in it. Tenfold.
I saw a light. I'll say that much. I saw a light.
Then the bell rang,
and nobody in HollowMere can tell you which way.

passages.heading: (no bell)
passages.text:
Ten for one, he said, ten for one,
and I'm in the pew where I told him,
holding what he held for me —
come down.

——
(half-spoken, the tune going out)
The stone goes up at dawn…
Somebody light the pink one…
Don't go down the stair…
Who preached at dusk tonight…

He prayed for the strength of ten, and HollowMere heard a debt.
This town has never once let a debt go uncollected.

works.title: I Want to Hang
works.blurb: the Drifter's slow waltz: a nameless stranger who came to the end of the line to be chosen practises looking guilty at the well and the doorpost, reads the stone every morning hoping for his own name, and pleads with the bench for the rope, knowing his hanging buys time for the real knife.

passages.heading: I Want to Hang
passages.text:
*(waltz time, slow; no drum, just a chair creaking in three)*

Nobody comes to the end of the line
unless they're running, or hunting, they say.
I wasn't running. I wasn't hunting.
I paid one way to be picked.

——

One bag, one coat, one fare, no name.
In the bag, a knife I whittled out of pine
and blacked with stove polish till it shone like a sin.
A rag gone red with something that isn't blood.
A coat that came with somebody's trade:
you'd nod at it. You do.

I have never cut a thing that bled.
I have never held a thing that mattered.
I have never once been chosen.

So what does guilty look like, in this fog?
Somebody show me. I'll wear it.

——

Bell, and bench, and beam.
Acquittal, a fine, or the drop.
Don't acquit me.
Don't fine me.
I want to hang.
Choose me.

passages.heading: I Want to Hang
passages.text:
——

I learned to wash my hands at the well
at the wrong hour, where the shutters can see,
clean hands, and I scrub them like they're not.
I learned to leave one red thumb on a doorpost
where somebody careful will find it.
I learned to pass a lit door twice
and look back once, and not the third time.

Not too much. Too much and they laugh,
and a laugh is a town looking away,
and I have had a whole life of away.

Every morning I wet the rag again.
Every morning I read the stone with tomorrow on it,
slow, every letter, like a letter from home.
It's never me.
It's somebody who wanted the morning.
It's never me.

How guilty is guilty enough?
How long does a slip have to lie
before somebody writes my name on one?

——

Bell, and bench, and beam.
Acquittal, a fine, or the drop.
Don't acquit me.
Don't fine me.
I want to hang.
Look at me.

passages.heading: I Want to Hang
passages.text:
——

But I'm not the only one in a borrowed coat.
Somebody here washes at the well and means it.
Somebody here keeps the real one, warm from a pocket,
and tonight they'll be the loudest voice in the square
asking who did it,
and their finger will find me,
and I'll stand up straighter.

I know what my rope buys.
I know who it buys it for.
I don't know their name.

Every day you spend on me, the knife walks free:
another plate at the wake table,
another name on the stone that isn't mine.
And God help me, I'm grateful.
Whoever you are,
you're the only one in this town who ever needed me.

——

*(music stops; whispered)*
Dusk. They take the rope in.
They bolt the trap.
The crows walk the beam to keep me in sight.
I stand under it anyway,
like the last one at a dance, waiting to be asked.

passages.heading: I Want to Hang
passages.text:
They say the last man through the trap
went into the Gazette with no name,
because nobody could swear to it.
They say the rope comes off the Company mill
and gets billed to whoever drops.
Fine. Open me an account.
Put a name on it. Any name.

I never told anybody mine.
Not the conductor. Not the bench. Not you.
So if you choose me, what do you choose?
And who was all of this for?

——

*(music back, slower)*
Bell, and bench, and beam.
Acquittal, a fine, or the drop.
Hands go up at the bell like crows off a beam.
The town has spoken.
Say it's me.

——

*(half-sung, fading)*
I never wanted to die.
I wanted to be chosen,
and this town only chooses one way.
All my life the world looked straight through me.
A gallows is just a town that finally looks.

works.title: The Blade Sings at Dawn
works.blurb: the head sawyer's work song for the dawn of Monday 8 December 1952, when Mirek, Sawmill No. 6, is sentenced to the Blade on a short count the singer's own silence put on him, and the singer works the lever: "The Blade didn't sing for him. / I did.".

passages.heading: The Blade Sings at Dawn
passages.text:
*(no music; the wheel in the dark)*
Five to six, Monday mornin', December, fifty-two,
Ice on the race and the waterwheel turnin' like it's got someplace to get to,
Old rail bed by the trestle runs south, and none of us ever came up it,
PRODUCTION IS OBLIGATION on the gate, new paint on the old — somebody else's slogan, we just inherited it,
They tell you at the gate you're feedin' the furnace or you're fuel,
And the furnace never once ran cold, and the wheel never once ran cool.
Saw's been quiet all night. Saw's gonna sing before the bell.
Mondays like this it sings empty first — so the whole bunkhouse can tell.

——

PRODUCTION —
— IS OBLIGATION.
Wheel on the race and the carriage on the rail,
Quota on the board and your number on the nail,
PRODUCTION —
— IS OBLIGATION.
Feet by the bell and feet by the night,
Chalk don't lie and the Tallyman's always right,
Ten on the sawmill rack, and the rack don't care what you are —
The log on your rack at dawn is who you are.

passages.heading: The Blade Sings at Dawn
passages.text:
——
(storytelling cadence, low, under the saw)
Now Two's on the tail with his hands in his sleeves,
Taps the rail twice before every cut, like a man sayin' please,
Came in off a boat from a war that ain't over and won't be,
Says *thank you* to nobody, soft, like the last thing he owns free.
Seven sets the dogs and he talks to the logs like they're mules —
*Easy now, girl, easy* — Seven never learned any other rules.
And Six takes the board off the saw and he walks it out to the stack,
Counts every plank twice 'cause he ran a lathe once and he trusts a number to count him back,
Names every log as it comes off the carriage, low, in a language I don't have,
Folds his scrip every Friday into a paper bird before he spends half,
Hums somethin' under the saw all day that the saw won't let you hear,
Asks me every night what time it is someplace, and I tell him, and he nods like I'm near.
And me, I'm Five, on the lever, I'm the one sets the bite,
Cough since the thaw — crew calls it a cold, and the crew's bein' polite,
Used to stand on a crate in the rain and say UNION like a prayer,
Now I stand on a lever and say nothin', and nobody's countin' what's there.
Mess-hall men hum with no words when the whistle blows; we sing with ours, so somebody knows.

passages.heading: The Blade Sings at Dawn
passages.text:
——
(the count; flat, like the board)
Four hundred feet by the first bell — Tallyman chalks it on Six,
Eight hundred by noon, and the wheel takes its buckets and ticks,
Twelve hundred's the quota, eleven-sixty's a Monday,
Forty feet short is a Monday, and Monday comes round every someday.
I pull the lever. Six takes the board.
The Tallyman chalks what Six can hold.
Offbearer's count is the count goes up on the slate,
So whatever the lever don't cut, it's Six who comes up late.

——

PRODUCTION —
— IS OBLIGATION.
Man comin' in on Friday's train, so the quota goes up for his eyes,
Fifteen hundred feet, and the wheel don't turn faster for a man in a tie,
PRODUCTION?
— is obligation.
Short on a Monday, your week goes down the race,
No store, no bread, no paper bird, and a hungrier face,
Ten on the sawmill rack, and the rack's a ledger, not a star —
Who owes who, when the log on your rack at dawn is who you are?

passages.heading: The Blade Sings at Dawn
passages.text:
——
(beat drops out; the platform at dawn)
WEIGH THE TEN.

WEIGH THE TEN.

CIRCUIT JUDGE, FLOWN IN THIS MORNING.

NUMBER SIX. SHORT FORTY.

ACQUITTAL. SCRIP FORFEITURE. THE BLADE.

MONDAY THE SEVENTEENTH. SCRIP FORFEITURE.

CIRCUIT JUDGE, FLOWN IN THIS MORNING.

NUMBER SIX. SHORT FORTY.

ACQUITTAL. SCRIP FORFEITURE. THE BLADE.

passages.heading: MONDAY THE EIGHTH —
passages.text:
(beat rolls back in, slow and heavy)
Billet goes on the scale. Billet comes off the rack.
Judge goes back to the airstrip. They'll fly him in again when they want him back.

——
(darker, slower)
Acquittal's back to the carriage — that's the mercy, that's the prize,
More feet for the same bread, the same wheel, the same skies,
Forfeiture's your week in the race, every cent of scrip gone,
And the Blade's the carriage with a man on it, where the log belongs.
Same rail. Same bite. Same lever. Same hand.
What the saw lets go of, the chute takes down to the race, and the wheel don't understand.
Race runs red for a minute. Then it runs clean.
Nobody looks. Nobody counts. Nobody says what they've seen.
Then they plane your billet blank, white wood where the number burned,
Brand it fresh for Friday's train, and a new man wears what you earned,
Wears your wood and your slot and your quota, and never knows who's gone —
That's the whole of the Blade. That's all. And the shift goes on.

passages.heading: MONDAY THE EIGHTH —
passages.text:
What's a number worth on a fifty-two quota?
Forty feet of pine?
And who chalked it — the Tallyman,
or the man on the lever who kept still?

——
(drops to almost a whisper, deliberate)
Monday the seventeenth, the forty was mine.
Cough on the lever, I held the bite back, I was slow on the line,
The cough took the forty and Six took the chalk,
Tallyman turned to the crew and said *Whose?* — and nobody'd talk.
And I didn't talk.
Judge said forfeiture. Six said *okay*. That's all Six said.
No paper bird that Friday. No store. Camp ration and a heel of bread.
Three weeks, and his belt ran out of holes, and Seven punched him a new one with a nail,
Ribs come up through his shirt like the carriage rail,
Knuckles gone white as the planed wood, hands shakin' on the board,
Still countin' every plank twice. Still trustin' what the chalk would record.
Then the man off the train, and the quota went up for his week,
And a hungry man carries less board than a fed one, however you speak,
Monday the eighth the forty was Six's, honest and true —
Was it? I built it. I built it out of keepin' still, start to through.

passages.heading: MONDAY THE EIGHTH —
passages.text:
Did he know?
He looked at the lever once, on the seventeenth, the way you look at weather.
Then he went back to countin'. He never said. We never talked about it, ever.
Whether that look was him forgivin' the man at the lever, or him knowin' all along who built his forty, I'll never hear it from a mouth the Blade sang shut.

His name was Mirek.
He named the logs for places he'd left, so somebody'd say 'em out loud.
He folded the birds for a child he couldn't send 'em to, and kept 'em in a cigar box, and never once was proud.
He hummed the whole shift long under the saw, so the saw would let it pass,
And Saturday night in the bunk I finally caught the tune —
It was a lullaby. For somebody small. He never told me whose.

I pulled the lever. I watched the chalk. I kept my wood.

passages.heading: MONDAY THE EIGHTH —
passages.text:
——
(dawn; the lever)
PRODUCTION —
— is obligation.
Lever's mine on a Blade mornin' — that's the order, that's the trade,
Saw runs empty, one long note, and the whole camp hears the Blade,
PRODUCTION —
— is obligation.
Mirek on the carriage where the log should be, lookin' at the wheel, not me,
Hummin' — and this time I can hear it, 'cause the saw ain't bitin' yet, and the race is runnin' free.
Two taps the rail twice. Seven says *easy* — and don't say *girl*.
One voice short on the answer, and it's the quietest sound in the world,
Ten on the sawmill rack, and nine of us standin' where we are —
The log on my rack at dawn is who I am. That's the charge.

——
(half-spoken, fading as the wheel takes up)
First bell…
Somebody roll the first log…
Friday's train's bringin' a new Six…
Keep your wood…
Keep your wood…

passages.heading: MONDAY THE EIGHTH —
passages.text:
The Blade didn't sing for him.
I did.

works.title: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
works.blurb: the dockhands' work song as the shantyman's confession: paid by the Smuggler-Blackguard to sing louder over the crate, the saffron, the vault and the ferry strongbox, he keeps singing while Petit-Yann is framed by a seal in his loaf, fined by the noon bell and given to the Hearth at the nine o'clock supper on 9 September 1789; the ferry brings the news and takes the smuggler away, and the shanty becomes the Commons' song with Yann's name in it.

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
*(no music; rope on the bollard)*
Four in the mornin', end of August, eighty-nine,
Fog on the bay, and the foghorn moanin' the one note it knows, same as mine,
PORT-AU-LEVAIN — BY DECREE OF THE SOVEREIGN SOURDOUGH COUNCIL, cut in the arch at the head of the quay,
Mornin' Ferry don't wait on a soul — what misses her stays. What stays is me.

——
*(Yann takes the answer, a breath high)*
HAUL AWAY —
— for the Mornin' Ferry,
Gold on the Gallery, white on the Guild,
Burlap on the Abbey and the red crust on the quay,
Every platter in the Hall has gotta be filled,
And it's never been the Gallery fillin' one for me,
HAUL AWAY —
— for the Mornin' Ferry,
She takes out the cod and she brings back the tax,
The loaf on your platter at dawn is who you are —
So haul, boys, haul, and don't look back

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
——
*(storytelling cadence, laid back, heavy)*
Now Marrec's on the winch with a wheeze like a bellows with a hole,
Says the fog gets in his chest and charges rent on his soul,
Old Maela guts on the planks and she sings the low line flat,
Forty years flat, and nobody's told her, and nobody's gonna do that,
Nolwenn, twelve, chalks the crates with a stub the size of her thumb,
Counts out loud so the Counting-House can't say she's dumb,
And Petit-Yann on the rope, takin' the answer a breath too high,
Hauls with us by day, and by night in the dish pit he kneels where the old seal's ground in dry,
Three weeks Unregistered, copper short, and the tariff don't bend,
Seal struck off his bread, so he presses his thumb in the crust instead —
Says that way he'll know it's his. Says a man should know his own bread.
Keeps a ferry token in his pocket he never once spent.

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
Four, the salt for the Counting-House, weighed on the Counting-House scale,
Five, the saffron, stamped for the Apothecary, sweeter than the sail,
Six, the gold leaf in paper for the Gallery's cloches, light as a lie,
Seven, the customs crate — Crown wax, Crown chain, and nobody's to pry,
I haul the salt. I haul the gold.
I haul whatever the Gallery's sold.

Then up off the Salt-Flats, boots white to the knee,
Comes a sea-dog in a coat with no colour I could see,
Not gold, not flour, not crust, not burlap — nobody's man,
Opens the coat just enough: a pocket-mortar, small as a hand,
Don't point it. Don't need to. Just lets me look.
Then he asks me the one thing, quiet as a hook:
"Which crate's the Crown's?"
And I told him.
Silver piece in my palm, and he closes my fingers on it slow —
"Sing it loud tonight, shantyman. Louder than you know."

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
——

HAUL AWAY —
— for the Mornin' Ferry,
Night shift under the lamps and the fog comin' in on the slates,
Sing it to the bottom of your lungs and a little past that, mates,
HAUL AWAY —
— for the Mornin' Ferry,
Silver in my boot and the crew askin' why I'm callin' so strong,
The loaf on your platter at dawn is who you are —
So haul, boys, haul, and don't count the crates

——

First night, a crack, down under the second refrain,
Like a cask stove in — so I sang the refrain again,
Mornin', the customs crate's stood open, Crown wax broke in two,
And a silver piece on the lid with PROOF-READER scratched through,
Nolwenn wouldn't touch it. Maela crossed herself twice.
Master Proof-Reader come down himself at seven and didn't look at it twice,
Put it in his apron the way a man puts away what's his,
And nobody on this wharf has seen it since, or asked what it is.

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
Second night, glass, off the west side, under the low line,
Maela sang it flatter, and the flat covered it fine,
Mornin', the Apothecary's short of its saffron, every thread,
And short of the vials the register counts. That's all the Inquisitor said.

Third night, the Counting-House, iron on iron, three streets up,
Ledger-Clerk shot every deadbolt home, and every deadbolt held like a sieve,
Mornin', the gold reserve's gone, and the brass seal off the Clerk's own desk,
And the Gallery's sendin' down for a name, and the Gallery don't much care whose name is next.

Three nights I sang, and three nights the island slept,
And three silver pieces in my boot is the only count I kept.

——
*(darker, slower)*
Monday, the seventh, dusk, and I go up to the Hall like you do,
Look at my own seal on my own loaf, see it's still true,
Gilded platters nearest the Hearth, silver gone yellow with the heat,
Flour-white in the middle, red crust at the back where the draughts come in off the street,
Aboyeur comes down the Hall with the dusk loaf, calls no name,
Sets it on the empty platter nearest the fire — *for a name under seal* — same
As every night since before my grandmother. Nobody asks. I don't.
And at the back, by the red crust, by my own platter — the coat.
At Yann's.
Cloche up in one hand. Cloche back down.
I went back down to the wharf. I sang the night shift, loud as he paid.

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
Wednesday the word comes down the quay off the dawn judgment:
Audit on platter nine. Loaf with no thumb in it. Bailiff cracked it. Counting-House seal.
Fine's four onces of copper, the weight of the seal, by the noon bell, or the Hearth.
Yann on the rope, sayin' "That ain't my bread. There's no thumb."
Saying it to the rope.
I had the sea-dog's silver in my boot. Three pieces.
Noon bell.
I was haulin'.
And the sea-dog on the wharf that afternoon in gloves —
Never wore gloves in his life.

——

*(beat drops out)*
WEDNESDAY. NINTH OF SEPTEMBER. NOON BELL.

BY ORDER OF THE MORNING JUDGMENT.

PLATTER NINE.

YANN LE GOFF. PLONGEUR. RED CRUST.

THE CRATE. THE SAFFRON. THE VAULT.

FINE UNPAID.

TRIAL BY FIRE.

SUPPER AT NINE.

*(beat rolls back in slow and heavy)*
Gallery up in the gold with the menu cards tucked in their sleeves,
Quartet tunin' a fifth, and the Abbot in his burlap wouldn't bless it — kept his hands in his sleeves,
And Yann on the stage, hummin' the answer, a breath too high,
Waitin' on the call. Found me in the crowd. Waited.
I never gave it.
They gave him to the Hearth.
Menu's up on the board by the Gallery stair by three: the fish, the wine, the saffron bread.
His platter's bare by morning.

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
What's a shantyman worth on a burnin' day?
Who calls the time, if not the one that's paid?
And who'd have heard him answer, if I'd called?

——
*(half time; nobody takes the answer)*
HAUL AWAY —
HAUL AWAY —
Gold on the Gallery, white on the Guild,
Burlap on the Abbey and the red crust on the quay,
One platter in the Hall that won't be filled,
And it was never gonna be the Gallery fillin' it for me,
HAUL AWAY —
She takes out the cod and she brings back the tax,
The loaf on his platter at dawn was who he was —
So haul, boys. Haul. Don't look back.

——

Twenty-third, mornin', and she comes in out of the white,
Deckhands shoutin' it down before the rope's even tight —
Paris. A fortress taken in July. The King's own walls.
The Third Estate sittin' as the nation, in the King's own halls.
Marrec let go of the winch. Maela put down the knife.
Nolwenn set the chalk on the crate, first time in her life,
And a Crown man in a coat comes down the plank behind the paper, grey from the crossing, hat in his hand,
And nobody bows. And nobody hauls. And nobody's paid. And nobody's sure where to stand.
And I open my mouth, and the shanty's what comes, because the shanty's all I've got —
HAUL AWAY —
— the fortress is down —
First new line anybody's put to it in a hundred years, and it went up the Wharf, and up the Flats, faster than his coach.

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
Then one dawn after — don't ask me which, the fog don't keep a calendar —
She casts off with the cod and the mail and a coat with no colour aboard,
Crack out over the water like the crust breakin' at six,
Strongbox gone. Sea-dog gone. Ferry gone under him.
Some say inland. Some say the reef.
She came back in a fortnight with a mainland crew and no box.
She brought the news in. She took him out.
One crate, one shelf of saffron, one vault, one ferry — four,
And a fifth he never touched with his hands: a song. He paid for it. It's mine.

——
*(drops to almost a whisper, deliberate)*
So here's the count the Counting-House never kept.
He asked which crate. I said.
I saw the coat at Yann's platter. I sang.
The fine was copper by the noon bell, and his silver was in my boot. I hauled.
On the stage he waited for the call, a breath high, the way he always did,
And I kept my mouth shut — me, the one man on this rock whose whole trade is openin' it.
Thumb in every loaf so he'd know his own,
And they gave him to the fire for a loaf with no thumb in it.
Ferry token in his pocket, never spent. I don't know where it went.

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
But he never paid me to keep quiet.
He paid me to sing.

——

Now it goes up the hill — wharf to the dish pit, dish pit to the Flats, Flats to the Square,
Apprentices, Plongeurs, the gutters, the Unregistered, every red crust that's there,
Under the Gallery windows at supper, crowdin' the lane,
And somebody put him in it. Somebody put in his name.

HAUL THEM DOWN —
— from the Gallery,
Gold on the Gallery, white on the Guild,
Burlap on the Abbey and the red crust in the Square,
Every platter in the Hall is gonna be filled,
And Petit-Yann's the answer, and the answer's everywhere —
HAUL THEM DOWN —
— from the Gallery,
Same stage, same bell, same cloches, same fire,
The loaf on your platter at dawn is who they'll say you are —
And I'm the one that calls it. Every night. Louder. Higher.

passages.heading: Shanty for the Morning Ferry
passages.text:
——
*(half spoken, fading slow like the beat's dying)*
Haul away…
Marrec, mind the winch…
Nolwenn, chalk the crates…
Somebody tell Maela she's flat… no… don't…
Platter nine's bare…
See you at the ferry…

Every dawn the ferry goes, and every dawn the bell,
And the song I sold for silver is the one they sing so well.

They sing him now like the Gallery lit him alone.
I sang loud enough to cover a crate — and I've been singin' over it since.

works.title: Six Things a Hand Can Make
works.pov: first person (Ada Kerrow, the camp smith)
works.blurb: Ada Kerrow's forge song at Grounds 99, Thursday 11 December 1952: six materials (timber, stone, tin ore, pine resin, herbs, mushrooms) and the six things a hand makes of them (torch, snare, spade, lockpicks, lantern, crowbar), a verse each with what it cost; the refrain runs from "Don't tell me who it's for" to "Somebody tell me who I was for", and the turn is her brother Carl, the name on the list.

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
*(no music; hammer on the anvil)*
Thursday, December, fifty-two, and the hearth's not out. It don't go out.
Men stand in my door to call it the warmest light in the camp, and they stand there long, and I let 'em.
It's warm 'cause it's working, boys. A light is only a fire with a job.
Left hand healed shiny. I keep it out of the trough.

——

Six things in the hills, and six things in the hand,
Bring 'em in where it's lit, where the whole yard can see whose hands,
Nothing gets made in the dark in this camp, nothing gets made unseen,
Every hand in this room is a hand somebody's counted clean —
Bring it to the forge, I'll make it.
Don't tell me who it's for.

——
*(hammer, steady, one for each)*
One for the timber, off the yard and the saw,
Saw's run quiet since Monday, and nobody says what it saw.
One for the stone, off the yard, cheapest thing in the camp,
Only thing they carry me that nobody died for. Stone don't need a lamp.
One for the tin ore, from the seam, and the seam wants a spade,
And the spade wants my basin, so every lantern's mine at both ends of the trade.

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
One for the resin, off the pines, sticky as a debt,
Reverend used to thumb it on us at the gate, resin on the brow. He's not back yet.
Gone since the fourth. The collar still blesses at the gate, the same words, the same height of hand.
I don't look whose neck is in it. I'm a smith. I don't have to understand.
One for the herbs, out of the woods, and everybody wants 'em,
The ones who hand out the jobs want 'em, and the snares want 'em, and I can't tell you which is worse to be asked for, so I don't.
One for the mushrooms, up out of the adits, cold and pale as a palm,
Only thing they bring to my door I can't make into anything.
Somebody wants 'em. Never me.
Thank God for one thing in this camp that isn't mine to make.

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
——

Six things in the hills, and six things in the hand,
Bring 'em in where it's lit, where the whole yard can see whose hands,
Nothing gets made in the dark in this camp, nothing gets made unseen,
Every hand in this room is a hand somebody's counted clean —
Bring it to the forge, I'll make it.
Don't tell me who it's for.

Six for the hills. And six for the hand.

——
*(quench hiss)*
Timber and resin, that's a torch, and a torch don't need my fire.
Any man can make his own torch, and that's the saddest thing I know.
It's for the ones caught out past the whistle, between the bunkhouse and the pines.
Wolves won't cross a flame. They won't. They wait at the edge of it, patient as clerks.
Sawmill Five went out Tuesday at the Roll with his hands in his pockets and no light.
Dawn, at the treeline: his boot, and his foot still in it, laced.
His jacket in strips down the slope, like somebody sorting rags.
A drag line in the needles into the pines, wide as a man's shoulders, then narrower.
In the one pocket left, a spoon he was whittling for nobody. Half a bowl. A good half.
Ridge has a saying: *the whistle you did not answer.*
I don't know which whistle Five didn't answer. I know he whittled.

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
*(hammer)*
Timber and herbs, that's a snare. Somebody orders one most weeks.
I don't ask who. The tag on it tells you all it does:
holds whoever steps in, and logs the name.
That's all a snare is, boys. Holds whoever steps in, and logs the name.
It don't care whose foot.
Neither did the list they read to somebody I ironed a shirt for.

*(hammer)*
Timber and stone, at my basin, a spade, for the Workings crew:
*dig tin ore out of a seam*, and the ore comes back to me.
Every spade I hand out comes back to me as ore.
Some come back without the man.
There's one on the rack now, the handle worn to one man's grip, his thumb's dip in the ash.
Nobody asks for it. Nobody's hand fits.
And some nights a spade goes out for what isn't ore,
And comes back clean, and nobody brings me anything.

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
*(hammer)*
Tin ore, at my basin: picks. For whoever wants in.
I make 'em. I don't ask what door, and I don't ask after.
The camp says it like a hymn: *locks keep people out, never in.*
Nothing on my hut is locked from the outside. Go and look.
I could make a pick for every door in this camp,
And not one of them's the thing that keeps me here.

——
*(hammer slower)*
Then the lantern. *Three tin ore from the seam. I will make you a lantern for it.*
I say it to every one of 'em. Same words, every time, like the Reverend's.
*Good ore. This burns bright.* It nearly always does.
It's for every man they send down. The detail man fills his before he goes in the water,
Every one of 'em fills it, don't let the bunkhouse tell you different,
'Cause down there they live below the last lamp, and a man wants to be the last lamp, not below it.
Little Hob came up still hooked on a hand that wouldn't let go of the bail.
I cleaned him. That's my work.
This one's Patience. I'm sealing her now, under my breath. You didn't hear it.
Patience, go down. Come back up.
Come back up with him.

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
*(hammer, heavy)*
Timber and tin ore: a crowbar. Heaviest thing I make, and the plainest.
Says it on the tag: *break a locked door; it stays broken.*
For whoever wants in and don't care who knows it.
The yard says the crowbar goes to whoever never holds the knife.
I let the yard say it. I hand it over. I don't ask.
It's the honest one of the six. What it opens stays open.

——

Six things in the hills, and six things in the hand,
Brought in where it's lit, where the whole yard could see whose hands,
Nothing got made in the dark in this camp, nothing got made unseen,
Every hand in this room was a hand somebody'd counted clean —
I brought it to the forge. I made it.
Don't tell me who it was for.

——
*(beat drops out; the whistle)*
FIFTEEN SECONDS.

BANK THE TROUGH. LEAVE THE FIRE.

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
WHO'S GOT A TORCH.

NOBODY'S OUT. NOBODY'S OUT.

THE BUNK BY THE DOOR IS EMPTY.

DON'T ANSWER THE WHISTLE.

DON'T ANSWER IT.

*(beat rolls back in, slow)*
A bunk without a man gets the light, and the light found the bunk by the door.
The rack'll write him *absent* by morning, and my hearth's still going behind me, lit for nobody.

——
*(at the bunk; almost a whisper)*
Carl.
Six things a hand can make in this camp, and I've made every one of 'em for somebody else.
Yours made a seventh.
A name. Off a list. In a pressed shirt I ironed.
There's no tool for that in my forge. I've looked. I'm the best smith in this camp, and I've looked.
A crowbar's door stays broken. A said name stays said.

Who's the torch for? Who's the snare for?
Who was I for?
Did you need to? Did they ask? Did it cost you anything at all?

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
I could make a pick for the gate. I never have.
Wrong tool. There's no lock on what keeps me.
The men need lanterns, and I'm the one who makes 'em, so I stay, and I keep it lit,
and I call that a choice, 'cause it's the one thing in here I get to call one.
Our old lantern off the dump's still under my bunk. I could fix it by supper. I haven't.

I know who it's for.

——

Crowbar and lantern, picks and spade, snare and torch, back down the line,
Mushrooms and herbs and resin, and ore, and stone, and the pine,
Bring it in where it's lit, where the whole yard can see whose hands,
Every hand in this room is a hand somebody's counted clean —
Bring it to the forge, I'll make it.
Somebody tell me who I was for.

——
*(half-spoken, fading with the hammer)*
Three tin ore…
Good ore…
Bank the trough, not the fire…
See you at the whistle…

passages.heading: Six Things a Hand Can Make
passages.text:
A hand can make six things in this camp, and every one of them goes out the door.
The seventh thing a hand can make is a name, and nothing in this forge can unmake it.

works.title: Don't Miss the Train
works.pov: first person (the platform hand, Arthur's brother)
works.blurb: a platform ballad for the last train out at dusk on Saturday 23 December 1893, sung by the Ballad of the Iron Beast's platform hand: the leavers (a drummer on his tonic trunk, a Mill Row family a fare short, a man with a pressed flower in his Psalms), the town that stays, Pruett's spoken call of LAST TRAIN OUT, one heavy case handed up unremarked; at the whistle he finally takes Arthur's ticket out of the hatband and gives it to Ernie, who climbs the step, looks back once, and steps down to stay for him; the refrain turns from "don't miss the train" to "we just stood where it left us".

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
*(no music; boots on frozen planks; wind off the north)*
Quarter to four in the evenin', December the twenty-third, ninety-three,
Coach road went Tuesday under the white, and the white's still comin' for me,
HOLLOWMERE — EST. BY THE RAILROAD EXPANSE, sign iced stiff on its chain,
Whole town's out on the boards for once — and nobody standin' in threes for the train

——

Step on up, snow on the boards, keep your hat in your hand,
Wasn't saints laid this line, boys, and it wasn't the pioneers' hand,
Barons own the mill and the bank and the dirt where you stand,
You want bread, you want news, you ever hope to go —
Seven days' walk to a soul, and tonight it's all snow,
Here she sits on the spur, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
HollowMere, end of the line, wash the mud off your name,
And whatever you do, boys — don't miss the train

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
——
(storytelling cadence, laid back, heavy)
Hoods were out last night, flour sacks and torches, the lot,
So we come down one at a time and we stand apart like we're not,
There's a drummer in checks come up for Harold's sale,
Sold nothin', bought nothin', sits on his tonic trunk, pale,
There's a Mill Row woman with the beddin' roped tight,
Three kids and two fares, and she's done the sum twice,
Smallest wears her boots round her neck by the laces,
Savin' the soles for the other end, wherever that place is,
There's a man with a Bible, a flower pressed flat in the Psalms,
Won't say where he's goin', holds it shut in both palms.

Car 2's empty tonight, first time since I come,
Nothin' to sign for, nothin' to unload, nothin' to bring home,
I lift their trunks. I lift their beds.
I lift whatever they couldn't sell.
And what do you carry out of a town
when the year's in the Company's name as well?

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
——

Step on up, snow on the boards, keep your fare in your hand,
Ticket out costs a year, and the Clerk's had the year in his hand,
Five days, boys, and nothin' comes up, and nothin' goes down the line,
Five days of the white and the pines and whatever's behind,
Here she sits on the spur, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
She's the last for a while, boys, and they're tellin' you plain —
Whatever you do, don't miss the last train

——

Now Len's on the trunks singin' spike-time to the lift,
Clem reads the manifest out loud, the parts nobody asked for, every line of the shift,
Jack Rudd grins at the drummer and the drummer looks at the floor,
And Ernie, twelve, with the bucket, wipin' snow off the step by the door,
Askin' Pruett where she goes after us —
and Pruett ain't told him yet.

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
Mrs Grieves has the Lantern lit, one lamp in the glass,
Long coats on the bank front, watchin' the bank, watchin' us pass,
They come up for their Baron. Their Baron fell on these boards. They stayed.
Nobody's told 'em to go, so they stand where they're paid.
Down on the dock there's a lantern, Nora's, bought dear at noon,
So Cyril can see where she is, and Cyril's three weeks drowned,
Agnes'll have the stone's name by mornin', before anyone asks,
And the Vicar didn't come down to bless the cars.
He's not been himself since Sunday, they say.

And somewhere on these boards, wavin' her off like the rest,
Stands whoever did for the Baron on the fourteenth, hand to the chest,
And the bench at the end where they found the railyard man on the twelfth —
Snow on it, smooth as a sheet. Nobody's sat there since.

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
Then I slip in my one, outbound, Ma's name in my hand,
*Merry Christmas, Ma. The West agrees with me, Ma* — in Arthur's hand,
I sign it Arthur. I tie off the bag. I heave it aboard.
Last bag of the year. Last lie of the year, Lord.

——
(beat drops out; Pruett on the step, punch in his hand)
LAST TRAIN OUT.

LAST TRAIN OUT.

LINE'S SHUT TILL SHE CLEARS.

CAR THREE IS FULL.

NOBODY RIDES IN CAR THREE.

FARES ON THE STEP. FARES ON THE STEP.

A PASSENGER BOOKED IN IS A PASSENGER COUNTED OUT.

ERNIE. GET THAT BUCKET OFF MY STEP.

(beat rolls back in slow and heavy)
Nobody asked how many in the back car, and nobody said,
Car Three don't get asked. Car Three just gets fed.

——
(darker, slower)
Last of 'em up is a passenger with one case, carried low,
Hands it up to me, and I take it, and the weight goes right through,
Heavy as the mail on a Monday, heavy as a man,
I set it in the car with both arms and I take back my hand,
Didn't look at the face. Didn't look at the boots in the snow.
Freight is freight, and the Company don't ask, so don't I.
Somethin' pressed in my palm, cold and round, and I shut my fist on it slow —
Ain't opened it yet. Ain't goin' to. Some things a hand don't need to know.

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
And out past the end of the platform, where the lamp gives out,
Somethin' stands at the tree line. Don't board. Don't wave. Don't shout.

Who counts what goes out of here, if not the hand that lifts it?
Who asks what's in a case, in a town that sells its keys at noon?
And who'd hold the last train for a question, with the white comin' down?

——

Step on up, light's goin' down, take your hat off your head,
She brought the bread and the whiskey, the priest and the lead,
She brought the Baron and the dogs and the letter sealed black,
She took the ones we couldn't keep, in a box, in the back,
Now she takes the ones that paid, and she leaves us the rest,
Five days of nothin' at all comin' up from the east,
Here she goes, whistle and steam, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
Last train don't wait, boys — and she won't come back for you, all the same

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
——
(drops to almost a whisper, deliberate)
But I had a ticket.

Arthur's. In the hatband since the back car. Never punched past Tuesday.
I took off his hat. I took out his ticket. I held it up in the snow.
Thought: now. Get on. Go where he didn't go.
Pruett on the step with the crescent die up in his hand —
and I didn't get on.
I put it in Ernie's hand.

Go on, I said. Go see where she goes after us.
Go on. You always ask.
And he climbed to the step, twelve, with the bucket still in his fist,
and Pruett brought the punch down to the paper —

He looked at me once. He stepped back down.
He stayed for me. He stayed in this town.

Gave it me back, warm from his hand.
"Who'd fill the bucket," he says, "if I'm gone?"
And I took it back. I put it in the band. I was glad.
God help me. I was glad.

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
Never punched past Tuesday. Still.

So which of us taught him that?
The one who stepped down for me —
or the one who stood here and let him watch?

——

Step on up, snow on the boards, keep your hat in your hand,
Barons own the mill and the bank and the dirt where you stand,
You want bread, you want news, you ever hope to go —
Seven days' walk to a soul, and tonight it's all snow,
There she goes round the black pines, red lamp into the white,
Iron Beast — that was Arthur's word — she don't wait, don't explain,
HollowMere, end of the line, wash the mud off your name,
Nobody missed the last train, boys — we just stood where it left us. Again.

——
(half-spoken, fading slow like the beat's dying)
Dusk whistle…
Somebody's runnin'… a woman, a boy… down the boards after her…
Red lamp's in the snow…
Somebody get Ernie off the tracks…
Nothin' till it clears…
See you at five, boys. There's no five.

passages.heading: Don't Miss the Train
passages.text:
Don't miss the train, they tell you, and nobody here ever has —
we just hand the ticket to the next boy, and watch him give it back.

works.title: Trips Are Like Exes
works.blurb: Prose-poem on self-discovery and impermanence via a travel/relationship duality.

passages.heading: Trips Are Like Exes
passages.text:
Trips are like exes— We’d like to think it’s all their fault when it goes wrong, Love the memories, but wouldn’t ever go back. Yet we take another trip, another chance, Finding ourselves while we are out looking for others. Turns out maybe every trip has a story, And every story has two sides.  
Like Jekyll and Hyde, we run and we hide from the truth. Life’s ugly, love’s got a metallic aftertaste, But in the end, we’d drink poison to feel more alive. We flirt with death at every chance for celebration— Birth, betrothal, or betrayal, we always celebrate. That’s what life’s about: To plan the party, crash it, and clean up after it. Because for fuck's sake, we’ve only got today.  
But the most beautiful part Is finding yourself after a trip. You were broken and lost, Your ego dissolved, your inner self bare. The moment that you thought would bring the ultimate peace Was actually just the moment you lost what you loved.  
When you are freed from your ego, you yearn for your life. Not that you are in any peril, But for a moment, your mind is forced outside itself. Then comes that moment when your self collects back to you, Like a pool of identity in the shards of the after-party. That cleaning up is you coming back, Choosing to be you, And watching as every sliver that is you comes back.

passages.heading: Trips Are Like Exes
passages.text: “In the end we’d love to think it’s all beautiful or ugly but instead the ugly is fucking beauty and every beauties got an ugly side” PART 1

works.title: Growing Up
works.blurb: Mortality and memory through a grandfather relationship.

passages.heading: Growing Up
passages.text:
Growing up is realizing that no one dies of old age.  
Just another fairytale; they don’t mention their pain.  
But why? Youth clings to illusion and fades faster than it,  
and with its passing you see those who died are no different than you and me.  
It is sad, but it is true; that is why we give the passing their due—  
we lay them in boxes their lives’ worth can barely afford.  
Bountiful blessings fall upon deaf ears, past curses forgotten from the years,  
loved ones who never knew them look teary-eyed down at a stranger.  
Go on, pray to some God born from a manger; no plea will bring them back.  
Once the light is extinguished, there’s no coming back.  
Death is neither sad nor happy; like life, it is the tool by which we measure.  
Every point has an end, or else it defies its premise; every life has a death that makes you live.  
So I learned to measure life by its textures: peanuts in bobbing in a cold Coke, baseball on the weekends, the faint smell of dirt under his nails.  
Saturdays were baseball on the tv, the crack of a bat, him calling out names like  he knew the players.  
He built raised beds the way some men pray—measured, squared, patient—  
each seed tucked in like a promise he could keep; soil under his nails smelled of time.  
His office was a pile of paper and tiny things, a life in clutter;  
when I was small I called him an archivist, later I called it what it was: hoarding.  
Still, those piles were his language—how he said he mattered.  
He loved in small rituals: peanuts in Coke, a game on the radio, a row of tomatoes.  
For it is simple to see that life is full of what you look for—  
not why for or who for, but the looking you do when you don’t see.  
Through each breath you are living life, and through each thought of the future you are closing in on death.  
No sermon will bring back the ordinary; only the echo of habit remains.  
So plant your beds, keep your odd comforts, learn the geometry of a double play,  
notice the textures—the fizz, the crack, the dirt, the shuffle of paper—and hold them close.  
Only you can decide what your last breath will look like.  
Make it beautiful, make it memorable, make it a… CRESCENDO!!!

works.title: Am I Me Enough
works.blurb: Self-worth and love, moving toward self-acceptance.

passages.heading: Am I Me Enough
passages.text:
“Am I Me Enough?”

I remember it like it was yesterday — being young.  
I would’ve said young, dumb, and in love,  
but the truth is youth was the only thing I ever lost  
while trying to prove I was enough.

For to be so in love  
that it drives you toward something foolish —  
well, that must’ve been good love.  
The kind pirates plunder,  
kings cling to,  
and paupers pity from afar.  
A treasure so bright it blinds you  
into believing you’re worthy of it.

And wasn’t that always the question?  
Not is this love real,  
but am I real enough for this love.  
Every heartbeat felt like a test,  
every promise like a wager,  
every kiss like a crown  
I wasn’t sure I deserved to wear.

And so I spent whole seasons  
trying to polish myself into something worthy—  
sanding down my softness,  
sharpening my silence,  
learning how to love like a man  
who never asked for anything in return.

passages.heading: Am I Me Enough
passages.text:
I mistook endurance for virtue,  
mistook sacrifice for proof,  
mistook my own breaking  
for a sign I was finally doing love right.  
I kept offering pieces of myself  
like coins into a wishing well,  
hoping the splash meant something,  
hoping someone would hear the echo  
and call it devotion.

But the truth is,  
I wasn’t chasing people—  
I was chasing permission.  
Permission to be held,  
to be chosen,  
to be seen without earning it.  
Every goodbye felt like a verdict,  
every silence like a sentence,  
every almost‑love like a mirror  
asking the same old question  
in a new, cruel light:  
Was I ever enough for anyone  
if I was never enough for myself.

But time has a way of softening the blade,  
of turning questions into quiet companions.  
I learned that worth was never something  
I could win by bleeding for it,  
never something another person  
could stamp onto my chest like a medal.

passages.heading: Am I Me Enough
passages.text:
I spent years trying to be chosen,  
never realizing I was the one  
doing the choosing all along.  
And maybe that’s the cruelest trick of youth—  
believing love is a door someone else must open,  
when all along the hinges were in my hands.

So was I good enough?  
Maybe that was the wrong question.  
Maybe the truth is simpler,  
gentler,  
truer:

I was growing.  
I was learning.  
I was becoming.

And in the becoming,  
I found a version of myself  
who no longer begs for permission,  
who no longer trades pieces of his heart  
for a glimpse of belonging,  
who no longer mistakes being chosen  
for being worthy.

Now, when I look back,  
I don’t ask if I was good enough.  
I ask if I was honest,  
if I was trying,  
if I was becoming someone  
I could stand beside without flinching.

And maybe that’s the quiet miracle of it all—  
that after everything,  
after the longing and the losing,  
after the crowns I didn’t feel fit my head,  
I finally learned to wear my own name  
without apology.

passages.heading: Am I Me Enough
passages.text:
I finally learned  
I was enough  
because I was mine.

works.title: When You Know to Much
works.blurb: Creative ambition and defiance in the face of mortality.

passages.heading: When You Know to Much
passages.text:
When You Know to Much

It pains me to know so many beautiful words have leapt from my mind without me even catching hold.  
It pains me to know I could have written something beautiful, something that could have lasted.  
Maybe I’m foolish to believe the words bumbling around in my head like a beehive would mean anything on paper.  
I want to be great, I say. But I don’t know what to call greatness. I want to be happy, I think. But still I never know joy.  
For who am I to be great—like Shakespeare or King Arthur? One was a drunk and a womanizer. The other was a fairy tale told long ago.  
Are we to keep telling our kids of fae or troll, to let their imaginations run wild with things that go bump in the night? Only for them to grow old as I do now and find it was never true.  
Or should we slay the beautiful creatures that dance in our dreams, call forth misery from adulthood’s fate, and let myth vanish from our lives?  
I cry out one last time to whoever could be listening. Still no change comes that would matter. Because time is the end of all, and it never stops. Maybe that’s why joy fades and light diminishes. Why we wish to be something more is because we know we are slowly becoming less.  
The child in us weeps every day. Will you dry his tears, or tell him never to cry again?

passages.heading: When You Know to Much
passages.text:
Some may think I’m crying over a child, over childhood at its loss. But no—know that I weep for someone else. Myself.  
The world grew around me. I did not grow for the world. They made me into a jest. They made me small so they could stand tall. They defiled what was sacred and called it comedy.  
But here’s what they didn’t know while they laughed:  
I was watching.  
I may not be great. But I can be vain. And vanity—oh, vanity is the one thing the destroyed understand perfectly. We who have nothing left to lose see the game without the mercy of blindness. We speak past you, through you, into the void where those who come after might hear.  
You built your idols on facts you ignored. You called it destiny. You called it talent. You called it greatness.  
But I know the secret now: there is no difference between a god and a joke until someone decides there is. And I have decided.  
So let me laugh—joyful, bitter, knowing. Let me spit gold that tastes like ash. Let me build mountains from the wreckage you left me. Let me push the great ones from the heights not because I’m stronger, but because I’m already falling, and I’ve learned how to fly on the way down.  
This is the power of the defiled: we move without fear. We speak without hope. We climb without asking permission from those who never owned the mountain anyway.  
My words aren’t great. They’re mine.  
And that’s more than enough to shake what was never real.

works.title: Inherited
works.blurb: Generational cycles and becoming your parents.

passages.heading: Inherited
passages.text:
Inherited

I remember the nights I tried to stay awake to see my father’s headlights touch my window.  
The way you would sleep in on the weekends because you were tired.  
My heartaches when you weren’t there to play catch.  
But now I know the noose money became as it trickled out like water, pushing you further out to sea.

My mother yelled not out of anger but fear.  
I felt like we were at odds but the truth is I fought while you protected.  
I believed you were my greatest enemy only to find you were the only one defending me.  
I thought you meant to break me but you were the one who made me.

You cared for me longer than I have memory.  
You cried for me before I had fears of my own to cry about.  
Yet you still bore them. Even when I added to them.

passages.heading: Inherited
passages.text:
I’m not sorry for being young.  
I’m sorry for doubting your love when you never showed us contempt.

Now I see you.  
You were no older than I am now when you became a mother—  
just 19 facing the world with such courage.  
A caretaker. A protector. A dream builder in the dark.

I thank you for all the times you weren’t there dad because I needed you to be somewhere else.  
I thank you for the nights you slept because exhaustion was all you could muster.

You felt the pain deeper than I ever could as just a child.  
You bore it with honor.  
And now I grieve that suffering—the kind you never let me see,  
the kind I can only know now that it’s too late to unknow  
and the suffering ill never know because you spared me.

But here is what keeps me awake now:  
I see exactly why you had to leave.  
I see exactly why you had to yell.  
I understand the aftermath of survival.

passages.heading: Inherited
passages.text:
And I am standing at the threshold of becoming what you were,  
I know will make the same choices.  
I know will not be there when they need me.  
I will seem angry to gain obedience because sometimes cruelty is mercy.  
I will stretch myself thin in ways they cannot comprehend  
until they stand where I’m standing now,  
understanding everything,  
unable to change anything.

My children will feel what I felt.  
They will doubt me.  
They will grow into the terrible knowledge that I did the best 
but it was never enough.

And they will stand at their own threshold,  
terrified they’ll do the same.

The cycle doesn’t break.  
It just gets inherited with fuller sight.  
We see it coming and we cannot stop it.  
We only bear it with whatever honor we can find.

The bridge between childhood anger and adulthood understanding  
is learning that both things are true at once:  
You saved me.  
You hurt me.  
And I will do both to them.

passages.heading: Inherited
passages.text:
This is what clarity costs.  
This is what it means to grow up and become your parents,  
not despite understanding their pain,  
but because of it.

works.title: Was I Good Enough
works.blurb: Self-worth, loneliness, and family, a companion piece to "Am I Me Enough".

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
“Was I Good Enough”

I remember being young, sprawled across the couch,  
no fear in my body except the quiet tremor of my thoughts.  
I watched anime until the sky bruised purple,  
dodging deadlines, dodging myself,  
dodging the question humming under my ribs:  
Was I good enough?

I worried about my friends—  
if they liked me, if I mattered,  
if the girl on the playground  
ever saw me the way I rehearsed in my head.  
Funny how early doubt learns your name,  
how it follows you like a shadow  
that grows longer than your legs ever did.

I guess that’s the curse of a soft heart—  
to sit among friends  
and still feel set apart.  
Nights I begged for a call, any call,  
just to drown out the echo in my chest.  
A phone ringing in another room  
felt like someone else’s life calling me  
while mine stayed pressed  
beneath the weight of the question.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
I grew up measuring my worth  
by the noise I could pull from other people—  
a laugh, a text, a name spoken like a vow.  
I stayed awake for signs I wasn’t drifting  
too far to be found somehow.  
But most nights, it was only me, myself, and I—  
three shadows sharing one body,  
three voices asking why  
I still wasn’t enough for myself.

Some mornings we get along.  
I’ll make breakfast without rushing,  
choose fruit instead of skipping the meal,  
and for a moment we sit at the same table  
like three people learning how to feel  
without fear of failing.

Other days we argue in the mirror.  
Me wanting to slow down,  
myself replaying something someone said last week,  
I caught in the middle,  
trying to keep the peace  
between two versions of me  
who both believe they’re the one  
who wasn’t good enough.

Some nights we surprise each other—  
I’ll let a thought pass without chasing it,  
myself won’t turn a small mistake into a prophecy,  
and I will breathe like I’ve been practicing for years.  
Those are the nights we feel almost whole,  
almost clear,  
almost worthy.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
But there are still moments  
when one of us storms off inside my chest,  
slamming a door only I can hear.  
Moments when I fall back into old habits,  
Looking for someone else to fill the silence  
instead of sitting with the three of us  
and learning how to steer  
my own life.

Some days the sun hits my hands just right,  
warm enough to feel like someone holding me  
without asking for anything in return.  
It’s strange how a little light  
can feel like a memory of love  
I never fully got to earn—  
or thought I didn’t.

I think about the past more than I admit—  
the way my mom yelled when I was too young  
to understand she was drowning too,  
how my dad’s absence filled the cabinets  
but emptied the room,  
how my brother’s anger cracked the walls  
long before I learned it was pain  
trying to bloom  
in a house that didn’t know how.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
And I carried all of it,  
quietly,  
like a child holding a box too heavy  
but too proud to set down—  
as if endurance could answer the question  
no one ever asked me out loud.

But lately, something’s shifting.  
I feel it in the small things—  
the way the morning air forgives me,  
the way a soft breeze brushes my cheek  
like an apology I never asked for.  
I catch myself smiling at nothing,  
letting the sun warm my hands  
without comparing it to anyone else’s touch,  
as if warmth itself is proof  
I might be enough.

We don’t talk enough about the way  
a stupid coincidence can make you laugh  
harder than it deserves,  
how that tiny burst of joy  
can soften the sharpest nerves  
and remind you you’re still alive.

We forget to honor the moments  
when a sunrise catches us off guard,  
or a sunset paints the sky  
like it’s trying to mend what’s scarred.  
Those times we smile for no reason  
and feel our own heart warm in return—  
those are the moments that teach us  
what we once had to learn  
from someone else.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
Sure, I miss the warmth of a kiss,  
the safety of a hug,  
the feeling of someone choosing me  
without hesitation.  
But I found something quieter,  
something steadier than infatuation—  
a love that doesn’t leave  
when the room goes silent.

I found myself.  
Not in a self‑help,  
“love your flaws” kind of way,  
not in the watered‑down guru garbage  
that tries to sell healing like a trend.  
I mean the real thing—  
the kind of love that grows  
when you sit with yourself long enough  
to call yourself a friend  
and believe it.

I like my own company now.  
I trust it.  
Me and myself don’t leave  
when it gets heavy.  
We stay,  
we breathe,  
we laugh at nothing,  
we watch the sun rise and fall  
like it’s a show made just for us—  
steady, ready,  
finally enough.

I realized, in a life we may tell one or countless others  
that they are our whole world,  
that we’d choose them in every lifetime,  
that we’d die for them—  
and don’t get me wrong, I love that.  
But maybe we forget to ask  
if we’d do the same for ourselves.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
Would I choose me  
in every version of my life  
or only when I’m easy to love?  
Would I stand by myself  
when the room goes quiet,  
when the thoughts get loud,  
when the world feels too heavy  
for one pair of hands?

Maybe the real promise—  
the one no one teaches you to make—  
is learning to choose yourself  
with the same tenderness  
you once saved for everyone else.

And maybe that’s what love looks like now:  
not grand declarations,  
not dying for someone,  
but living with myself  
in a way that feels like choosing me  
every single time.

works.title: In Search Of Truth
works.blurb: Existentialist prose-poem on truth and self-deception.

passages.heading: In Search Of Truth
passages.text:
In Search Of Truth:  
Elijah W. Skinner

The lengths we go to chase our perceived truths often stretch beyond the reach of our own comprehension.  
We build scaffolds of belief— not to ascend toward reality, but to shield ourselves from its raw, unfiltered glare.  
In our hunger for clarity, we craft versions of truth that feel digestible, symmetrical, safe.  
Not because they are real, but because they are bearable.  
Factual reality: cold, indifferent, unyielding— demands surrender. 
But the mind, ever defiant, prefers a substitute: a truth softened by narrative, shaped by bias, stitched together with the thread of familiarity.  
We do not always seek what is true.  
We seek what can be held without burning our hands.  
There is a moment, quiet, unannounced— when the false truth begins to rot.  
Its symmetry cracks.  
Its safety suffocates.  
Its sweetness turns sour in the mouth.  
And reality begins to press in— not with force, but with the quiet weight of something that has been put off.  
To face it is not to conquer it.  
It is to kneel.  
To let it burn.  
To let it strip away the scaffolds until only the raw truth remains.  
This is not clarity.  
This is nakedness.  
When we lay ourselves barren we are able to be seen, and to see. 
This is the only place truth can be witnessed without illusion.  
This is not the end of seeking.  
It is the end of hiding.  
You no longer chase truth.  
You must live it.

works.title: The Unfamiliar
works.blurb: Growth and courage, written in second person.

passages.heading: The Unfamiliar
passages.text:
The Unfamiliar

To rise from the dust of the ordinary  
into the rare air of the extraordinary,  
one must step beyond the borders of the known,  
To know what can not be known.

The familiar is a warm cage-  
its bars invisible,  
its floor worn smooth by the pacing of your own feet.  
It will not harm you,  
but it’s fate is a hollow death.

The unfamiliar waits outside,  
its shape shifting in the half-light,  
its voice a language you have not yet learned.  
It will not promise safety,  
but it will promise change.

To ascend,  
you must open your arms to what unsettles you,  
let it press its strange weight into your skin,  
let it teach you the names of things  
you once feared to touch.

For only in the company of the unknown  
does the self shed its husk,  
and in that agonizing act of shedding the old 
the beginning of something new unfolds.

passages.heading: The Unfamiliar
passages.text:
And as you move into the heart of the unfamiliar,  
you will feel the ground tilt,  
the air sharpen,  
the horizon pull at your ribs.

This is how ascent begins—  
not with triumph,  
but with a single step taken  
before you feel ready.

Followed by the toil of beginning 
again and again 
with that experience forever more 
As it presses itself into you deeper

The extraordinary is built  
from moments like these.

And when you cross that trembling threshold,  
the world will not applaud.  
It will simply rearrange itself around you,  
as if it had been waiting  
for your arrival all along.

The sky will feel wider.  
Your breath will feel truer.  
And the person you once were  
will watch from a distance,  
grateful you did not stay with them.

works.title: The Knife I Chose
works.blurb: Betrayal and cyclical harm, written in third person.

passages.heading: The Knife I Chose
passages.text:
The Knife I Chose

The night swallows her footsteps,  
each one a drumbeat of fear against the hollow streets.  
Shadows stretch long and hungry,  
the evils of the world at her back,  
their breath cold on her neck.

She runs toward the only light she knows—  
a figure waiting in the dark,  
familiar, steady,  
a harbor she has clung to in storms before.  
Her chest heaves, her pulse a frantic hymn,  
and when she reaches him,  
she falls into his arms  
as though the world might finally loosen its grip.

But the embrace is not salvation.  
It is the moment the blade finds her—  
cold, precise,  
sliding between ribs with the intimacy of a whispered secret.  
Her heart clenches,  
not only from the steel,  
but from the truth that blooms with it:  
trust has teeth,  
and wolf’s don’t only hide beneath sheep’s skin

passages.heading: The Knife I Chose
passages.text:
Warmth spreads across her skin,  
thick and clinging,  
the metallic scent of betrayal rising with the steam of her breath.  
The night does not pause.  
The shadows do not retreat.  
And in that final clarity,  
she understands—  
the knife was always there,  
waiting in the arms she thought would save her.

The blade is still there,  
buried deep,  
its cold edge pulsing with her heartbeat.  
Each breath is a ragged thread,  
but she clings to it—  
not because she cannot pull away,  
but because the thought of facing the night alone  
is a greater terror than the steel in her chest.

The world’s evils still prowl beyond these arms,  
and here, at least,  
she knows the shape of the monster holding her.

Her hands rise, trembling,  
fingers brushing the jaw of her betrayer  
as though memorizing the lines of a face  
she has always known would end her.  
She draws him closer,  
their foreheads almost touching,  
and with the last breath she owns,  
she presses her lips to his—  
a kiss not of love,  
but of surrender to the only warmth left to her.

passages.heading: The Knife I Chose
passages.text:
Her body slackens,  
the weight of her falling into his grasp.  
Blood hums against her skin,  
sticky and slow,  
and yet a faint smile curves her lips—  
not joy,  
but the quiet relief  
of someone who has chosen  
the pain they understand  
over the darkness they do not.

And yet—  
she does not die.  
Not in body, at least.  
For this is not an ending,  
but an inheritance:  
a story older than memory,  
repeated like a sacred curse,  
etched into the laws of this world  
where love and ruin  
so often share the same embrace.

works.title: The Stripes Remain
works.blurb: Resilience and redemption, reads as a rebuttal to "The Knife I Chose".

passages.heading: The Stripes Remain
passages.text:
The Stripes Remain

She said, “A tiger can’t change its stripes.”  
She spoke it like a sentence passed,  
as if my flaws were carved into the marrow,  
as if my shadow was born of nothing but my own rot.  
And in that moment, I believed her.  
That was my first defeat.

I fell.  
Not once, but again and again,  
each failure a stone dragging me deeper.  
I learned the taste of ash,  
the weight of silence,  
the slow suffocation of being seen only as the sum of my sins.

But the trial did not end in the pit.  
It began there.  
I walked through fires that stripped the flesh from my pride.  
I descended into depths where the air itself conspired to crush me.  
And in those depths, I did not die.  
I endured.  
I endured until endurance became my crown.

passages.heading: The Stripes Remain
passages.text:
When I rose, it was not as the man she left behind.  
The stripes remained,  
but they were no longer her prophecy.  
They were my regalia —  
marks of survival,  
sigils of the battles I had bled through.

Now I stand above the ruins,  
not cleansed,  
but sovereign.  
Not forgiven,  
but unbroken.  
The throne I claim is carved from the bones of my trials,  
and the crown I wear was forged in the heat of my own damnation.

She will never see the man I became.  
And that is my final triumph —  
for the one who swore I could never change  
will never know how high I have risen.

works.title: For My Papa
works.blurb: Grief and legacy, a companion piece to "Growing Up".

passages.heading: For My Papa
passages.text:
For My Papa

I would be dishonest if I said my heart wasn’t heavy.  
The pain of his passing is a burden—  
but it’s a burden I will gladly carry,  
because it is the weight of love,  
and the blessings of his memory.

My papa, more than anyone else,  
taught me that when you love someone,  
you accept that there will be pain.  
For better and for worse—  
those words should never be confined to wedding vows.  
They are a way of living,  
a testament to the choice to love,  
to care,  
to stand beside someone no matter the season.

No one embodied that more than my grandparents.  
Their love overflowed into the branches of the family tree they built.  
Many of us here today would not be here  
if not for the commitment they showed.  
They are the roots of a great oak,  
digging deep into the mantle of the earth,  
holding us steady in a world of shifting ground.  
Even now, with his passing,  
he holds us strong.  
His memory will live forever in all of us.

passages.heading: For My Papa
passages.text:
People say not to judge a book by its cover—  
and the same is true of life.  
My grandfather was born in 1949,  
and today, as we close his casket,  
the story of his life does not end.  
The chapters remain with us—  
in the way we speak,  
in the way we love,  
in the way we carry ourselves through this world.

Though we have lost his presence,  
we have not lost him.  
He is woven into us,  
a golden thread running through the fabric of our lives.  
And as long as we live,  
his story will never close.

works.title: Darkness
works.blurb: Cycles of violence and retaliation resolving toward forgiveness.

passages.heading: Darkness
passages.text:
Darkness

To answer shadow with shadow  
is to feed the very night you wish to end.  
Strike for strike, wound for wound—  
the cycle closes in,  
a serpent devouring its own tail.

Darkness does not starve  
when given more of itself.  
It swells,  
it thickens,  
it learns your name.

Only those who have walked its corridors  
and felt its cold breath on their skin  
can choose to turn,  
to lift a lantern instead of a blade.

Light is not the absence of shadow—  
it is the defiance of it.  
It is the hand that refuses to strike,  
the voice that refuses to echo hate.

And when light is offered  
where darkness once reigned,  
the night does not vanish—  
but it begins to retreat,  
step by reluctant step,  
until the horizon remembers the sun.

works.title: Past, Present, and Future
works.blurb: Self-transformation and groundedness.

passages.heading: Past, Present, and Future
passages.text:
Past, Present, and Future

I am but a vessel —  
neither shackled to the ruins of my past  
nor tethered to the mirage of my future.  
Behold the fragments of who I was,  
woven with the tender threads of what I am becoming.  
Like all living things,  
I am caught in the endless turning of metamorphosis —  
never still, never finished,  
forever shedding, forever forming.

The path beneath your feet  
is the loom upon which your destiny is woven.  
Stand tall, with the poise of one who knows their own weight,  
and let no misstep cloud the horizon of your sight.  
Sink your roots deep into the soil of your being,  
for without knowing yourself,  
you risk becoming a ghost  
wandering through the corridors of your own life.

A flower, though radiant, cannot still the hunger in our bellies.  
If all the world’s flora were only petals,  
our bodies would starve.  
Yet if every plant were only sustenance,  
stripped of beauty,  
our spirits would wither.  
So it is with humanity:  
if all were teachers,  
wisdom would smother joy;  
if all sought only comfort,  
our minds would dull,  
and our days would pass like smoke.

passages.heading: Past, Present, and Future
passages.text:
Every taking demands its recompense.  
Nothing in this world comes without a price.  
The natural order knows this well —  
even the plants, breathing in the air,  
return it as oxygen,  
a quiet covenant with all who live.

What some call flaws,  
others name beauty —  
like a weed in a garden  
that refuses to bow to the gardener’s design.  
So too with us:  
if our worth is unseen,  
perhaps it is not we who are lacking,  
but the garden itself  
that fails to recognize  
the rare bloom in its midst.

works.title: Love
works.blurb: Childhood trauma and distrust within family.

passages.heading: Love
passages.text:
Love

I never pray for love.  
Why would I?  
I grew up in a house where love was sharpened,  
where it glinted in the light like something beautiful  
until you felt it slide between your ribs.

In that place, love was not a gift—  
it was a lesson,  
a rulebook written in invisible ink  
that only appeared when you broke it.  
I learned early that love was never unconditional,  
only conditioned—  
a currency you earned by obedience,  
by silence,  
by swallowing the truth whole and smiling as it burned.

I was conditioned to love my mother  
because that was the role assigned to me,  
because the world said  
a child must love the woman who bore them.  
But her hugs were snares,  
closing around me with the soft weight of a trap.  
Even as her arms wrapped tight,  
my body remembered  
what her hands had done before,  
and I felt myself recoil,  
a shadow pulling back from the flame.

passages.heading: Love
passages.text:
I was conditioned to love my father  
because his wallet was always open,  
but his heart stayed locked.  
He gave in bills and coins,  
in gifts that glittered but never warmed.  
Even his embraces came with a price tag,  
the paper rasping against my soul,  
reminding me that nothing he gave  
was ever truly free.

So I learned to keep love at a distance.  
To build a moat around my heart  
and salt the earth between myself and anyone  
who might try to cross.  
Because no one I love can wound me  
if I wound myself first—  
if I lay the blade to my own skin  
before they ever get the chance.

And maybe that is the truest thing I know about love:  
that for me,  
it has always been a shadow  
I watch from across the room,  
never daring to step close enough  
to see if it might be warm.

works.title: From Ashes to Ascendancy
works.blurb: Childhood abuse recast as resilience and reclamation.

passages.heading: From Ashes to Ascendancy
passages.text:
### I. The Seeds of Burden  
At eight, a weight of sorrow pressed on tender frame,  
The world dismissed my worth and cloaked me in its shame.  
A teacher’s scorn declared that I was trouble in a guise,  
Yet lonely halls became my strength, where silent hope would rise.

They threatened, “Stop your tears or face a harsher fate,”    
But every sequestered tear forged courage over hate.  
With honors bright as beacons and diplomas to defy  
The twisted words they threw at me, I soared from every lie.

---

### II. The Tower of Silence  
Before me loomed the giants—monsters cloaked in human guise,  
Whose vile, forbidden acts stole trust and dimmed the skies.  
In that crushing, fateful moment, innocence was torn apart,  
Transforming dreams of gentle grace into chains upon my heart.

passages.heading: From Ashes to Ascendancy
passages.text:
Their breach of sacred boundaries etched a scar I can’t ignore,  
Yet even in that darkest hour, from pain I learned to soar.  
Though shadows linger long in echoes of the acts they wove,  
I lit a flame of inner strength no terror can remove.

---

### III. The Stolen Narrative  
They penned a tale in twisted ink, a story not my own,  
Distorting truth with crafted lies until my voice was overthrown.  
Voices rose to mute my plea, to cage the truth inside,
