Yet from the silence of that theft, a rebel soul replied.

I reclaimed each stolen line and reshaped every wounded part,  
Transforming manufactured history into a testament of heart.  
No puppet strings of false accounts can bind what is set free—  
I own my truth, my scars, and now I write my destiny.

---

### IV. The Shield of the Moment  
In storms of doubt and bitter trials, I stand a fortress strong,  
Holding back the ghosts of past, rejecting every wrong.  
With every steady heartbeat, I summon fierce and steady power,  
Defying threats and bitter voices with a spirit that won’t cower.

passages.heading: From Ashes to Ascendancy
passages.text:
I arm myself with memories turned into badges of my fight,  
Each step a rhythmic anthem carved in defiant, pulsing light.  
The silence after all their venom bursts with victories untold—  
In reclaiming all I once had lost, I transmute the dark to gold.

---

### V. Epilogue – Rising in Resilience  
Those hollow words that bound with “I love you, but” like chains,  
Could never root in a resolve that triumphs over pains.  
The blaze of hate and anguish that scorched my tender days  
Now fuels a vibrant courage, igniting ever-brighter rays.

Today, my eyes hold embers that no threat can disbelieve,  
For I rise each day unbroken—a phoenix born to weave  
A life of raw resistance, a story fiercely self-made.  
A survivor’s truth affirmed in every step and every shade.

works.title: A Crown Without a Kingdom
works.blurb: Mortality and the impermanence of ambition, argued in a generalized voice rather than confessional first-person.

passages.heading: A Crown Without a Kingdom
passages.text:
A crown without a kingdom

We are not the architects of our fate. 
We are the sculptors of a stone we did not choose. 
Its grain was set before our first breath— its flaws, its fractures, its hidden veins of weakness.

Every strike of the chisel is not creation… it is revelation.

Whether born in the filth of the gutter or the halls of kings, all men are bound to the same laws: Time is finite, but the map stretches on without end, and yet the hunger for completion is never sated.

The pauper who climbs finds the summit barren; the noble who inherits finds the air thin.

Both learn the same truth— the game was never meant to be won.  
There is no finish line… only death.

Contrast gives this world its form. Sweetness is born of bitterness.  
Light is crowned by shadow.  
Value exists only in the presence of its opposite. 
And a blank canvas is not void—its value emerges from your actions.

passages.heading: A Crown Without a Kingdom
passages.text:
Time is the salt that makes the feast worth tasting. 
Without it, there is no urgency. No weight. No worth.

This design is deliberate; no final quest, No ultimate reward. 
Only the eternal cycle—acquire, decay, replace.

Every man dies, but few will learn to live.

When he departs this world, his followers will gather. 
His work will remain—unfinished, unresolved. 
But this… this is not tragedy. 
It is inevitability.

What greater ending than this: To know that those who loved you will carry forward your final chapters.  
When your quill slows… and falls…  
theirs will rise, and the writing will begin anew.

So I say this: do not seek to conquer the world, do not dream of the crown, for all of this is vain. 
Carve your stone knowing it will never be complete, revel in every moment, breathe, and result of your actions.

March knowing the road has no end. For the game is not meant to be won… it was meant to live, to love, and do it again all before Time runs out.

works.title: How It Is
works.blurb: Poverty, inequality, and indifference.

passages.heading: How It Is
passages.text:
How It Is

The first homeless man I ever saw  
His clothes, brittle as the wind, clung to him like a second skin  
My parents whispered he didn’t work hard enough—that he had earned his place beneath the overpass  
I nodded, believing I’d never be like that  
I saw the world exactly as I was told it was

Most of what I saw pressed against my ribs, heavy

Poverty—sprawled in quiet corners, invisible until you learned to see it  
Hardship—etched into the backs of hands, into the cracks of worn soles  
Hunger—lean and hollow, curling around ribs like a slow, patient fire  
Overdose—bodies turned to stillness, faces emptied of time  
Pain—woven into the fabric of existence, stitched into shadows

I asked why people would choose this  
Why they would drift instead of stand, break instead of build

passages.heading: How It Is
passages.text:
Years passed, and I learned:  
“How it is” isn’t how it has to be

No one had to starve  
No one had to suffer  
No one had to taste the bitterness of being forgotten

So why?

passages.heading: Because that’s just the way it is
passages.text:
I watched the world forget,  
watched people step over suffering like cracks in the sidewalk,  
like it wasn’t worth bending down to acknowledge.

They whispered reasons under their breath—  
*They should have tried harder.*  
*They must have done something wrong.*  
*You can’t save everyone.*

Their voices curled into silence,  
settling into the empty spaces between convenience and indifference.

I saw them turn their heads at hunger,  
walk faster past the hollow-eyed ghosts of the system’s failure,  
tighten their grips on purses and convictions,  
because sympathy costs too much.

I asked why—  
why the world carries wealth in its pockets but lets children starve,  
why comfort is built on the backs of the broken,  
why suffering is the price of stability.

Years passed, and I learned:  
It isn’t just “how it is.”  
It’s how we allow it to be.

No one had to turn away.  
No one had to forget.  
No one had to accept pain as collateral for progress.

passages.heading: Because that’s just the way it is
passages.text:
So why?

Because it’s easier than change.

I watched them feast,  
watched their tables bend beneath the weight of their indulgence,  
watched them drink until their laughter slurred,  
until hunger became a rumor,  
until excess rotted inside them, turning their stomachs sick with privilege.

They carved the world into portions,  
sold the sky in parcels,  
hoarded the sun in bank vaults,  
turned land into numbers, lives into assets,  
until nothing was untouched by price.

Their children never hungered, never reached, never wondered.  
They lived on money they never earned,  
slept in beds they never built,  
walked streets where no footstep before them was truly their own.

With nothing to strive for, they found misery in luxury,  
crafted suffering from silk sheets and golden halls,  
called it *ennui*, called it *emptiness*,  
never once tasted the bitterness of having nothing.

I asked why—  
why wealth could grow but never fill,  
why abundance could rot but never nourish,  
why they ate the world only to leave it hollow.

passages.heading: Because that’s just the way it is
passages.text:
Years passed, and I learned:  
It isn’t just “how it is.”  
It’s how it was bought to be.

works.title: My Wish
works.blurb: Authenticity, self-acceptance, and autonomy.

passages.heading: My Wish
passages.text:
My wish

My wish is not for material worries.  
I do not beg for gold.  
I do not wish to never grow old.  
My wish is not wealth like winter flurries.

My wish is not for love never-ending.  
I do not groan for fable.  
I do not grovel for a seat at the table.  
My wish is not for a will unbending.

No my wish is to be me.  
Not better or worse.  
Not to live with remorse.  
My wish is to be.

My wish is to be me.  
No matter who it angers.  
No matter the strangers.  
My wish is to be, who ever the fuck that my be.

works.title: The Sun's Bright Light
works.blurb: Gratitude and vitality through nature imagery.

passages.heading: The Sun's Bright Light
passages.text:
The sun's bright light, a golden hue,  
Forever young, yet ancient too.  
Its beams stretch wide from corner to ledge,  
With my eye I see the sky, where azure sings and pledges.  
As it draws near, its glow is clear,  
A gentle warmth that I hold dear.  
I recall what I've always known—  
Like a tree in December, its light has shone.  
For it is life, and it gives us breath,  
A radiant gift that conquers death.

works.title: Taking All From the Rich
works.blurb: Satirical critique of wealth inequality, argued rather than confessed.

passages.heading: Taking All From the Rich
passages.text:
Taking all from the rich, to give to the poor  
Is the same as taking from the poor, to give the rich more.  
The world doesn’t need another Robin Hood,  
Just someone who’s willing to do something good.

For though King John wore the villain's crown,  
Two wrongs can’t make a right; they just drag us down.  
In the end, it’s a dirge we all must face,  
A cycle of heartache in an endless race.

works.title: Today's Wine
works.blurb: Impermanence and present-moment mindfulness.

passages.heading: Todays Wine
passages.text:
Todays Wine

Today's wine is particularly fine,  
Exquisitely crafted, a true divine.

For yesterday's wine has slipped from our grasp,  
Its taste lingers sweet, but it doth not last

And tomorrow's wine has yet to delight,  
For it’s future’s promise, not here in our sight.

Today’s wine is ours, to savor and share,  
Though it may not be perfect, it’s still worth a care.  
Remember, not all things are destined to last,  
For memories linger, but they are the past.

Embrace the present, let your spirit flow,  
For today is a gift; in this moment, we grow.

works.title: The Daybook of Crumb's Ovens
works.blurb: Tamsin Crumb's daybook for Saturday 21 October 1893, room by room through the four back rooms of Crumb's Ovens, with one sack and the sweepings, three dead, the island's arithmetic of loaves and the unsigned papers she folds into the bread.

passages.heading: I. The cold room. The island's hour.
passages.text:
Up before anyone.

The cold room has a door to the shop, a shelf for the crock, a gap behind the crock where a hand can go, and a place where I am found out. This morning that place is the flour bin. One sack and the sweepings. No flour came Friday. None will come today.

Recipe: one spoon of yesterday, one cup of flour, water to the second knuckle. Stir on the island's hour, not the mainland's. The clock on the wall is the Company's. The crock keeps the other one.

I feed the crock. I feed the town. I feed the dead.

Three nights now, they say, since Aldous Vane. The wire said it, or the square did. I could not tell you which, and nobody in this town would think to ask me. I did not cry. I fed the crock at the hour, and the crock rose, and I took that for an answer, because it was the only one I was given.

passages.heading: I. The cold room. The island's hour.
passages.text:
People used to ask whether I came inland for him or for the cup. I still do not know. I know the spoon. I know the hour. I know that what rises in this crock is the cup's life and not the cup, and that the cup went where he went.

Who feeds the cup now?

passages.heading: II. The mixing room. Four.
passages.text:
I don't know. That is the first thing I knead into the dough every morning: I don't know.

Recipe for a Rumour Loaf: flour, water, salt, a fist of the daughter, and one folded paper. Fold the paper twice. Lay it flat under the fold of the dough. Shape it tight so nothing shows at the seam.

The papers come to me unsigned. Under a coin on the counter. Under the door before light. Once, inside a glove someone handed back across the counter. I have never written one. I have folded every one.

I do not read them. I read them. I bake them anyway.

This week the slips go to the Tribunal, and a day is all it takes to harden a rumour into an indictment, and the gallows stands at the Bell. I cannot tell you whether any paper that passed through my hands ever reached the trapdoor. I can tell you I did not ask.

passages.heading: II. The mixing room. Four.
passages.text:
This morning I cut into a loaf I shaped last night, to test the crumb, and there was a paper in it already. Folded twice. Laid flat. Not mine. It could have been a customer's hand reaching over the bench while my back was turned. It could have been the boy who carries the baskets. It could have been my own hands, tired past remembering. I write all three down and I choose none.

If I do not know what I carry, am I innocent of it?

passages.heading: III. The oven room. Five.
passages.text:
The oven answers that, the way it answers everything: no.

The oven is clay. Vane's men built it behind the tents before there was a town to put it in, and the town grew up around it like a crust. Recipe: fire it till the walls go white. Rake it. Swab it. Bake out yesterday's proof. Do not open the door to look.

On Thursday night, or Wednesday (the week runs together now), someone emptied the till. They left a gold coin on the hearth-lip, the way you tip for good bread. They left a boot in the flour dust, long in the stride, the toe toward the back door.

I swept it.

I sweep every night. That is my alibi, and it is theirs. The Detective came with his case file the next noon and asked whether anything was out of place. I said the floor was clean, and that was true.

passages.heading: III. The oven room. Five.
passages.text:
I cannot spend the coin. Gold asks where it came from. So it sits behind the crock, in the place a hand can go.

Up before anyone, and still somebody was here first.

What is a gold coin worth in a town where flour comes by train, and the train brought none?

passages.heading: IV. The proofing room. Before the train.
passages.text:
Less than a sack of flour. Exactly what I did next.

The proofing room is the only room in this house that belongs to tomorrow. Recipe: shape, cover, set in the cold, and leave it alone to become what it is going to be.

Three dead. Dora Finch. Wilf. Percy. One loaf to every mourner and three to each of the dead. That is the island's arithmetic, four hundred years old, and I have one sack and the sweepings.

The Company recognises no custom of mourning, the Articles say, and then they tolerate my table and write: "No rent shall be assessed on the three loaves set for the dead". The bread of the dead is the only bread in HollowMere the Company takes no cut of.

But who is the bread for?

This part is mine, and nobody else's. I cut the mourners' loaves to halves. Every living mouth at that table will get half, so that every dead one keeps three. Nobody ordered it. Nobody will thank me for it. I did it with the scraper in one stroke, the way you do a thing you have already decided.

passages.heading: IV. The proofing room. Before the train.
passages.text:
And there is more. On my way in, before the crock, I went to the stone with tomorrow's date, as I have gone every morning this week, and read the new name on it. I have not written that name in this book. I will not write it here.

But three more loaves are proving under the cloth at the end of the bench, made from the living's flour, and they are not for Dora, or Wilf, or Percy.

Did I bake for a death, or does a death come to be baked for? Nobody has seen the name cut. Nobody has seen me shape these.

Is it grief, done early, or an order filled?

passages.heading: V. The wake table. Station Rush.
passages.text:
I do not answer. I set the table.

Ten plates. Three for the dead, three loaves to each. Six for the halves, heaped. The tenth I set for whoever remains, and leave.

I know who bought which loaf. That is the whole of my office.

Dora Finch bought the end of the rye and held the seal up close to read it, through spectacles mended with thread, as if a crumb could have writing on it. Wilf paid for a heel once in the key of G, on my step, because he had no scrip and I had no mind to refuse a tune. Percy came in with three marbles and his bootlace undone and asked every time whether the dead ones were for eating, and every time I said, not by you.

I press a crumb into each loaf and seal it in candle wax, white on the dark crust. Every mouth that eats carries off a small hard piece of who is gone.

passages.heading: V. The wake table. Station Rush.
passages.text:
At the rush the Undertaker's boy comes in with his cap in his hands. Four, he says. Make it four. I ask him four for whom. He looks at his paper and says the paper says four. I count the dead I know of and get three, and the numbers will not lie down together. I do not bake it. I do not refuse it. I look at the tenth plate, already set.

The mourners sit. They eat the halves. Nobody says the loaves are small. Nobody has to.

Up before anyone, flour to the elbows, and the dead fed first.

The island taught me to feed the dead. HollowMere taught me who goes hungry for it.

works.title: Hopscotch
works.blurb: the counting rhyme chalked under the lantern on the square: ten squares, ten children with grown-up names, a stanza each for a landmark of HollowMere, and a refrain about hopping the stone and not looking down.

passages.heading: chalked under the lantern on the square
passages.text:
One for the bell, and the bell brings the town.
Alfie counted the gallows stairs: thirteen up, and none come down.
Alfie climbed in a crate on the morning train.
The crate went east. It never wrote.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Two for the pump, two hands on the iron.
Nell pumped first and Nell drank first.
Fever by Friday. Ribbons, blue.
Nell rode the back car east.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Three for the lantern we chalk it under.
It keeps the wolves off. It keeps us in.
Sid chased his shadow to where the light stops.
Where does the light stop?
Sid knew. His cap's on the fence.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Four for the Lantern, sign and all.
The barman carried it into the mere.
Flo swept the floor for a penny a night
and finished the cups when Mrs Grieves wasn't looking.
Something in a cup was not sugar.
Flo's broom is still by the door.

passages.heading: chalked under the lantern on the square
passages.text:
*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Five for the oven, up before light,
ten plates on the wake table, laid out right.
Peg stole the heel off every loaf.
One for each mourner and three for the dead:
three on Peg's plate,
and nobody took the heel.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Six for the manor, where the clock stopped
at eleven forty-seven and stayed.
Ted wound his gran's clock every night
and told the time by the train.
Rent comes due when the sun's straight up.
Ted went to the mill to pay it with his hands.
He's at the loft window. He doesn't wave.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Seven for the well, and the ladder down.
Winnie dropped pebbles and counted the splash.
Winnie threw her stone and the stone went in.
Winnie went down the ladder to fetch it.
We counted for her.
We are counting still.

passages.heading: chalked under the lantern on the square
passages.text:
*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Eight for the chapel and the Company bell.
Lil sang loudest, always a beat ahead.
Lil went up to the rope to ring it in.
The hymn came out one voice short.
There's a glove in the rope.
Nobody says whose.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Nine for the pines, and the pines aren't empty.
May was scared of the dark,
so May walked toward every light.
There was a light in the fen. May walked.
Who's holding the lantern out there in the fen?

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Who chalks it fresh when we're all in bed?

But the tenth square isn't chalk.

Ten for the stone with tomorrow's name.
I hopped every one of them. That's the rule:
you never land where the stone is lying.
Alfie. Nell. Sid. Flo. Peg.
Ted. Winnie. Lil. May.
I hid. I watched. I remember.
I can read. I read it.
I won't read it out.

passages.heading: chalked under the lantern on the square
passages.text:
*Ten chalk squares and one of me.*
  *Throw your stone. It's your turn now.*

Nobody's out in HollowMere.
Everybody's next.

works.title: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
works.blurb: a triptych for the three world-state figures: a widower at Hale Barn prayed over by both faiths who takes up the rusted fork, a man the Line owes eleven weeks riding as freight and reading the Baron's manifest, and a town waiting on a train that stopped sending flour, each doing a sum that does not come out.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
## I. The Apostate. Hale Barn, and the Bell.

The fork is rusted. I know why. I left it out in the wet the week she coughed, and nobody has forked hay since. Rust is what iron grows when nobody asks it for anything.

She talked to the goat as if the goat kept the accounts. She was not afraid of the pelt on the door; a wolf that has already lost, she said, can't hurt anybody. She prayed every night and never told me to whom. I thought there would be time to ask. The fen-cough came up out of the fog in October, and it did not leave time. It left the barn, and me, and the goat, and the goat has kept no accounts since.

Then they came. Not before. After.

One came by day with a candle. He was new off the train, his collar still white from back east, and he told me everyone in this town comes to him to confess sooner or later, and he could wait. One came by night with ash. I never saw a face. I saw what was left on my door in the morning, under the pelt: a mark in ash and something darker, still wet at the edges.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
They prayed for my soul. They prayed for my vote at the Bell. They prayed for my hands, which are strong, and which a man in my state might put to anything. They prayed over me in the lane, and in the chapel porch, and on my own step, and each side prayed louder when it found the other had been there first.

Not one of them prayed for her bread. Not one of them prayed for her breath. Where was either of them the week she coughed?

I couldn't put that question down. So I put down everything else.

I took the fork off the wall. I scraped their mark off my door with the tines until the wood came up pale. I walked to St Brannock's with the fork on my shoulder and put out his candle in the porch with the haft. One stroke for each of them. Fair. The first fair thing done in that barn since October.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
Now they pray against me, both of them. They cross the lane when I carry the fork, and I carry it everywhere. I stand at the Bell with it, and nobody asks me to put it down, and nobody asks me what it's for. There's talk at the Lantern that if anyone ever puts the new man in the ground, he'll come back tenfold. Talk. If it's true, that's ten more of him praying at me.

Whichever church takes this town, both will have prayed over me once, and I will have the rust to prove I never answered.

I was owed one god. I was sent two, and neither one brought bread.

## II. The Stowaway. A crate stencilled for Thorne Junction.

The platform lantern is lit. She lights it first; she always lights it first. Through the slats I can read the sheet clipped to the car door, if I keep my eye to the gap and my breath slow.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
I read what goes. I read what comes. I read what a town is worth.

The Line owed me eleven weeks. I laid its ties out past Thorne Junction before the banks went, and when the banks went the paymaster went with them, and nobody wrote down where. If they wouldn't carry me as a man, I'd ride as cargo. Cargo gets where it's going. Cargo gets counted.

Flour comes in ninety-eight-pound sacks. I weigh less than two of them now. What is a man worth by the pound?

I came in under the bakery's flour, on the Wednesday. I ate it in the dark, raw, a fist at a time, paste on my tongue. I ate this town's bread before it was ever bread. I didn't think of that then. I think of it now, every morning, at the hour the ovens ought to smell of something and don't.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
They found me with the Baron's freight manifest in my hand. They put me off at the Siding, by the rule, and I walked the last of it through Gallows Wood with something in the pines keeping pace and never coming closer.

But I had read it. And I kept reading, every morning after, over a porter's shoulder on the platform, all the way down.

Flour: six, six, six, five. Then a word where the number should be. *Cancelled.* Powder: two, two, two, three, six. Lead: three, three, three, four, eight. No flour. Twice the powder.

I'm no ledger-man. I can't tell you what a Baron means by anything. I can tell you what two columns mean when one goes down and the other goes up in the same week, in the same car, under the same lamp.

Who reads a manifest and doesn't learn the town's price?

Tonight the sheet is outbound. Car 3. *Coffin, outbound. Coffin, outbound. Coffin, outbound.* The remarks column says what each of them is taking along, a small thing apiece, the thing they'd have reached for. Nobody's remark says bread.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
I'm riding east with them. I'm owed a fare, and eleven weeks, and my name on a pay sheet somewhere back east. I've paid my way in the only coin they don't print: the dark, holding still, among the dead.

A man who rides as freight learns what he weighs. A town that waits on freight learns what it's worth.

## III. The Starving. The square, the wake table, the Bell.

We were told: if you want to eat, you wait for the train. We were told, and we waited, and we were good at waiting. Waiting was the one thing in HollowMere the Company never charged rent on.

The first time, it was one Friday. One word on the sheet. One sack and the sweepings at Crumb's, and the mourners' loaves halved so the dead could still have theirs. Then, on the Monday, the sacks came back. Six of them, white on the platform, like a promise kept.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
That was the cruelty. It came back once. It taught us to keep waiting.

Now the sheet says nothing where the flour should be, and we have stopped asking.

The rent still comes at midday. The scrip goes three to the dollar, then four, then five. The wake table still has ten plates. The wolves come closer to the fence, because wolves can count too. Somebody leaves gold at the bakery for bread there isn't, and we have learned you cannot chew gold. A woman stands on a box at the Bell and says what we are all thinking, louder. A man stands near her with a rusted fork, and nobody prays for him now. A crate goes out at dusk heavier than it came in.

We were calm. Then we were frightened. We have said the next word once before, and the Baron came down off the train behind his dogs. We can feel it in our mouths again, where the bread should be.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
Mothers chew the crust first and hand it over soft. A child counts the crumbs on the board before she lets anyone sweep them. The tinners eat with their caps on, the way the dark taught them, as if the roof might come in on supper. Nobody here is a lesson. Everybody here is hungry in their own way, and that is the last thing still ours.

What is a company town when the company stops sending the town?

Agnes reads the stone to the Row at dawn now, before anyone looks at the board. We used to ask whose name. Now we ask whether there will be loaves enough for the wake.

We were owed the train. We were the bargain, and we kept our half. We are the line that isn't on the manifest.

The plate on the wake table at dawn is who we are. And the plate is empty.

passages.heading: The Apostate, the Stowaway, the Starving
passages.text:
One was owed a god. One was owed a fare. We were owed bread.

Nobody came to pay. Everybody came to count.

What you are owed and what you are sent: the difference is the town.

works.title: Resin-Seal
works.pov: first-person (Rev. Elias Moss; then his collar; then the Pack)
works.blurb: the camp chaplain Rev. Elias Moss blesses men at the gate with their names and writes them up on Fridays, dies at the hollow pine on 3 November 1952 asking a man for his name, and his collar tells how the blessing goes on at the gate from 10 November in numbers, while the Pack answers him and the Howl comes on the full moon of 1 December.

passages.heading: Resin-Seal
passages.text:
```
CHAPEL HUT — STORES ISSUE
ITEM ............ RESIN, PINE, 1 TIN
ISSUED TO ....... CHAPLAIN (CIV.)
PURPOSE ......... MORALE
CHARGED TO ...... ████████ LIAISON
```

## I. The Chaplain. The gate, Mon 6 Oct to Mon 3 Nov.

The gate says PRODUCTION IS OBLIGATION. I stand under it at six with a tin of pitch and a cold thumb. The ridge gang comes through in twos, on its way up Widow-Maker Ridge, and I bless them.

The tin was my father's. He kept a church I will not name here, because this place takes the names of things and does not give them back. The pitch goes on the brow in one stroke of the thumb, the way he taught me, and I say what he said:

*Pitch on the brow. Pine at your back. The Lord on the ridge. Go up a man. Come down a man. Keep the wild out of the mind.*

passages.heading: Resin-Seal
passages.text:
That is the blessing as the guards hear it. It is not the whole of it.

The camp gives me numbers, stencilled on a jacket and burned into a billet. It does not give me names, so I take them, one a morning. I learn one true thing about a man. The next morning I put his name inside the blessing, between *go up a man* and *come down a man*, low, under the wind, where the guard at the post hears only an old preacher mumbling. I will not write their names here either. Each was said once, into the pitch, and that is where they are kept.

I bless the man who whistles through a broken tooth and stops when the dogs look up.
I bless the man who keeps a bootlace from home in his cap and has no boots it fits.
I bless the man who will not tell me his name, because the last man who asked for it wrote it down.

passages.heading: Resin-Seal
passages.text:
He was right not to. I wrote things down.

Every Friday there is a form called a Pastoral Return. It has a carbon, and a letterhead somebody has inked over before it reaches me. *Spiritual condition of personnel. Attendance. Remarks.* I filled it in every Friday, in my good hand: who prays, who has stopped, who cries in the wash line where he thinks the water covers it. I told myself the paper was the price of the gate, the gate was the price of the names, and the names were the price of my sleeping. Do you see how a ledger balances, if you let it?

One morning in October a man flinched at the pitch. He was not flinching at me. He flinched at the tin coming toward his face, as if it were a lamp held too close. That Friday I wrote one word beside his number: *unsettled.* The next week his number walked out past the woodshed at night between two guards, toward the hollow pine. He came back in the morning and stood his roll. He came back every morning after that, thinner each time, the way a stair wears down. First his belt went in a notch. Then his cheeks went in. Then his wrists were rope. By the end of the month his knuckles were white as chalk, and he ate at the mess table like a man who could not get to the bottom of the plate.

passages.heading: Resin-Seal
passages.text:
Did my word walk him out there? Or was he already walking, and my word only kept step with him? I have asked it every night since. Nobody at that office answers a chaplain's questions. They only take his answers.

What does pitch keep out, if the gate let it in? Whose mind was I keeping the wild out of, his or mine?

On Monday the third of November he came through the gate last. This time he leaned in to the thumb, and he asked me to say his name. I did not know it. In four weeks of mornings I had learned that he hums in the wash line and never takes a lamp into the dark. I had not learned his name. So I said his number. I will not write it. I have written enough numbers down. He said *amen* before I had finished. I never heard a man say it so like a door closing.

passages.heading: Resin-Seal
passages.text:
I have one more Return to write, and I will not write it. Tonight I will go out to the hollow pine and give him the only true one: *I wrote you down. I am sorry. Tell me your name.*

I gave them their names back one morning at a time, and every Friday I gave their words to a man with a pen. I was a good shepherd. I was a good shepherd to the ledger.

passages.heading: II. Roster. Tue 4 Nov.
passages.text:
```
STAFF ROSTER — CIVILIAN — TUE 4 NOV 1952
CHAPLAIN (CIV.) ......... not at work for reasons of religion

CHAPEL HUT — INVENTORY
RESIN, PINE, 1 TIN ...... present
COLLAR, CLERICAL, 1 ..... not found
ACTION .................. none required
```

## III. The Collar. The woods, the night of Mon 3 Nov. The gate, from Mon 10 Nov.

I am linen and starch, and I was his for thirty years. I know a throat. I knew his. It swallowed on Fridays when he wrote the Return. It went still when he said *Lord* and meant it, and it went still less often than you would think.

On the night of the third he did not take me off. He always hung me on the nail. That night he wore me out past the woodshed, past the kilns, into the cold by the hollow pine. The cold there is wrong. It is colder under the boughs than out on the open snow, the way a cellar is colder than the yard.

passages.heading: II. Roster. Tue 4 Nov.
passages.text:
He found the man sitting against the pine with his knees up, the way a boy sits.

I tell you what I was on. The Reverend's pulse, quick. His breath, short. His throat working on the words he had carried out there: *I wrote you down. I am sorry. Tell me your name.*

The man said his number.

So the Reverend opened the tin and blessed him. Pitch on a brow that was mostly bone. He blessed him in the dark, with nobody to report it to. I want that written somewhere that is not a form.

Then he did what he had never once done. He put his own name inside the blessing, for himself: *Go up a man, Elias. Come down a man.*

Then the breath on me that was not his. Hot, in that cold.
Then the jaw.
Then my starch went soft and red, and his pulse under me ran fast, then slow, then nothing, and the nothing was so cold.

passages.heading: II. Roster. Tue 4 Nov.
passages.text:
I was taken off him in the morning. I was not folded.

Now I am on someone else.

This throat runs hot in the frost.
This throat swallows before *amen*, the way a man swallows who learned the word under a lamp while someone wrote it down.
This throat has a pulse as slow as something sleeping out the winter, and it does not quicken when the dogs go by.

The skin of it is drawn tight as a drumhead over the windpipe, with nothing between the two. The hair at the nape is too coarse for the comb, and it grows back faster than hair should. The ear tips are frostbitten black and do not seem to hurt him. And the jaw. The jaw has come forward. When he chews, something at the hinge clicks against my edge, a joint set wrong, like a gate that no longer meets its post. Under me there are marks I can feel and cannot read: small, in rows, healed in a hurry. I am cloth. I do not know what was done to him. I know it was done in order.

passages.heading: II. Roster. Tue 4 Nov.
passages.text:
On Monday the tenth he stood where the Reverend stood, under the gate, with the Reverend's tin. My starch had been brushed brown. The guard at the post looked at me and nodded. A collar is a collar. Nobody looks above one. That is what a collar is for.

He says the blessing, every word of it. Where the Reverend put a name, he puts a number. *Go up a man, Nine. Come down a man.* The men say *amen*. None of them ever heard his own name in it. Each only ever heard the number in his own ear, where the name had been. So the blessing sounds the same. It sounds the same, and it works the other way.

At night in the hut he says his own number to himself, twice, the way a man checks a lock. He hums one line of something that is not a hymn, a tune with a dance in it, from somewhere with a river. He thumbs pitch onto his own brow, waits, and wipes it off. Some nights he cries, and the crying comes out of that jaw wrong. I cannot tell whether he is mocking the blessing or begging it. In thirty years on the Reverend I could not always tell that either.

passages.heading: II. Roster. Tue 4 Nov.
passages.text:
Was the blessing ever the Reverend's? Or was it only the shape of his mouth, and the shape is all it needs?

They took the names out of the blessing, and it still worked. I have been a collar for thirty years. That is the first thing that has frightened me.

passages.heading: The Timber-Stalker
passages.text:
You said come down a man. I came down quiet.

I walk the log decks at night, and the old rail bed past the broken trestle, where the ties have rotted to the shape of ties. It runs south, farther than anyone here has walked it. I leave no print on it. I count my steps in my mother's language, so that one count in this camp is not theirs.

Quiet is the only thing here they never issued.

passages.heading: The Pit-Fiend
passages.text:
You said come down a man. I came down owed.

I work the Workings by lamp. When a man is alone where the drift narrows, I stand in it, and I do not move, until he gives me what the camp gave me: less. I keep an empty matchbook from a dance hall back east. There is nothing in it. I keep it because it closes.

I like it, Reverend. Write that down. You wrote down everything else.

passages.heading: The Den-Keeper
passages.text:
You said come down a man. I am not one, and I came down anyway.

I keep you in the deep woods, under the boughs, where nobody has reported you. While nobody finds you, your collar walks. I know what that makes me. I keep you anyway. Nobody else in this place would keep anything for you.

The frost keeps you better than I can. Your face is grey and whole. Your throat is not, so I laid pine across it, the way you would lay a cloth on a table. Your hands are whole. I folded them on your chest with the thumb out, because that was the part of you that worked.

I hang what the camp throws away on string around us: a bent spoon, the key off a ration tin, a lid with no can. When anything comes, it rings. Every night I tell you the roll, the way you told God the names. Ten of ten, Reverend. Ten of ten.

passages.heading: The Den-Keeper
passages.text: Somebody here should be a sexton.

passages.heading: The Alpha-Born
passages.text:
You said come down a man. I say it myself now.

I have no collar and no tin. The pines weep pitch for nothing, and I take it on my thumb. I say it with no name and no number: *Go up. Come down. Keep the wild.* If they find you tomorrow, the words stay in my mouth. They were never in the collar.

I have come down something that does not need you to say it.

passages.heading: The sixth
passages.text:
I said *amen* because everyone did. And because his thumb was warm, and nothing else is warm in November.

## V. The Howl. Mon 1 Dec into Tue 2 Dec.

```
YARD BOOK — FOREMAN HASK — TUE 2 DEC 1952
Structures, surface damage, cause: animal (?)
  Bunkhouse ............ lines, 5, at the reach of a man
  Vane Sawmill ......... lines, 5
  Company Office ....... lines, 5
  The Forge ............ lines, 5
  Chapel hut ........... lines, 5
Repair: sand and creosote. Priority: low.

NIGHT LOG — MON 1 / TUE 2 DEC 1952
00:00  Midnight Roll. All racks: ten of ten.
02:10  Widow-Maker Ridge: figures, 6. Sound, sustained.
       Duration: 15 sec (timed on the roll-call watch).
       Moon: full. Colour: red (kiln smoke, burn-off).
       Searchlight: traversed ridge. Figures: not found.
06:00  Dawn Roll. All racks: ten of ten.
       Incident: none.
```

Six of them were on the ridge at ten past two. All six stood by their bunks at six. Every billet on every rack weighed true. I was on the throat that led them, and I can tell you what fifteen seconds is in this camp. It is the time they give you to be where you belong. The six took it and used it for the other thing. The jaw under me opened wider than a jaw should, and the sound went out over the pines. Then they came back, and they belonged.

passages.heading: The sixth
passages.text:
He blessed the ridge gang at the gate that morning, under the motto, with the Reverend's tin, and the guard nodded at me.

What is a blessing for, if it keeps nobody out?

It was never a lock. It was a name said once, where nobody could write it down. The Reverend knew that, which is why he said the names low, and why, at the very end, he said his own. They know it too, which is why they say none at all.

Moss put the names in so God could find them. They took the names out so nobody would. The log on your rack at dawn is who you are, and every one of them was there.

works.title: What the Dish Pit Knows
works.pov: first-person, eight voices of the Old Brigade
works.blurb: eight voices of the Old Brigade under the Hall, 1787 to May 1793 (the Plongeur, the Commis, the Apprenti, the Croissant Rassis and the Sin-Eater), each a section and a year: the plates that come down from the gallery, the Champignon's seal under a kneeling knee, the Critique's empty chair, the Commis's question about whose ash goes down to the Mother, Armand's sea-pinks, and the refrain that every plate comes down.

passages.heading: I. Le Plongeur, 1787
passages.text:
I kneel on a word I cannot read.

It was a seal once, the seal of Le Champignon, the office of the first heresy. When they abolished the office they ground its seal into the dish-pit floor, so that someone would always be kneeling on it. Someone is me. Before me it was my mother. My knees know its letters better than my eyes know anything.

I did not choose the floor. I did not choose the water. I did not choose whose plates.

The Council's book says the Plongeur is penance, by sentence or by birth. Mine was birth. I was born to this floor the way a loaf is born to its platter, and nobody asked the loaf.

In the spring they gave a salt-raker to the Hearth for a crumb. It was the heel of a gilded loaf, found in his cap. I did not see it. Down here you hear it. The music comes first, through the south doors from the Square. Then the bell. Then every cloche in the Hall lifts on the one note, like the whole Gallery drawing breath.

passages.heading: I. Le Plongeur, 1787
passages.text:
He whistled through the gap in his teeth. He mended my bucket once with a cod-bone needle and would not take a copper for it. His name was Mathurin. I say it once because no one upstairs said it at all.

Then the supper came down.

Crust with the gold leaf still on. A cream sauce left to skin. Three sugared swans, one with its neck bitten through.

I know what it cost. It cost one Mathurin.

What the dish pit knows: every plate comes down.

At dusk the Aboyeur walks the Hall above me, calling every loaf by its owner's name. I hear him through the floor. The first loaf of the night he sets on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal, and he calls nothing at all. I do not ask whose. Nobody below the Hall asks. Nobody above it does either.

Who washes the plate a death was eaten off? I do. Who asks what it cost? Only the water, and the water does not repeat it.

passages.heading: I. Le Plongeur, 1787
passages.text: The loaf on your platter at dawn is who you are. The plate in my sink at dawn is what you did.

passages.heading: II. Le Commis, 1788
passages.text:
Ninety-one steps. I carry flour down them, and water, and ash. I set them at the foot of the vat and I climb back up without touching the glass. A Commis may carry, but may never feed the Mother. That is the whole of my office. I have done it four years without a crumb of complaint, and without a crumb.

The Gallery's flour. The Gallery's water. The Hearth's ash.

Whose ash? The duty does not say. I have not asked. I carry it.

In the autumn the Gallery gave the Hearth a boy for a tassel. He had cut it off a cloak in the crowd on the Wharf: gold thread, a thumb's length of it. The Fire was set for the sixth bell. Then a lady of the Gallery remembered the fish. Fish will not wait. So the Fire was moved to after the fish course, so that the cloches could be lifted on the bell and the soup would not go cold.

passages.heading: II. Le Commis, 1788
passages.text:
He kept a pocket of odd buttons. He sorted them by colour on the Wharf steps: bone, horn, brass, and one of real silver he would not trade for bread. His name was Yannick. The island called him the Cutpurse, which is what it calls every boy with quick hands. Then it called him nothing.

That night I carried the Hearth's ash down and the Gallery's bottles up. Down, up. Down, up. Everything to her. Nothing from her.

Did I ever eat a loaf I carried for? Did anyone ever hand me back so much as a heel? You know the answer. You have eaten it.

But hands that only carry learn the weight of everything, and the taste of nothing.

I carried their plates down and their ash down, and I called it work.

passages.heading: III. L'Apprenti, 1789
passages.text:
There are several of us. We are the ones who watch. The disgrace of our office is speaking, so here is everything I did not say.

I saw a washerwoman fall behind on her yeast-tax in the wet spring, when her youngest had the cough. I did not say it.

I saw the Ledger-Clerk's stamp come down on her platter: UNREGISTERED. I did not say it.

I saw the Inquisitor ask, the Bailiff take and the Chancellor decide, in the order the law gives them, as neatly as a menu. I did not say it.

She stitched each of her children's initials inside their caps in blue thread, so that she could find them by feel in the dark. Her name was Soizic. The island calls her the Debtor now, the way it gives every Unregistered death that name, as if owing were all she ever did.

I saw the Gallery choose their seats for the Square by the gilt on their sleeves. I saw a lady of the Gallery ask whether the bell might be rung a quarter-hour early, because her boat had the tide at seven. It was rung early.

passages.heading: III. L'Apprenti, 1789
passages.text:
I did not say it. I did not say any of it.

Is a watcher a witness? Is a witness a hand? If I had spoken, whose platter would have been empty that dawn: hers, or mine, or both?

Silence was my office. I kept it better than they kept their word.

passages.heading: IV. Le Plongeur, September 1789 – 1790
passages.text:
On the twenty-third of September the news came in on the Morning Ferry. I heard it in the water before I heard it in words. That night the supper for the Crown's man came down uneaten.

Full plates. Cold plates. Plates no one would sign for.

In all my life of plates I had never seen a full one come back. I stood with my hands in the water and did not know what to scrape.

Before the month was out the Gallery gave the Hearth one of its own, and the Square that watched was red.

Then the lower rooms filled. Dockhands, Plongeurs, apprentices, the Unregistered. Red crust was pinned to their sleeves where the Guild wore flour-white and the Gallery wore gold. They stood in my dish pit because it was the one room in the Sacred Kitchen nobody above us had ever wanted.

In 1790, the year the Abbot died, the new faith came down the stairs. It had been a heresy. Now it was the Commons' religion. They knelt where I kneel, on the Champignon's seal, and they called the floor holy. They called it an honour to kneel there.

passages.heading: IV. Le Plongeur, September 1789 – 1790
passages.text:
I have knelt there since I was born.

If the floor is holy now, what was I? The saint, or the rag?

They made my penance their prayer, and asked me to move over.

passages.heading: V. L'Apprenti, 1791
passages.text:
The kitchen has a committee now.

Plongeurs and Commis sit at the command desk, where the Chef once ordered the day's bake. The tribunal's table stands in front of Le Critique Gastronomique's chair, empty for two hundred years. No one sits in it. The Council kept it empty so that no one could overrule the Council. The committee keeps it empty for the same reason. Nothing it decides can be overruled by a chair.

I am its clerk. Speaking was the disgrace of my office. Now speaking is my duty. I read the denunciations aloud from the expediter, where the Aboyeur stands to call the loaves, and my voice carries the length of the Hall.

In the summer they gave the Hearth a cadet of a gold-leaf house. It was for a gilt button worn on a fast day. A crumb, the other way round.

It was the same bell. It was the same cloches, lifted on the same note. The supper after was the same, and red crust ate it. The plates went down the same stairs to the same sink.

passages.heading: V. L'Apprenti, 1791
passages.text:
He pressed sea-pinks in a psalter. He was nineteen. He had never once been down the kitchen stairs, and on the last morning he asked me, quietly, which way they went. His name was Armand.

But I had watched this before. I knew the words before they gave them to me.

They gave me back my voice and told me what to say with it.

passages.heading: VI. Le Croissant Rassis, 1792
passages.text:
Lamination is patience in folds. The disgrace of the office is haste.

I was the Tourrier for thirty years. I folded butter into dough, and gold leaf into the butter, for the Gallery's pastry. The thinner the leaf, the more they paid. The more they paid, the faster I folded.

I folded for their weddings. I folded for their christenings. I folded for the suppers after the Fire, and I did not ask whose Fire.

Now the committee has given me the title that is not an office. Le Croissant Rassis. The stale one. It stands on a card in the front-of-house case, and I sit in the case above it, hard as a rock under the case lamp, so the island can learn what a man is worth who folded gold for the Gallery. Children tap the glass. Their mothers let them.

Am I stale because I was kept too long, or because I was kept at all?

passages.heading: VI. Le Croissant Rassis, 1792
passages.text:
I laid gold on bread for people who sentenced bread. I know it. I knew it with every fold.

Haste was my sin. Theirs is the same, in a redder coat.

passages.heading: VII. The Sin-Eater, spring 1793
passages.text:
They pay me a copper and I eat a crust over the empty platter, and the sin goes into me and not into the ground. That is the island's custom, older than the Council. Nobody writes it down. Everybody pays.

I ate for Mathurin. I ate for Yannick. I ate for Soizic, whom the island calls the Debtor, and her children paid me in buttons because they had no copper. I kept the buttons.

Now the gold-leaf houses send for me. They pay better. The crust is finer.

Sin tastes the same on gilt as on burlap.

The Sot sings at every Fire. He sang for the Gallery's suppers and he sings for the committee's. It is the same tavern song, the same wrong note in the third line. Nobody has ever stopped him. Nobody has ever needed to. The stage never changed, so why should the song?

In April a thing came off the Morning Ferry in crates and a great deal of straw, with a Paris mark burned into the wood. The National Razor, they call it. They set it up beside the Hearth. One stage. Two instruments. I did not look at it long. It is a thing, and things are not what I am paid to eat for.

passages.heading: VII. The Sin-Eater, spring 1793
passages.text:
Now the feeding hand waits upstairs for the Commons' tribunal. He is a Vane, of the only house whose hand has ever touched the Mother. They have asked me to be ready with a copper's worth of crust. Ready is not needed. Nobody can tell me which I will be.

I have eaten the sins of both halves of this island, and I am still hungry.

passages.heading: VIII. Le Plongeur, May 1793
passages.text:
I am on my knees on the seal.

The others went up. Plongeurs sit at the command desk now. Apprentices read from the expediter. The faithful come down and kneel beside me, and go back up. I stayed where I was born.

The committee's plates came down tonight. It is the same porcelain, and the gilt rim is chipped now. There is red crust in the crumbs where gold leaf used to be. I scrape them the same way. The water does not know the difference.

At dusk the Aboyeur set the first loaf on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal. He called nothing, as he did the night I was born, as he did every night of the Gallery and every night of the Commons. No revolution has moved that loaf an inch. I do not ask whose.

The feeding hand is upstairs. His tribunal is at dawn. I do not know if his plate will come down to me tomorrow, or who will have eaten off it, or whether his platter will stand empty when the cloches lift. I will not know until the plates come down.

passages.heading: VIII. Le Plongeur, May 1793
passages.text:
What the dish pit knows: every plate comes down. Every hand that eats is a hand I wash after.

They changed the colour of the crust. They never changed who kneels.

works.title: Sayings of the Fork
works.pov: first person (Agnes, No. 21 Pump Row), addressed to Edith
works.blurb: at dawn on 12 December 1893, the morning after Rose, Agnes of No. 21 Pump Row climbs to Edith's stone in St Brannock's churchyard with her bitten arm bound and says every saying the Row has instead of the name, in ten sections (Pump Row, Lights, Wolves, Water, Doors, Hiding and counting and the bell, Bottles and watches and faces, What we don't give sayings to, The fork, The stone), each saying turning out to be someone's habit or death worn smooth.

passages.heading: I. Pump Row, first light
passages.text:
*Say it before they ask, and it is only news.*

That one is mine. I made it myself, on this lane, going up.

I am Agnes, of Pump Row, the door next to yours, Edith. Every morning it is the same three things: the shawl, the lane, the stone. Then I come back down with a name in my mouth and call it in at the doors before anyone has their boots on.

This is a young town with old sayings. Some came in on the Line in people's mouths, from back east and from further than that. Some we made here, after the drain, and they took faster than weeds. Harold says *before the drain* about everything, bread included. Nobody laughs any more, because it is a saying now, and you don't laugh at a saying.

We say it about the bread. We say it about the weather. We say it about the dead, because the dead are weather here.

passages.heading: I. Pump Row, first light
passages.text:
How old does a saying have to be before it is true? Two deaths old. One death is bad luck. Two is a custom.

You never learned them, Edith. You said *two weeks* about the rent, as if saying it carefully enough could bring it down to one. That was your saying. It never took.

*A saying is a thing said twice by people who were right once.*

passages.heading: II. Lights
passages.text:
*Keep a candle lit and the wolves keep their distance.*

We teach that one first. The children have it before their prayers.

A window is not a light to a wolf. Nor is the moon. Nor is the moss. A wolf is afraid of a flame, and of nothing that only looks like one. So we say: carry it. A lit window is for the people inside it.

A lantern carried is a lantern owed. The Lamplighter goes round at dusk and lights the town's lanterns for scrip. She leaves the fourth one on the square till last, the one over the chalk and the well, and we say you don't walk under that one until it's lit.

*A dark lantern walks two ways, the careful and the guilty.* We say it of anyone we see with the shutter down. Nobody says which of the two they are.

*Not every light over the fen is Fennick's.* Follow none you did not see lit.

passages.heading: II. Lights
passages.text:
And what does a candle keep off, besides wolves? Nothing. I have sat up with one all night. The rest come indoors.

*A flame keeps the wolves off. Nobody ever said what keeps the rest.*

passages.heading: III. Wolves
passages.text:
*A wolf runs a short mile and goes home.*

That is what we say. Run if you must, and run toward a flame. Never go into the wood unlit at dusk. A wolf has a home and goes back to it, which makes it kinder than some.

What it kills, it leaves where it fell. A body in the mud with the throat opened. The coat in strips. Fur. Claw marks on the fence post. Never a footprint. The wolves do not come back for what they leave, and they do not wipe their feet.

I say all this with my arm bound to the elbow. On Wednesday, before light, at the pump, one did not go home. I have the saying in my mouth and its teeth in my arm, and the saying is still right, mostly. Mostly is what a saying is.

There is a girl who strayed at twilight, got cornered, and was brought back. She tells the truth now, about everything: the price of eggs, whose step is dirty, what she saw. The town finds her harder to bear than the wolves.

passages.heading: III. Wolves
passages.text:
*The wolves get blamed for what the wolves did, and for what they didn't.* It is the easiest thing to say at a door. Wolves, we say, and we shut it. But Doc Mallory bends over a body, and sometimes the word the Doc writes down is knife. And sometimes there is a thread on the door frame, and wolves don't wear scarves.

*Wolves leave fur. Nobody ever found a wolf's thread.*

passages.heading: Never wash at the well after dark.
passages.text:
It isn't the water. It's who sees you at it.

A wet bucket at dawn is a question. A clean rag has done nothing yet. A bloody rag has done it once. We say these over the washing, and we laugh, and we look at each other's buckets.

Hattie had the wash-house at the foot of the Rise. She wrote to her son back east every week. On her shelf she kept a jar with the lid on. In it was one button off every dead man's shirt that came down to her to be washed for the box. Something of him kept back above ground, she said, and no one would miss one.

Since Hattie, the Row has a new saying: *Keep one button back.* The women say it at the tub. Not all of them know why. That is how you know it has become a saying: it has stopped being Hattie.

passages.heading: Never wash at the well after dark.
passages.text: What does the well remember? Don't ask me. I only draw from it.

passages.heading: V. Doors
passages.text:
*A lock keeps people out. It has never once kept anyone in.*

A broken door stays broken. A key that opens every door leaves a hand on every door. A lock put on from outside does not last the night. *Horace knows your last house, never your hour.* We say that to the young ones when they go walking out. They blush, and they should.

And you, Edith. Your bolt was shot from the inside. Your blanket was straight. I brought your name down the Row myself, and I could not tell anyone the day.

But the lock kept nobody in, Edith. It did not keep you.

Your letter to your sister is still on your table. It is folded once, not finished, with the stamp lying loose on top. I have looked at it through your window every morning since. I have not gone in and posted it. Should I have? Whose letter would it be, if I did?

passages.heading: V. Doors
passages.text: *Bolt the door for the living. The dead were never the ones coming in.*

passages.heading: Don't count the dead twice.
passages.text:
The children get this one from the hiding game. Whoever opens a hiding place is written into it. Quiet feet are a bad sign, or a child. Children see height and scarf, so we teach them to look at boots, not faces. Whoever finds it says it, and the body stays where it is: we move the living to the square, not the dead.

Elsie counted her eggs twice into her apron every morning, behind the Row. She named her hens after Company officers. The one called the Clerk laid nothing. They found her in the hen run with her back to the fence and the eggs in her apron. Eleven, the Undertaker said, as if she hadn't known.

Since then: *don't count the dead twice.* What does it mean? Nobody agrees. That's how you know it's ours.

And who rings a bell for nothing? Nobody, the first time. The second time, it is whoever was left standing nearest the rope.

passages.heading: Don't count the dead twice.
passages.text: *A bell rung for nothing is a bell rung for you.*

passages.heading: VII. Bottles, watches, faces
passages.text:
*Never take a bottle from a woman who keeps two.*

It is said of Mother Moll. It isn't fair, and it's said anyway.

Stand by one door a night, and never the same door twice. A bandaged man wakes knowing the height of whoever came for him. Everyone tells the Vicar sooner or later, so tell him early, while it's small. Wenna's dead have only a few words between them, so ask them short. The Gamekeeper does not go alone.

Trust her height. Faces are lent. Blood on a coat can be paint. A noise in the lane can be thrown. The knife has an heir.

The one we say lowest is this: watch the hands of whoever asks loudest who did it. I have asked loud. Everyone on the Row has. So at the bell we watch each other's hands, and that is a kind of prayer too.

Whose face did you borrow this morning, to come out in?

passages.heading: VIII. What we don't give sayings to
passages.text:
*When you hear feet and see nobody, don't answer.*

Mother Moll says the fog is in everyone's chest. Stan Pike had it. Arthur had it. We hear it through the walls at night and we say *bless you*, which is not a saying, only a hope.

We say the wolves. We say the wisps. We do not say the Gallery.

Reg and Norman sit at the mouth with their hats on their knees. Reg cracks his knuckles in the order of the old levels, top to bottom. Something is asleep down there, and the mere-rot wakes it. That is all anyone on the Row will put into words, and we use as few as that.

A saying is a kind of name. You don't name a thing you want to stay asleep.

Gives you away to what? Don't ask me that either.

*In the wood a light keeps you. Under the Gallery a light gives you away.*

passages.heading: IX. The fork
passages.text:
*Every trade comes to a fork, and the fork comes at night.*

Tamsin at the ovens can bake to the Clerk's list or to her own. Bar has two roads behind the bar, and only one of them is the street. The Undertaker signed for a roll of lead on the platform. We all saw him, and nobody asked what it was for. The Clerk posts the scrip in the morning and counts it at noon, and the two numbers have stopped agreeing.

Nobody says which way any of them went. We say: *Nobody chooses a fork. You find you have walked one.*

And here is the road's fork, where the lane splits below the churchyard. Up the one way to the stone, or out the other past the post at the edge of Gallows Wood. *At the fork, take the lit side*: every child on the Row has that one. The post is still burning out at the wood's edge. Up the other way, the sky is coming grey over the stone. Which is the lit side, at first light?

passages.heading: IX. The fork
passages.text:
I could read the name and carry it down first, the way I always do. Or I could walk out past the post and let the Row learn it from the bakery and the boy and the cart. They would learn it either way. The town is ahead of the stone now. If I don't read it, does it stay uncut? It doesn't. It never has.

You never had a fork, Edith. You had a bolt and a blank.

*The lit side is not always the safe side. It is only the side you can be seen on.*

passages.heading: Carry in what you love at curfew.
passages.text:
That one is Rose's. Every night at curfew she took her geranium in off the sill, the only flower on Pump Row, holding it against her like something that might wake. Rose died yesterday. Last night nobody carried it in. It is still on the sill, in its tin.

Every saying is somebody. It is Nora on the dock, answering two notes with two notes, though nobody whistles first now. It is Elsie counting twice. It is Hattie's one button. It is Rose's tin of red at the window. It is your two weeks, Edith. We say them so we don't have to say who.

I take the lit side. I go up. Under the binding my arm aches the way the sayings say a bite will before weather. The stone is where it was. I read it, and the name is in my mouth, ready, before anyone has asked.

passages.heading: Carry in what you love at curfew.
passages.text: *A saying is a name worn smooth. Say it first, and no one has to hear whose it was.*

works.title: Will-o
works.pov: first person (Old Fennick, the lighthouse keeper of the mere)
works.blurb: Old Fennick's confession in six sections: his steady light against the bog-wisps' lights that lure walkers off the path and in, the five seconds when a wisp blinds his own lantern and he cannot tell which light is his, and Cyril's drowning on 29 November, which he goes over without settling ("Was it theirs? Was it a hand? Was it mine, gone out for five?").

passages.heading: I. Which is mine
passages.text:
Dusk below the Fenwood, and I climb.

Once it was the oak, limb over limb, at nineteen. Now it is a pole. My knees count the rungs for me, and the can knocks my hip on every one.

I keep it lit. I keep it trimmed. I keep it for nobody, going nowhere in particular.

There is no lake now to bring a boat home across. There is a fen, and a town on the lip of it, and a light on a pole at the edge of the two, and an old man under the light. That is the whole of the arrangement.

On Saturdays I fill my can at the Lantern, and Mrs Grieves puts it in her book. If you bring me oil I will take it, and I will tell you what you paid for it, so you know that I know. Nobody pays me to burn it. The Company pays the Lamplighter by the post, in scrip. She passes my pole and does not reach for it. If she reached, I would stop her.

passages.heading: I. Which is mine
passages.text:
What is a light for, if it brings nobody home?

A light is not for where you are going. It is for knowing where you are.

passages.heading: II. The others
passages.text:
Out on the fen there are other lights.

Low. Lower than any arm would carry them. Moving against the wind. Moving when nothing moves. Never twice in the same place.

They are not lanterns. Nobody holds them. They lead walkers off the planks and in, and the fen does the rest.

Mine is steady. Theirs are not. I say it the way my father said it of his. The same height every night. The same place every night. The same colour every night, since before this town had a name to put on a stone.

But I hear what people say. They have stood at the end of the planks, they say, and could not tell which one was mine. They say it kindly. They think it is a thing about the fog.

I take it the way I took the lake. Personally.

If you cannot tell them apart, what is steady worth to you?

passages.heading: II. The others
passages.text: Steady only saves the ones who wait long enough to see it stay.

passages.heading: III. Five
passages.text:
One of the low ones comes nearer. Mine goes out.

I have not touched it. The oil is in it.

One. A walker on the planks looks for the steady light.
Two. Finds only the ones that move.
Three. Steps toward the nearest.
Four. Steps again, and there is no plank.
Five.

Mine comes back. I did not light it.

Here is what I have not told the box at St Brannock's, or the Lantern, or my father, who is not here to hear it. Up on the pole, in the five, I cannot tell either. In the five, I have wanted to go.

Who keeps a light that goes out when it is wanted most?

Five is long enough to choose wrong, and too short to choose again.

passages.heading: IV. Two notes
passages.text:
Cyril fished the channels. In fog he whistled two notes, high and then low, so that Nora on the dock would know where he was on the water, and she answered with her own. I heard them from the pole for years, the way you hear your own heart. Some nights I lifted a hand to them, though no hand could be seen through that.

Low water was circled on the chart at the Lantern, and he went out at the circle.

Two notes. Nora's two. Two notes again. Then none.

Was mine lit? I will not tell you it was dark. I will not swear to you it was burning. I was on the pole, and I was counting, and I do not know what I was counting.

They brought him in at noon. I went down to look, because I had heard him every night and I owed him that.

passages.heading: IV. Two notes
passages.text:
Face down in a channel that would not cover a boot. One boot gone. A fist of reed he would not give up. Fen in his mouth, and the mouth open, as if on the first note. His eyes open too, turned toward the marsh edge, where the pole stands.

They wrote *drowned*. A man does not go under in water that will not reach his shin. Everyone who stood in it knew that, and nobody had another word.

Was it theirs? Was it a hand? Was it mine, gone out for five?

Nora whistles from the dock every evening. I do not answer. I am not the one she is calling, and I am the only one who hears.

passages.heading: V. The one under the water
passages.text:
You will want to ask about the other one. Everyone does, sooner or later: the lantern under the black water by the old oak, still burning, as steady as mine.

Don't ask me who keeps it lit.

I have heard it is my father's lamp, gone down with the limb. I have heard it is the sign of the old Rusty Lantern, carried into the mere by a barman who never came up. I have heard both. I say neither.

What I will say is this. When I was nineteen, nobody had drowned in my keeping, and I was proud of it the way a young man is proud of a thing that is his. When the limb went I watched the lamp go under, and I stood and waited for it to go dark.

I did not trim it. I did not fill it. I did not ask.

So what is a keeper whose first light keeps itself? And if there are two steady lights on the fen now, how would you know which one the fen is keeping?

passages.heading: V. The one under the water
passages.text: I keep the light I can reach. The other one keeps something I won't name.

passages.heading: VI. Steady
passages.text:
There is someone at the end of the planks tonight, counting. I can see the light stop and the head turn. One light. Two lights. Five. Maybe it is the Lamplighter on her way back. Maybe it is you.

I will climb. I will trim. I will stand under it till the fog goes, the way I stood under the oak when there was water to stand beside.

It will not be enough. It has not been enough since the lake went. One of the low ones is coming in now, not steady, nearer than it was.

If you are the one counting, hear me once.

"Wait five before you follow anything. Wait five, and then wait."

Every light on the fen is a promise, and the fen keeps every one but mine.

works.title: The Lavender Field
works.pov: first person (Nora, Cyril's widow), written the day after
works.blurb: the Vicar's memorial as one villager saw it: Nora, Cyril's widow, at the Bell on the night of Sunday 17 December 1893, watching twenty-one seconds of a lavender field and a lone orange tree under a blue sky "in squares, like a net held up to a lamp", reading his last words verbatim with a finger in the air, then turning to find the robes standing at the back; the next morning she calls it a dream at the pump, and puts his words across the Clerk's counter, unsigned.

passages.heading: The Lavender Field
passages.text: *HollowMere. Written Monday, the eighteenth of December, 1893, on the dock, about the night before.*

passages.heading: I.
passages.text:
Sunday. The seventeenth. After dusk. The Bell.

I came because the stone said THE VICAR at dawn, and Agnes read it to the Row the way she reads them all, and the Row went to its doors and looked up the slope.
I came because the chapel bell did not go when the service ended.
I came because the dock is no place to be after dark when nobody is going to answer anyway.

Somebody rang the Bell. I don't know who. In this town that is enough.

We were fewer than had been in the pews. You could count the dark doors on the Row and know who wasn't there.

What do you bring to a wake when nobody has said there is a body?

passages.heading: II.
passages.text:
It came where the square should have been. It was in front of every face at once, and I can't tell you where it came from.

A field. It came in squares, like a net held up to a lamp, each square its own colour. A colour I have no word for. Somebody at the pump said *lavender* this morning. I let them have the word.

Hills, bent. The whole field leaning the way the reeds lean off a boat's wake.

One tree, near, standing over the rest. Fruit on it the colour of a lamp-flame.

And the sky. Blue. Not fog-white. Not mere-grey. Blue. Cloud on it thick as wool before carding.

It slid past the way the bank goes by when you're rowing. Then it came toward the tree, the way the dock comes to you when you ship the oars.

There was music, and St Brannock's has no organ.

passages.heading: II.
passages.text:
I counted it. I count the way I count between Cyril's two notes and mine: high, low, and then the wait before I answer. One. Two. Nobody else was counting. I'm sure of that, and I don't know why it matters.

Twenty-one.

There was nobody in it. I looked for a face out of habit, his. Nobody. That was how I knew it was his.

passages.heading: III.
passages.text:
Then the words came, under it, white, standing the way the Gazette's type stands, with no voice to them.

I read slow. I read with a finger, and there was no paper to put it to, so I put it to the air, and the words waited for me. They waited the way he did on the bank of the channel, the day I took the Seal and couldn't find what to say.

*"In the end I sought nothing else but to serve God.*
*And serve him I did.*
*With this death's last breath I pray this prayer: may the Almighty grant me the strength of ten in the next life.*
*And in return, tenfold my own."*

Strength of ten. I can mend ten fathom of net in an evening. I can't think what he meant to carry with it.
Is a prayer still owed if nobody hears it said? Is it owed if the whole square does?

passages.heading: IV.
passages.text:
It went out like a lamp turned down, not blown.

We looked round, all of us, the way you look round at a wake for the widow. I know how that looks. They looked at me that way on the twenty-ninth.

And the robes were there.

At the back, under the eave, where a man stands to hear a town out. The collar I knew. The black from the collar down. Standing still, watching the place where the tree had been.

Whoever was under it had watched it with us. Had they counted too?

Who wears a dead man's coat to his wake?
Who stands at the back of a man's memorial and keeps so still?
Who among us looked longest, and was seen looking?

People looked at the robes, and their shoulders came down. I watched it go along the square like a gust going down the Row. It was easier. A coat is easier than a field.

passages.heading: IV.
passages.text: I said, *He's here,* to nobody. Then I said, *They're here.* I don't know which of those was the lie.

passages.heading: V.
passages.text:
I said dream.

I said dream at the pump this morning, with my bucket, the way you say fog.
I said dream because a dream cannot be taken to the Constable.
I said dream again tonight, on the chapel step, because at dusk the robes stood up in the pulpit and preached, and the town went in to hear it, and so did I.

The Undertaker wrote *drowned* for Cyril, in water that would not cover a boot. He wrote it because the line wanted a word. I let it stand, because I had no better one. I know what it is to let a short word stand. I have been doing it since the twenty-ninth.

And this too. This morning I turned over the twine account and wrote his words on the back in my plain hand, slow, every one, the way they had waited for me. I took them down the hill and put them across the Clerk's counter. He was reading something in his drawer and did not look up. I did not sign.

passages.heading: V.
passages.text:
I reported him the only way this town allows. Unsigned.

The pump says the Postmaster cut the bag from the east and there was a second copy in it, word for word. The bag came sealed.

Who wrote that one?

I didn't sign because the robes had seen who read slowest. I read slowest. I always have.

passages.heading: VI.
passages.text:
This evening I whistled from the dock, the two notes, high, then low, the way I do every evening. Nobody answered, the way nobody does.

At the same hour, up the slope, the robes preached, and the town answered. *Amen.* Aloud, together, through the fog. I could hear it from the boards.

That is all I know that the town doesn't. I know how the quiet sounds when the dead are really gone. I have heard it every evening since the twenty-ninth. Tonight I heard the town answer something that is not him.

I took the Seal for the house. The house is me now. I don't know what that makes the Seal.

passages.heading: VII.
passages.text:
Nobody in HollowMere has seen a blue sky since the fog came off the mere. Last night every one of us saw one, and this morning not one of us had.

A dream is what a town calls the thing it saw together and will not report.

works.title: Eight Phrases
works.blurb: the V2 Medium as Wenna's last ring with chalk, Sunday 3 December 1893, at Hattie's body: eight counts and eight things the dead may say, each block opening onto one of the winter's dead or the living who ask after them (Mabel, Cyril and Nora, the hanged man, Hattie and the Watchman, Maud), with the refrain that she does not tell; the dead on the knife's side may lie, and the one liar she is sure of in every ring is herself, answering Jory's nightly question with what he needs to hear.

passages.heading: IT WAS DARK.
passages.text:
Sunday night, and Hattie on the board where Doris and the Undertaker laid her out. Chalk round her in one line with no gap, from a twist of paper with three sticks left in it. Three candles: one at her head, one at her feet, one in my hand. Then I count. The dead get eight counts, a held breath's length, and eight things they may say. Never a ninth. The dead are poor in words. Eight is all they have, and they share them.

One. *It was dark.* I have heard that one more than all the others put together. Dark in the lane behind the Lantern after eleven, where Mabel went in her boots lined with hymn sheets, the alto line marked. Dark on the channel. Dark under the Bell. What use is a phrase that is true of every death in HollowMere? Everyone here dies after the lamps. The living hear it from me and nod, as if I had brought them something.

passages.heading: IT WAS DARK.
passages.text: I do not tell.

passages.heading: I KNEW THE FACE.
passages.text:
Two. A man can come down the Row in a coat that is not his, with a walk that is not his, and say good morning in a voice he has borrowed for the day. A ghost who says it knew the face is telling me about a coat. What the dead saw is not what the dead know, and it is the second one the living come to me for. How would the dead know the difference, when the living never have?

I do not tell.

passages.heading: NOT THE WOLVES.
passages.text:
Three. Since the wolves started walking the fence, the town has wanted this phrase and been afraid of it in the same breath. A wolf is a sorrow. A wolf is weather.
