If it was not the wolves, it was a hand, and the hand passed you the bread at the last wake. Which would you rather I brought up out of the ring, a wolf or a neighbour? Nobody answers that. They ask me what was said instead.

I do not tell.

passages.heading: BY THE WATER.
passages.text:
Four. Cyril, on the Wednesday. I drew my ring on the dock before they carried him up to the Undertaker, out of a channel that comes to the ankle at low water. In fog he whistled two notes, high then low, so Nora would know where he was on the water, and she answered with her own. Nora stood outside my chalk with the nets over her arm and asked what he said. I gave her nothing. She whistles the two notes off the dock in the evenings now, and nobody answers, and I could.

What does a drowned man owe the dock? What does the woman with the chalk owe the wife? *By the water* is a phrase I knew before HollowMere. Another man went into the water at the end of this Line, and the first train came in without him on the platform.

I did not tell Nora.

passages.heading: IT WAS NOT ME.
passages.text:
Five. The man the Tribunal hanged on the Tuesday. His name is a blank in their book and in the Undertaker's, and I will not be the one to fill it. I drew my ring at the foot of the gallows pine after they cut him down. There was waxed thread in his coat pocket, and I left it there.

Here is the rule I learned before I learned the eight: the dead who were on the knife's side may lie. They keep their side after. So *not me* from a hanged man is worth nothing, and if he says nothing, that is worth nothing too. If the dead can lie, what is a Medium for?

I have an answer, and I do not like it. There is one liar I am sure of in every ring I draw. I have been sure of it since the first train.

I do not tell.

passages.heading: TELL HIM.
passages.text:
Six. Back in this room. Hattie. Doris told her the news before I came in, the way Doris always does; she said so at the door. Over Hattie's copper, in white capitals, HATTIE: the one word she could write, chalked where she would see it first thing every morning. A son back east, and a letter every week, a line at a time through the Postmaster, for a scrip. A jar of buttons on the shelf, one off every dead man's shirt she washed for the box, so that something of each of them stayed up here.

The Watchman is at the door. They took his lantern off him today, and he holds his hands as if it were still in them.

passages.heading: What did she say?
passages.text:
*Tell him.* Tell whom? The son who will get no letter this week? The man in the doorway with nothing in his hands? The phrase is the same two words, whoever it is for.

I do not tell him.

passages.heading: I AM COLD.
passages.text:
Seven. Maud, the Monday Car 3 took her out. She took her Rotgut as a wage, never as a gift, and darned both of Bar's cuffs so they matched. I held her ring that night behind the back car, with all eight laid open, and she picked none. She has not picked one since. She never said much, living.

I have envied her ever since: eight counts with every word open, and nothing taken. Who needs a Medium to know the dead are cold? There was a cold once that smelled of rain, under the hill, and I was not there for it. I was in a room over a laundry, ironing other people's collars, waiting for a letter in pencil.

I do not tell.

passages.heading: HAS IT COME?
passages.text:
Eight. The only question among them. Seven of the phrases are for the living. One is for me.

Jory. I have not said his name tonight until now. I came on the first train to meet a man who had written that he would meet it. He did not. Every night since, in every ring I draw for him, he picks the same one.

passages.heading: Has it come?
passages.text:
And I say what a living woman would say. It has. He asks again. I say it again.

In my pocket, a small wooden spoon with a notch for the thumb, the bowl still rough. I do not say who gave it to me.

That is the liar I am sure of. The dead may lie to keep a side. I lie to keep a man asking.

Eight. Hattie's flame leans. She has chosen. I heard it. It is hers.

Tomorrow I take the chalk to Harold's step, three stubs in a twist of paper, and ask him to keep it out of my reach, to learn whether Jory asks without the ring.

The rule says the knife's dead may lie. It was never written for the one who answers them.

I do not tell the living what the dead know. I tell the dead what they need to hear.

works.title: The Dream Book
works.pov: first person (Ernie, 12, platform crew), his own book
works.blurb: the last open trope, "it was all a dream", settled by refusing it: Ernie, twelve, of the platform crew, keeps a book on the back of a Company form pad from Monday 1 January 1894, writing down what he saw at night (the train that came up the shut line, the robes going down the slope empty, walkers with no lanterns, Percy and his marbles, and his own step up onto the last train and back down); every morning his mother says it was a dream, and every margin holds a station name he copied off something real.

passages.heading: The Dream Book
passages.text: *HollowMere. Kept by Ernie, of the platform crew, on the back of a Company form pad Clem gave me. Begun Monday, the first of January, 1894.*

passages.heading: Head note.
passages.text:
Clem's book counts who comes off at Day and who gets on at Dusk. It doesn't count what you see at night. Nobody's book does. So this one will.

Mam calls them dreams, so it's a dream book. I didn't name it. I only keep it.

My rule is the kind Clem has. I only put a name in the margin if I copied it off something I could put my finger on in daylight. A dream doesn't leave you anything to put your finger on.

Every morning of my life Mam said on the step what every mother here says, while she pinned my collar: *Keep to the light, and don't miss the train.*

Since the year turned, she says, *It was a dream.*

passages.heading: Monday, 1 January.
passages.text:
Friday. Fog at the Rush. The line was shut, and a train came up it anyway.
Pruett in the door of the private car with his punch in his hand, not using it.
One off the private car. The fog stood off him. An iron crosier as tall as he is.
The crew took their hats off. I took mine off. Clem wrote that he couldn't say which way he meant it. Neither can I.

That's all of it. I was on the boards with the bucket. I saw what the boards saw and no more.

Mam, at the clock, this morning: *No train came Friday. The line's shut. It was a dream.*
Then she set the clock by the up-train, the way the rule says every clock in the Grant has to be set.

She set it Friday night too. It was the first time since the twenty-third.

So what did she set it by?
If Friday was a dream, why is our clock right?

passages.heading: Monday, 1 January.
passages.text: I'll tell the truth here, because it's my book. I wanted it to be a dream. Then nothing would have come up the line for anybody.

passages.heading: [Margin, pencil, large capitals:]* WIDOWS CUT
passages.text: Copied Friday, at the Rush, off the tender, where the tank man at the Cut chalks up the water he lets go. The chalk came off on my finger. It's still on the cuff of my coat. I haven't brushed it.

passages.heading: Monday, 8 January.
passages.text:
Saturday, the thirtieth. Dusk. The square full.
A light came down on the chapel step, as wide as the pump.
I was too short for the step. There were backs in front of me. I saw what came down the slope.
The robes. Over the rail, down the slope, nobody in them.
I ran after them. The fog had them first.

Mam: *It was a dream.* She said it with her boots on under the blanket. That's how she sleeps now, as if she means to get up.

passages.heading: [Margin, pencil:]
passages.text:
You can't copy a name off a light. When Clem hasn't got a name he leaves a blank, so I've left one.

Is a thing a dream because it left you nothing to copy?
Is a blank a lie?
Then Clem's book is full of lies, and he's the most honest man on the boards.

passages.heading: Monday, 15 January.
passages.text:
Thursday night. From our window you can see the end of the boards.
People walking past it, one behind another. No lanterns. No sound. No hurry.
Going the way that goes to the Gallery mouth.
I counted them the way Clem counts, under my breath. When I knew one of the coats I stopped.
I'm not writing whose.

Then I saw Mam. She wasn't in her bed. She was at the other window, her shape on the glass, watching the same way I was.

Friday morning, at the clock: *It was a dream.*
Friday evening she barred the door before Curfew. She's never barred it before.

So now I know what a dream is in our house. It's a thing two of us saw at the same time and neither of us will say. It has to be called something.

I think I know why, too. Whatever you say you saw, somebody up the square writes you down for it. Mam is keeping us out of everybody's book.
Except mine.

passages.heading: [Margin, pencil, large capitals:]* GALLOWS WOOD SIDING
passages.text: Copied off the board at the end of the boards, the one that points down the line. Under it the frost had prints going over the rails in a line. By noon the prints were gone. The board wasn't.

passages.heading: Monday, 22 January.
passages.text:
Percy, at the Lantern, on a Tuesday. Three marbles. He wouldn't play for keeps. He never would.
I let him win one. He gave it back.

Mam: *It was a dream.* She said it soft. This time it was.

This one was a dream. I know the difference.
That's how I know the others aren't.

passages.heading: [Margin, pencil:]
passages.text:
There's nothing to copy. Percy never came on the train. He came in on Tuesdays.

Where do you put a friend in a book that only keeps what's real?
If I wrote his name in capitals, would that make him one or the other?
Percy goes in the middle of the page, with the dreams. Small. Where he'd sit.

passages.heading: Monday, 29 January.
passages.text:
This week Mam said it first, before I'd said anything. At the clock:
*You never went near that train. You dreamed it.*

The pump told her. The pump tells everybody everything, a week late.

So here it is, in my book, in my hand.

Saturday the twenty-third. The last train out. Arthur's brother took Arthur's ticket out of his hatband and put it in my hand. *Go on,* he said. *You always ask.*
I always ask where she goes after us. Nobody's ever told me.
I climbed to the step with the bucket still in my fist. Pruett brought the punch down to the paper.
I looked back once. I stepped down. I gave it back warm.
I said, *Who'd fill the bucket if I'm gone?*

It wasn't the bucket.

Maybe it was him, with his hand still out, and nobody on the boards to stand next to after.
Maybe it was where she goes after us, that nobody's ever told me, and I was afraid to be the first to find out.
Maybe it was Mam, who would have heard it at the pump a week late, and gone on setting the clock for one.

passages.heading: Monday, 29 January.
passages.text:
If it was a dream, I never gave it back.
If I never gave it back, I'm gone.
Which boy does she want at the table?

passages.heading: [Margin, pencil, large capitals:]* THORNE JCT
passages.text: Copied off Arthur's ticket. Arthur's brother took it down out of the band for me, stood there while I did it, and put it back. I copied the name. I didn't look to see if it was punched.

passages.heading: Monday, 5 February.
passages.text:
No dream this week. I slept. Nothing to call anything.

This morning Mam found the book open on the table. She looked down the margins, at the capitals going down the side of every page. She didn't say anything about the Cut, or the Siding, or the Junction.
She put her finger on the last one. I copied it this morning off the sign on the boards. It's the first word I ever copied, in October, when Clem said I could have the foot of every page.

*That one's real,* she said.

It's the only one she'll let be. The name of where we're standing.

passages.heading: [Margin, pencil, large capitals:]* HOLLOWMERE
passages.text:
I keep the clock she set by a train that didn't come.
I keep the prints that never crossed the rails.
I keep the step I never got down from, because I was never on it.

She can call it what she likes. She's keeping me out of everybody's book, and I'm keeping her in mine.

A dream doesn't leave you the spelling. Everything in my margins did.

works.title: Dear Katie
works.blurb: an amends letter reckoning with a past relationship's harm and the author's own role in it.

passages.heading: Dear Katie
passages.text:
Dear Katie,

I don’t think I’m writing this for you. In truth, I’m writing to get something off my chest.

I loved you even when it wasn’t good for both of us. I was so consumed by your love that I lost sight of my own. I craved your approval so much that I ignored my own feelings. I ran through every stop sign in what I called love, but it was just a hormonal cry for help because I was alone in this scary world, navigating changes I couldn’t comprehend. I was filled with hate that came from twisted feelings of love.

I pushed you away because losing you meant not being able to be with you. But truthfully, I didn’t even know what that meant. Love isn’t just sex. I knew that, but then again, maybe I thought the only way you’d love me like I loved you was if I was good at sex. I wanted something for you that I didn’t even want. In my hurry to please some idealistic version of our love, I crossed both our boundaries and created so much shame in our friendship that I left.

passages.heading: Dear Katie
passages.text:
I didn’t just leave physically; I left emotionally, mentally, and with all my presents. I went from a force of love in your life to just another example of the shitty men who leave. I fear I might have failed to keep my promises to you and to my younger self. I meant to be there for you, but I put myself first and became selfish, twisted, and alone. I used my time to cause harm when I could have sought to heal myself sooner and helped those around me find their way to healing as well.

That’s why I’ve come to the conclusion that in order to heal myself, I must first accept and apologize for doing harm to others when I was in pain. My actions were not my best, and I seek to amend them in the present.

I can’t predict the future or change the past. Instead, I’ll focus on the present moment and appreciate the experiences that come my way. I’ll see people for who they are and understand that no one is a mere object of my desires.

works.title: Five Letters at the Fork
works.blurb: five unsent letters, one for each townsfolk trade on the night it reaches its evolution: Tamsin Crumb to the dead Aldous Vane, the Postmaster to his sister who cannot read, the Undertaker to Father Bray, the Bartender to the drowned barman (written twice, one for the stove), and the Company Clerk to Ivy Cotter the night after the Baron falls, with the writ in his drawer.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
> *Mail that has been read shall be resealed and stamped. The stamp is not evidence of reading.*
> Articles of Incorporation and Bylaws of the Thorne & Expanse Line, Art. VI §2

---

## I. The Baker, to Aldous Vane
*Thursday, 26 October 1893. After the oven is raked.*

Dear Aldous,

I am not writing this for you. You are eight nights dead by the town's count, or the wire's, and no ferry I know of carries letters to the Hearth. I am writing because the crock did not rise on the hour tonight, and I need something in this house to answer me.

Up before anyone. Down after everyone. In between, I have been deciding things.

No flour came Friday last. None Saturday. None Monday. None today. The last sack went into the dead's loaves and the living's halves, and I have the sweepings. I don't know what comes next. That is still the first thing I knead into everything: I don't know.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
On the Saturday I cut the mourners' loaves to halves so the dead could keep their three. I did it with the scraper in one stroke. Nobody thanked me. Nobody stopped me. That is what I have to tell you, Aldous. A scraper is a law if nobody stops it.

I cut the loaves. I set the plates. I chose the halves.

Who gave me that? You did, with the cup.

The gold coin is still behind the crock, in the place a hand can go. Gold asks where it came from. Tonight there are two. I did not put the second one there. I counted them on the island's hour and again on the Company's, and there were two both times.

Last night there was a sack on the cold-room step with the stencil scraped off it, and no note, and a boot in the frost. I could not tell you how long a boot, because I swept before I looked. I sweep everything. Whose boot? I write that I don't know, and this time I mean it, and I do not like how little it costs me to mean it.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
At the Shift the Clerk stood at my counter with his hat on and asked for my book: who bought which loaf, to set against the Indebted. The Company does not recognise my table, he said, but it would like to read it. I said the book was in the oven room. It was in my apron.

So here is the whole of it. I could bake to his list. I could bake to my own. I could take what comes to the back step in the dark and pass it on in the crust, the way I pass the papers, folded twice, laid flat. Every road out of this kitchen goes through my hands.

People used to ask whether I came inland for you or for the cup. I still don't know. I know what you did with the tin money and the custom. You built one thing in HollowMere the Company could not tax. You left it with me. You did not leave me the flour.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
Is it freedom, if there is only one sack of it?

I have decided. I did it the way you do a thing you have already decided, in one stroke. The step is empty now. The book is not in my apron. I fed the crock on the island's hour and it rose, late, and I took that for an answer, because it was the only one I was given.

The island taught me to feed the dead. Hunger taught me that whoever holds the scraper holds the town.

---

## II. The Postmaster, to Hester
*Tuesday, 7 November 1893. The kettle still warm.*

Dear Hester,

You can't read this, and that is why it is to you.

Every letter I ever sent home, the neighbour's girl read to you aloud at your own table. So this one I will not send. It is the only letter in this office nobody will open. I have read every other.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
The Company bought me a kettle. It is in the Articles: kept for the purpose at the Company's expense, which expense is charged to the mails. So the town pays for the steam that opens it. I have held every envelope in HollowMere over that spout, and steam has taught me three things. Who owes. Who lies. Who is leaving.

I know which letters go east and come back with no answer. I know how many Ivy Cotter wrote, and how few were answered. I know whose name Arthur's brother signs at the bottom of his letters to his Ma, and I will not write it, not even to you, who could not tell it from a fence-rail. I reseal them all. I stamp them. The stamp is not evidence of reading. The Articles say that too. They thought of everything but me.

This morning there was black wax in the second bag.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
Black wax is the Company's. It is exempt from the right to read. I am to deliver it unopened and unsteamed into the hand it names, and not write down that I did. In October one went past me altogether, straight to the Conductor. This one came through my bag, and lay on my sorting table, and the kettle was already on.

I steamed it.

One line, printed: *Burn the Letter & Keep Your Mundane Life, OR Accept the Baron's Contract.*

The name on the outside is someone I have sold stamps to. I have counted change into that hand. I know how it holds a pen. I will not write the name, Hester. Not even here.

If the stamp is not evidence of reading, what is a reseal evidence of?

Here is my confession, since this is the only page in the Grant nobody will steam. What I have read is worth more than my wage. I have known that since the summer. Once, in September, I let a man see across the counter that I knew what was in his letter. Only my eyes. He bought a second stamp he did not need, and paid for it in coin, and I let him. That was all. That was the first rung.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
When we were small I read your letters to you before you heard them. I knew your news first. I held it on my tongue for a whole breath while you looked up at me, waiting, and I liked that breath more than I should have. You trusted the reader. Should anybody?

It is resealed. The wax took the iron cleanly; you could not tell. It is out of my hands now. The kettle is back on the stove, where the Company keeps it.

Every letter in this town is read but this one, and this is the only one that tells the truth.

---

## III. The Undertaker, to Father Bray
*Sunday, 19 November 1893. Maud on the table.*

Dear Father,

Either you are in the ground somewhere I did not put you, or you are somewhere a letter from me cannot follow. The Articles say I receive every body within the Grant, by whatever cause and wherever found, the bed of the mere included. I never received yours. That is the first thing I have to confess, and it is not even mine.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
I write to you because you were the last man who sat with me over a body and did not ask what it was worth.

Maud is on my table. Doris laid her out at four and went home without her supper. I have done the inventory to the last button, as the Company wants it entered against the account. One darning needle, in her collar, threaded grey. A card of red wool. A card of brown. A thimble worn through at the crown. Eleven buttons, none of them off her own clothes; she kept the ones she cut from other people's mending in case they were wanted back. She took her pour at the Lantern as a wage, never as a gift. Last night she darned Bar's other cuff to match the first. She was square with everyone.

She had no household and no lodgers. Her effects are held thirty days, then sold, and the proceeds applied to the account. I priced the needle before I closed her eyes. I want you to know that. I want somebody to.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
Pruett counts the coffins going out and I count them coming in, and we have not always agreed. In October my boy carried a paper reading *four* to Mrs Crumb's when she had three dead to bake for. I write the number before I have the name. That is the trade. I will not tell you who the others were. I don't know that I could.

Does a person become a number at my table, or were they one already, and the table only finds it out?

The Company would like a Chief Coroner: a man who writes the cause in a fair hand, so the Tribunal can read it and the account can close. Here is my difficulty, Father. Maud's name was on the stone with tomorrow's date. She came into the Lantern at dusk anyway, and darned, and asked for her Rotgut as a wage. I cannot write *the stone*. I cannot write *the cough* and look at her hands. I have left the line blank. A blank is the most honest thing a coroner could sign, and the Company does not take blanks.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
Pig lead comes up in Car 2 every day for the railyard. Lead keeps a thing where you put it. I have been thinking about that, and I would rather not tell you why.

I measure everybody by eye. It is the habit of the trade, and I cannot stop it. Today I measured Bar coming in with his cap off. I measured my boy, who has grown. I measured the new Vicar in the chapel door, the way I measured you your first week, without meaning anything by it. I measured myself in the window glass after, and none of us came out a size I liked.

I have made up the box. I have entered what I entered.

You buried the dead for God. I bury them for the account. Neither of us was ever asked what they were worth, and only one of us wrote it down.

passages.heading: Five Letters at the Fork
passages.text:
## IV. The Bartender, to the barman who went into the mere
*Monday, 20 November 1893. After closing. Low water at two minutes past nine.*

I wrote it twice. One goes in the stove.

passages.heading: The first letter
passages.text:
You,

I don't know your name. Mrs Grieves carries you at the top of every page as a little lantern in ink, and nobody drinks on your line, so that is what I call you. I'm not writing this for you. I took your place behind the bar and never once asked what you would have done with it.

Maud darned my right cuff in October and the left one on Saturday, to match. Today I carried one end of her box to the back car. Both cuffs are mended now. I have to decide which hand.

On the Tuesday I stood the platform crew nine Rotgut for the strike. Mrs Grieves asked me whose strike. The one we're having, I said, and told her to put it on my own line. That night twelve men came to the back room for the Burial Club, and nobody was buried. Len had sung Stan out at the back car at Dusk. Arthur's brother still pays a Rotgut on a closed line every week. A round is a vote you can drink. They drank it.

passages.heading: The first letter
passages.text:
Who drowned you, the mere or the Company that named the saloon? You went in after its lantern. I'd like to think you were going after something of ours.

I'll open the back room Tuesday.

I'll leave your Liquid Courage on the slate, unpaid, the way she keeps it. Tuck says the lantern in the Fenwood is lit again. I don't ask who. A drummer told Mrs Grieves that every town at the end of a line drowns its barman sooner or later. She doesn't believe him. Neither do I.

A man who goes into the water for a lantern was never asked which way. I am being asked.

passages.heading: The second letter
passages.text:
You,

I don't know your name. Mrs Grieves carries you at the top of every page as a little lantern in ink, and nobody drinks on your line, so that is what I call you. I'm not writing this for you. I took your place behind the bar and never once asked what you would have done with it.

Maud darned my right cuff in October and the left one on Saturday, to match. Today I carried one end of her box to the back car. Both cuffs are mended now. I have to decide which hand.

In October Frank said a thing about the girl Nell's fever, and I had him out the door before Mrs Grieves had her hand off the tap. A stool went, and a tooth. I found the tooth two days later under the rail, and I kept it. I don't know why. On the Wednesday I took two shells off the train. The dogs came past the shutters, and I cleaned the gun on the counter and did not look at them. They looked at me. The gun lives under the counter so I don't have to.

passages.heading: The second letter
passages.text:
Who drowned you, and did anybody ever answer for it?

I've loaded what I loaded.

I'll leave your Liquid Courage on the slate, unpaid, the way she keeps it. Tuck says the lantern in the Fenwood is lit again. I don't ask who. A drummer told Mrs Grieves that every town at the end of a line drowns its barman sooner or later. She doesn't believe him. Neither do I.

A man who goes into the water for a lantern was never asked which way. I am being asked.

---

## V. The Company Clerk, to Ivy Cotter
*Friday, 15 December 1893. After the night wire.*

Dear Miss Cotter,

East or the back car, no letter of mine will reach you. I wrote *Settled. Departed by the Line* against your name. Somebody else wrote *Gone east*. They say a box went down the line with a thimble on a string in it. I have never asked which of us was right. You will not read this. That is why I can write it.

passages.heading: The second letter
passages.text:
You are the only entry I ever made that I still read. *In arrears by the price of a lamp-wick.* You paid the wick. You sat in the dark to pay it.

Yesterday the Baron came in on the train, and on the platform he stopped being the Baron. I was at the window of the Telegraph Room with the key under my hand, and I wired it east before the Constable had his whistle out. That is what I am for.

Every bed slept in, and every bed that should have been. In person, in scrip, at noon. On the ninth, Vera's bed on Mill Row stopped being slept in. It is still on my round.

On the sixth I entered Ada Brook of Mill Row, third door, Indebted: two weeks, to the Mill at Midday. That week she lost a grey scarf at the Rush, her mother's, darned in red where the moth had it. She had paid ahead for ten wake loaves at Crumb's, which is the kind of thing you do when you think there is a week coming you won't be in. That night the key woke, and the Eastern Office asked IS ADA BROOK LIVING. I sent back ADA BROOK LIVING STOP AT MILL STOP STONE IS RUMOUR. I had sent her to the Mill myself, at noon. I had not seen her since.

passages.heading: The second letter
passages.text:
Is a woman living because I wire that she is?

Today's train brought the writ. It is in the drawer, on Company paper, under the seal. It raises the Clerk to Heir to the Baron. The Articles let the Heir declare martial law and hold every power of the President, and keep the books besides. He signed it in his own hand in November, the week he came through with the dogs. It waited back east for him to stop.

He came through this office twice and looked at my rent book and never at me. He never wrote his name in any book of mine; the Company did that for him. My mother never said his name either. She said *the Line*, the way the women on Mill Row say *the weather*. The writ names the town where she kept rooms. I never put that town on any Company form. I have been through every one I ever filled in about myself, tonight, one by one. It is not there. The writ knows it anyway.

passages.heading: The second letter
passages.text:
There is more than one thing in this town called an heir. I am only the one with paper.

Here is the rest. The rate went three to the dollar, then four, then five. I post the rent in scrip and the Company counts it in dollars, and between the board in the morning and the box at noon there is a gap a careful man could live in. I am a careful man. Nobody reads my books but me. From tomorrow, if I want it, nobody may.

I was never the cruel one, Miss Cotter. I was only the one who wrote it down. Is that worse? You would know. You sat in the dark while I wrote.

I have signed. It wanted my name either way.

You sat in the dark to pay me. I sit in the light and keep the books. The name you sign at midnight is who you are.

works.title: Censored
works.pov: first-person (three letter-writers), with the censor's marks
works.blurb: three letters out of Grounds 99 under Standing Order 14, in their file copies with the struck matter still legible: Foreman Hask to his daughter, Ada Kerrow at the Forge to the brother who named her, and the Collier at the kilns to the mother of Tony, whose name is on the board and whose lamp still burns, a letter held and never sent.

passages.heading: Censored
passages.text:
> *Outgoing correspondence shall concern the writer's health, work and family. Names, numbers, places, weather, the condition of other persons, and any reference to the program shall be struck. Struck matter is lined through in the file copy and blacked in the copy sent. A letter that cannot be struck shall be held. The censor's mark is not a reply.*
> Grounds 99, Standing Order 14 (Correspondence)

---

## I. Foreman Hask, to his daughter
*Sunday, 19 October 1952. After the second roll. For Friday's train.*

Dear girl,

I am allowed to tell you about my health, my work, and my family. So.

My health is a cough I keep short. Short is the rule here for coughing. A long one gets you sent to the doctor. The doctor gives you the tonic, and the tonic gives you a longer one.

My work is the yard and the office. I give a man a crowbar and he gives me four timber, every day, and if he gives me three I write three. I keep the key to the office. I keep the yard. And I call the roll.

passages.heading: Censored
passages.text:
I have to tell you that part, because you asked what my work is. You were always a girl who asked twice.

At midnight the whistle goes, and the men have fifteen seconds to stand by their slots. Then I read the numbers out. Not names. Numbers. I am ███ on the rack myself, so I am not above them, only in front of them. I read out ███, ███, ███, and a man answers to each one, or he doesn't.

I'll tell you about one number, since numbers are what I have.

~~He came in with a neck like a bull and a laugh you could hear across the yard. He kept a comb in his breast pocket and combed his hair before every roll, as if the searchlight were a girl. By the third week I could count his ribs through his shirt from where I stand. By the fifth his skin had gone tight over his knuckles, white, like a glove a size too small. His cheeks went in until his face was the shape of what's under a face. He showed me his gums once, laughing, and touched a tooth, and it moved. His toes went black in his boots and he stood on them for roll anyway, because standing is the rule. At the end the hair came away in the comb and he went on combing. At the end he stopped answering to his number. He answered to the whistle, before I'd said anything, the way a dog lifts its head. Then one night his slot was empty and I said the number to nobody.~~

passages.heading: Censored
passages.text:
When a man doesn't answer, there are words for it. Here are the ones they let me write: transferred. Rested. Sent down. Gone to the Blade. The camp has a word for everything that happens to a man, and none of them is the thing.

My family is you. That is the only line in this letter nobody will touch.

It ██████ on the ridge Thursday. That is all I'll say about that.

I don't know who runs this place. I mean it the way a man means it when he has said it to himself a hundred nights. There are men on the rack who carry tales, and I don't know which ones, or to whom. I don't know whether the man I'd tell would be one of them. The telephone in the office is dead. It rang once last week. I picked it up. Nobody was on it, and nobody asked me afterward why I'd been in the office at that hour, which is worse than if they had. The ███████ ███████ does not need to ask. A dozen men in the mess have started humming together when the whistle goes, all at once, the same note, and I did not teach them that.

passages.heading: Censored
passages.text:
One more thing. It is not a number, so maybe it will reach you.

In the office drawer, under the payroll ledger with its torn page, there is an old freight tag. Card, gone soft. The ink has gone brown. It has one word on it: HOLLOWMERE. I asked about. Nobody here has heard of it. And separate from that, because I want to be honest about what I know and what I don't: there is an old railroad bed out past the ██████ ███████, over the █████████, and it goes ███. Nobody keeps it. The ties are mostly gone. It still goes.

I don't say the tag and the bed go together. I say a rail goes somewhere, and so does a tag.

If a rail goes somewhere, where does a man go who is called and doesn't answer? ~~Not down any rail. I have seen where. I have seen what he is when he gets there.~~

passages.heading: Censored
passages.text:
Don't write back about the rail. Write me about you. What you're reading, what you're cooking, whether the step is still loose.

I read the numbers out so nobody has to hear their own name. That is the kindest thing I do here, and it is not kind.

passages.heading: Your father
passages.text:
`PASSED. Struck as marked. CENSOR No. 4.`

---

## II. Ada Kerrow, at the Forge, to her brother Carl
*Sunday, 16 November 1952. The hearth banked. For Friday's train.*

Carl,

Health. Work. Family. In that order, they tell me, as if that were the order.

Health: my hands are good. The left one burned in ████████ and healed shiny. I keep it out of the trough now. I keep the trough clean, too. A clean trough is the one thing in this place I can make true by Sunday.

Work: I am the forge. The warmest light in the camp, the men say, and they stand in the door to say it. They bring me ore from the seam, and I tell every one of them the same thing: "Three tin ore from the seam. I will make you a lantern for it." When the ore is good I tell them, "Good ore. This burns bright." It nearly always is. They pick it as if their lives were in it.

passages.heading: Your father
passages.text:
I name each lantern while I seal it. Under my breath, not out loud. Not their numbers. Names I make up. Bess. Little Hob. Jenny Wren. It's a habit, and I'm keeping it.

The men take the lanterns down. Some of the lanterns come back up. Lanterns issued: ███. Returned: ███. You see how it is. I am not allowed my own arithmetic.

So I'll say it the other way. There are ten billets on a rack. I have made a lantern for every man on a whole rack. Then for a whole rack again. Then again. Then again. I don't count the lanterns that come back. I count the ones that don't, the way you count steps in the dark, and I am past the end of more racks than I like.

And some come back that I wish hadn't.

~~Little Hob came up in the ore cart on Tuesday under a tarp, still lit, still hooked on the man I made it for. Two of his fingers were through the bail and would not come out of it. They were blue to the nail, and the skin of that hand had gone loose and white and soft, like a glove you've been washing in. His face had been in water a long time. I did not know him by his face. I knew him by the lantern. He'd scratched a mark on the base with a nail, a little house, I don't know why. They sent the lantern back to me to be cleaned. I cleaned it. That is my work.~~

passages.heading: Your father
passages.text:
~~Another came up dry. A man walked it up the ladder himself, which they say is luck. His ears were black. The tips of his fingers were black and hard, like the end of a burnt match. His lips were split and gone grey. He handed me the lantern and asked if he could warm his hands at my fire, and I said yes, and he held them out to it and could not feel it, and he kept them there anyway, smiling, because he thought he ought to.~~

There is a house on the row that my forge cannot warm a nail in. I took a hinge to it once. I don't say which house, and I don't go back.

Family: you.

They don't let me write about why I'm here, so I will write about you instead, and you can work out the rest. You sat in front of the ████████ ██ ███-████████ ██████████ in a pressed shirt. I know the shirt. I ironed it for you in ████. They read you a list, and you said one name off it, and the name was mine.

passages.heading: Your father
passages.text:
Did they ask you to say it, or did you offer?

I don't need an answer. I have had a long time at the anvil to write your answer for you, both ways. Both ways you were frightened, and both ways I am here.

I make a light for every man they send down. Who made one for me?

You did, once. Do you remember? The tin lantern from the dump, the one we soldered on the back step, that leaked oil down your sleeve. I still have it. They let me keep it because it doesn't work. I have never fixed it. I could. I'm the best smith in this camp. I haven't.

I don't forgive you. I'm not cursing you either. I haven't the oil to spare for it.

You gave them my name. I give the dark a light. Only one of us did the work we were sent for.

passages.heading: Ada
passages.text:
`PASSED. Struck as marked. CENSOR No. 4.`

---

## III. The Collier, at the kilns, to Mrs. ██████
*Sunday, 14 December 1952. Clamp lit. Not for any train.*

Dear Mrs. ██████,

You will not know my hand. I sold your son charcoal.

I am allowed to write about my health, my work and my family. My health is the kilns. My work is the kilns. I had no family but the men who bought from the kilns, and Tony was one of them. So this letter is within the rules. I have read them.

I burned on this slope before there was a fence on it. Before there were numbers. Your boy would come up the skid road at the end of a shift, black to the eyes, and buy a sack for your stove. He lit his lamp at the kiln mouth because, he said, my fire was cheaper than his matches. It was a joke. He made it every time. I laughed every time. That is how you know a man, Mrs. ██████. By what he says every time.

passages.heading: Ada
passages.text:
He went down into the ████ █████ one morning and he did not come up. You know that much. They told you "lost". Here is the rest.

When the fence came, men came with it, from ███ █████ ████, in good coats, with maps that were wrong. They needed someone who knew the old workings. I knew them. I showed them the way down. I did not tell them who was still in it.

Why didn't I? I have asked it every night since, at the clamp. Because they were paying. Because they would have found it anyway. Because I was afraid. Pick one. I have picked all three, on different nights.

In ████████ they took me down again, to show the new men the water. So I have been to his light. I'll set it down plain, because you are owed plain.

There is a refuge at the bottom of the old workings, with a table and a bunk. His lamp is on the table, and it is burning. Brass, wiped clean, the wick trimmed. It has been burning all this time.

passages.heading: Ada
passages.text:
The men in the bunks say nobody fills it. That's a story for the bunks. They fill it. Every man they send down to the water fills that lamp before he goes in. The oil is the camp's. I have seen it go down in the cans.

Tony is not there. I looked for him, Mrs. ██████. I will tell you that much for myself. I'd have known him by his coat, which was his father's and too big for him, and by his left hand, with the two fingers short from the saw before he ever went under. There is nothing to know him by. The bunk is empty under its dust. The dust on the table lies thick and unbroken round the lamp, as if no one had ever sat there. Whatever took him took all of him.

I did not go in. I stood on the ledge above the water with the new men, and I looked at what was there instead.

passages.heading: Ada
passages.text:
~~The water comes up to the sill of the refuge and stops there. At the edge of the light, where the lamp gives out, there are men crouched. Or there were men. They have gone long, as if something had pulled them out at both ends. White like bread left in the rain. The skin drawn tight to the bone, the ribs standing out like the slats of a crate, the nails gone off their fingers and the tips black with frost. One still has camp issue on, his number stitched on the breast, the shirt hanging off him like a flag off a pole. Their chests don't move. Then one of them heaves, once, a great drag of air, and goes still again. They don't look at us. They look at the lamp. All of them. The way you'd watch a door for somebody due home.~~

~~Those are the detail men. They filled his lamp, and went into the water, and that is what came back to the sill.~~

passages.heading: Ada
passages.text:
That is what sits round your son's light now. The camp keeps it burning, and they keep it company.

His name is on the board in the Workings, from the last shift before the camp. Chalk. Most of them can't read it. I can. I don't say it to anybody. Who would I tell? Who would let me? Who would they send down next, for asking?

A man came on the Friday train with his own chair, ███ █████████-███████. Friday last they took another off the platform in a good coat, and since then nobody asks anything about anything. That is the weather here. That is all the weather I'm allowed.

My work is the clamp. Every man who comes to the kilns, I tell him: "Three good stones for the clamp, and take a torch with you." And when he has set them, I tell him, "It will hold. Keep that torch up." I say it to every one of them, every time. Like Tony's joke. It is how they will know me.

passages.heading: Ada
passages.text:
I don't know if you're living. I don't know if this goes past the fence. I am writing it so that it is written somewhere: he was a man who made the same joke every time, and paid in coin, and his name was Tony, and his light is still down there.

It will hold. Keep that torch up. A name on a board at dawn is who you were.

`HELD. Not to be forwarded. Writer to be spoken to. CENSOR No. 4.

works.title: Black Wax
works.pov: first-person, five letters (a Gallery house; the holder of slot forty; Bastien Leclou; the Committee of the Common Loaf)
works.blurb: five pigeon letters of the Black-Crust Contract: in 1788 a Gallery house buys a death from slot forty, and an old Apprenti accepts; a Plongeur, Bastien Leclou, writes to his sister and is found at his station with his hands in the water; in 1793 his sister, now the Committee's Secretary, sends the same bird to the same slot against the house of Maillard, and the slot-holder's last letter, never sent, says he has chosen twice.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
> *A cylinder is addressed to its slot, and not to a name. The slot is not a name. What is put in a slot is the slot's.*
> Ordinance of the Sovereign Sourdough Council, on the post-loft and the station slots

---

## I. A house of the Gallery, to the holder of slot forty
*The eve of the Feast of the First Loaf, November 1788. Black wax, a fleck of gold leaf pressed into it.*

To the slot,

You will forgive the paper. Its edge was gilt, and a servant has been at it with a knife. Badly. A house cannot write on anything else, and a house does not wish to be known by its edges.

We write on a small matter.

There is a man of the dish pit, a Plongeur by birth, called Bastien Leclou. On the third night of this month he stood in Gallows Square and counted the Hearth's dead aloud. He reached a number the Council has not published. On the fifth night, in the Tavern, he said a Council name without its title. Those are the whole of it. We do not add to them, because a house does not need to.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
You will find with this a vial of Nightshade Glaze. You will know what is done with it. A house does not write such things.

Our terms are three.

Before the Feast, so that supper is not disturbed.
Not on a Thursday. The Chancellor dines on Thursdays.
Quietly. We are giving the Feast.

We enclose the card so you understand the evening we are protecting:

*Cod cheeks in white butter. The First Loaf, gilt. A swan of spun sugar. Pears in the Abbey's wine. The cloches lifted at the eighth bell.*

What is one platter, against a Hall?

For your trouble, your platter will be registered for one year and your tariff paid to the token. You may lift your own cloche at dawn without fear. If you want the Morning Ferry, there is a place on it. We cannot raise you. We can keep you.

Answer in the same wax. Do not write the name back. The bird knows its loft.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
A house is not cruel. A house is only kept.

---

## II. The holder of slot forty, to the house that did not sign
*The same night, after the dusk loaf. In the same wax.*

To the house,

The bird came in late, after the seating, which no bird should. Nobody logged it. Nobody logs birds.

I am the old Apprenti. You know the office even if you don't know the man. L'Apprenti is the one who watches, and the disgrace of the office is speaking. In forty-one years I have not spoken once at my bench. They forbade my mouth. They forgot my hand.

So I will use the hand.

I have watched the bake. I have watched the Hall at the seating, every loaf called and every cloche set down. I have watched the Square on the mornings of the Fire: the cloches, the music, the bell, the supper after. I keep a list of everything I have watched. It is longer than any list of things I have done.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
My tariff is three weeks behind. The Ledger-Clerk has the stamp inked. I have seen the word on other men's platters, and I have watched what the Council stops feeding.

What is a man who only watches, if not a knife no one has picked up?

You have picked me up. I won't pretend I'm sorry. I want the stamp off my platter. I want to lift my cloche at dawn and find my own name under it. That is the whole of why. I will not dress it as anything better.

I know the man you mean. I will not write him back.

I will do the thing you ask, to the one you name.

Keep the ferry place. I have never been off this rock, and I am too old to learn the water.

You have bought a hand. You have not bought a witness. I was always both.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
## III. Bastien Leclou, to his sister at the dish pit
*The night before the Feast, 1788. Folded twice, with the comb inside.*

Agathe,

I'm putting the comb in with this, so you can't tell me again it isn't finished. It is. It's cod bone, from the big one off the Flats last spring. I've been rubbing it down with sand for a year because I wanted the teeth even. They aren't. Wear it anyway.

I've been frightened all week and I can't tell you of what. Nobody has said anything to me. Nobody has done anything to me. Maybe that's it.

You know what I do at dusk. The Aboyeur carries the loaf down the Hall and sets it on the empty platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal, and the night starts from that loaf. Then I stand outside the great doors and say the Unregistered names out loud, every one I know. There is one loaf I can't say a name for. I say the rest.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
Somebody has to. The board doesn't. The ledger doesn't. The Hall calls only the names that are paid.

And the count. I know they heard me count. I'd do it again. The Hearth has taken more than its number, and a number isn't a crime just because the Council won't print it.

Who counts the counters?

Here's a strange thing, and a good one. The old Apprenti, the one who's watched from his bench for forty years and never said a word, has started watching me. In the Square. In the Tavern while I mend the chairs. At the doors at dusk. I think he's the only one in the Hall who sees me. I nodded to him on the stair. He didn't nod back, but he can't, can he. It's his office.

Kneel on the seal, Agathe, because they make you.
Kneel on the seal, and count while you kneel.
Kneel on the seal, and don't let them tell you the number.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
I'll come down after the Feast with whatever they scrape off the plates. Cod cheeks, if the gallery leaves any. It never does.

They can take the number off the board. They cannot take it out of my mouth.

Your brother,
Bastien

---

## IV. The Committee of the Common Loaf, to the holder of slot forty
*March 1793, the week before the spring ferry. Black wax. The Committee found no other in the loft.*

Citizen of the slot,

The Committee of the Common Loaf, sitting in the Hall, has taken into common keeping the loft of the citizen formerly of the house of Maillard.

In it the Committee found: one bird, still wearing black wax on its ring. The house's copy-draft of a commission, November 1788, naming Bastien Leclou of the dish pit. And an answer in the same wax, unsigned, from a slot. It names no one. It says: *I will do the thing you ask, to the one you name.*

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
A slot that has answered once will answer again.

Bastien Leclou was found at his station in the dish pit at the dawn bell on the Feast-day, with his hands still in the water. The Hall ruled that he had died Unregistered. It fined his platter the cost of his own burial. His sister paid it on her knees, at the rate a Plongeur is paid, over two years.

The Committee encloses his last letter, so that you know what kind of house it is.

The citizen formerly Maillard is charged with these:

Gold leaf on the cuffs, in a hungry year.
White bread on his table in the black year.
The keeping of a loft.
Feeding the loft's birds by hand every morning, and giving them names. One of them is *Douce*. The Committee lists it because it was found in his own hand, and the Committee lists everything it finds.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
The Committee has taken into common keeping, from the Apothecary's register, the Nightshade Glaze the house left behind. A vial comes with this. You will know what is done with it.

Our terms are three.

After the Supper of the Equal Loaf, so that supper is not disturbed.
Before the spring ferry brings the Razor, so that the Committee is not obliged to share him with the Square.
Quietly. We are giving the Supper.

The Committee holds the Counting-House ledgers now. A ledger is read from the top.

The Hall is ours. The forms were always the Hall's.

*For the Committee, the Secretary, who knelt in the dish pit*

*In my own hand, and not the Committee's: the citizen enclosed was my brother. The comb came folded in his letter. I have worn it five years. I want it back. Send it with your answer. That is my surety and not the Committee's. I am not asking you whose hand it was in 1788. I am asking you to be a hand now.*

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
## V. The holder of slot forty, to Bastien Leclou
*March 1793, the night the bird came. No wax. Folded once and left in the slot.*

Bastien,

I'm writing to you because you are the only one on this rock who can't read it.

The bird is on the sill. It's the same bird. I would know it anywhere: it holds its left foot up when it waits. It flew to the only slot it knows, and the only slot it knows is mine.

Your letter came in with it. I have read it nine times. *I think he's the only one in the Hall who sees me.*

You were right. I was the only one who saw you. That is how I found you.

I watched you at the doors. I watched you at the chairs. I watched you on the stair when you nodded to me. I couldn't nod back. You thought it was my office. It was the vial in my apron.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
I said I wouldn't write you back. I am writing you back now, all of it, to a slot that cannot answer.

The Feast-eve. The vial. The dish pit at the dawn bell. Your hands in the water. That is all of it I will set down, and it is more than the Hall ever did.

The house kept me for a year, exactly as it promised, to the token. Then it stopped. In 1790 the Commons stamped my platter Unregistered anyway, for having been kept. I turned the ferry down because I had never been off the rock. That was the reason I gave. The truth is meaner. The Hall is the one place where my watching was ever worth anything, and I would not give it up.

Your sister has your comb in her hair. She wants it back. She is asking for it from the hand that killed you, and she says she isn't asking whose hand.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
Is it justice if the same hand does it twice?
Is it penance if I'm paid?
Is it anything at all, if no one ever reads it?

One bird. One slot. One hand.
Two masters. Two waxes. One hand.

I could refuse. Then the Committee reads the ledger from the top, and my answer of 1788 is near the top. I could take the ferry at last. It casts off at dawn, and the Razor comes in on the next one. I could do nothing. I have done nothing for forty-one years, and I know what nothing costs: it costs exactly what someone else decides.

So I will choose this time, and not be chosen. I will choose the house that bought me. I will choose your sister's surety. I will choose a man who names his birds, because a Committee told me to. I don't know if that makes me better or worse. It makes me the same.

passages.heading: Black Wax
passages.text:
At dusk, after the loaf, I'll seal the comb in the cylinder and write the answer under it. The same words. I have only ever had the one answer:

*I will do the thing you ask, to the one you name.*

This letter stays in the slot. It's yours.

A slot does not choose what is put in it. A hand does. I have chosen twice.

---

*[Cylinders I and II, and the draft of I: the loft of the citizen formerly Maillard, inventory of the Committee, 1793. III: enclosed with IV. V: unsealed, found folded in slot forty of the second rack. The answer sent at dusk is not in the inventory. The bird is not entered.]*

works.title: One Shot
works.pov: three letter-writers in first person (the Ranger, the Watchman, the Gamekeeper)
works.blurb: three letters, 4–6 December 1893: the Ranger gives her one white-threaded arrest bolt to the stood-down Watchman and writes to the Magistrate of the Territory why; the Watchman writes to the dead Hattie, in six numbered steps, how before dawn he spent the bolt on a wolf that had Agnes by the arm at the pump ("One shot, and the whole square went quiet"); the Gamekeeper hangs the wolf from the gallows beam, where the crows take its eyes by noon, and writes to the dead Aldous Vane his standing order for his own one shot.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
> *One shot, and the whole square goes quiet.*
> said in HollowMere

---

## I. The Ranger, to the Magistrate of the Territory
*Monday, 4 December 1893. Hale Barn, under the pelt. The goat watching.*

Sir,

You signed my paper standing up, in a room with one chair, and you did not look at me while the ink dried. One arrest, once, in the name of the Territory and not of the Company. I have carried it folded in my coat since. I am not going to send you this. I am writing it because your paper says a thing I did this morning cannot be done, and somebody ought to be told so in writing.

The bow I carry slung. The bolts I carry in the quiver. One I carry apart, in a loop on my belt, its fletching tied with white thread so that I cannot use it by mistake. That one is your paper. The rest is wolves.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
I have not used it. I have been in HollowMere longer than the talk that says the town is waiting for someone like me, and I have not used it once.

On Saturday night I was out past the Gallows Wood edge, where the planks stop. I go out there to count. The pack was at the den and along the far side of the Fenwood, and I counted them there by my torch. There were no wolves in the square. Not one.

At the foot of the Rise somebody cried that there were. The Watchman left the wash-house door to go and meet them, because that is what a lantern is for. Hattie died behind the door he left.

In the morning at the Bell a voice said it plainly: there were no wolves in the square last night. It said it louder than he had told the truth. It was true. I knew it was true better than anyone on that square. And it was used. It came down on his heel, and the square looked at his heel, and the voice said one more word, and the square took the word up until it belonged to nobody.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
They did not give him the rope. They gave him three months' scrip, and they took his lantern off him on the table beside the thread, and they stood him down.

I said nothing. I stood at the back with your paper in my coat and said nothing.

In November I told the new priest I was more afraid of being right than of being wrong. He told me to wait. I waited.

Here is what being right looks like in HollowMere. Cuffs. The square. A meeting that opens on a face already closed. Then the beam at the Bell, and the crows. If I am right, your paper does that. If I am wrong, your paper does that too. The paper does not know the difference. Only the hand does.

Is a right still a right when it changes hands at a pump?

This morning the Watchman came past the pump without a lantern. You hear him before you see him; he drags his left heel. They took the light off him and he walks the lanes anyway, in the dark, where the wolves do not run from him, because he does not know what else he is for.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
I did not give him my paper. I did not give him my name. I gave him the one shot.

The bow, and the white bolt, and nothing to go with it. I cut the loop off my belt and tied it to his sling, so he would carry it where I carried it. One, so that he would have to choose. He took them without a word. His heel went once on the stone, and he went on up the lane.

I kept the snare. I kept the torch for the den. The wolves were never what I needed a bow for.

The Territory gave me one arrest. I gave it to the only man in HollowMere who already knows what being wrong costs.

---

## II. The Watchman, to Hattie
*Wednesday, 6 December 1893. Before the Station Rush. No lantern.*

Hattie,

You paid me in sheets. You said it would be the first bed I'd had with no holes in it. It was. I still sleep in them. I sleep in them by day now, because the nights are not mine to sleep.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
You can't read this. Nobody in this town will hear me say the word *door*, so I am saying it to you. Door.

I left yours. Somebody cried wolves in the square from the pines side, high, pitched to carry, and I looked at your door, and I looked at the dark, and I went. There were no wolves. You came in humming with the last basket, the tune with no words left in it, and you thought I was still on your step. I know that from the vote. I don't know it from you.

Three months' scrip. My lantern on the table beside the thread. Stood down. Nobody stands at any door now. I walk the lanes in the dark instead, and if you hear a heel, it's mine.

There are two voices I have listened for at the Bell every morning since. The one from the pines side. The one at the table that said *rope*. I would know either of them in the dark. I don't know either of them by day. By day every voice at the Bell is loud, and every face asks who did it.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
On Monday the Ranger put her bow in my hands at the pump, and one bolt with it, tied with white thread, in a loop she had cut off her own belt. She did not say what it was for. She didn't need to. It was the arrest. I meant it for a voice. I will not write which, because I am not sure, and I was sure once at your door, and I was sure of the wrong thing.

This is last night. It took six seconds. That is as long as a wolf wants you. Then it goes home.

The last hour before light. Three lanterns on the square gone out. The fourth still burning, over the chalk and the well, because she lights it last. Agnes coming down the Row in the dark to be first at the stone, the way she is every morning, so she can tell the Row the name before it asks.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
The wolf came over the pump. They hunt the edge of the light, the town says, and never cross it. The mere-rot makes them bold. This one was bold.

**One.** I knew it was a wolf. Nobody had to cry it.

**Two.** The bolt on my sling was the arrest, and the arrest was for a voice.

**Three.** It had Agnes by the arm. Through the wool, through to the bone, shaking her the way a dog shakes a rag. Her blood on the pump handle. She did not scream. She said, *Oh*.

**Four.** Last time the wolf was a word behind me, and I ran toward it. This time it was in front of me, and there was nowhere to go that wasn't away from her.

**Five.** I spent it.

**Six.** One shot, and the whole square went quiet.

It lay at the foot of the pump with the white thread standing up out of its neck, and its jaw still shut on her sleeve. I opened the jaw with my hands. There was grey wool in the teeth, and some of her under the wool. Doc Mallory came down in a nightshirt and took her arm, and would not let me watch what the Doc did with it.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
Agnes lives. When she could talk, the first thing she said was not about the wolf. She had not been up yet. The Row would have no name today. She asked me to go up and read the stone for her. I didn't. I don't read stones.

The loop on the sling is empty. There is no arrest left on that paper. Nobody will be dragged to the square on my word. The voice is still loud at the Bell. I still know it in the dark.

Was it the right shot, Hattie, or only the sure one?

I couldn't keep your door. I couldn't keep my lantern. I kept the bolt for a voice, and I gave it to a wolf.

Once I ran from your door toward wolves that weren't there. Last night one was there, and I stood still and shot it. Neither one opens your door.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
## III. The Gamekeeper, to Aldous Vane
*Wednesday, 6 December 1893. Dusk. Hale Barn, the piece across my knees.*

Vane,

You paid me to keep the wood. My wages stopped with you. I keep it anyway. I have not gone to the Company window to ask, and nothing has come to the barn. You'll not read this. Dead men pay nothing and read less. You are the only one I answer to, and the only one who can't answer back, and that suits me.

The piece is across my knees. You paid for it out of my first wage, and I have oiled it every night since. It has one shot in it that is not for the wood. It is for the end. If they come for me, I'll not go alone. I made that bargain with myself the day you died, and I made it in your name.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
At first light I was at the Gallows Wood edge, where the planks start, and I heard one shot from the square. One shot, and the whole square went quiet. The pines went quiet with it. For the length of that quiet I thought it was mine. I thought I had fallen and not known it, and the piece had gone off at somebody on its own account. I put my hand on my own chest to see if I was there. I was. The piece was cold.

It was a wolf. The Watchman, with the Ranger's bow and no light, at the pump, and Agnes's arm in its mouth.

I went down and took it off the square. It is one of the den. I know them the way you knew your crates. Tonight I'll go past the den and count, and the count will be one short, and the short one is on the town's gallows.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
I hung it from the beam at the Bell. That is the wood's custom with a varmint: you hang it where the rest can smell it. Nobody stopped me. By noon the crows had it. The eyes first. Then the soft of the belly, opened from below, the crows going in and out of it as if it were a door. The white thread still in its neck. Grey wool still in its teeth. I left the wool.

So the beam at the Bell had a wolf on it this week, and not a man. It is the only thing I have seen on that beam that the whole town agreed was guilty.

At the Bell this morning there was talk. The wood came into the square, they said, and the wood has a keeper. Nobody put up a hand. Nobody said rope. But I felt the shot in the piece lift, the way a dog lifts its head at its name.

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
Here is the arithmetic, Vane, since you liked figures. If they had stood me on the trap this morning, I would have had my one shot. I would have had to take somebody. I do not know whom.

There is one voice at the Bell that has been louder than the rest since October. I could find it in the dark. I have found worse in the dark. But finding a thing in the dark is not the same as its being the one who came.

The new priest came out to the barn in November and sat with me and the goat. I told him about the one shot and where I was afraid it would go. He said, "Be sure." Nothing else. He preaches at dusk, I hear. I have not gone to hear it. The wood's not Christian. I'd be lying to it.

Be sure. The Watchman could be sure. A wolf on a woman's arm is sure. What is a face by lantern, at the end, when you are already going?

passages.heading: One Shot
passages.text:
What did you pay me to be sure of, Vane: the wood, or the town?

Who keeps the keeper's wood when the keeper falls?

I keep the wood. I keep the count. I keep the one shot.

So here is my order, written down, since there is nobody left to give me one. If I fall to a face I have seen by my own lantern, coming at me, I'll take it. That is the one who came. If I fall in the dark, the shot goes into the pines. The wood gets every shot I can't be sure of.

I have written it. I'll keep to it while the piece is mine to keep. I have kept your wood longer than I have kept most things.

One bolt in a wolf is the only sure shot this town has had. The rest of us carry ours like a vote with one hand.

works.title: The Red Crust
works.pov: first person (Aurèle de Sérigny, Citizen Mie), five letters
works.blurb: five letters of 1793 from a Gallery son who takes the red crust: at Candlemas Aurèle de Sérigny scrapes the gold from his cuffs before the Square and becomes Citizen Mie; he points the Committee to the window where Maillard feeds his birds, reads the dowager of Belcourt's sentence a second time when the lot falls to him, and votes with the nineteen against Évariste Vane on 2 May; his four letters to his mother go unreceived, and at Michaelmas he sends the steward the pinch of gold he kept back, weighed at "very nearly the fine".

passages.heading: The Red Crust
passages.text:
> *A white crust under a red wash is a Gallery loaf pretending, and is to be cracked before the Square.*
> The Recipe Book of the Great Hearth, the Red Crust, 1791

---

## I. Aurèle, of the house of Sérigny, to Madame his mother
*Candlemas, 1793, the night of the reading. Sealed with a thumb of crumb, there being no wax for citizens.*

Madame,

You will have heard the bell. You will not have come down for it, so I will tell you what it rang for.

At the first bell after Candlemas the committee read the Ordinances aloud in the Hall of Platters, as directed. Every article, the struck ones too, so that the Hall would hear what had been struck. When the reading was done they called me to the Square, and I went.

I have taken the red crust.

The Aboyeur lifted my platter from among ours, four chairs from the Vanes, and carried it down the whole length of the Hall to the far end, where the red crust's platters stand. He called its name as it passed, the way he calls every loaf. It was not my name. The committee has entered me in its book as *Citizen Mie*. They told me it means the inside of the loaf, which is the same in every loaf. I bowed when they said it.

passages.heading: The Red Crust
passages.text:
Then they gave me a knife from the dish pit, and before the rope pen I scraped the gold from my own cuffs. The leaf came away in flakes and fell into a dish held by a Plongeur, who did not look at me. Afterwards I ate my crust, standing. It tastes of nothing but bread.

Then I bowed to the Square.

You taught me that bow. You taught every child of the house in the long room, counting aloud. *Once to the Hearth. Lower to the gallery.* I gave the Square the first and not the second. Once, and not low. My knees remembered your counting, and I had to tell them to stop.

I have taken the red crust.
I have taken the far platter.
I have taken a name that is a crumb.

You will want to know why, and you will want it to be a better reason than it is.

passages.heading: The Red Crust
passages.text:
I am afraid, Madame. I have read the gallery's seating plans. I know which names are near the top, and I know a ledger is read from the top. That is one reason. The other is that some evenings I believe them, and on those evenings the bread does taste like bread and nothing worse. I cannot tell you which of the two lifted my hand tonight. I have been trying since the bell.

Is a man who changes sides to live a convert, or only a guest?

Come down. The Gallery stands in the rope pen at every sitting and is counted. You can stand there, or you can stand with me. They are twenty steps apart, and only one of them is in the rain.

I kept back a little of what came off the cuffs. It is mine, and it is small. I tell you so that you will not hear it from anyone else.

passages.heading: The Red Crust
passages.text:
A house can change its seat in an evening. It takes longer to change its knees.

Your son,
Aurèle ~~de Sérigny~~

---

## II. Citizen Mie to Madame his mother
*March 1793, the week before the spring ferry. Crumb seal.*

Madame,

Your steward writes that Madame does not receive the citizen. He wrote it in five words and signed it. I keep it in the book I keep the committee's minutes in.

I will write anyway. A citizen may write to anyone. It is in the new articles.

The committee did not take me for my conversion. I thought it would, and I was ready to be tested on it: the crust, the bow, the name. Nobody tested me. What they wanted was what I remembered.

Who sat where at the Feast of 'eighty-eight.
Which house had its loaves gilded double.
Whose window is whose.

They had the gallery's books by then, every seating plan back to 'eighty-seven, open on the rail. They could read the names. They could not read the rooms. A seating plan tells you who sat beside whom. It does not tell you who lowered his voice when the Chancellor came in, or which house fed birds from its upper window every morning, so that the birds knew it.

passages.heading: The Red Crust
passages.text:
I told them that. I told them which window the birds come to at the house of Maillard. I told them the citizen formerly Maillard feeds them by hand every morning and gives them names. I did not know the names. They found those for themselves, written in his own hand. The committee lists everything it finds.

The Secretary took it all down. They say of her that she knelt in the dish pit, as if it were a rank, and I think in that room it is one. Every plate I ever ate from at a Gallery supper went down to her sink. I could not look at her while she wrote, so I looked at her pen. She wrote my words exactly. She did not make them larger.

What is a turncoat but a man who knows where the other coat was hung?

The committee thanked me. Then, because there is a form for thanking and they keep the forms, they thanked me a second time.

passages.heading: The Red Crust
passages.text: They did not take me for my heart. They took me for my memory, and it is the only part of me that was ever the house's.

passages.heading: Mie
passages.text:
## III. Citizen Mie to Madame his mother
*Friday, 29 March 1793, after the ferry. Crumb seal.*

Madame,

Your steward writes that Madame's platter is a fortnight behind. He did not write anything else. I think he meant me to understand that he was not allowed to.

On Lady Day the Gallery gave its ball in the Hall. Out of habit the house's printer sent me a card, addressed to a name the committee's book no longer carries. He is paid by the year. I did not go in. I stood with the Commons outside the south doors in the Square and heard the hautboys through them. I did not look for you. I tell you so, because you will want to know whether I looked, and the answer is that I kept my eyes on the man in front of me until the music stopped.

On Tuesday the Razor came off the Morning Ferry, in crates stencilled for the committee. Guild carpenters put it together beside the Hearth, and the consort played while they did it. No one had told the consort to stop.

passages.heading: Mie
passages.text:
On Thursday they drew the lot at the committee's supper.

You know the article. You have heard it read every Candlemas of your life. *The sentence is read twice, once by the High Chancellor, and once by a member of the Gallery chosen by lot, who shall be thanked.* The committee has retained it in every particular. The question was whether my name went into the bowl. They took it gravely, the way they take everything. They ruled that Citizen Mie is red crust at the platter and gold leaf in the bowl. They did not laugh. I did not laugh. The ruling was entered.

The bowl gave them my name.

This morning, at the dawn sitting, I read the sentence of the dowager of the house of Belcourt for the second time.

You remember her. She carried her linnet's cage to the gallery window every morning of her life, so that the bird could see the harbour. At my first ball, when I was twelve and had been counted through my bows a hundred times, she danced with me because nobody else would, and she told me I bowed like a man apologising.

passages.heading: Mie
passages.text:
I read it to her from the paper. I did not look up until the end.

She thanked me. As the article requires.

I read it in my own voice.
I read it in the house's voice.
I read it in the voice you taught to bow.

The citizen formerly Maillard did not come before us. His name was on the committee's list in the week before the ferry, and before the ferry it was off it. No one struck it in my sight. I did not ask. Not asking is the form.

The Secretary wears a comb now, of cod bone, the teeth not quite even. I do not know where it came from or what it means. I noticed it because she touched it twice while the lot was drawn, and I have learned this spring to notice what people touch.

A sentence read twice is not twice as true. It only has two men to thank.

passages.heading: Mie
passages.text:
## IV. Citizen Mie to Madame his mother
*Thursday, 2 May 1793, after the sixth bell, at the committee's table. Crumb seal.*

Madame,

They tried Évariste Vane this morning. I am writing to you from the gallery, where the supper is waiting.

I sat in a gilded chair. Red crust sits in them now. Mine was four from where the Vanes used to sit, because the ushers follow the stenographer's plan and the stenographer has not changed her hand.

The south doors opened at the fifth bell, and the Square sang. Évariste was brought up from the cold pantry and set on the stool. It is the same stool. He bowed to the Square, as the Order now says, and not low. You taught him too, Madame. He was in the long room with me, counting.

The President read the charge. Then she had the stenographer read Exhibit 1, which is the Book of the Morning Judgment for the eleventh of March, 1788, read in full and standing.

passages.heading: Mie
passages.text:
I was there in 1788. You were too. I had forgotten it, and this morning I learned that I had not.

The seating was read out: the house of Vane first, and then the rest by precedence. We were the rest. Then the boy, Toinot, of the shaping bench. A bite of a gilded heel, weighed. Eleven grains. The fingernail held out over the rail. Then what he said, which the ruling would not have as testimony and the stenographer wrote down anyway: a square of sailcloth, flakes of gold leaf scraped from our crusts in the dish pit, pressed flat to be counted, for his mother's tariff. *It came to very nearly the fine.* The cracks of a loaf coming out of the oven. Ice going on the mill pond.

Then the supper card, read as served. Quince, after the Fire.

I ate the quince, Madame. I remember now that it was good.

passages.heading: Mie
passages.text:
The whole of the reading, I had my hand on my coat, over the place where the twist of paper is.

Évariste said he sat at the supper and did not speak for the boy. He did not make that into a defence. Then he asked who would go down at dawn, if his hand were stopped, since no hand but a Vane's has fed her since the Bringing. Nobody answered. The Wardens turned out his coat on the trial table: a handkerchief, a pencil, a little tin with his daughter's leaven in it, dried grey. They gave him water. He took it in the hand that does not feed her. He keeps the other from bread.

Then the committee voted, and I counted with them.

Nineteen for the Razor. Four against.

I was one of the nineteen.
