**The look.** A tinner on a timber at the gallery mouth, with his hat on his knee. On Sundays he sits there instead of in chapel. He would not come to me, so I went to him.

**Name, as given.** Norman. "Reg is the other half of the pair."

**Carries.** A lantern, a watch, chalk and rope. The Company issues them to the hands of a shut mine, so that the hands have something to hold.

**Wants.** "Work in pairs. The shut hands together. Vote on what I saw."

**Confessed.** He was on the shift of the last plug. He was Jory Kitto's pair. A pair goes down together and comes up together. He came up.

That is all of it. He has said it to the gallery mouth every Sunday since, and now he has said it to me, and he does not think it has made any difference to either of us.

passages.heading: No. 14
passages.text: I asked him whether any other tinners come to confession.

passages.heading: Eleven of us left," he said. "None come.
passages.text: I went back to the vestry that night, turned to No. 8, and wrote one word on what is left of it.

passages.heading: Where this soul stands.** *With the parish.
passages.text:
**Said.** Nothing.

**Seal.** Taken. He put it in the hat on his knee and put the hat on.

---

passages.heading: No. 15
passages.text:
**Tuesday, 14 November 1893. In the box, while the square rioted.**

**The look.** A plain coat, a lantern like Len's, and a voice like a dozen voices at the pump. At first I thought it was Len. It was not Len. Len's watch runs slow and ticks loud, and this one had no watch that I could hear.

passages.heading: Name, as given.** None. "You don't need it.
passages.text:
**Carries.** Under the coat, the shape and weight of a crowbar. It knocked the wall when the coat moved. In one hand, set down on the shelf and taken up again, a small tobacco tin with a loose lid. In it were things that were not theirs: a thread of blue wool, a little nap of hat felt, a pinch of chalk dust folded in paper.

**Wants.** A townsman's words, said easily, and the ease was what was wrong with them: "Do my share in pairs. Vote on what I saw."

**Confessed.** "I said I was with him at the pump. I was at the pump."

That was the whole of the first part. It was said twice, so that I would have it right.

Then: tonight they had broken a door. The door was already broken, they said; they had only finished it. Outside, the riot was going down the square toward the bank. We could hear it through the wall: the bell going, and glass. They were very calm.

passages.heading: Name, as given.** None. "You don't need it.
passages.text:
**Where this soul stands.** *Not learned.* I had spent riot night on another soul before this one knelt. God forgive me, I chose another.

**Said.** The next day, at the meeting by the bell, someone asked whether a man had been at the pump the night before. I said that he had. I had it from this box. That is more than the seal allows. I said it because I was asked, and I was asked because someone knew I could answer.

**Seal.** Taken, quickly, into the tin with the other things.

> *In the margin, pencil, a small hand:* Who asked you to?

---

passages.heading: No. 16
passages.text:
**Wednesday, 15 November 1893. The post at the Gallows Wood edge.**

**The look.** A woman in a man's coat, standing under the Lamplighter's lantern. The Baron's train was in at the platform with the Pinkertons on it, and their dogs.

**Name, as given.** Not given. She said a name is a thing the Company writes on a warrant.

**Carries.** A crossbow, slung. Bolts in a quiver, and one kept apart in a loop on her belt, its fletching tied with white thread so that she cannot use it by mistake. A snare, coiled. A torch, unlit, for the den.

**Wants.** "The wolves. One arrest. And to be right."

**Confessed.** She hunts wolves for the bounty. The pelt on Hale's barn door is hers. She has been in HollowMere longer than the talk that says the town is waiting for someone like her.

She holds the right of one arrest, once, on a paper from the Territory and not from the Company. She has not used it. The bolt on her belt is the arrest. The Baron's men are on the platform today, she said. If she is right about anyone, they will be the ones who do something about it. She is more afraid of being right than of being wrong.

passages.heading: Said.** "Wait.
passages.text:
**Seal.** Declined.

> *In the margin, pencil, a small hand:* Did she?

---

passages.heading: Saturday, 18 November 1893. The Constable's office.
passages.text:
**The look.** The window boarded where the riot broke it. A desk with a case file on it. A man who sat very straight, the way men sit who were once paid by the minute.

**Name, as given.** Not given. He said the Constable deputised a Detective, not a man, and may undeputise either.

**Carries.** A magnifier on a ribbon. A notebook. A lens for close work. A fingerprint kit in a tin box, the powder like soot. The stamp.

**Wants.** "Verified clues. The board narrowed. The village does the rest."

**Confessed.** He kept time in the railyard before this, and he still counts minutes. He counted ours while we talked, and told me at the end how many there had been.

The morning after the riot he stamped a thing *Verified* before he had verified it. The town needed a stamp more than it needed the truth, he said. A stamp on the board stops a mob in a way a truth does not. He did not tell me what he had stamped. He asked me not to ask, and I did not.

passages.heading: Where this soul stands.** *With the parish.
passages.text:
**Said.** Nothing. "A man who cross-references does not need a priest to agree with him." Those were his words. I write them down as his.

**Seal.** Taken. He stamped the back of the card with his own stamp before he put it away.

> *[Lower margin: a thumbprint, in ash.]*

---

passages.heading: No. 18
passages.text:
**Monday, 20 November 1893. Behind the back car, as Maud went out at Dusk.**

**The look.** A woman in a thin coat, mended at the elbows more times than I could count, walking beside me behind the back car.

**Name, as given.** Wenna. She came on the first train, to meet a man who had written that he would meet it.

**Carries.** Chalk for the ring, in a twist of paper. A candle. A small wooden spoon with a rough bowl, which she keeps in her pocket. She showed it to me and did not say who had given it to her.

**Wants.** "To hear the dead. To hear one of them stop."

**Confessed.** She did not go back east. She meant to, on the next train, and the one after. She stays because he still asks about the train. Every night, in the ring, he asks whether it has come. She tells him it has. He asks again.

passages.heading: No. 18
passages.text:
Tonight Maud is in the ring, she said, and has not yet said anything. Maud never said much in life either.

Wenna does not tell what the dead know, and I did not ask her to. The bell rang for the train. Bar carried one end.

passages.heading: Where this soul stands.** *With the parish.
passages.text: **Said.** Nothing. At the platform I lit her candle from mine.

passages.heading: Tuesday, 5 December 1893. In the box.
passages.text:
**The look.** A plain coat, which tonight did not pretend to be anything.

**Name, as given.** None.

I have heard this voice before, and I cannot find the page. Afterwards I went back through the book with the candle, one to eighteen. I came to No. 8 and its cut edge, and stopped there, and went on, and did not find it.

**Carries.** Something heavy under the coat that knocked the wall. A small tin. And a long thing wrapped in a rag, laid on the shelf by the grille while we talked and taken up again before the end. There was chaff on the rag. It had come from under some sacking.

passages.heading: Wants.** "To finish what was started. Alone, now.
passages.text:
**Confessed.** "Someone is gone, and the town does not know it yet."

Nothing more about that. Not who. Not how. Not where. I asked whether it was a death to be confessed. The voice said no: it was a death to be carried. Then it asked me the hour. I have no watch, and I said so.

**Where this soul stands.** I spent the night on this soul. *With the other.*

**Said.** Nothing. The seal. ~~Nothing. The seal.~~ I have told no one. I have told no one. I have told ~~

**Seal.** Not asked for. Not offered.

> *In the margin, pencil, a small hand:* Count the pages.

---

passages.heading: Wednesday, 6 December 1893. The vestry. My own.
passages.text: **The look.** I do not know it. A coat too good for the mud, they said at the pump in October. The mud has seen to that.

passages.heading: Name, as given.** —
passages.text:
**Carries.** A candle. ~~A watch.~~ See No. 11.

**Wants.** "To know where each of them stands. To say only as much as saves them."

**Confessed.** I have walked behind the back car for Maud. For Elsie. For Mabel. For a man from the bell whose name the Gazette would not print. Half the boots that walked behind him, he had mended. For Cyril, drowned in water I could have stood up in. For Hattie, who took in washing and gave it back folded.

I bought Liquid Courage and drank none.

On my first day I let a child's lie stand. I have let it stand every day since.

- No. 8: I learned where he stood, and wrote it, and it is gone, and I did not say.
- No. 15: I said, and should not have.
- No. 19: I learned, and I have not said.

Gold has been left at Crumb's more than once. Nobody has confessed to leaving it. I do not know that it is a sin to leave gold. I know that nobody leaves it for nothing.

passages.heading: Name, as given.** —
passages.text:
Someone burns letters in the vestry stove. I find the wax in the ash, black, run like tar.

There is ash on the margins of this book, and I did not put it there.

Agnes reads the stone to the Row at dawn. I have begun to stand behind her and listen with the others. I will hear tomorrow's name tomorrow.

**Where this soul stands.** *Not learned.* No one has spent a night on me.

passages.heading: Seal.** —
passages.text:
> *In the margin, pencil, a small hand:* Hymns: as on the wall.

---

passages.heading: No. 21
passages.text: *[Ruled in pencil, in the small hand, as the others are ruled.]*

passages.heading: Seal.
passages.text: *The page that bears your number at dawn is who you are.*

works.title: Four Notices
works.pov: multiple (Company print; four hands on the backs)
works.blurb: the Constable's four wanted notices of December 1893 (the Zealot, the Activist, the Bandit and the Hitman), each a Company front that names the deed and leaves the name blank, and each turned overnight so that the square reads a back in another hand: the candle-keeper, a railyard sleeper, Tamsin Crumb, and the one who burned the black-wax letter.

passages.heading: Four Notices
passages.text:
*The board in the square, the Constable's corner. Four notices, as found, December 1893.*

---

passages.heading: The Board
passages.text:
A notice posted on the board in the square is lawful notice to every person within the Grant. The Articles say so. They also say it holds whether the notice is read or not, and whether the person can read or not.

The board stands by the pump. Most of it belongs to the Gazette and to the ledger slips nobody admits to writing. The Constable keeps the left-hand corner. He pastes his notices there at the Station Rush, face out, with four tacks to a sheet and flour paste from Crumb's Ovens.

By the next Rush a notice has often been turned. Someone has taken it down, written on the back and pasted it up again face-in. What the square reads over its morning water is then a hand, not the Company's print. Nobody is seen doing it. Paper is short in a Panic year, and the back of a notice is a page. The Constable turns them out again, and by the next Rush they are turned.

passages.heading: The Board
passages.text:
Four hung in December. Each is for a killing, or for what a killing was for. The Company names the deed and prices it in scrip, at three to five to the dollar and falling. Then it leaves the face blank, as the Gazette does, for the Town to fill in.

The Company prints the deed. The town writes the rest. Nobody writes the name.

---

passages.heading: THE ZEALOT
passages.text:
*Date: torn away below the fold. The tacks are still in it.*

For marking five buildings within the Grant in ash and in blood: the door of St Brannock's, the grille of the Company Bank, Crumb's Ovens, the Mill, and the Station.

For desecrating St Brannock's, contrary to Article VIII.

The Company does not allege that the Vicar is dead. The Vicar preaches at dusk.

The Company's three particulars:

- **Height:** as the Vicar's.
- **Scarf:** none. A stole.
- **Hat:** none recovered.

**Trace:** candlewax, on the sill of every building marked, and on the Vicar's cuff.

**Persons sought in association, known as the Dark Positions:**

- **The Minion.** Keeps a body from being found. The Company is advised that a power is kept for as long as a body goes unfound. Bone chimes have been reported after curfew in Pump Row and at the Fenwood edge.
- **The Mob Boss.** Raises mobs against the Vicar and against every soul the Vicar has brought to faith. Shakedowns have been reported. No complainant will give a name.
- **The Cultist.** Sets the altars and recruits. Those recruited carry the faith from door to door, without the Company's licence.
- **The High Priest.** NOT SOUGHT. The Company is advised that if the Zealot is taken, the High Priest finishes it.

passages.heading: THE ZEALOT
passages.text:
If six gather at an unlicensed altar, in the Flooded Gallery or in the desecrated chapel, the Town will be told that the sky has turned and the Bell tolls backward. The Company does not recognise a crimson sky. Under Article VIII, the Bell is rung in the ordinary order only.

The Company takes no side between faiths. It will treat with whichever holds the town.

**Reward:** 200 scrip.

**Name:** ____________. Unverified. The Town may supply it.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
*Pencil, in an upright hand that presses hard. There are wax spots on the paper.*

I keep the candles at St Brannock's. I kept them for Father Bray and I keep them for the new one. I trim the wicks, I scrape the drips off the brass, and I save the ends in a box by the font. On Saturdays I melt the ends down at my own table, and the Row has light it did not pay the Company for. That is the only theft I have ever done, and I confessed it.

I went to him in October, the week he came. He asked my name and used it. Nobody had used it in a year. I told him three things. I will not write them here, because they were his.

Now I count.

One. The wax on the sills is ours. I know a chapel drip from a tallow dip with my eyes shut. My box is lighter than I left it.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
Two. At dusk he said my name the way the Company says it, as if he were reading it off a sheet.

Three. At the door I spoke to him about the second of my three things, and he did not know it.

Four. Men came to my door on Thursday at curfew. They did not come to hurt me. They came to tell me which way the town was going, and that a woman who lives alone with a box of candles should go the same way. I have opened the door to nobody since, except to him.

They say he said this, at the end:

"In the end I sought nothing else but to serve God. And serve him I did. With this death's last breath I pray this prayer: may the Almighty grant me the strength of ten in the next life. And in return, tenfold my own."

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
I did not hear it. I was not there, and nobody I know was there. The words go round the Row like a loaf passed at a wake, and every hand that passes them on is sure.

So I have worked it out at my table, the way the Detective works things. If he preaches, he is not dead. If he is dead, the one who preaches is not him. And if he is dead, the town says he will come back ten times himself: a field of lavender, one orange tree, a blue sky over them, an iron crosier, a light standing up out of the ground like a pillar.

I have seen none of it. I keep the candles.

I have not gone the way the town is going. I am still his. I no longer know which of them that makes me.

passages.heading: THE ACTIVIST
passages.text:
Saturday, 16 December 1893. *Reissued. The notice of 16 November is withdrawn.*

**For the assassination of the President of the Company, Mr C. Thorne, on the platform, on Thursday 14 December.**

For Fire in the Mill: the loft, on Tuesday 14 November. The Indebted were turned out. The Company does not enter the Indebted by name.

For Dynamite on the Tracks: four sticks, unfired, under the last mile below Gallows Wood Siding.

For conspiracy against the Company Bank and its vault.

For Public Unrest under Article X: the soapbox at the Bell, held beyond the Shift.

The Company's three particulars:

- **Height:** middling.
- **Scarf:** red, as half the railyard wore on 14 November.
- **Hat:** a man's, felt, found at the soapbox. She did not come back for it.

**Trace:** black powder. Powder is delivered daily to the railyard, by the Train.

**NOTICE OF REDEMPTION.** If she is taken, or gives herself up, the Town will vote at the Bell on her Redemption. If she survives the vote, she will be restored to the rolls as Townsfolk under Article X. Her speech will be struck from the record. Her account will not.

passages.heading: THE ACTIVIST
passages.text: **[ CONSTABLE — HOLLOWMERE ]** *Countersigned below the stamp, in a narrow hand.*

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
*A railyard pencil stub. The hand is unsteady on the figures.*

I sleep in the railyard bunks at ninety cents a bed, and I am two weeks behind. Every other week I send a postal order east to a girl who thinks I cook for a hotel. I read the reward three times before I understood it. Then I worked out how many of my weeks it was, which is the only way I know how to read a number. It is a lot of weeks.

I was in the square on the fourteenth of November. Everybody was. I stood near enough to the soapbox to have seen her face, and I didn't look at it. I looked at her hands, because they were black at the nails with powder, the same as mine and the same as everyone's from the yard. Powder comes up on the Train every morning, and we load it with our hands. If black under the nails hangs a woman, it will hang the whole railyard.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
I was on the platform on the fourteenth of December. I heard it and I did not see it, because I was looking at the train, the way everybody looks at the train. Then there was a hat on the boards, and the Pinkertons had their dogs out, and nobody in the town was looking at anybody.

Now there is to be a vote.

They say it is about her. It isn't. The Bell will be asking whether we forgive the hand that loosened the grip, and so whether we forgive ourselves for cheering when it did. That is what the vote is for.

Only the grip did not loosen. Look at the foot of the front. The countersign is not the Constable's, and it is not Thorne's, which I never saw. It is a hand I have seen before, and I cannot think where. I don't like that I can't. The reward is paid at the Midday Rent.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
Thorne came by train and left by train. Whoever signs now doesn't need the train. He is already here.

They say Thorne had no sons. They say it the way people say a thing they have been told to say.

I know how I will vote. I am not writing it down.

passages.heading: THE BANDIT
passages.text: Monday, 11 December 1893. *Reissued from the Gazette of Thursday 7 December, with additions.*

passages.heading: Scores:
passages.text:
1. **Crumb's Ovens.**
   - *First.* The week of 16 October, Wednesday or Thursday night; reported 5 December. The till was emptied. A gold coin was left on the hearth-lip. A bootprint in the flour dust, long in the stride, the toe toward the back door.
   - *Second.* Monday night, 4 December. The till was emptied. One gold coin was left on the counter, as a tip.
2. **The plate of St Brannock's.** Sunday 10 December, after the dusk sermon. A brass casing, .45, spent, was found standing upright where the collection had been. No shot was heard.
3. **The Company Bank, the vault.** Not yet.
4. **The Daily Train, the express safe.** Not yet.

The Company's three particulars:

- **Height:** short, by the bootprint in the spilt flour.
- **Scarf:** grey wool. Thread found caught on the till.
- **Hat:** none recovered.

By report: a bandana, and a six-shooter.

**Traces:** flour dust; a brass casing (.45).

passages.heading: Scores:
passages.text:
Gold tendered within the Grant is scrip until proven otherwise.

**Reward:** 300 scrip.

**Name:** ____________. Unverified. The Town may supply it.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
*Pencil. Flour in the creases of the sheet. Tamsin Crumb's hand.*

I am the robbed, so they say I may write.

There are three gold coins behind the crock in my cold room, in the place a hand can go.

The first is October's. The till was emptied on the Wednesday or the Thursday night (the week ran together). The coin was on the hearth-lip, the way you tip for good bread, and there was a boot in the flour dust, long in the stride, the toe toward the back door.

The second came on the twenty-sixth of October, and I did not put it there. Nobody had been at my till that night, but somebody had been behind my crock. Somebody knows the place a hand can go. I fed the crock that morning at the island's hour as I always do, with my back to the door, and I have fed it that way every morning since, because there is no other way to feed it.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
The third is the fourth of December's. It was on the counter this time, and the print was short.

The two prints do not agree. One is a long stride and one is a short one. I have stood in both, in my own flour, to see. I fit neither, and I fit both, depending on how I walk. So it was two men, or one man walking two ways, or a man and a woman. Half the women of Mill Row are short. So am I. Grey wool is what a mill town wears. And I sweep. I always sweep. That is the trouble with having a baker for a witness.

On the Tuesday after the fourth, a woman paid me in full, in scrip, for ten wake loaves for her Row, and asked that the Row not be charged. I will not lay the one beside the other. Scrip is scrip. Everyone in this town has some, and none of it is theirs.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
On Sunday they took the plate at St Brannock's and left a spent shell where the coins had been. The bakery gets gold and God gets brass. I do not know what that says about the bread.

I cannot spend the coins. Gold asks where it came from, and the Company says gold is scrip until proven otherwise. I have three proofs, and I will not show them.

I have been robbed by someone who tips. I would rather it had been someone who didn't. A thief who takes is only a thief. A thief who pays is keeping an account.

*Tag: everything is owned, so everything can be taken, and someone is keeping count.*

---

passages.heading: THE HITMAN
passages.text:
Tuesday, 12 December 1893.

For the death of ____________, a man of the railyard bunks who came up the Line in October. He was found at the Station Rush on the bench by the platform lantern. The Gazette prints no unverified name, and neither does the Company.

By a needle, or a small-bore pistol. The Doctor's autopsy places the death before curfew ended.

The Company's three particulars:

- **Height:** unknown. No print on the boards.
- **Scarf:** none.
- **Hat:** felt, brown, common.

**Trace:** a seal of black wax, broken, on the boards beside him. No letter was found.

**NOTICE REGARDING BLACK WAX.** Correspondence sealed in black wax is correspondence of the Company and is exempt from the right to read (Article VI). The Company acknowledges no contract and offers no reward.

He will be on the Dusk train. So will others.

**Name:** ____________. Unverified. The Town may supply it.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
*Ink, from a bottle nearly dry. Small writing, to fit.*

It came in the mailbag in November and was put into my hand at the window. The Postmaster did not look at it, and he did not write down that he had given it to me. Black wax, no sender. Inside, one printed line:

Burn the Letter & Keep Your Mundane Life, OR Accept the Baron's Contract.

Under the line, a name. I knew the name.

I burned it in the stove before I had finished being afraid. I kept my mundane life. Here it is: the rent at the Shift; the kettle on at five; my neighbour's lamp, which I trim for him because his hands shake. That is the size of it. I chose it, and I would choose it again. Write that down too.

I knew him. He was always early for the Train. He sat on the bench by the platform lantern an hour before the Rush every morning, in case it came early, which it never has. He kept his scrip in a sock and a one-way ticket in his hatband, and he was saving toward the date on it. January, he told me. He said it the way people here say "back east", as if it were a place you could already see from the platform. I will not write his name on the back of the Company's paper.

passages.heading: Back
passages.text:
But I burned it, and he died anyway, on his bench, with black wax on the boards beside him.

So there was another letter, in another bag, to another hand, and that hand did not burn it. Nobody starts as the Hitman. I know that now from the other side. Somebody finishes as one.

Burning it kept my life the size it was. It did not keep his any size at all.

They say on the platform that the Baron is dead now, and that the contract was his. They say the wax still comes.

The Train comes at the Rush, and the bag comes with it. Check yours.

*Tag: nobody starts as the Hitman; somebody always finishes as one.*

---

passages.heading: The Board, at Dawn
passages.text:
The Constable pastes the four face-out at the Station Rush. He uses fresh tacks and fresh paste. He stands back to see that they hang straight.

By dawn they are turned again: four backs to the square and four hands where the print was. Under every front there is the same line, set by the Company in the same type. Nobody has filled it in. Everybody has read it.

*The blank on the board at dawn is who you are.*

works.title: Persons of Note
works.pov: first-person (the Postmaster, with the Clerk's margins)
works.blurb: the Postmaster's who-to-ask guide for persons arriving by the Daily Train, handed across the sorting table on 11 December 1893: the landmark figures, those who keep terms, the law, the house and the wood and those who come by train, each with where to find them, what they ask, what they give, what not to say and what post they get, under the Clerk's pencilled approvals, and ending on the persons not entered.

passages.heading: Persons of Note
passages.text:
*Who to Ask in HollowMere. For the Use of Persons Arriving by the Daily Train.*
*Issued from the Post Office & Telegraph Room, HollowMere, Coldwater Territory. December 1893.*
*Copy handed across the sorting table, Mon. 11 Dec.*

> *Approved for issue. — Clk.*

---

Nobody comes to the end of the line without a reason. I do not ask yours. Your letters will tell me, or the lack of them will.

This is a list of who to ask. It is not a list of who to trust. The Company prints the one and not the other.

passages.heading: Before You Ask Anyone
passages.text:
1. Ask by daylight. After Curfew, the answers come from people you did not ask.
2. Ask in pairs. The town counts alibis in twos, and so should you.
3. Pay in scrip. It was three to the dollar in October. It is five now. Do not ask what it will be.
4. Rent is collected at the Shift, by the Clerk, from everyone under a roof. A guest is under a roof.
5. Do not read the stone in the churchyard aloud. Agnes reads it to the Row each dawn. Let her.
6. Do not follow a light in the fen unless you know whose it is.
7. Don't miss the train.

> *Rule 5 is not Company policy. — Clk.*

---

passages.heading: Mrs Grieves — the Drowned Lantern
passages.text:
*Where to find her.* Behind the bar, from Station Rush until the shutters come across at Curfew. After the shutters, what burns in there is her business.

*What she asks.* That you pay your tab, and that you never try to close anyone else's.

*What she gives.* Whiskey off the train, four cases a week with one short-filled, which she notes and does not complain of. A lantern on loan if you need one, and she will not ask where you mean to carry it.

*What not to say.* Do not count the frames behind the bar out loud. There were six when I last stood there: drowned sailors, one frame empty, and one face nobody admits to hanging. Do not ask after Frank. Bar, her hired man, keeps the sawed-off under the counter. Do not ask him which side of the strike it is for. He has been asked, and he has answered both ways.

passages.heading: Mrs Grieves — the Drowned Lantern
passages.text:
She keeps a line open for Arthur, who died of the cough last winter. His brother pays for a Rotgut on it every week. She has never struck the line through.

*Post.* None. She says anyone who wants her can walk in.

**Old Fennick — the light at the marsh edge**

*Where to find him.* At his light below the Fenwood, every dusk. On Saturdays he is at the Lantern, filling his can.

*What he asks.* Nothing. If you bring him oil he takes it and tells you its price, to show you he knows.

*What he gives.* He will tell you which light is his, which is worth more than it sounds. Stand at the end of the planks on a fog night and count the lights on the fen. One of them is steady. Ask him which.

*What not to say.* There is a lantern under the water by the old oak, and it burns. Do not ask him about it, and do not ask him who keeps it lit. Some say it is the lamp he kept when there was a lake, gone down with the limb that held it. Some say it is the sign of the old Rusty Lantern, carried into the mere by a barman who never came up. Fennick has heard both, and he says neither.

passages.heading: Mrs Grieves — the Drowned Lantern
passages.text:
He was nineteen when he had a lake to keep. He is old now, and his light guides nobody anywhere in particular. He keeps it all the same. The Lamplighter lights the square and does not light his, and he would not let her.

*Post.* None that I have carried.

**Father Bray — St Brannock's (not to be found)**

*Where to find him.* You will not find him.

passages.heading: What he asks.* —
passages.text:
*What he gives.* The bell. He had it off the Company for the chapel, and it hangs at St Brannock's still.

*What not to say.* Do not say he died, and do not say he fled. Either earns you a look across the bar. Both together earn you a drink, because the town says both, and says them louder after the second pour. The Gazette answers no enquiries regarding Father Bray, and neither do I.

The town remembers that he darned his gloves in red wool. It remembers this the way you remember a man's hands.

Letters still come for him from back east, in two different hands. I hold them. I do not send them back, because there is nowhere certain to send them.

For confession, go to the new Vicar, who came up on the train on the seventeenth of October with one trunk. He preaches at dusk. Everyone in HollowMere confesses to him sooner or later; he is patient, and it is a small town. Say what you came to say. When you leave, look at who is kneeling at the back, and do not let them see you look.

passages.heading: What he asks.* —
passages.text: *Post.* See above.

passages.heading: Doc Mallory — Mallory Apothecary
passages.text:
*Where to find the Doc.* At the bench by day, and at the Bell whenever it rings. At other hours, upstairs under the green lamp in the loft, at times you should not be passing.

*What the Doc asks.* Your name, for the stock book. Every bottle on the shelf has a line in that book, and every line has a name and a date. Give a true name.

*What the Doc gives.* Salts and bandages. Notice of the fen-cough, posted on my board and in the Gazette and worded as the Company asks: *miasma*. And when it comes to it, the hour you died, which is the one thing in this town that breaks an alibi.

*What not to say.* There is a shelf marked NOT FOR SALE with one slot empty. Do not ask what stood in it, or when it went. Mallory knows both.

*Post.* Tonics for the morgue come up crated on the train. I sign for them, and Mallory signs again. Nobody has explained to me why it takes both of us.

passages.heading: Tuck — the ferry post, marsh dock
passages.text:
*Where to find him.* At the post where he ties the ferry, which has a tar line on it at the water's edge. Or out in the channels, when the fog allows.

*What he asks.* A fare. Scrip or a crust: I have seen him take both and could not tell you which he prefers.

*What he gives.* The crossing. And what he has seen, if you wait for it. It was Tuck who said the lantern in the Fenwood was lit again. Gulls follow his ferry out and do not follow it back.

*What not to say.* Do not ask him to pole toward the lights that are not steady. Do not ask anything of him after dusk.

He cannot read. When the Gazette comes up I read him the front of it on the platform, the stone's name first, because he asks for that first. He ties the ferry with a knot nobody in this town taught him, and he will not say who did.

passages.heading: Tuck — the ferry post, marsh dock
passages.text: *Post.* None.

passages.heading: Tamsin Crumb — Crumb's Ovens
passages.text:
*Where to find her.* At the ovens before anyone wakes, flour to the elbows. The wake table and its ten plates stand out front.

*What she asks.* The name of your dead, if you have any here, and the count of your mourners.

*What she gives.* Wake loaves, the island way. She came up with Vane from the island, before the Line. One loaf goes to each mourner and three to the dead, each with a crumb token sealed in wax. Keep the token. People here keep them.

*What not to say.* Do not ask what her bread is raised on. Do not ask about the fourth wake in October, the one she could not account for. And do not tip her in gold. Gold has been left in her shop before, and she did not care for it.

Her flour has come up short on the train since October. Mourners' loaves are halved so that the dead get theirs whole. A woman of Mill Row paid ahead for ten loaves of her own, and I carried the receipt. On the seventh the stone had her name. Whether she has needed the loaves is not mine to say.

passages.heading: Tamsin Crumb — Crumb's Ovens
passages.text:
*Post.* Flour, short.

---

passages.heading: Harbourmaster Pell — the marsh dock
passages.text:
*Where to find him.* At the dock, by the skiff, which lies pulled up with a stone in it.

*What he asks.* His terms, which he states the same way every time:

> "The skiff leaks. Bring me resin and a plank of timber and I will lend you a lantern."

*What he gives.* The lantern: lent, not given. He will want it back, and he will want it back lit.

*What not to say.* Do not call it a marsh dock to his face. HollowMere has no harbour. He keeps the title out of courtesy or out of habit, and you will keep it too. Do not ask him why a fen three hundred miles from any sea keeps a tide. He has a chart with the next low tide circled, and he does not explain it.

Nora has mended her nets on his boards since the twenty-ninth of November. She does not need you to say anything at all.

passages.heading: Harbourmaster Pell — the marsh dock
passages.text: *Post.* Years back, a tide chart came up the Line addressed to *the Harbourmaster, HollowMere*. There was no such office. He signed for it anyway.

passages.heading: Mother Moll — the charcoal hut, the Fenwood
passages.text: *Where to find her.* Past Gallows Wood, beyond where the planks give out, by the charcoal clamp that is always smoking low. The hanging oak is close by, and so is the den. Her door is shut. Knock once.

passages.heading: What she asks.
passages.text:
> "Four sprigs of herb, dear. The fog is in everyone's chest."

*What she gives.* A twist of paper for the chest. I have never heard of anyone who took one complaining of it.

*What not to say.* Do not stand in front of the den, and do not ask her about the oak. She keeps two bottles. Do not ask her for the other one.

*Post.* None. The Fenwood has no box.

Up the Line, they say, there are others who keep terms: a foreman on the BlackPine yard, a woman at a forge, someone at the kilns. Men come down saying so. I have had no letter from any of them, and I enter it as said.

---

passages.heading: The Constable — the Constable's Office & Morgue
passages.text:
*Where to find him.* In the office. At first light, at the door of whoever is behind with the rent.

*What he asks.* That you keep the peace. He keeps the rest: the cuffs, the whistle and the key.

*What he gives.* Under Article IX he may deputise you, and he may undeputise you without cause.

*What not to say.* Do not declare Unrest. The word belongs to him or to the soapbox, and you are neither. Do not ask him who held the Detective's office before the man who holds it now.

The Watchman, who drags his left heel, used to report at this door. He was fined and stood down after Hattie. You may still hear a heel in the lanes after dark. I do not say whose.

*Post.* Wires from the Eastern Office, which come in at the key. The Clerk works the key. I carry the slips across the square, folded.

passages.heading: The Detective — a desk at the Constable's
passages.text:
This is an office, not a name. The man who holds it kept time at the railyard before he was deputised. He has a magnifier, a case file and a stamp.

*Where to find him.* Wherever something has been left lying.

*What he asks.* What you saw, and the hour you saw it. He will want to look at your watch.

*What he gives.* A stamp on your statement. Sometimes, NO CASE.

*What not to say.* Do not tell him the last one was careless. The Gamekeeper says there was a last one, who went into the Fenwood at dusk after a light, with a book like his under his arm, and did not come out on the side he went in. He has heard this. He has written it down himself.

*Post.* A file came addressed to that desk before the desk had a man at it. Where it went is not entered here.

passages.heading: The Detective — a desk at the Constable's
passages.text: > *Office established for the list. — Clk.*

passages.heading: The Judge — the bench under the Bell
passages.text:
*Where to find him.* He comes up on the train for a sitting and goes down again at dusk. Between sittings the bench stands in the square under a tarpaulin against the fog, with the gallows behind it and the rope taken in.

*What he asks.* Nothing of you, until you are standing in front of him.

*What he gives.* One of three verdicts, painted on a board for those who cannot read: Acquittal. A Heavy Fine. Death. Death comes at an hour he sets, never during the Shift. The Company does not lose the work.

*What not to say.* Say nothing at the bench before he records the only words he is permitted to record. After *The Town has spoken*, nothing you say will be entered.

He last sat on Tuesday the twenty-eighth of November. That evening they hanged a man who mended boots. I never carried a letter for him, and so I never had his name.

passages.heading: The Judge — the bench under the Bell
passages.text:
*Post.* None comes to him here. A carbon of every verdict goes down by the Dusk train to the Eastern Office.

---

passages.heading: Widow Vane — the parlour
passages.text:
*Where to find her.* In the parlour, by day. She does not stand when you come in. At night she is in the bedroom, with a candle. The town says she cannot sleep; that she sleeps with it lit, to see who comes; that she lights it to be seen from the lane by someone in particular. Pick one. She will not tell you which.

*What she asks.* Who sent you.

*What she gives.* Nothing. Lord Aldous Vane's will was read in that room, and it leaves everything to whoever remains when the last lantern goes out. Horace, Butler at the manor these twenty-two years, will come down and see you out.

*What not to say.* The portrait over the letter box hangs turned to the wall. Do not turn it unless it is your work. She will let you, and she will watch whether you do. Do not speak of the island. Lord Vane is three nights dead, and he has been three nights dead for longer than three nights.

passages.heading: Widow Vane — the parlour
passages.text:
*Post.* Crepe, four yards, paid in scrip, entered at the Company Store the morning the wire came. The wire came in at the key, which the Clerk works and I do not. I carried the slip across the square to her, folded. I did not read it. Nowhere else in this guide do I say that.

> *Read it. — Clk.*

passages.heading: The Gamekeeper — Gallows Wood and Hale Barn
passages.text:
*Where to find him.* At the near edge of the wood, where the planks start. Or in Hale Barn with the goat, oiling his fowling piece, under a wolf pelt nailed to the door. The nails are old. The pelt is not.

*What he asks.* That you keep to the planks.

*What he gives.* He knows where the den is. He gives you that, and only by telling you not to go there.

*What not to say.* Vane paid him to keep the wood. Vane is dead, and he keeps it anyway. Do not ask him why. Do not come up behind him. Do not come for him at all: if anyone comes for him he will not go alone, and he means to take the right one.

*Post.* His wages stopped with Vane. Nothing has come for him since, and he does not come to the window to ask.

passages.heading: V. Those Who Come by Train
passages.text:
**The Pinkertons — the platform, when the town riots**

*Where to find them.* Off the Baron's car. Mr C. Thorne travels with an escort of nine and four dogs. They came up on the fifteenth of November, the day after the riot, and again on a Saturday after. They stood at the platform all day, and went down at dusk.

*What they ask.* Nothing of you. They ask the Constable.

*What they give.* A quiet square, and the dogs.

*What not to say.* Do not speak to the dogs. Do not be on the soapbox at the Bell when the car comes in.

*Post.* They carry their own, and so does he.

---

passages.heading: VI. Held at the Window
passages.text:
Mail does not stop because a person has. These are held, and I enter them so you will not ask me for them.

- **Elsie**, 25 Nov. A seed list from back east, sent for every autumn. She never once planted from it. She liked to read the names.
- **Mabel**, 27 Nov. A card from a niece, with a pressed flower that has gone the colour of the card.
- **Cyril**, the fisher, 29 Nov. Twine, ordered on account. Nora has the account.
- **Hattie**, the washerwoman, 2 Dec. A letter in her own hand, sent back from back east: *not known at this address*. She had written the address from memory.
- **Vera**, of the mill, 9 Dec. A paper of fifty needles, paid ahead.
- **Ada Brook**, Mill Row. One letter, which I have put in neither pile.

---

passages.heading: VII. Persons Not Entered
passages.text:
The Gazette prints no name it has not verified, and neither do I. What follows are not persons. They are things the town says and things left lying, and I enter them as the town leaves them.

They say someone walks after dark in a face that is not their own. When the town asks loudest who did it, count the voices.

They say there is always a second, who never holds the knife, only the alibi; and that if the first falls, the second picks it up. Nobody has proved it. Nobody has stopped saying it.

A bandana. Gold left where nobody pays in gold. A match struck at the mill. A voice at the soapbox after the Shift, which the Constable has not yet called Unrest. Someone at the back of St Brannock's every dusk, who kneels and does not sing.

There is a glove in the chapel rope. I do not know whose it is.

passages.heading: VII. Persons Not Entered
passages.text:
There is a stone with tomorrow's date on it. It shows a new name every morning, and nobody has seen a name being cut. Whether it kills or only knows, I cannot tell you. I can tell you that Agnes has not missed a morning.

And this. If a letter comes for you sealed in black wax, I did not open it. I could not have told you whose it was before it came. It comes in the bag like the rest, and it comes for whoever is here.

> *Nor could I. — Clk.*

---

The train comes in at Station Rush. The train goes down at dusk. The mail goes with it.

I keep a kettle for the purpose, at the Company's expense, charged to the mails. Write what you like. Write it as if I were reading.

The envelope in my rack at dawn is who you are.

passages.heading: VII. Persons Not Entered
passages.text: Don't miss the train.

works.title: The Tally Rack
works.blurb: the yard's Tally Rack roll and grain-density register for the Dawn Tribunal of Saturday 20 December 1952: ten billets weighed for the camp's ten offices and trades, their brands, debts, sins and forks, and a rack that comes out 3 lb 6 oz heavy because an oak billet stands in a pine slot, with "A.K." under the brand of slot 8.

passages.heading: The Tally Rack
passages.text:
`▇▇▇ / ▇▇▇ / ▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇ — ANOMALY UNKNOWN`
`GROUNDS 99 — YARD`
`DECLASSIFIED IN PART`

**TALLY RACK ROLL AND GRAIN-DENSITY REGISTER**
*For the Dawn Tribunal, Sawmill platform, Saturday 20 December 1952, first whistle.*
*Entered by: Slot 0. Counter-initialled: Slot 5.*

passages.heading: PRODUCTION IS OBLIGATION.
passages.text:
> *Order of the Circuit Judge, Fri. 19 Dec., 23:40, steam restored. Following the interruption of steam this night, and one person of grade not accounted for, all ten billets of the yard rack to be weighed before the Tribunal sits.*

---

passages.heading: Standing Order on the Rack
passages.text:
1. Every person on Grounds 99 has a billet. Grade does not exempt. The program took the slogan with the site, and the rack with the slogan.
2. This is the yard rack. It holds the camp's ten offices and trades. Each work crew keeps its own rack, numbered 0 to 9: the Workings, the sawmill, the bunkhouse. A number means nothing without its rack.
3. The billet carries the number, the trade, the debts and the sins. You are told once, at the intake office: *you're either feeding the furnace or you're fuel.* The billet says which.
4. Woods by work. Pine for light work: the tally, the ridge, the office. Fir for fire work: the boilers, the infirmary, the kilns. Oak for heavy work, and for the law that goes under ground.
5. Nominal weights: pine 4 lb 2 oz, fir 5 lb 10 oz, oak 7 lb 8 oz. Tolerance two ounces either way. A billet out of tolerance is a billet in the wrong slot.
6. Brands are burned at the Forge, with irons from Ada Kerrow and charcoal from the Collier's kilns. Neither is on this rack. Neither is asked.
7. At the Midnight Roll Call you have fifteen seconds to stand by your bunk. Then come the searchlights, the masks and the dogs. A billet without a body is entered *absent*. A body without a billet is entered *surplus*.
8. The log on your rack at dawn is who you are.

passages.heading: The Ten Billets
passages.text:
**Slot 0 — Head Tallyman**
*G99-0117. Pine.*

*Classification.* Enemy of the state. Trusty.
*Brand.* TALLY · 0117 · G99.
*Trade.* Keeps the rack and this register, and holds the only key to the scale's weights. Weighs any billet at night and says whether it was carved, counterfeited or swapped.
*Debts.* The yard's quota, which is his. Eleven cord short in November. Carried.
*Sins.* Kept the count.
*Remarks.* I weigh my own billet last, with my eyes shut. I know what it weighs. Tue. 9 Dec.: forty scrip found on the store counter, unclaimed, and entered as lost property. Not since claimed.
*Weighed.* 4 lb 2 oz.

**Forks.** A — Counterfeiter / B — Quota Boss. Marked: ______

**Slot 1 — Powder-Monkey**
*G99-2290. Oak.*

*Classification.* Prisoner of war.
*Brand.* POWDER · 2290.
*Trade.* Issues caps and powder from the niche in the Workings. Each night he sets the dye-cap on this rack's latch. The next hand to lift the latch goes red and stays red.
*Debts.* The niche count is short ▇▇ sticks and ▇▇ caps, carried since Tue. 11 Nov.
*Sins.* Answers for the count.
*Remarks.* He counts the caps aloud before he signs, in a language this register has no column for. He ends the count the same way every time, on a word that is not a number. Latch cap fired on the night of 19 Dec. Hands at roll were not inspected, because there was no light.
*Weighed.* 7 lb 8 oz.

passages.heading: The Ten Billets
passages.text:
**Forks.** A — Demolitionist / B — Ordnance Master. Marked: ______

**Slot 2 — Scaler**
*G99-0384. Pine.*

*Classification.* Enemy of the state.
*Brand.* SCALE · 0384.
*Trade.* Measures standing timber on Widow-Maker Ridge. Watches the camp through the surveyor's scope, and reports any long-gun, any carried load, anything dragged across open ground.
*Debts.* One scope lens, cracked. Charged.
*Sins.* Reports what he sees. For 19 Dec.: saw nothing. For 1 Dec.: kept indoors by order.
*Remarks.* He draws each tree in the margin of his tally before it is cut. He has asked about the old bed by the broken trestle: the sleepers rotted out, the ballast still level, running south off the camp map. He was told it is not on the map. Entered as asked and answered.
*Weighed.* 4 lb 2 oz.

**Forks.** A — Poacher / B — Ridge Tracker. Marked: ______

**Slot 3 — Boilerman**
*G99-1702. Fir.*

passages.heading: The Ten Billets
passages.text:
*Classification.* Prisoner of war.
*Brand.* BOILER · 1702.
*Trade.* Keeps the steam that runs the saws, the lift and the heat. From the boiler house he can vent any building or close it.
*Debts.* The boiler main, Tue. 11 Nov. Repairs charged to his billet, not his crew's.
*Sins.* The pressure log for 19 Dec. is not with this register.
*Remarks.* He lays two fingers on a valve before he opens it, the way you would on a wrist. Then he taps twice. He says the camp loses heat somewhere under it, more every week, and he cannot find where. He says one line comes back to him rimed with frost on the inside. He did not lay that line. Entered as said.
*Weighed.* 5 lb 10 oz.

**Forks.** A — Saboteur's Stoker / B — Iron Master. Marked: ______

**Slot 4 — Company Doctor**
*G99-0051. Fir.*

*Classification.* Other.
*Brand.* INFIRMARY · 0051.
*Trade.* Treats Lung-Rot with the oxygen tonic and does the autopsies: cause, and time. The program also measures the Lung-Rot. Tonic is issued against the measurement, not against the cough.
*Measured.* Weekly, for the program: weight, chest, how long a breath holds. Entered beside what the measuring leaves:
- ribs standing out like the slats of this rack;
- skin gone tight and grey across the knuckles, then across the face;
- fingers black from a cold the infirmary stove does not reach;
- three of those fingers on the infirmary table, weighed like billets and entered;
- a lung on the same table, black right through, entered by the ounce;
- a man who coughed until there was nothing left to cough, and went on.
*Debts.* Lime, infirmary requisition: one sack more than the infirmary uses, first week of November. Not explained. Not asked.
*Sins.* Fourteen certificates since October signed *exposure*. Exposure covers what the camp needs it to.
*Remarks.* He keeps one autopsy out of the file, in his own coat. He knows each patient by the cough before he sees the number. One of them hummed the same four notes until the measuring took the breath for it. Since Fri. 12 Dec. no findings are referred upward. Dr Ambry's case is sealed and is not with this register. He was not told why, and he says so, to the rack. Two clean autopsies and the officer may deputise him. He has had two. He has not been deputised.
*Weighed.* 5 lb 10 oz.

passages.heading: The Ten Billets
passages.text:
**Forks.** A — Back-Alley Sawbones / B — Chief Surgeon. Marked: ______

**Slot 5 — Security Officer (Camp Investigator)**
*G99-0005. Pine.*

*Classification.* Staff.
*Brand.* SECURITY · 0005. Burned Mon. 6 Oct., over his objection, which is entered.
*Trade.* Soot-dust kit and ledger magnifier. Lifts coal-dust prints, wood chip, and three traits from a scene.
*Case File.* ▇▇▇▇▇▇ — ~~verified~~ / ~~not verified~~.
*Debts.* None in scrip.
*Sins.* Counter-initials this register.
*Remarks.* He smells his hands after roll. He wants to know whether he has been near powder.
*Weighed.* 4 lb 2 oz.

**Ladder.** On verification, the suspect goes to the Warden's custody.

**Slot 6 — Mine Warden**
*G99-0006. Oak.*

*Classification.* Staff.
*Brand.* WARDEN · 0006.
*Trade.* Restraints, the coal-slug riot gun and the brass horn. Locks down the adits and the mill.
*Debts.* None in scrip.
*Sins.* Carries the fifteen seconds.
*Remarks.* He polishes the horn where his mouth goes, and nowhere else. He has not been seen to blow it twice for the same man.
*Weighed.* 7 lb 8 oz.

passages.heading: The Ten Billets
passages.text:
**Ladder.** On cuffing, the suspect goes to the platform.

**Slot 7 — Circuit Judge**
*G99-0007. Pine.*

*Classification.* Staff, flown in.
*Brand.* JUDGE · 0007, three times: Mon. 17 Nov., Mon. 8 Dec., Thu. 18 Dec. The first two are struck through with the edge of the iron. He is flown in for each tribunal and re-branded on each arrival. The rack does not remember him between sittings. It is made to.
*Trade.* Sits at dawn on the Sawmill platform. Lays out the Case File, orders the ten weighed, and gives one of three verdicts: Acquittal, Scrip Forfeiture, the Blade. *The Blade* is the camp's word. He uses it too.
*Record.* 17 Nov.: Scrip Forfeiture. 8 Dec.: the Blade (sawmill rack, No. 6).
*Remarks.* He will not touch the rack. He points. He arrived Thu. 18 Dec. with his own weights for the scale. They were checked against mine and agree.
*Weighed.* 4 lb 2 oz.

passages.heading: The Ten Billets
passages.text:
**Slot 8 — Felling Hand**
*G99-3318. Oak.*

*Classification.* Prisoner of war. War: not specified.
*Brand.* FELL · 3318.
*Trade.* Fells and bucks on the skid road, and hauls what he fells.
*Debts.* Quota short four days in five. Tonic owed.
*Sins.* A slip, folded small, found in his lunchbox at roll. It is an enlistment. Department: ▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇. Addressee: illegible. Terms: *success to the agency of this camp.* Retained. He says it was not his tin. Tins are not numbered.
*Remarks.* He saves the crust of his ration. It is not found on him at roll and not found in his bunk. His billet is old oak from stock, re-planed. On the underside, where the plane did not reach, an older brand shows: **A.K.** The yard reads it as the smith's, Kerrow's, from when she proved her irons. She has not been asked. Nobody has asked the wood.
*Weighed.* 7 lb 8 oz.

passages.heading: The Ten Billets
passages.text:
**Forks.** None listed for his trade.

**Slot 9 — Kiln Hand**
*G99-4471. Fir.*

*Classification.* Enemy of the state.
*Brand.* KILN · 4471.
*Trade.* Tends the clamps under the Collier and carries charcoal to the Forge.
*Debts.* Arrived owing.
*Sins.* His classification.
*Remarks.* He hums at the shift whistle. He is not alone in it: he keeps time with others who do not bunk near him. Entered: under observation; to the mess hall after roll.
*Weighed.* 5 lb 10 oz.

| Rack on the beam scale, tared, 05:40 | 59 lb 4 oz |
| Difference | 3 lb 6 oz |

The difference is oak less pine. It is not fir less pine, which is 1 lb 8 oz. It is not oak less fir, which is 1 lb 14 oz.

So an oak billet stands in a pine slot. The pine slots are 0, 2, 5 and 7.

Every figure above is in this hand. Every figure above is exact.

Billets not re-weighed. Whistle at 06:00.

works.title: The Density Audit
works.pov: first-person (the Master Proof-Reader, in the register)
works.blurb: the Master Proof-Reader's night register of Tuesday 8 September 1789: ten platters weighed for the Hall's ten offices, from Le Levain of the house of Vane to platter 9, Yann Le Goff called Petit-Yann, a dockhand who works the dish pit; the Gallery's bread is declared and never weighed, the rack comes out four onces heavy, and a stolen Counting-House seal is found in the one loaf with no thumb-press in it, the fine unpaid at eleven in the morning.

passages.heading: The Density Audit
passages.text:
`HALL OF PLATTERS — ARCHIVE OF THE MASTER PROOF-READER`

**REGISTER OF THE DENSITY AUDIT**
*Night of Tuesday the 8th of September 1789, from the dusk loaf to the sixth bell of Wednesday the 9th.*
*Kept by the Master Proof-Reader under the standing order of the High Chancellor. Countersigned by the Chancellor's clerk, by seal.*

passages.heading: BY DECREE OF THE SOVEREIGN SOURDOUGH COUNCIL.
passages.text:
> *Standing order of the High Chancellor, given at the command desk, for the quarter of Saint-Michel. The Hall of Platters to be weighed entire, as at every quarter, and this register laid on the trial table before the Dawn Tribunal sits.*

---

passages.heading: The Standing Rule of the Hall
passages.text:
1. Every soul on the rock has a platter. The long racks behind the Hearth hold the town's, and the journeymen weigh them. This rack holds ten, the platters the Council audits by office. An Unregistered platter is moved to the tenth place of this rack, where the Council can see it.
2. Loaves go by rank, and each rank has its weight. The Gallery's loaf is gold leaf, 4 livres. The Guild's is flour-white, 2 livres. The Commons' is red crust, 1 livre. An Unregistered platter gets the dish pit's issue loaf, 10 onces, with the seal struck. The tolerance is one gros either way, and a loaf outside it has been touched.
3. The bread of the Gallery is not handled by trade. Its weight is entered as the house declares it. The Proof-Reader lifts no gilded cloche.
4. The Abbey's bread is not on this rack. It sits at the Vault altar under burlap and is weighed by God.
5. At night the cloches are lifted by the Proof-Reader alone. At dawn each owner lifts his own. An Unregistered loaf is cracked by the Bailiff, because an Unregistered hand may not touch silver.
6. The platter nearest the Hearth carries no number and does not stand on the rack. It is not weighed and it is not entered.
7. As the Council painted it over the door: *the loaf sitting on your silver plate at dawn is who you are.*

passages.heading: Dusk
passages.text:
The Morning Ferry had cast off at dawn. Nothing was signalled from the mainland. The fog took the harbour lamps before six.

At six the Aboyeur carried a loaf down the Hall. He called no name. He set it on the platter nearest the Hearth, for a name under seal, and the night was reckoned from it.

The Ledger-Clerk closed the tariff desk at the half hour. Nine platters of this rack paid or remitted. Platter 9 was Unregistered, carried three weeks.

A complaint came down from the gallery at seven, and I wrote it as received. Crusts had gone from the gilded platters. *The Unregistered steal.* On that complaint the Spice-Master coated cloche 9 with Bitter-Citron Oil. It goes on clear and shows nothing until a hand lifts the cloche. Then the oil is off the silver and on the hand, yellow, until morning.

At the midnight proofing bell the Iron-Wardens locked the Hall from outside.

passages.heading: The Ten Platters
passages.text:
**Platter 0 — Le Levain, of the house of Vane, the eldest line**

*Colour.* Gold leaf.
*Seal.* A hand above a crock.
*Tariff.* Remitted, by courtesy.
*Loaf.* 4 livres, nominal.
*Declared.* 4 livres.
*Note.* The feeding hand. It is the only hand the Mother knows, and in the Hall it is always gloved, by right. I have kept this register eleven years and have never seen it bare. The left glove is worn thinner than the right. It is the left that feeds.

passages.heading: Platter 1 — High Chancellor
passages.text:
*Colour.* Gold leaf.
*Seal.* The Mother in her glass.
*Tariff.* Remitted, by courtesy.
*Loaf.* 4 livres, nominal.
*Declared.* 4 livres.
*Note.* He has never sat a Tribunal hungry. He keeps the card of what he ate in his sleeve until the verdict is entered, and then he gives it to his clerk to file, so that the archive holds his suppers beside his sentences.

**Ladder.** The last rung. He presides at the Dawn Tribunal, orders the cloches lifted, and gives one of three verdicts: Acquittal, a Guild Fine, or Trial by Fire in the Great Hearth.

passages.heading: Platter 2 — Master Proof-Reader
passages.text:
*Colour.* Flour-white.
*Seal.* A balance.
*Tariff.* Paid, in copper.
*Loaf.* 2 livres, nominal.
*Weighed.* 2 livres, exact.
*Note.* This hand. I weigh the issue loaf of platter 9 on the same pan the Chancellor's loaf would go on, if it were weighed. The ordinance does not say I may not. Tampered loaves audited this season, before tonight: two.

At the end of August a silver piece was left on the lid of the customs crate at the East Dock, on the night the crate was opened. My office was scratched into it with a knife point. I took it to the Ledger-Clerk. She has no column for silver left to an office by no one. It is in my apron.

**Evolutions.** A — The Black-Market Baker / B — The Archivist. Neither entered.

passages.heading: Platter 3 — Spice-Master
passages.text:
*Colour.* Flour-white.
*Seal.* A citron.
*Tariff.* Paid in yeast tokens at eleven at night, after the desk had closed. Entered by courtesy. The Commons do not get the courtesy.
*Loaf.* 2 livres, nominal.
*Weighed.* 2 livres.
*Note.* She tastes nothing she sells, and she says that is the whole of her art. She oiled cloche 9 on the gallery's word and asked to have the word written down. It is written above, at seven.

**Evolutions.** A — The Toxicologist / B — The Alchemical Purifier. Neither entered.

passages.heading: Platter 4 — Tide-Watcher
passages.text:
*Colour.* Flour-white.
*Seal.* A lamp.
*Tariff.* Paid.
*Loaf.* 2 livres, nominal.
*Weighed.* 2 livres.
*Note.* Nothing signalled. The sweep went out at nine and at eleven and showed him fog, he says, the way a blind man is shown a wall. In the mornings he counts the Wharf lamps back aloud, one by one, as the fog gives them up. He has never once said a lamp was missing, and he counts as if one might be.

**Evolutions.** A — The Wreck-Looter / B — The Harbor Master. Neither entered.

passages.heading: Platter 5 — Hearth-Warden
passages.text:
*Colour.* Flour-white.
*Seal.* A poker crossed with a key.
*Tariff.* Paid.
*Loaf.* 2 livres, nominal.
*Weighed.* 2 livres.
*Note.* Behind the Tavern bar he keeps a boy's shoe. An apprentice left it there and never came back for it, and the Warden does not say where the boy went. Tonight two apprentices were shackled to the stone pillar until the morning bell, for singing. He did not write down what they sang. I asked him, and he said it was the Wharf's song and that it had a new verse.

**Evolutions.** A — The Mutiny Boss / B — The Ironside. Neither entered.

passages.heading: Platter 6 — Ledger-Clerk
passages.text:
*Colour.* Flour-white.
*Seal.* An open book.
*Tariff.* Paid, and the receipt made out to herself.
*Loaf.* 2 livres, nominal.
*Weighed.* 2 livres.
*Note.* She blows on every line she writes, even a line already dry. Every fifth bell she opens the seal drawer of the Counting-House and counts what is in it. At the fifth bell tonight she came to the Hall and reported **the Counting-House seal missing from its drawer.** One seal, brass, 4 onces. She reported one.

**Evolutions.** A — The Customs Embezzler / B — The Council Regent. Neither entered.

passages.heading: Platter 7 — Inquisitor-in-Training
passages.text:
*Colour.* Flour-white.
*Seal.* A lens.
*Tariff.* Paid.
*Loaf.* 2 livres, nominal.
*Weighed.* 2 livres.
*Note.* He is nineteen and holds his breath when he dusts, so as not to blow the evidence away. With the magnesium powder and the Ledger Lens he lifted one print of flour dust from the floor beside the rack. **The print has a heel.** The trades do not wear heels. He drew no conclusion and I enter none.

**Ladder.** His dossier is unverified, so it does not go up to the Bailiff.

passages.heading: Platter 8 — Guild Bailiff
passages.text:
*Colour.* Flour-white.
*Seal.* A shackle.
*Tariff.* Paid.
*Loaf.* 2 livres, nominal.
*Weighed.* 2 livres.
*Note.* He carries the iron staff and the brass shackles. He has never closed a shackle on a gloved wrist, and he says his warrant does not reach that far. I have read his warrant. It does not say.

**Ladder.** When he cuffs the prime suspect and brings him to Gallows Square, he goes up to the Chancellor's rung.

passages.heading: Platter 9 — Plongeur, Commons
passages.text:
*Colour.* Red crust.
*Seal.* Struck. **UNREGISTERED**, carried three weeks.
*Tariff.* Unpaid.
*Loaf.* The issue loaf, 10 onces, nominal.
*Weighed.* **14 onces.** *Tampered. Foreign object, about 4 onces.*
*Note.* He hauls on the Wharf by day. At night he works the dish pit, kneeling where the old seal of Le Champignon is ground into the floor. Since his own seal was struck he has pressed his thumb into every loaf he is issued, where the seal used to be. The loaf on platter 9 at the second bell bore no thumb.

Each quarter he asks me what his loaf weighed. I tell him, and he says it is more than he thought it would be. He keeps a ferry token he has never spent.

His name, which the struck seal does not carry: Yann Le Goff, called Petit-Yann.

Cloche 9 was dry of oil when I lifted it at the second bell. A hand had lifted it before mine. My hands were clean, and the Inquisitor-in-Training has entered that he saw them.

passages.heading: Platter 9 — Plongeur, Commons
passages.text:
**Evolutions.** None listed for his trade.

---

passages.heading: The Balance
passages.text:
At the fourth bell the whole rack went onto the Great Balance of the Hall against the Council's weights, tared.

| | |
|---|---|
| Sum of entries, platters 0–9, declared and weighed | 22 livres 14 onces |
| The rack on the Great Balance, fourth bell | 23 livres 2 onces |
| Difference | 4 onces |

Platter 9 is 4 onces over its nominal, and those 4 onces are already in the entries. The Balance finds 4 onces more.

The Ledger-Clerk reported one seal missing, at the fifth bell. A seal weighs 4 onces. The rack carries the weight of two.

The eight loaves I weighed are within their gros, all but platter 9, which is entered. The two I may not lift are entered as declared.

After the fifth bell I entered a request that the declared bread be weighed. It went up to the gallery and came back down before the sixth, under seal:

passages.heading: The Balance
passages.text:
> *Ruling of the High Chancellor, from the gallery. The bread of a house is the word of that house, and its weight is its word. The Council does not weigh a word. Whoever asks to lift a gilded cloche asks to weigh the house beneath it, and his asking is entered so that it may be remembered. Refused.*

It is entered.

---

passages.heading: The Cracking of the Crust
passages.text:
The Great Proofing Bell struck six, and the Hall came in to the Hearth.

Each owner lifted his own cloche. The Gallery's were lifted with gloved hands, and the loaves were cracked *by the house, and found sound by its own report.* The Guild's were cracked at the trial table, before the Chancellor's clerk. All seals were their own.

Platter 9 was cracked by the Bailiff. In the crumb lay the seal of the Counting-House. The Ledger-Clerk claimed it, wrote the receipt, and blew on it.

Hands were shown palms up at the Hearth. The Guild's were clean. The Commons' were clean, platter 9's among them. The Gallery was gloved, as is its right, and was not shown.

The Inquisitor-in-Training laid the print with the heel on the trial table. The Chancellor looked at it and asked whose heel. No one answered, and it was not asked a second time.

passages.heading: The Cracking of the Crust
passages.text:
The verdict of the High Chancellor, as his clerk took it down:

> *The oil proves a lifting. It does not prove a lifter. A seal was found in a loaf, and a loaf is who you are. A Guild Fine of four onces of Guild Copper, being the weight of the seal, payable at the Counting-House by the noon bell, so that the Hall may be swept before the Gallery sups at nine. Unpaid at noon: Trial by Fire in the Great Hearth.*

The Bailiff cuffed platter 9 and took him out through the south doors to the Square. He went up a rung for it.

The Aboyeur took the dusk loaf from the platter nearest the Hearth, as at every dawn. It is not eaten.

Fine: unpaid at the time of this entry, eleven in the morning.

Platter 9, weighed again empty of the seal: 10 onces. Nominal.

passages.heading: The Cracking of the Crust
passages.text: The entries again, with platter 9 at its 10 onces: 22 livres 10 onces. The rack on the Great Balance, weighed again with the seal taken out: 22 livres 14 onces. It is 4 onces over. No one has reported anything missing that weighs 4 onces.

works.title: Pledged and Unredeemed
works.blurb: Harold, the oldest man on the Grant, keeps a pawn counter behind his step and has never sold a pledge; when a Company writ of 15 December forces a forfeit sale for 23 December, he writes up every ticket's owner so the town knows what it buys (Ivy's lantern, the Drifter's tin knife, Horace's study key, the lake man's watch lent to the Vicar, the lost Detective's notebook, Flo's skeleton key, Gert's stolen jet brooch, a sealed alibi paper, Wenna's chalk, the Watchman's irons and empty-looped crossbow, the Gamekeeper's fowling piece with its shot untaken, Moll's second bottle held with no number); the sale goes item by item, the Clerk buys the study key, and at dusk Harold hands Flo's key to a stranger holding her half-ticket, by his own rule.

passages.heading: Pledged and Unredeemed
passages.text:
*Book of Pledges. Harold's step, HollowMere. Kept since before the drain.*
*Pages for 1893, written up for the paper under the Bell.*

---

Everything in this room came over my step with someone who meant to come back for it. I lend on the meaning to come back. The thing itself is only what I hold while I wait.

passages.heading: Terms of the Step
passages.text:
1. I lend on what can be carried over the step. Nothing that breathes. Nothing that is bread.
2. Thirty days, and a ticket in two halves. You keep one half and I keep the other. Whoever brings your half is the owner, as far as the step knows.
3. I lend in scrip and I am paid back in scrip. It was three to the dollar in October and it is five now. What it does in between is the Company's business, and has been since the drain.
4. I do not ask why. I write down what I am told.
5. At thirty days the thing is mine. I have never sold one.

---

passages.heading: The Paper under the Bell
passages.text:
The Baron fell on the platform on Thursday. On Saturday the sixteenth the Clerk nailed a paper under the Bell in his own hand, and stood beside it while the Row read it. I have never known him stand beside a paper before.

> *Under the Articles an account survives the man. Every article held against scrip upon the Grant is an account. All such articles held at Harold's step shall be cried at the Midday Shift on Saturday, 23 December, inside their days or out of them, and the sums set against the lines of those who pledged them. A list to be posted by the holder.*

Nowhere on it is the word *forfeit*. I looked for it. A Company paper that will not use the Company's word has been written by a man who has not yet got used to his hand.

I am the holder, so I post the list. I have done it my way, which the paper did not forbid. A pawn counter is where a town puts what it cannot trust itself to keep. If the Company means to sell those things back to the town, the town can at least know what it is buying, and from whom. So under every article I have written who brought it, why it came, and why it never went home.

passages.heading: The Paper under the Bell
passages.text:
I list only this year. The rest of the room is from before the drain: a lake man's ring, a christening cup, four watches that stopped when their owners did, an oar with a name burned into the blade. The Company has no paper that reaches back that far, and it cannot cry what it never wrote down.

---

passages.heading: The Tickets
passages.text:
**No. 4061. Monday, 16 October.**
*Article.* One lantern, tin, the glass whole. The wick trimmed short and hardly burned.
*Name on the ticket.* Ivy Cotter, of the mill.
*Lent.* Four scrip and some coppers, which was what she was short.

She sat in the dark of an evening to save the wick, and the whole Row knew it. That afternoon she counted her fare out on my counter from a paper twist, coin by coin, the way she had saved it, and it came out four short. The lantern was the last thing she owned that she had not been sitting in the dark beside. I would have lent on the coat. She said she needed the coat for back east.

Two boxes went down to the platform that day: Bert Haddon and the girl Nell. The next morning, the crew say, Ivy Cotter stood on the platform in her grey coat with her fare in a paper. I did not see her go. Mrs Grieves has written *Gone east* against her, and I write what Mrs Grieves wrote, and say so.

passages.heading: The Tickets
passages.text:
*Why it has not come back.* Nobody who has gone east comes back for a lantern. It is the only lantern on my shelf that has never been lit. Since the wolves came down to the fence at the end of November, four people have asked me for it. They hunt the edge of the light, and in a winter like this a lantern is worth more than anyone ever lent on one.

*For Saturday.* Cry it.

---

**No. 4068. Tuesday, 24 October.**
*Article.* A knife. I have written *knife, tin*, because it is tin, painted to look like steel, with the paint gone off the edge.
*Name on the ticket.* Smith.
*Lent.* One penny.

A stranger off a train, in a coat cut for a bigger town than this. They wanted the ticket to say *knife*. I wrote *knife, tin*. The stranger read it upside down, laughed, and said that would do: a paper was a paper. The penny did not interest them. What they wanted was a paper with a knife on it and a name, in a hand that was not their own, in a book the town could be shown.

passages.heading: The Tickets
passages.text:
*Why it has not come back.* The stranger does not want the knife. They want it found. Every dawn they pass my step going up to read the stone, and every morning on the way down they stop and ask whether anyone has asked about the knife. Nobody has. I say so, and the stranger looks sorry for me.

*For Saturday.* Cry it. On the list, under it: *It is not a knife. Whoever buys it, be told.*

---

**No. 4070. Friday, 27 October.**
*Article.* One key, brass, a study key. Worn bright at the bow where a thumb has counted it.
*Name on the ticket.* Horace, Butler to the house of Vane.
*Lent.* One coin, which he did not ask for.

He came in his mourning band and stood, because he would not sit in a shop in front of its keeper. He laid the key on the counter teeth up, so that I could see the bite, as if I could know a study key by its teeth. I could not. He could.

passages.heading: The Tickets
passages.text:
He asked to borrow nothing. I made him take a coin. A pledge with no sum on it is a gift, and I do not take gifts from the manor.

"The ring is no longer my count," he said. "Your book is."

He said nothing more, and I did not ask. The town says there is a key in the barn and a key under the chapel, and stops counting at two. I make it three. I do not say so on the square.

*Why it has not come back.* He passes my step every day. He writes his round in the day-book before he walks it, and has done for twenty-two years. He has never once written this step into it.

*For Saturday.* Cry it. I went up to the Bell and told the Clerk that a key to a dead man's study is not an account. He wrote down that I had said so. Then he entered the key on his own copy of the list, in his own hand, with the rest.

passages.heading: The Tickets
passages.text:
**No. 4077. Wednesday, 8 November.**
*Article.* One pocket watch, silver, a good movement. Too fine for anyone on the Grant to have bought here.
*Name on the ticket.* Nobody. I asked twice. "Nobody. Write it." I wrote it.
*Lent.* Full value, without haggling.

The voice knew a pawn counter. It had stood at one before, or at many. It set the watch down face up, with its hand flat beside it, the way you do when you want the broker to see you will not snatch it back. Nobody does not haggle. I should have known by that.

It looked longer at the shelf behind me than at the money: the brooches, the christening cup, the lake man's ring. "Somebody's grandmother's, all that," it said. "Every bit."

On Saturday the sixteenth, the Vicar saw the watch in my window. He came in, asked the price, opened the back with his thumbnail the way a man opens his own, and shut it again. I offered it to him for nothing, and my terms be hanged. He would not have it.

passages.heading: The Tickets
passages.text:
"Let whoever pledged it come back for it," he said. "I should like to see who."

So I lent him another, off the old shelf: a lake man's watch from before the drain that nobody had come for in thirty years. No ticket. I am told he set it by the clock in the Telegraph Room on Sunday afternoon. That evening he went up the slope.

*Why it has not come back.* The pledger and the owner were each waiting for the other. Neither is coming now, or both are, and I cannot say which. The lake man's watch has not come back either. Whoever has been preaching in those robes since Sunday has not brought it.

*For Saturday.* Not on the list. It was never a pledge, only a theft with a ticket on it. The Articles have a word for a man who lends against a thing like that, and I have entered that word against myself on the back board of this book. I wind the watch on Sundays.

passages.heading: The Tickets
passages.text:
**No. 4079. Friday, 10 November.**
*Article.* One notebook, Company paper, written to the back board. A strap.
*Name on the ticket.* Detective. He gave his office and not his name.
*Lent.* The price of a can of oil, and a wick.

He was the one before the one there is now. He kept the book shut while he stood at my counter, with his thumb inside it to hold a page. He said he would fill another by the far side and come for this one on Monday.

"I keep a copy of everything," he said. "This is the copy."

*Why it has not come back.* He went into the Fenwood at dusk after a light, with the next book under his arm, and did not come out the side he went in. That is the Gamekeeper's account, and the Gamekeeper does not say things. Lights hang low over the fen that are not lanterns. Old Fennick's is steady and the others are not. I do not know which one he followed. I have never read his book. The pages are dry. The Fenwood is not.

passages.heading: The Tickets
passages.text:
*For Saturday.* Cry it.

---

**No. 4090. Monday, 27 November. Station Rush.**
*Article.* One key, iron, plain, longer than a house key, no tag. Out of the sweepings.
*Name on the ticket.* Flo.
*Lent.* One penny.

A hand came under the shutter before I had it up: a child's, with chalk in the creases of the knuckles and a broom callus at the root of the thumb. I knew the hand before the voice. Flo sweeps the floor at the Lantern for a penny a night.

passages.heading: Under the crew bench," she said. "Penny?
passages.text:
I said it was somebody's. She said everything is somebody's. I gave her the penny, tore the ticket, and put her half into the hand, and the hand went.

While I was writing it up, the Undertaker's boy ran past my step for the cart. They had found Mabel in the lane behind the Lantern.

The town says a key like that opens any door, and tells on you afterwards. Where it lay, it left a black mark on my counter, and another on my thumb. I have scrubbed both. Neither will come off.
