*Why it has not come back.* The Undertaker went round the Row in November looking for the children and could not find five. Flo was one of them. Her broom stands propped by the Lantern door every morning, and nobody sees the hand that props it. I saw it. I may be the last one who did.

passages.heading: Under the crew bench," she said. "Penny?
passages.text:
*For Saturday.* Struck. I struck it late on Friday night and put the key in my own drawer. A child's penny is not an account.

---

**No. 4091. Wednesday, 29 November.**
*Article.* One mourning brooch, jet, with a plait of grey-brown hair under the glass. Her grandmother's. The hair was her grandfather's.
*Name on the ticket.* Gert, Pump Row, fourth door.
*Lent.* Six scrip, which is less than the pine.

On Tuesday the Tribunal hanged a man who mended boots. The Company billed the gallows pine to Gert's account, and at Midday it entered her Indebted. She came to me next morning with her boy of eight behind her, carrying the empty basket so the Row would think she was going for washing. She scrubs her step every morning, though the mud is back by noon. She asked whether it would keep. I said everything keeps here.

On the night of Wednesday the thirteenth it went off the shelf, and my half of its ticket went with it. Pell's chart had low water circled that night. Nothing else was touched, not even the lake man's ring beside it. One soul had stood at my counter in November and looked a long while at that shelf. I need not write more than that, and I will not.

passages.heading: Under the crew bench," she said. "Penny?
passages.text:
*Why it has not come back.* It was not there to come back. Gert comes on Saturdays and stands at my window looking at the place it stood. The Saturday after, I paid her its value out of my own drawer, and her half of the ticket came back over the counter. It is the only ticket I have ever redeemed from my side.

*For Saturday.* Gone. The Clerk has entered the loss against Gert's line anyway. I have paid that too.

---

**No. 4096. Saturday, 2 December.**
*Article.* One paper, folded three times and sealed, with a name written on its face. It weighs nothing.
*Name on the ticket.* The name on the paper. I will not copy it here.
*Lent.* One penny.

It came at a quarter past five, before the lamps. The pledger asked me to write the hour. I write the hour on every ticket. This time I was also asked to say it aloud, so that we both heard it. A quarter past five. A plain coat. Clean hands, that had never pawned anything in their life: they did not know where to put themselves on my counter.

passages.heading: Under the crew bench," she said. "Penny?
passages.text:
Hattie was dead by the next light. On Sunday morning the Detective, the one there is now, came to my step and asked to see Saturday's page. I showed it to him. He put his finger on the hour and the name and copied both into his own book, and thanked me. Then the Tribunal sat, and the Watchman was fined, and his lantern was taken from him on the table.

The paper was nothing. My book was the alibi.

I have never broken the seal, and I never will.

*Why it has not come back.* Once the hour was in my book, the paper had done its work.

*For Saturday.* Cry it, sealed.

---

**No. 4097. Monday, 4 December.**
*Article.* Chalk, in a twist of paper: three sticks worn to stubs.
*Name on the ticket.* Wenna.
*Lent.* One penny.

She came on the first train to meet a man who had written that he would meet it. I knew him. Jory Kitto, a tinner. He drowned at the last plug, and he lies in the first plot behind St Brannock's. She never went back east.

passages.heading: Under the crew bench," she said. "Penny?
passages.text:
She told me that every night, in her ring, he asks whether the train has come. She tells him it has, and he asks again. She wanted one night without the ring, to learn whether he would ask anyway, and she asked me to keep the chalk out of her reach. Chalk is worth nothing. I lent on the reach.

At Dusk she came back to my step, though not for the chalk.

"He asked anyway," she said. Then she went down to the platform to watch the train go out.

*Why it has not come back.* She does not need chalk to hear him now.

*For Saturday.* Cry it.

---

**No. 4098. Tuesday, 5 December.**
*Article.* Irons, one pair, Office issue, with the key on a string through the chain.
*Name on the ticket.* The Watch.
*Lent.* A quarter of the fine.

I heard his heel on my step before the knock: one short scrape, then nothing. A Heavy Fine of three months' scrip, the lantern taken, stood down. The irons are not his. They are the Office's, and the Constable has not asked after them.

passages.heading: Under the crew bench," she said. "Penny?
passages.text:
"I've stood by enough doors," he said. "Let them stand by yours."

A crossbow hung on his back that he had not carried on Saturday. I did not ask whose. The square says it was the Ranger's, and that she gave it to him on Monday. He does not say.

*Why it has not come back.* No wage, no lantern. He still walks the lanes after dark with nothing in his hands. At night I hear the heel go past.

*For Saturday.* Cry it.

---

**No. 4099. Friday, 15 December.**
*Article.* One crossbow, string slack. On the stock, a loop for a single bolt to ride apart in. The loop is empty, with a knot of white thread still in it.
*Name on the ticket.* The Watch.
*Lent.* The rest of the fine.

The same man, the same heel, ten days on. I asked about the loop, which breaks my fourth term, and he answered, which surprised me.

passages.heading: Under the crew bench," she said. "Penny?
passages.text:
"Wednesday. At the pump, before light. It had Agnes by the arm."

That was all he said. The square told me the rest. The wolf had come up out of the dark to the pump. The bolt went through it behind the jaw. Agnes's forearm was opened in four places, two above and two below, deep enough to see what holds a hand on. The Gamekeeper hung the wolf from the gallows beam by its hind legs. It stayed there two days, its lips drawn back off its teeth and the fog beading on its fur, and the crows had the eyes by noon. Agnes lives. She has missed one morning at the stone, that one.

The Baron fell on Thursday. On Friday his escort stood on the square in their long coats, looking at anyone with anything slung on their back.

"A bow with nothing in it," he said, "is a thing a man gets looked at for."

passages.heading: Under the crew bench," she said. "Penny?
passages.text:
*Why it has not come back.* He has taken his one shot. There is nothing left to redeem it with, and nothing left to redeem it for.

*For Saturday.* Cry it.

---

**No. 4100. Monday, 18 December.**
*Article.* One fowling piece, single barrel, the stock dark with years of oil.
*Name on the ticket.* Vane's man.
*Lent.* A can of oil.

On Sunday morning the stone said THE VICAR. On Monday evening, they say, the Vicar preached. The Gamekeeper did not go up to hear him. He came to me in the morning with the gun across his arms, the way a man carries a child he does not know how to hold.

"He told me to be sure," he said. "I'm not. And whoever's up there preaching hasn't told me anything."

I told him it would be cried on Saturday, by the paper under the Bell.

passages.heading: Then let the Company hold it.
passages.text:
*Why it has not come back.* If they come for him now, he will go alone. That is better than taking the wrong face with him. Its one shot is still in it.

*For Saturday.* Cry it.

---

passages.heading: Held, not pledged
passages.text:
**No number. Friday, 8 December.**
*Article.* One bottle, brown glass, corked.
*Name.* Mother Moll.
*Lent.* Nothing.

She brought me her second bottle, the one she keeps on the far shelf so that a hand reaching in the dark cannot take it by mistake for the first. She asked me to hold it.

I told her my first term: nothing that breathes. "This is the other way round, Moll."

"So it is, dear," she said, and set it on my counter anyway.

I would not put a sum on it, so there is no ticket. While she watched I sealed the cork in wax and put the bottle in a biscuit tin on the top shelf, where my own hand would have to fetch a chair to reach it. I asked her when she would come for it.

passages.heading: Ask me after.
passages.text:
*Why it has not come back.* She is not yet certain. Every morning I look at the wax, and every morning it is whole.

*For Saturday.* Not on the list. The Company cannot cry what was never pledged.

---

passages.heading: Saturday, 23 December. The Midday Shift.
passages.text:
Last night the hoods were out after Curfew, flour sacks with holes cut in them, with torches. Nobody came to the Bell in threes this morning. They came singly and stood apart. The escort stood along the bank front in their long coats.

The Clerk ran his finger down my list and said it balanced.

**Ivy's lantern** went first. Nora bought it at three times what was lent. She said it was for the dock at dusk, so that Cyril could see where she was. I wrote down what she paid.

**The tin knife** had no bid. The stranger stood at the back of the square and watched nobody bid. It came back to my shelf, and on the way past the stranger looked sorry for me again.

**The study key** went to the only bid, at the sum lent and the interest to the penny. The bid was the Clerk's. He put the key in his waistcoat pocket, and it clicked against another key in there on a brass tag. While the money was being counted, Horace came up the square with his day-book open at a page already written: *Key, bought back.* He stood a long time looking at his own line. Then he closed the book and walked his round anyway.

passages.heading: Saturday, 23 December. The Midday Shift.
passages.text:
**The notebook** went to the Detective at the sum lent. He did not take it home. He read it where he stood, on my step, turning to the last written page. Then he asked me the hour. I opened Nobody's watch, the Vicar's, and told him. He wrote the hour down. He did not tell me what was on the page.

**The irons** went to the Constable at the sum lent, for the Office. He made the Clerk write that the Office had paid for its own irons.

**The crossbow** went to one of the long coats. "For the wolves," he said, and he did not mean the wolves.

**The sealed paper** had no bid for a while. Then a penny came up through the crowd from hand to hand, and the paper went back down the same hands. I did not see which hand it stopped in.

**The chalk** had no bid.

passages.heading: Saturday, 23 December. The Midday Shift.
passages.text:
**The fowling piece** had no bid. Everyone on the square knew whose it was, and the Gamekeeper stood at the edge with his hands empty. I have entered: *Not sold. Nobody would.*

**The brooch:** *Gone.* Gert was there. She looked at the place on the list where it was written.

---

passages.heading: Dusk, the same day
passages.text:
The shutter was half down. A hand came under it, and I did not look past the hand. My fourth term is that I do not ask.

It held Flo's half of the ticket, folded small, the way a child folds a thing to keep it in her fist. The paper had gone soft, with a crease of chalk dust along the fold. Beside it lay one penny.

"Redeeming," said the plain coat.

I took my half out of the drawer and laid the two halves together. The tear matched.

My second term says that whoever brings your half is the owner, as far as the step knows. I have kept that term since before the drain. I kept it tonight. I put the key in the hand. The hand took it without hurry, and the shutter came down.

I wrote it: **No. 4090. Redeemed.** It is the only redeemed thing in a book of unredeemed ones.

passages.heading: Dusk, the same day
passages.text:
Then I asked the shutter where she was. I asked it once, and I asked it too late.

The black is still on my thumb. The town says a key like that tells on you afterwards. It has told on me.

---

passages.heading: The last page
passages.text:
Agnes came down the Row at first light with her arm bound up in a sling, and called the stone's name to every door before anyone asked. I heard it from behind my shutter. I have not written it here.

The half-ticket in your pocket at dawn is who you are.

works.title: The Two Roads
works.pov: three readers in three hands (the island card-woman, 1789; Wenna, 1893; Slot 0, 1952)
works.blurb: the story-mode cast arcs as fifteen cards in three suits read on three nights by three readers who never know of each other: the island's masters read for their apprentices on a salt-cod crate on Saint John's Eve 1789; HollowMere's keepers read by Wenna with the Lantern's house pack on Christmas Eve 1893, the first night with no train; Grounds 99's trusties read for the Head Tallyman from a dead man's fifty-one-card deck on 17 December 1952; each card a face and two roads, given as fortunes and never as fates.

passages.heading: The Two Roads
passages.text:
*Fifteen cards. Three hands. A card shows the face. It falls one of two ways. The falling is a fortune, and the face is only where you stand tonight.*

---

passages.heading: I. Cloches
passages.text:
*Port-au-Levain. The eve of Saint John, Tuesday the 23rd of June, 1789. Read at the Smuggler's Wharf on a salt-cod crate turned over. In the reader's hand.*

On the mainland tonight they light a fire on every hill for Saint John. The Council allows the island one fire, and it is not mine. So the Hearth burns as it burns every night, the Hall sends its music down to the water, and up there the Gallery lifts its cloches to a bell. That is our Saint John.

My cards are painted the Paris way. A ferry brought the fashion two summers ago in a lady's trunk, and the lady's maid sold it to me when the lady tired of it. The backs are painted as silver domes, so I call the suit Cloches. To lift a card is to uncover a dish.

One Guild Copper a card. I read the masters for their apprentices. Only an apprentice wants to know which way a master will go, because the apprentice goes the same way a step behind, carrying.

passages.heading: I. Cloches
passages.text:
I do not read the Gallery. The Gallery does not ask what will become of it. It decrees, and the Square was built to hear it. Their footmen come down in gold-edged livery and pay double to ask anyway, for their lords' amusement. I take the coin and lay nothing. They go back up laughing, and the coin stays on my side of the crate.

The beam from the reef crosses the crate four times between the proofing bell and the six. I read between passes.

A card has a face, and it falls one of two ways. The face is where a man stands tonight. The way it falls is a fortune, and a fortune is no more a fate than weather is.

passages.heading: The Master Proof-Reader
passages.text:
*Face.* He weighs the Wake Loaves at night and lifts every cloche on the island himself, except the gilded ones. The Gallery's bread is entered at whatever weight the house declares. He writes that number down as if he had weighed it, and his hand does not shake. That is the hard part of the office.

*One way: the Black-Market Baker.* If silver comes to him by the crate, a loaf may leave his scale heavier than its flour. Something in the crumb that is not crumb goes out past the Wardens on a platter they will not lift, because he already has. The card does not show what it is. Cards never do.

*The other way: the Archivist.* He keeps the density book, and every swapped platter on the island is in it to the ounce. The book could be read aloud to a swapper, privately, the night before the Dawn Tribunal, at a price. A scale is a confession nobody has asked for yet.

passages.heading: The Master Proof-Reader
passages.text:
*Laid for.* His apprentice, a boy with flour in his eyebrows. At the end of each night he sweeps the scale pan into his own palm and eats what he sweeps. He asked me whether that was stealing. I told him it was weighing.

*How it lies.* Upright, pointing at the crate. "Silver comes by the crate," I told him. He looked down at the crate I was reading on. It was salt cod. He laughed and paid.

passages.heading: The Spice-Master
passages.text:
*Face.* The Apothecary, the kettle in the window, a register line for every bottle. He coats the cloches with Bitter-Citron Oil. A hand that lifts a cloche not its own goes yellow to the wrist and stays yellow a week. The Wardens look at hands before faces.

*One way: the Toxicologist.* A jar with no label on a shelf where every other jar has one. When a house buys the Black-Crust contract, somebody has to glaze the crust. The Guild calls it Nightshade Glaze. That name is all the card says, and all I will.

*The other way: the Alchemical Purifier.* Draughts against a rot that is not yet in the Vault, for a crowd that is not yet a crowd. The card is painted with a cup held out to many hands. I do not know those hands yet.

*Laid for.* His apprentice. His palms are yellow from the cloches he oils, and sand, lye and prayer will not scrub them clean. The Wharf takes him for a thief. He showed me his hands before I asked for the copper, the way honest ones always do, and it cost him something.

passages.heading: The Spice-Master
passages.text: *How it lies.* Either way up, the same hand pours.

passages.heading: The Tide-Watcher
passages.text:
*Face.* The lamp on the reef. Four times a night the office turns it landward and sweeps the town. It keeps the customs ledger of what comes in and the ferry tally of who goes out. It is the only office on the island that sees all of us and never sees the Hearth.

*One way: the Wreck-Looter.* Fog, and a manifest that could say anything, because in fog nobody can see the gangplank to argue. A barrel entered as salt that is not salt. A crate entered as lost that is not lost.

*The other way: the Harbor Master.* The gangplank held and dockhands deputised with a ribbon round the arm, on the day a Crown's man who is not yet on any ferry steps off one. The card shows a man in a coat too good for the crossing. I have never seen him. The card has.

*Laid for.* A dockhand who counts the beam's passes aloud, one to four, so he knows when to be indoors. On four he goes home whatever the cards say. He paid on three.

passages.heading: The Tide-Watcher
passages.text: *How it lies.* Face down, and it would not stay down. "The light doesn't choose which," I told him. "The weather does." He said the weather belonged to the Council too. Then the fourth pass came across the crate, and he went.

passages.heading: The Hearth-Warden
passages.text:
*Face.* The Port Tavern. He carries the iron poker across his shoulders like a yoke and keeps stone pillar shackles. He keeps the tavern's order, and its rum cellar, and the rum cellar is a cellar.

He is the only master who came himself. He paid one copper, not double. He is Guild, and he wanted me to know he knew the price.

*One way: the Mutiny Boss.* Someone the Wardens want, kept under the floor among the casks, and the apprentices rising with the poker on their side for once. I did not read this road in the card. I read it in the faces queued behind him on the wharf, every one of them an apprentice, every one waiting to hear it.

*The other way: the Ironside.* The mounted harpoon gun over his bar unlocked and turned on the smugglers of this wharf. My wharf. The card shows a man on a stair, looking down into water.

passages.heading: The Hearth-Warden
passages.text:
*Laid for.* Himself. When I had read it, he took his copper back off the crate and put it in his apron. On the next pass of the beam he laid it down again in the same place and said nothing. I do not know what he decided in between.

*How it lies.* Crosswise, with neither road up. I told him so. He said a poker lies crosswise too, and that is the only way it gets heavy.

passages.heading: The Ledger-Clerk
passages.text:
*Face.* The tariff desk in the Counting-House. He takes the nightly yeast-tax in Guild Copper and Yeast Tokens and in no other coin, and he shoots the iron deadbolts.

*One way: the Customs Embezzler.* The Counting-House gold, taken in the noise of somebody else's robbery, and out on the Dawn Ferry before the noise stops. The card shows a door standing open, with a ferry small in one corner.

*The other way: the Council Regent.* Every bolt on the island shot at once, on his word, if a man who has not yet come survives a night that has not yet come. The card shows the same door, shut.

*Laid for.* His apprentice, a thin one who never stops counting. Without being asked, he sorted my coppers by their mint, counted them right, and pushed the pile back to my side. He will make a Ledger-Clerk.

*How it lies.* Upright, whichever way you turn it. Both roads go through a door he holds the bolt of.

passages.heading: The Ledger-Clerk
passages.text:
After the fourth pass, someone in the queue asked me to lay a card for the empty platter nearest the Hearth. It is the one the Aboyeur sets at dusk, for a name under seal. I said a card is laid for a name. Under seal, there is no name to lay it for. She said that was why she had asked.

I put the Cloches back in the crate. The Hall's music stopped as I shut the lid, as if it had been waiting for me.

A ferry will come with news. Every year one does.

---

passages.heading: II. The Lantern Pack
passages.text:
*HollowMere. Sunday, 24 December 1893. Christmas Eve, the first night with no train. Read at the back table of the Drowned Lantern. Pencil.*

I was at the end of the boards at Dusk. There was nothing to watch go. The last train went yesterday, full of people with cases. The storm has the line now, and nothing comes up it until the storm lets go.

I have no chalk. It has been behind Harold's step since the fourth, on a ticket, a penny lent against my reach. Without chalk there is no ring, and without the ring the dead keep their own counsel. They like it that way. I do not tell what they know in any case.

So tonight it is the living. Mrs Grieves keeps a pack behind the bar for the drinkers, dealt for rounds and fought over. One card is creased down the middle where a thumb went through it the night of the fight that got into the Gazette. She lent me the pack without asking what for, and entered nothing.

passages.heading: II. The Lantern Pack
passages.text:
Cards are for the living. The dead have had their turn.

I lay five, for the five who keep things in this town: the bread, the post, the dead, the bar and the rent. A card has a face, and it falls one way or the other. Which way is a fortune. Nobody in this town needs telling that a fortune is not a promise. They are paid in scrip.

passages.heading: The Baker
passages.text:
*Face.* Crumb's Ovens. Up before anyone, flour to the elbows. One loaf to each mourner and three to the dead, each with a crumb token sealed in wax. Tomorrow's wake table is already set out front, ten plates in a storm.

*One way: the Fence.* If gold comes as a tip, her oven may give back bread heavier than the flour she put in, and it will go past the Constable on a mourner's plate. Gold has come. On the fourth of this month a coin was laid on her counter as a tip, by somebody who did not wait for change.

*The other way: the Ration Tyrant.* If the mill burns, or the last mile is fired, the last flour on the Grant is in one kitchen, and the town eats when the hand on the scraper says it may. The mill loft burned in November. Four sticks lie unfired under the last mile, and the storm has the rest of the line.

passages.heading: The Baker
passages.text: *Laid for.* Herself, though she would not sit. Tamsin Crumb came in at nine with loaves for Mrs Grieves's Christmas board and stood in her shawl while I laid it. She had already fed the crock tonight, on the island's hour. She said so the way another woman says she has wound the clock.

passages.heading: Both doors are open, Mrs Crumb.
passages.text:
She said that was true of every oven, and went home.

*How it lies.* It would not lie still. I laid it three times. The pack is old and the table is not level, and I do not think either of those is the reason.

passages.heading: The Postmaster
passages.text:
*Face.* The Post Office and Telegraph Room. A servant of the mails, under oath, with a kettle the Company charges to the mails.

*One way: the Extortionist.* A second book beside the Company's, kept where the steam cannot reach: who owes, who lies, who is leaving. Read to the right man the night before a vote.

*The other way: the Handler.* The black wax comes in the bag like the rest of the mail, and it comes for whoever is here. This road is a hand from the shadows for whoever opens it and accepts. Or it is the hand that keeps for itself what was meant for them.

*Laid for.* Himself. He sat across from me with his hands flat on the table and asked me to read the card to him aloud. He has read every letter in this town before the one it was meant for. I read it. He listened the way a child listens, looking up. Once he said "Hester", only that, and did not explain her.

passages.heading: The Postmaster
passages.text: *How it lies.* Pointing at him. He did not touch it. On his way out he said nobody had read anything to him since he was small. I did not ask him what it had been like.

passages.heading: The Undertaker
passages.text:
*Face.* He bags the dead and inventories their pockets for scrip. He enters the number before the name. That is the trade.

*One way: the Grave Robber.* A box lined so that what is laid in it stays laid, and a favour in return from whoever wants it kept that way. Robes go on walking that ought to have stopped.

*The other way: the Chief Coroner.* The cause in a fair hand with the hour beside it, for the Constable, so that somebody's alibi breaks on his table.

*Laid for.* Himself. He measured me by eye while I dealt, crown to boot, as he measures everyone, and I let him. He said I would take a narrow box. I said I had been told so. He said Maud's line in his book is still blank. He has not written a cause. He said it as if it were the card's business.

passages.heading: The Undertaker
passages.text: *How it lies.* Pointing away from both of us. "The first train through will decide nothing for you," I said. He said nothing ever decided anything for him. He only entered it.

passages.heading: The Bartender
passages.text:
*Face.* Bar, Mrs Grieves's hired man. He pours stout that changes a man's mood, puts the shutters up for curfew, and listens.

*One way: the Union Boss.* The cellar opened under the boards for someone this town spared and never named, and a brawl staged at the right hour so that the law cannot get in the door.

*The other way: the Vigilante.* The sawed-off from under the counter, if the robberies turn to blood, and justice taken by the hand that pours.

*Laid for.* Himself. I laid the card twice, because he asked me to lay it again. Mrs Grieves watched from the tap. He keeps a tooth in his waistcoat, a man's tooth, from October. He turned it over in his fingers while I dealt and put it away when I looked. The drowned barman's Liquid Courage is still on the slate above him, unpaid.

*How it lies.* Once each way. He said that was about right.

passages.heading: The Company Clerk
passages.text:
*Face.* The rent ledger, the key in the Telegraph Room, every bed slept in and every bed that should have been. Nobody likes him, and he does not ask them to.

I laid this card unasked. At ten he stood in the Lantern door with his hat on and snow on the hat, and did not come in. Rent falls on a Monday, Christmas or not.

*One way: the Embezzler.* Now that the vault has been opened, a careful man's books could be made to say what he needs, and a case could go down on the morning train. The next morning train is Friday.

*The other way: the Heir.* A man to be guarded, guards, and the whole town locked down by one hand. The card is a king. But the man to be guarded is not on it. The guards are. Seven of them.

*Laid for.* The hat in the door. Before he turned to go he said one thing, not to me: "Miss Cotter paid the wick." I do not know her. I wrote it down because he said it as if somebody ought to.

passages.heading: The Company Clerk
passages.text:
*How it lies.* Pointing at the door, where he was standing. "Either road wants your signature," I said. He touched his hat and went out into the snow.

Mrs Grieves asked whether I would lay one for Jory. I squared the pack and laid none. He would only ask me whether the train has come, and tonight I could not tell him it has.

The pack goes back behind the bar, to be dealt for rounds again.

---

passages.heading: III. Fifty-One
passages.text:
`GROUNDS 99 — YARD`
`FORKS — SUPPLEMENTARY`
`NOT WITH THIS REGISTER. NOT FOR THE TRIBUNAL.`
*Wed. 17 Dec. 1952. Tally office, at the stove, 23:05 to roll. Entered by: Slot 0. Not counter-initialled.*

The Tribunal sits Saturday, first whistle. The register is complete except for five lines. Under each trusty's billet the form prints *Forks*, an A and a B, and *Marked: ______*. The form does not say who marks it, or by what. I have kept the lines blank since October, waiting to be told. Nobody has told me.

The Powder-Monkey ends his count of caps on a word that is not a number. I sent to the Workings for their No. 7, the interpreter at intake, to put the word into the register. He came with a deck of cards in his shirt pocket. It was Fitch's. Fitch was the Workings' No. 2, went down on 5 Dec, and is on no board now. Fifty-one cards. No queen of hearts. Fitch played solitaire with it every night and said he would win without her.

passages.heading: III. Fifty-One
passages.text:
No. 7 said he could not give me the word, but he could give me the forks. Entered as offered.

His rule. Red for A, black for B. The colour says which road is nearer tonight, not which road is walked. A card is not a finding.

Entered as said.

**Slot 1 — Powder-Monkey**
*G99-2290. Oak.*

*Face.* Issues caps and powder from the niche in the Workings. Each night he sets the dye-cap on this rack's latch, and the next hand to lift the latch goes red.

*One way (A): Demolitionist.* A cart on the coal track that should not be pushed, for whoever is breaking this camp from inside. The niche count has been short since Tue. 11 Nov. The card shows no more than that, and neither does this sheet.

*The other way (B): Ordnance Master.* Charges found and made dead. Flash-caps for the Warden that blind and do not kill.

passages.heading: III. Fifty-One
passages.text:
*Laid for.* Him, in his absence; he was at the niche. While he shuffled, No. 7 said the word under his breath, once, and did not say it again. I asked what it meant. He said it is what you say at the end of a count so that the count is finished and has not just stopped. He said English has no column for it either.

*Drawn.* Nine of clubs. Black. B nearer.

**Slot 2 — Scaler**
*G99-0384. Pine.*

*Face.* Measures standing timber on Widow-Maker Ridge. Watches the camp through the surveyor's scope and reports any long-gun, any carried load, anything dragged across open ground.

*One way (A): Poacher.* The ridge has places the scope does not see, because the Scaler knows where he does not point it. Goods off camp, south, along a bed that is not on the map.

*The other way (B): Ridge Tracker.* Blazes in the pines marking where the pack runs, so that the Warden can hunt it.

passages.heading: III. Fifty-One
passages.text:
*Laid for.* Him. He was in the office with his tally and sat for it. He draws each tree in the margin before it is cut, and he was drawing one while No. 7 shuffled. On 1 Dec he was kept indoors by order. He did not say what he heard that night, and I did not ask. It is not a column.

*Drawn.* Three of diamonds. Red. A nearer. He finished the tree.

**Slot 3 — Boilerman**
*G99-1702. Fir.*

*Face.* Keeps the steam for the saws, the lift and the heat. From the boiler house he can vent any building, or close it.

*One way (A): Saboteur's Stoker.* A main opened at the right minute, a corridor gone white so that nobody can see who walks through it, a dark that lets someone pass.

*The other way (B): Iron Master.* Steam cut to the lift and the Foundry doors sealed on the alert. Nobody passes.

passages.heading: III. Fifty-One
passages.text:
*Laid for.* Him, not present; he was on the main. No. 7 asked me what he does with his hands. I said he lays two fingers on a valve before he opens it, the way you would on a wrist, and taps twice. No. 7 laid two fingers on the card before he turned it. The Boilerman says one line comes back to him rimed with frost on the inside, a line he did not lay. I enter it again here because nobody has answered it.

*Drawn.* Jack of diamonds. Red. A nearer. No. 7: "Nearer is two nights or two years. The card has no calendar."

**Slot 4 — Company Doctor**
*G99-0051. Fir.*

*Face.* Lung-Rot, and the oxygen tonic, issued against the program's measurement and not against the cough. Weekly: weight, chest, how long a breath holds. On an infirmary card I have seen, in his hand: ribs standing through a shirt like the slats of this rack. Knuckles gone tight and grey, then the face. A breath counted and counted until the count was all there was of it, and the man breathing a little after the count stopped, as if no one had told him.

passages.heading: III. Fifty-One
passages.text:
*One way (A): Back-Alley Sawbones.* Lime, and a collar that walks at the gate after the man inside it has gone. No. 7 says a card can show a road already walked, and then it is not a fortune but a footprint. The infirmary requisition for the first week of November is one sack of lime more than the infirmary uses. Not explained. Not asked.

*The other way (B): Chief Surgeon.* Autopsies for Slot 5, cause and time in a fair hand, and men brought back off the table who were going.

*Laid for.* Him. He came in at 23:30 for the stove and stood at it. He keeps one autopsy in his own coat. He knows each patient by the cough before he sees the number. One of them hummed four notes until the breath went, and he asked whether the cards had those four notes in them. Dr Ambry's case is sealed and is not with this sheet either.

passages.heading: III. Fifty-One
passages.text:
*Drawn.* Six of spades. Black. B nearer. He said, "Nearer than what," and went back to the infirmary.

**Slot 0 — Head Tallyman**
*G99-0117. Pine.*

*Face.* Keeps the ten logs and this register, and holds the only key to the scale's weights. Runs the grain-density checks. Says whether a billet was carved, counterfeited or swapped.

*One way (A): Counterfeiter.* An agency man's money left where it can be found, and a brand on a blank billet that the Forge never burned. Tue. 9 Dec.: forty scrip found on the store counter, unclaimed, and entered as lost property. Not since claimed.

*The other way (B): Quota Boss.* The yard has been eleven cord short since November, and the quota is mine. Read out at the Sawmill Tribunal, a shortfall can be laid on whichever billet I choose.

*Laid for.* Myself, last. I weigh my own billet last, with my eyes shut, and I shut them for this. No. 7 turned the deck over one card at a time, all fifty-one, face up on the table. Then he squared it. He said the colour that would have told me belongs to the card that is not there. I asked what that meant. He said Fitch would have told me I could win without her.

passages.heading: III. Fifty-One
passages.text:
*Drawn.* None.

---

Forks, slots 0 to 4. *Marked:* ______. Not marked. Returned to the register as they were.

23:59:45. Whistle. No. 7 put the deck in his shirt pocket and went for his bunk with fifteen seconds. His rack is not mine.

The card on your table at dawn is not who you are. It is only which way you were facing.

works.title: The Architecture of Being
works.blurb: Four movements on duality, greatness, choice, and becoming, built from claim, parable, and closing aphorism.

passages.heading: The Architecture of Being
passages.text:
The Architecture of Being

The Weight of Being Human  
	Don’t fear the inevitable. It seems simple enough, but that includes death, heartbreak, and every uncomfortable threshold we’d rather avoid. We are simple creatures, if you consider our chaos simplicity. For that’s what we are — chaos. We adapt, overcome, and change when faced with any challenge or adversity.  
	And beneath all that movement lies a single truth: humanity is a creature of duality.  
To be human is to be both weak and strong, dumb and brilliant, fragile and relentless. We live suspended between opposites, and the only sane response is presence — the willingness to stand inside the tension rather than flee from it.  
	We will never eat our cake and have it too. We must either sit with hunger or want; our eyes crave the cake, our soul hungers for it — which will you feed? Desire is the compass, but deprivation is the teacher. The question is moot, however: how can you live without satiation, and how would you find the substance from which to feed yourself without craving?	
	A man doesn’t know how much he values water until he is in a desert, how much he values his family until he is alone, how much he would give to receive that which he is in want of. This is the paradox of being human: we only recognize meaning when it threatens to disappear.  
	The trick to being human is that we can only see the story from our own eyes; take into account the biases of the viewer and it becomes that much harder to discern fact from façade.  
	Never let your mind linger on your past — you don’t live there anymore — nor reach too far into the future, because you are not welcome there yet. The present is yours, and life a present; it only means as much as you give it meaning.  
	Think of the moment you cup your hands under cold tap water after hours in the heat — how the shock, the relief, the clarity all arrive at once. That is presence.  
You don’t water the grass for tomorrow; you water it for the day you see it green and alive. That day is only real when it is present.

passages.heading: The Architecture of Being
passages.text:
The Hymn of the Living  
	Greatness isn’t about luck, wit, or grit. It’s not for the few, the holy, or the lords of vast wealth.  
Greatness is not a crown worn by the powerful, but a fire rekindled by the broken.  
	Greatness was taken from the lowest to be given to those who have all but want. Farmers, young men, and the innocent all march to the cry of a war started for the profiteers, the powerful, and the greedy. None of those who die will see the riches they bleed for, and those who they fought for will cleanse their spoils of sacrifice. Not even their families will have ease in death.  
	But greatness does not die in the trenches; it dies in the quiet rooms where no one speaks to one another anymore. For to be brought low, humbled, and left for dead is not the end of greatness—it is the beginning of it. What is greatness but to make silk of dirty rags, feasts from table scraps, and grand cathedrals out of ruined stone.  
	Think of a grandmother’s hands kneading dough in a dim kitchen, the soft rhythm of survival passed down through touch—that is greatness, not the gold on a king’s table.  
Halls filled with children’s laughter and elderly hymns are richer than all those kings have tread. But children grow up, and elders pass in the night. Greatness fades as families lose their lineage, inheritance, and history.  
	Isolation becomes the new hymn, and vanity distorts the echo.  
For no one in isolation is great; greatness is born in love, devotion, and the care of others. No one given to vanity will find the peace of their own becoming, for they have traded their birthright of greatness for the hollow image of another.  
	Vanity and isolation appear to be opposites, but they are two sides of the same coin—one clinging to the eyes of others for worth, the other crushed by the mere thought of being seen. This constant question am I enough must stop being asked, answered, and overlooked.  
	How can freedom be free if we never act freely? We ask to drive but never leave the trunk. We sit in the darkness of our thoughts, blinded by the confines we built, silenced by doors we closed because it felt impossible to stand between them and their closing.  
	Our mind becomes our enemy only because we make it such a place.  
We are not meant to burn alone in the dark. Greatness begins the moment we stop setting fire to ourselves.

passages.heading: The Architecture of Being
passages.text:
The Doctrine of Choice  
	You have a choice — maybe not in where you begin, or why you were placed in this life, but always in how you live it. We move through the world as if everything is outside our control, as if we are passengers in our own story, but that illusion only survives until we look closely. Life will take things from you without asking: jobs, people, certainty, comfort. You don’t choose to be fired, to lose, to be betrayed, or to feel pain. But in the moments when life strips you bare, one thing remains entirely yours: your response.  
	This is the heart of choice — not control over circumstance, but sovereignty over your becoming. You can choose peace over war, calm over panic, love over hate, and greatest of all, hope over mourning. These choices do not erase suffering, but they shape what suffering becomes. They turn wounds into wisdom, endings into thresholds, and grief into a form of knowing.  
	When my grandfather died, I refused to see it as the moment I lost him. Instead, it became the moment I finally understood him — the moment his life became a story I could hold, examine, and learn from. To shed a tear is not a choice; the body grieves on instinct. But to let the tear linger, to let it fall with intention, to allow it to bring a moment of peace rather than despair — that is a choice.  
	Choice is not loud. It is not dramatic. It is the quiet turning of the inner wheel. Think of the way morning light spills across a kitchen table — soft, unannounced, indifferent to your plans or your pain. You cannot summon that light or delay it, but you can choose to sit in it. You can choose to let it warm your hands, your face, your spirit. Presence is not given; it is chosen.  
	We cannot choose tomorrow, and we cannot rewrite yesterday. But we can choose the posture we take toward the present. We can choose to stand in it fully, without flinching, without running, without numbing ourselves to its weight.  
	And this is where the emotional arc of choice reveals itself:  
first awareness, then acceptance, then action.  
	Awareness that life is not ours to command. Acceptance that suffering is not a punishment. Action that transforms circumstance into meaning.  
	Life will always offer you storms, but it will also offer you the stillness between them. And in that stillness, you decide who you are becoming. Choice is the quiet architect of a life — shaping you not through grand decisions, but through the small, repeated acts of courage that no one else sees.  
	You cannot choose the world you inherit, but you can choose the world you build within it. And that is enough to change everything.

passages.heading: The Architecture of Being
passages.text:
The paradox of Becoming  
	Most people never see the bigger picture of their own lives. The accumulation of their choices stays invisible until it’s too late, or until someone else points out what they’ve become. We rarely recognize the moment we step into the life we once prayed for, because becoming requires presence — and presence is the one thing we abandon most easily.  
	So many look back at their “prime” only to realize they were living in a different life entirely, one they never fully inhabited. We stay loyal to versions of ourselves that no longer exist. We keep showing up to a past that has already closed its doors. The best moment isn’t just now — the only moment is now.  
	Becoming is a strange, quiet transformation. You only become something when you stop trying to prove you’re becoming it. Identity doesn’t arrive with fanfare; it settles in like dawn light through a window — unnoticed until the room is already bright. Why do we work so hard to justify being ourselves when the only time we will ever truly be ourselves is in this exact breath?  
	Some people die having never felt at home in their own skin. They spend their lives trying to belong to a world that never asked them to change in the first place. I mourn for those who alter their bodies, their voices, their souls just to feel acceptable. Not because change is wrong, but because belonging built on imitation is a fragile home. You can only be yourself, no matter how hard you try to be anything else.  
	Feel pride in being one of one. There will never be another you — only replicas, echoes, approximations. Don’t become a replica. Become an original.  
	You only realize yourself when you allow yourself to be yourself. Becoming is not a performance; it is a surrender. It is the moment you stop rehearsing your life and finally step into it. The trick to becoming is forgetting you started.

works.title: What is The Power of Art
works.blurb: An anaphoric chain of artistic lineages argues that neglecting artists costs a culture its meaning.

passages.heading: What is The Power of Art
passages.text:
What is The Power of Art

The first hands to make art belonged to our long‑forgotten ancestors. With charcoal‑smeared palms, they pressed their stories onto cave walls and created the earliest record of human memory.

Those marks weren’t elegant. They lacked contrast, polish, and technique. But they meant something. Even when survival consumed every waking moment, humans still made art. They honored beauty. They spoke to the future. We stand today on the bones of humanity’s past, lifted by scaffolding we never saw raised and hands we never learned to praise.

Across centuries, countless artists lived and died in service of making the world more beautiful. Painters filled halls with meticulous devotion. Musicians carved melodies that still echo in our chests. Unknown architects shaped skylines that expanded our imagination. Writers gave us worlds we could never enter without their life’s work.

passages.heading: What is The Power of Art
passages.text:
Yet society has forgotten to honor them. Artists are dismissed as myth‑makers, dreamers, or people without “sensible” professions. And still, the world complains about its lack of beauty — as tasteless facades rise, films grow predictable, and music feels copied and hollow. We forget why artists matter.

There would be no Star Wars without George Lucas, no Lord of the Rings without J.R.R. Tolkien, no Starry Night without Vincent van Gogh, and beyond them are the countless creators they inspired. Imagine how many voices, visions, and worlds would never have been born if even one of these works had been lost.

There would be no Michelangelo without the chisels of Donatello, no Donatello without the revival sparked by Giotto, and no Giotto without the nameless icon painters who first dared to give spirit a human face. Each artist is a continuation of another’s unanswered question.

There would be no Frida Kahlo without the surrealists who fractured reality, no surrealists without the symbolists who blurred dream and waking life, and no symbolists without the romantics who insisted that emotion was worthy of worship. Every movement is a torch passed hand to hand.

passages.heading: What is The Power of Art
passages.text:
There would be no James Baldwin without Richard Wright’s fire, no Wright without Zora Neale Hurston’s folklore, and no Hurston without the oral storytellers who carried entire worlds in their voices. Literature is a lineage of breath.

There would be no Hayao Miyazaki without Osamu Tezuka, no Tezuka without Walt Disney, and no Disney without Winsor McCay’s impossible imagination. Animation is a chain of dreams that refused to stay still.

There would be no Kendrick Lamar without Tupac, no Tupac without Gil Scott-Heron, and no Gil Scott-Heron without the poets of the Harlem Renaissance. Music evolves because someone keeps listening backward while moving forward.

There would be no modern architecture without Frank Lloyd Wright, no Wright without Louis Sullivan, and no Sullivan without the classical builders who first imagined that space could shape the soul. Every structure stands on the shoulders of another.

Art is not a series of isolated miracles. It is a continuous inheritance — a relay of vision, technique, rebellion, and devotion. Every artist is both a descendant and an ancestor, shaped by those before them and shaping those yet to come.

passages.heading: What is The Power of Art
passages.text:
If we continue to treat artists as expendable, the world will not collapse all at once. It will dim slowly, quietly, almost politely. Beauty will thin out. Wonder will become rare. The future will inherit a world built only for function, never for feeling.

When we stop seeing artists as artisans, we forget that they are builders — not of walls or roads, but of meaning. Their craft shapes the invisible architecture of a culture: its symbols, its stories, its sense of what is possible. Without them, a society may still stand, but it will no longer live.

If we keep dismissing the artist, we will raise generations who know how to produce but not how to imagine. We will create cities that are efficient but soulless, technologies that are powerful but empty, and lives that are comfortable but devoid of awe. We will inherit a world that works, but does not move us.

passages.heading: What is The Power of Art
passages.text:
Art is not decoration. It is direction. It tells us who we were, who we are, and who we might become. When we fail to honor the hands that shape it, we sever ourselves from the very lineage that made us human.

And so the question is not whether we can afford to value artists.  
The question is whether we can afford not to.

Because if even one artist’s voice is lost, an entire branch of the future goes silent. And if enough branches fall, the tree stops growing.

If we continue to overlook the artist, the loss will not announce itself. It will arrive quietly — in the stories that never get written, the songs that never find their first note, the paintings that never touch canvas because the hands that would have made them were told their craft had no worth.

Somewhere right now, a child is drawing on scrap paper, humming a melody, building a world out of nothing but imagination. And somewhere else, another child has already stopped. Not because they lacked talent, but because no one told them their vision mattered. That is how beauty dies — not in flames, but in forgetfulness.

passages.heading: What is The Power of Art
passages.text:
Every artist you love was once a trembling beginner who needed one person to say, “Keep going.” Every masterpiece was once a fragile idea that could have been abandoned. Every cultural shift began with someone who refused to let their imagination be dismissed as impractical.

If we do not honor artists, we will inherit a future built only by what is profitable, never by what is meaningful. We will live in a world engineered to function, not to feel. A world where children grow up efficient but empty, where adults forget how to dream, and where humanity survives but does not soar.

But it doesn’t have to be that way.

We can choose to protect the hands that shape our inner worlds. We can choose to value the artisans of emotion, memory, and myth. We can choose to tell the next generation that beauty is not a luxury — it is a lineage, and they are part of it.

passages.heading: What is The Power of Art
passages.text:
So let this be the moment we remember.

Let this be the moment we lift the artists still among us, honor the ones who came before, and safeguard the ones yet to be born. Because somewhere in the future, an artist will look back at us the way we look back at those charcoal‑stained ancestors — and they will either thank us for believing in them, or mourn the world we left behind.

The future is watching.  
The next artist is listening.  
And what we choose to value now will decide whether their voice ever reaches us.

works.title: The Creative Codex of the Mythic Architect
works.blurb: A taxonomy of signatures, structures, systems, and domains for building transmedia creative universes.

passages.heading: The Creative Codex of the Mythic Architect
passages.text:
The Creative Codex of the Mythic Architect

The Creative Codex isn’t a manual, a style guide, or a lore bible. It’s something far more alive. Think of it as the internal physics of a creative universe—a system that explains why your worlds feel the way they do, why certain symbols return again and again, and why some ideas evolve while others fade. It’s a living architecture that holds the rules, the rhythms, and the emotional gravity of your creative life.

At its heart, the codex is a system of systems. It breaks creativity down into four layers—signatures, structures, systems, and domains—and shows how they combine to generate meaning. These layers aren’t tied to any one medium. They move freely across writing, art, music, film, games, and whatever new forms emerge in the future. The codex is transmedial by design.

passages.heading: The Creative Codex of the Mythic Architect
passages.text:
It also draws from everywhere: history, philosophy, psychology, mythology, anthropology, semiotics, ecology, physics, and your own biography. It’s both a map and the territory. It explains how meaning is made, how symbols evolve, and how collaborative mythmaking—between humans, cultures, and even AI—can be done with intention and integrity.

What follows is a walk through the codex’s architecture, its interdisciplinary branches, and the new frontiers it opens.

passages.heading: The Four Layers: The Architecture of Meaning
passages.text:
1. Signatures — The Smallest Sparks of Meaning

Signatures are the atoms of your creative universe. They’re the smallest units that still carry emotional or symbolic charge. A color. A gesture. A shape. A musical interval. An archetype. A recurring emotional tone.

They work like morphemes in language—tiny, but loaded.

A spiral. A minor third. A red brushstroke. A ring of power.  
Each one is a seed that can grow into something larger.

2. Structures — Patterns That Organize Meaning

Structures are what happen when signatures combine. They’re motifs, themes, patterns, arcs, and recurring shapes of story or emotion.

The hero’s journey. Forbidden love. Light versus darkness.  
A triangular composition. A sonata form.

Structures are the syntax of creativity. They give shape to the raw material.

3. Systems — The Laws That Govern Meaning

Systems are the rules and dynamics that determine how meaning behaves. They explain why repetition strengthens a symbol, why emotional climates shape stories, and why motifs evolve over time.

passages.heading: The Four Layers: The Architecture of Meaning
passages.text:
Foreshadowing and payoff. Memetic drift. Emotional atmospheres.  
Ecological interdependence. Narrative tension.

Systems are the grammar and physics of your creative world.

4. Domains — Worlds Built From the System

Domains are the fully realized worlds, genres, or mythologies that emerge when signatures, structures, and systems interact long enough to form a coherent whole.

Middle-earth. Surrealism. Jazz.  
Any world with its own logic, atmosphere, and symbolic ecosystem.

Domains are where meaning becomes inhabitable.

passages.heading: Interdisciplinary Branches: Where the Codex Expands
passages.text:
The codex grows by absorbing insights from many fields. Each discipline adds a new dimension to how meaning is created, transmitted, and transformed.

History reveals how symbols evolve across time.  
Philosophy asks what art is and why it matters.  
Psychology maps the emotional and cognitive engines behind creativity.  
Mythology provides the deep grammar of archetypes.  
Anthropology explains ritual, culture, and symbolic transmission.  
Semiotics decodes how signs generate meaning.  
Narrative theory explains how stories shape time and experience.  
Worldbuilding ecology shows how environments become symbolic.  
Creative physics models emergence, evolution, and collapse.  
Personal thematic DNA roots the codex in your lived experience.

Together, these branches turn the codex into a multidimensional creative organism.

passages.heading: New Frontiers: Where the Codex Pushes Beyond Itself
passages.text:
The codex isn’t static. It keeps asking bigger questions.

Temporal Physics  
What happens when time isn’t linear? When stories loop, branch, or fold?

Symbolic Biology  
What if symbols evolve like species—mutating, competing, going extinct?

Emotional Climate  
How do collective moods shape meaning across a world or narrative?

Collaborative Mythmaking  
How do humans and AI co-create myths without losing agency or integrity?

Transmedia Ontology  
How does meaning migrate across books, films, games, and digital spaces?

Ritual Mechanics  
How do repetition, initiation, and boundary-making generate transformation?

Archive Consciousness  
How does a creative universe remember, forget, and reinterpret itself?

These frontiers turn the codex into a creative physics engine—capable of modeling not just stories, but entire symbolic ecosystems.

passages.heading: Implementation: Bringing the Codex to Life
passages.text:
To make the codex real, you need tools, practices, and protocols:

Creative assessments to map your thematic DNA.  
Workshops and labs to prototype motifs and systems.  
Feedback loops to measure resonance and evolution.  
Archive systems to track versions, mutations, and genealogies.  
AI-driven engines to support adaptive learning and transmedia mapping.  
Ecological simulators for symbolic evolution.  
Ritual design kits for transformative experiences.

The codex becomes a living system—one that grows with you and your collaborators.

passages.heading: Conclusion: A Creative Physics Engine for Infinite Worlds
passages.text:
The Creative Codex is more than a framework. It’s a living universe. A grammar of worlds. A mythic engine that generates meaning across mediums, cultures, and time.

It integrates the smallest signatures with the largest domains.  
It blends emotional climates with symbolic evolution.  
It honors personal biography while enabling collective mythmaking.  
It adapts, evolves, and expands into new frontiers.

In an age where creativity is increasingly collaborative—between humans, cultures, and intelligent systems—the codex becomes a partner in the evolution of meaning itself.

It is a testament to the mythic architect within you: ever-adaptive, ever-becoming.

works.title: How to Help People
works.blurb: A personal essay on learning to secure your own mask before you can help anyone else.

passages.heading: How to Help People
passages.text:
How to Help People

When I was younger I carried a strange conviction: that somewhere inside me lived a destiny to save the world. It wasn’t the loud kind of heroism you see in movies, but a quieter, sacrificial certainty—an idea that if I could throw every ounce of myself at a problem, someday the pieces would fall into place and I would know, in the marrow of me, that I had mattered. I imagined a life of obsession and small victories, a ledger of good deeds that would let me rest easy when the work was done.

For years I chased that ledger. I measured my worth by how much I could give away, how many people I could lift, how many problems I could carry until they were no longer mine. There were nights I stayed awake thinking of solutions, mornings I missed because I had been up planning someone else’s rescue. The impulse felt noble, but it also began to hollow me out. The more I gave, the less I recognized the person doing the giving.

passages.heading: How to Help People
passages.text:
The turning point came in a moment as ordinary as any other: an airline safety demonstration on a flight I almost slept through. The attendant’s voice—calm, matter-of-fact—said the line that had always sounded like a cliché: secure your own mask before helping others. It landed in me like a small, stubborn truth. If I became a liability, my efforts would do more harm than good. If I lost myself in service, there would be no one left to serve.

So I changed the shape of my mission. I stopped treating self-care as indulgence and began to see it as preparation. I learned to align helping others with my own goals—so that my compassion had roots and my generosity had boundaries. I still wanted to make a difference, but I no longer wanted that difference to be the only thing that defined me. Helping people became part of a life I loved, not the whole of it.

passages.heading: How to Help People
passages.text: There is a fierce selfishness in loving your life, and it is the kind that saves others. Our lives are the only things in this world that belong to us alone; everything else we touch we share. Hold that life close, tend it, and you will find that the help you offer is steadier, wiser, and truer. In the end, the world doesn’t need a martyr so much as it needs people who are whole enough to give without losing themselves.

Building dreams from the top down

Michelin Star Chef - I want tons of successful restaurants and Michelin Stars. I want to train with some of the greatest chefs in the most renowned European, South/Central American, African, and Asian restaurants from around the world. I want to create food that has never existed in ways that were never thought of. I want to bring an alien/new flair to food that turns the world upside down.

Renowned Artist - I want my art to leave an impression on future artists. I want reach like Van Gogh, with the influence of Picasso, and the beauty of Rembrandt.

Singer - I want to be a singer. I don’t care if I’m the best or even if I make it big I just want a few songs that people can relate to and gives a whole new meaning to the world I have felt something all along

works.title: Shoot for the Moon
works.blurb: A mother's saying about aiming for the moon unspools into aphorisms on risk, fear, and complacency.

passages.heading: Shoot for the Moon
passages.text:
Isn’t it funny? Just How mothers seem to have the most beautiful sayings for the dullest questions? Maybe it’s cause they have all the answers, or eyes in the back of your head? Well I’ll tell you this much, for more moments than we can recall they watched us grow observing our reactions to life just to formulate the perfect solution for the obstacles they saw in their future. A good father can make a man but an attentive mother no matter the flaws can make the most beautiful people.

My beloved mother with all her perfections and flaws once told me more times than I can count; that the stars are yours for the taking just shoot for the moon. A cheap twist on an old and popular quote if you ask most, but if you ask me there is no deeper pool of wisdom that could produce a saying so impactful. I speculated in my earlier understandings that if I shot for the moon i would inevitably miss the mark and fly endlessly into the void. However I don’t believe it could be proposed as an act of chance or a streak of luck; that when i finally did launch myself into the void aiming so far from the moon that i had no directory in sight. I realized in the depths of uncertainty opportunity shines brightest. So maybe instead of waiting to see the light of a dawn that is not promised reminisce among the stars.

passages.heading: Shoot for the Moon
passages.text:
For so long i feared just how deep the undertow of change would suck me down into the abyss of darkness that we so believe is waiting for us. Yet here we are afraid to try and relocate ourselves to a more suitable environment while the one we are in promises much less than which we so quickly regard.

Anytime you allow yourself to build up a negative how daunting falling into 
but i never took into account that all I accomplishing in my fight against vulnerability was chasing dark side of the moon

Often times we would rather live a life mediocrity fearing that we will land to far outside our definition of success  
To realize we are already slipping through the cracks in the foundation of existence

Our soul is a flower that modern systems seek to extinguish  
For if a field of wild flowers stands before the teeth of the tiller of revolution, inevitably they are crushed

passages.heading: Shoot for the Moon
passages.text:
Sacrifice the beauty of a thousand small groups for one homogenous group that represents their history  
Silence the voices around the campfire and pour in the advertising of new infomercials

Society isn’t broken it just has the wrong goal in mind, we have to become apart of the change we seek  
Counting on your neighbors to pull their weight before you is pending your success on a chance that is never promised

Waiting for others to change is the system that has failed the world we are in now  
We hold our neighbors accountable but not our own household, we chastise instead of reaching out

Yet we wonder why we are sick, we can’t give someone else the cure and not use it yourself  
We spread the wave of negativity every time we push away a positive thought

Seize not just the moment but the narrative in witch your story is told, 
why wait for others to tell the story you already know by heart

passages.heading: Shoot for the Moon
passages.text:
Yes the constant tracing of the wound that is self improvement never stops hurting  
But your heart beats a little stronger each time you extend or receive a warm gesture
